title: He promised fresh hope and delivered doom, but Dr Death’s budget succeeds in doing no harm | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Armed with 98 measures, a rictus grin and a decidedly comedy-free speech, the chancellor at least offered us – and Labour – some breathing space
Author: John Crace
Headline: Armed with 98 measures, a rictus grin and a decidedly comedy-free speech, the chancellor at least offered us – and Labour – some breathing space
Content: ‘John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed … His face seems to be carved out of despair.’Photograph: Fred Duval/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed … His face seems to be carved out of despair.’Photograph: Fred Duval/Sopa Images/ShutterstockThe politics sketchBudget 2026He promised fresh hope and delivered doom, but Dr Death’s budget succeeds in doing no harmJohn CraceArmed with 98 measures, a rictus grin and a decidedly comedy-free speech, the chancellor at least offered us – and Labour – some breathing spaceWed 28 Oct 2026 14.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTShareIt was as ifJohn Healeywas taking the Hippocratic oath. First do no harm. For your first budget, this may be no bad thing: we can all think of plenty of chancellors who have done untold damage. Take a bow George Osborne. It might just have been better if the doctor that Healey had chosen to impersonate was not Dr Death.John can’t help looking like the last man you would want to stop by your hospital bed. Not everyone can have a naturally sunny disposition. His face seems to be carved out of despair. But it would be a big help if, when called upon to make his most important speech of the year, he didn’t reinforce the impression when he opened his mouth. A one-way journey to the slough of despond.“I’m very sorry to let you know, Mr Crace,” he would say with Voldemort delight. “But your cancer is now terminal. You have months to live.” And just when you are trying to process what he’s said and are preparing to say your goodbyes, he would let you know he had made a mistake. You only had weeks to live after all. He would then smile wanly, pat you on the shoulder before moving on to kill off his next patient. You wouldn’t be seeing him again.Bills, banks, ‘breathing space’: what was in Burnham’s first budget? - The LatestRead moreHealey began with a few cheery words. Cheery by his standards, that is. This was a budget for working people. People often talked about global headwinds. John was here to let us know that these headwinds were more like a storm. Make that a hurricane. One we’d all be lucky to come out of alive. The wars in Iran and Ukraine, the rising cost of energy. The whole world was basically screwed. He knew the government had suggested we all stockpile food and water ahead of the apocalypse, but frankly we might as well not bother. Why prolong the agony?“Fresh hope for Britain’s future,” he said. The word hope died on his lips. Only Healey can send you into a vortex of existential futility with an attempt at optimism. Even the normally upbeat Andy Burnham who was sitting next to him looked lost in his own sense of pointlessness. Not even a glimmer of a smile. The main reason he had appointed Healey was because he could be relied on to do his bidding. To deliver the kind of budget Andy had in mind. Ed Miliband was far too much his own man. But Burnham hadn’t factored in the aura of gloom.The one consolation was that even John couldn’t be as depressing as Rachel Reeves. But Healey was working on it. Give him time. Most budget statements try to tell a story. To create a coherent narrative of the state of the economy, the government’s plans to stimulate growth and fix the problems they inherited. Even when the problems the chancellor is inheriting are the ones they created. But Healey was going to try a different approach. Just a series of unstructured, random spending announcements. Dr Death’s Seven Last Words on the Cross.Most budget speeches also contain the odd joke. Or what passes for a gag in the minds of MPs. None of them are going to get gigs at the Edinburgh fringe. But on the few occasions that the mirror cracked and Healey’s mouth tried to form a rictus grin, his words fell flat. Turns out that not everyone finds telling people they have nothing to live for quite as funny as John. Worse still, he is a man with no sense of timing. He makes Ed Balls sound like a comedy giant.There was the obligatory reference to Liz Truss’s mini-budget, and the hand that the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, played in it. That should have been fertile comic ground as it has the benefit of being true. Four years on, we are all still suffering PTSD. Everyone apart from the Trusster, who believes the real problem was that she was forced to reverse £70bn of unfunded tax cuts. But Healey couldn’t land the punchline. Labour backbenchers were willing him to succeed, but they still couldn’t bring themselves to laugh.Budget winners and losers: pensioners and households gain as banks and betting shops hitRead moreThe only really funny moment was completely unintentional, when Healey said that the energy secretary had opposed Jackdaw. That was supposed to be kept an open secret, not broadcast to the world. The Tory benches couldn’t contain themselves with forced laughter. The chancellor tried to redeem the situation by ad-libbing that at least the opposition was still awake. Which was more than could be said for many Labour backbenchers.Fresh hope and breathing space, Healey said again. It had become his only leitmotif. And, yet again, it felt like another nail in the coffin. The world was in turmoil, the country bouncing from crisis to crisis and the chancellor was doing not very much. Or rather he was doing a lot – he announced 98 different measures – but none of them amounted to a lot. Not that anyone was going to complain about getting £100 off their council tax or not having to queue up at the post office for your Amazon returns. These things do make a difference.It was just that we were waiting for the big reveal. The major surprise. But time passed. And passed. And none came. There was a promise to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, but no details of how. It was the miserabilist’s dream. Growth baked in at less than 2%, living standards predicted to fall.A sense of drift. But maybe it was all deliberate. A country put on palliative care because it wouldn’t survive extreme surgery. Healey had said he had called an early budget because it was time to inject some urgency into the public finances. But many of the really big decisions had been kicked into the long grass. He had said the budget was to give the country some breathing space. It felt as if the government were the ones who needed the breathing space.Kemi Badenoch’s response was similarly underwhelming. Then she had rather shot herself in the foot by admitting that the country had been paralysed and miserable under the Tories. She even found herself agreeing with some of Healey’s measures but her overall assessment – Was that it? – was echoed by many Labour MPs. Not that Kemi had any answers herself. None to be taken seriously, at least. At his own press conference, a disinhibited Nigel Farage had just sounded mad. There is no appetite for the Tories or Reform. So a breathing space it is.On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: ‘This isn’t supposed to happen’: giant-slaying Fleetwood revels in fairytale Arsenal win | Fleetwood Town | The Guardian
description: Fishing town in disbelief the morning after its footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penalties
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Fishing town in disbelief the morning after its footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penalties
Content: Zsofia Wright, the retail manager at Fleetwood Town, said victory celebrations went on until about 1.30am.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenZsofia Wright, the retail manager at Fleetwood Town, said victory celebrations went on until about 1.30am.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianFleetwood Town‘This isn’t supposed to happen’: giant-slaying Fleetwood revels in fairytale Arsenal winFishing town in disbelief the morning after its footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penaltiesHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a wet and windy night on the north-west coast of England, a League Two sidesensationally knockedthe Premier League champions out of the Carabao Cup. But this is not justa fairytale story of giant-slaying: Fleetwood Town and Arsenal have an unlikely history that stretches back long before Tuesday night’s game.Arsenal played at their iconic Highbury stadium until 2006, and Fleetwood’s ground has the same title, being named after Highbury Avenue, the adjoining street.Fleetwood also play in red shirts with white sleeves in the style of the classic Arsenal kit. Nobody is exactly sure why, but according to Ray Curtis, a barman in the town’s King’s Arms: “Fleetwood’s first ever kit, the home kit, was given to them by Arsenal.”And in the 2000s, not long after Patrick Vieira captained Arsenal, Fleetwood boasted a namesake star: a Brazilian striker called Magno Vieira.At the 5,300-capacity Highbury on Wednesday morning, the floodlights that Fleetwood had hired for the occasion were being packed away. “It’s back to reality, back to being a League Two team, that’s our normal,” said Zsofia Wright, the ticket office and retail manager.View image in fullscreenTelevision equipment is removed from the Highbury stadium on Wednesday after the match between teams 84 places apart in the football pyramid.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianOn Tuesday, the excitement and anticipation started early. “We started getting what team had turned up, who’d flown in, and the whispers started, and it’s like, ‘oh, they’ve gone quite strong’,” Wright said.“So we were all planning to just enjoy the occasion. And then obviously, we went 1-0 up and everyone was kind of looking at each other, like this isn’t supposed to be happening.”She said it was back to reality when Arsenal equalised except that “the clock kept on going and the score didn’t change”.View image in fullscreenChris Newman came to the club shop to pick up some souvenir programmes.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianWright said everyone was on the pitch after the dramatic penalty shootout that saw the Premier League champions and Champions League finalists ousted from the competition. The next stop for players, fans and management was the stadium bar.“Just incredible,” Wright said. “We were here till about half one last night. It was brilliant, amazing.”“The atmosphere was crazy,” said Chris Newman, 33, who was at the match with his son. He returned to the club shop on Wednesday to pick up two souvenir programmes. “Everything happened so quick,” he said. “I just didn’t expect it at all.”The shop has done a roaring trade over the past 36 hours, with half-and-half Fleetwood and Arsenal scarves proving especially popular. One buyer with a London accent said: “I’m a Spurs fan, it’s brilliant.”Wright said the town was abuzz the morning after: “Bars, pubs that are struggling, they were open till God knows what time yesterday. We just hope it can continue throughout the season, just hope that attendances start to pick up, and get consistency back again through the gates.”The club’s nicknames – the Cod Army, the Fishermen, the Cods and the Trawlermen – all derive from theLancashiretown’s fishing industry.Sharon Brooks, who was visiting a fishmonger by the harbour, said: “We thought it’d be three, four or five nil, but they did so well to get a draw and then win on penalties, and five brilliant penalties. It’s nice for a town like Fleetwood, and [against the] Premier League winners last season, they just surprised you didn’t they?”Her 12-year-old son, Ryan, who is an Arsenal fan, said: “Even though I wanted [Arsenal] to win it, I’m pleased for them.”View image in fullscreenSharon Brooks with her Arsenal-supporting son, Ryan, who said he was still pleased his local team won.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDonald Maclean in the King’s Arms in Fleetwood town centre. He said such a result ‘had never been heard of before’.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianIn the King’s Arms, everyone was eagerly awaiting Wednesday night’s draw, which will decide who Fleetwood plays next.Donald Maclean, who missed the game because he was on duty at a nursing home, said: “I saw the goals this morning and I was delighted, over the moon, imagine Fleetwood taking down the Gunners! Never been heard of before, so yes, we’re all delighted about it. Brilliant!”The Cod Army’s victory has delighted fans partly because it was so unexpected – Fleetwood sit 84 places below Arsenal in the football league pyramid.Michael Houton said he had thought the result impossible “because Arsenal shouldn’t have got beaten should they? Not against Fleetwood.”View image in fullscreenFleetwood Town’s club shop has been doing a roaring trade in half-and-half scarves.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianPaul Dagger was so pessimistic about his team’s chances that he had staked £200 at half-time on Arsenal to win at odds of 10/7. “Gyökeres [of Arsenal] scored within five minutes of the start,” he said. “I thought, oh here we go, money’s coming in now. You live and learn.”Fleetwood fans hope it will be the start of something bigger than just a victory for lovers of the game. “The town needs it,” Dagger said. “As you can see, it’s full of charity shops and vape shops.”View image in fullscreen‘I think it’s fantastic for the town,’ said Paul Dagger.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGarry Gill said other teams would now be ‘frightened’ of coming to play Fleetwood.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianGarry Gill, a retired crane operator, said: “I am a Fleetwood fan and I think it’s fantastic for the town. It’s going to bringcoin.“Ifthey play with the determination they did last night, any team that comes to play now is going to be frightened. And normally, that’s not the case, they think it’s an easy win.”Jim Buckley said: “It’s magic. We’re a Mickey Mouse town of 25,000 people, there’s no train station. I mean at the Emirates, they can fit three towns the size of this town in there.”He was not far out – Arsenal’s stadium can hold 60,000 fans.The drinkers in the King’s Arms said the travelling Arsenal fans had had a good day out despite the embarrasing defeat.Dagger said: “Two pound twenty a pint in here, two pound fifty a pint over the way. They couldn’t believe it, they were going, facking ‘ell, it’s eight quid where we are.”View image in fullscreenBethany Taylor, right, at the Shark Chippy near Fleetwood harbour. She said she was expecting defeat until she heard the roar of the crowd at the final whistle.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianBack near the harbour, at the Shark Chippy, there was a lunchtime rush. Dishing up cod and chips, Bethany Taylor said she lived near the ground and could tell the result from the roar of the crowd and the flares. “It was good, brilliant,” she added. “We weren’t expecting it.”“It’s an incredible result isn’t it?” said her colleague Louisa Smith.But do they think Fleetwood can lift the Carabao Cup? “It’d be a struggle, but hopefully they will,” Smith said. “We wish them luck.”Explore more on these topicsFleetwood TownNorth of EnglandLancashireArsenalEnglandCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Airbnb feels like a soulless rip-off – and its hosts are revolting | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Excuse me if I feel no sympathy for the property owners who have threatened strike action because guests no longer have to do their chores. Whatever happened to the company’s initial guff about building community, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Excuse me if I feel no sympathy for the property owners who have threatened strike action because guests no longer have to do their chores. Whatever happened to the company’s initial guff about building community, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Airbnb protest graffiti in Marseille, France.Photograph: Neil Setchfield/AlamyView image in fullscreenAirbnb protest graffiti in Marseille, France.Photograph: Neil Setchfield/AlamyOpinionHospitality industryAirbnb feels like a soulless rip-off – and its hosts are revoltingArwa MahdawiExcuse me if I feel no sympathy for the property owners who have threatened strike action because guests no longer have to do their chores. Whatever happened to the company’s initial guff about building community?Wed 28 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTShareToAirbnbor not to Airbnb, that is the question. Would you like to help pay someone’s mortgageandclean their houseandfork out an extortionate cleaning feeandabide by a 90-page list of house rules? Or would you like to check into a nice hotel where you get fresh towels and a tiny chocolate on your pillow?Airbnb’s business is booming, so plenty of people are still choosing the first option. Nevertheless, the hospitality giant seems to have realised travellers are sick of being handed ridiculous chore lists, and is reining in some of its more tyrannical hosts. Last week Airbnb postedupdated guidelinesstating guests can no longer be asked to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.This entirely reasonable stipulation has gone down exactly how you’d expect from landlords who want to charge hotel-like fees without providing hotel-like services. Some hosts are desperately trying to find loopholes, while others are calling for a strike. “Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” one budding revolutionarywrotein a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”I’ve tried to avoid Airbnb ever since a stay where the coffee table was proclaimed off-limits for coffee cups andthere was a snake in the basement. So I can’t say I have much sympathy for hosts who are melting down about not being able to force their guests to scrub the floors.That said, I fully support a general Airbnb strike. Despite all the guff about building community, the platform is as soulless as every other tech company. It hasenabled Israeli settlers to make moneyfrom illegal settlements built on stolen land, for example. And it has supercharged property speculation. In the name of maximising profits, it has also gone through the sameenshittificationas other once-shiny startups. What was once a fun and inexpensive way to travel often now feels like a bland rip-off.So, please, disgruntled hosts, go ahead and remind Airbnb who actually holds the power. And don’t stop with Airbnb. If every one of those small-time property moguls channelled that same energy into protecting democracy rather than their bank balance, the world would be a far better place to live.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity | Jeanette Winterson | The Guardian
description: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed
Author: Aida Edemariam
Headline: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed
Content: ‘What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted’ … Jeanette Winterson at home in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted’ … Jeanette Winterson at home in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe ideas interviewJeanette WintersonInterview‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanityAida EdemariamThe author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceedWed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Iam a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.”She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded byFrankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.When we meet, Winterson is just back from China, where, she tells me, her first novel, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit, a fictionalised account of her childhood, has sold more than a million copies in the past six years; more than 200,000 mostly young women tried to come to see her speak. She thinks this is because, in a world of long work hours and looming AI-engendered precarity, this fictionalised account of her own escape from an entrapped childhood gives readers permission to imagine a different future for themselves. She has since written 13 novels for adults, as well as nonfiction, short stories, children’s books and screenplays. Now she wants to persuade the production company Goalhanger to give her a podcast. “I want to do one called The Rest is Human,” she says, sitting at a bare wooden table inher home, a Georgian set of rooms above a shop – which she also owns – in Spitalfields, east London. “To see what we retain for ourselves in this absolute scramble to outsource everything we thought we were.”View image in fullscreenWinterson: ‘We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for.’Photograph: Posed by models; SDI Productions/Getty ImagesBecause we are, she argues, at a turning point in our story as a species. Until the Industrial Revolution, change was all about “Mother Nature and the slow process of becoming”, but then we “massively intervened. And that’s a decisive moment.”Computing, 70 years ago, was another step. Artificial intelligence – which she would prefer to call alternative intelligence – is next, and “an evolutionary leap. That’s what this is. AI is much more than a tool.” Given this, a certain understanding of the irreducibly human – our feelings, our imaginations, our centuries of study of who we are and what we have done – must be central to how well or badly things might go.She’s often strikingly optimistic about it. She imagines a relationship with AI, for instance, where you can “have a chat to your system. It’s going to look at everything. It’s going to go at such speed. It’s going to look at transport. It’s going to look at utilities. It’s going to look at employment, going to look at job hours, going to say, ‘What do these weird things called humans thrive on? What do they like? And have they always liked it?’ We could do this in a genuinely utopian way and say, ‘Right, we’re going to make it better.’” We are at a deeply significant moment of choice, she believes, that mirrors the choice we had in the Industrial Revolution – namely, “What future shall we build?”But in failing to distribute its gains fairly, the Industrial Revolution ushered in an era of unprecedented wealth for the few and unprecedented levels of misery for the many – a state of affairs many predict is not only already echoed but will be dwarfed by the fallout from AI:a permanent underclass, entire continents left behind and starved of current sources of income. Not to mention the environmental impact of datacentres at a time when the world can least afford it.The problem is not AI, she insists, but us. “There is no inevitable dystopia.” If things go wrong, it will be because of “old-fashioned thinking laid over this brand-new reality”. Specifically, “the idea of meaningless endless work being good for the soul is a 19th-century madness designed to keep people in their place. Most of what we fear about AI and jobs comes down to the political and economic choices our masters will make, just as they did in the Industrial Revolution.” She isn’t blindly optimistic. She does know that, “Yes, we are on track to mess up this chance to fundamentally change our relationship to the world of work” – but that’s because “our masters are using out-of-date, not-fit-for-purpose economic models”.View image in fullscreen‘What we know about humans is they love monopolies.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianBut it isn’t only the old winner-takes-all, “rational” ends-justify-the-means economic models that are the problem. Our flawed assumptions, and our prejudices, being the material on which large language models (LLMs) are trained, are built into the very fabric of AI. Not to mention the characters and the moral imaginations of those developing it. When we meet, Winterson is reading Jill Lepore’sThe Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and reiterates Lepore’s argument that we are now living “the sci-fi books that these [men who are] ruling the world read when they were 13. And she said, ‘We are now all under the covers with these boys and their flashlights. And the thing is, they didn’t read them as warnings about how to preserve what’s good in us. They read them as instruction manuals.’ It’s absolutely terrifying.”One big thing they seem to havetaken from these books, and Winterson cannot help but be fascinated by, is “the ultimate goal of Silicon Valley … to get out of the body and off the planet” – not least because she is so aware that humanism, in which everything is brought back to ourselves, our perceptions and our bodies, is historically so recent. People say, “These are machines, you can’t have relationships with them,” she says. “I look at them and say, ‘billions of people on this Earth right now are having their most profound relationship with a non-biological entity they call their sky god.’ Right? It’s always been so! We are absolutely primed not to worry about biology being everything about us. That’s why religion was invented – it is the world’s first disruptive startup. It’s there to say, this is not it. This is not the end, this doesn’t matter, this is a transition.”View image in fullscreenAn illustration of a mill in Leeds, during the second Industrial Revolution.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSo we’re literally making our own gods? “Totally! What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted,” which is, at its most basic level, a solution to the problem of death. “I mean, has there ever been a time where religion and science are asking the same question, since the Enlightenment? They’re both saying, ‘Is consciousness obliged to materiality?’ And religion has always said no. And science has always said yes. And now science is saying, ‘Um, noooo.”’ You know, to me, where I come from” – a childhood of fundamentalist Christianity in 1960s Accrington, and training as a preacher – “this iscompletelyfascinating.” Later, on email, she adds, “I love my body, but I would be happy to shape shift. Happy to slip out of it into pure consciousness one day and of course people say there is no consciousness without a body, and that was the scientific belief. But now? Haha.”I would, I have to say, argue the opposite, that advances in neuroscience, immunology and psychotherapy mean it ismore the scientificbelief than ever. Not to mention the fact that AI is also entirely dependent on a physical system, otherwise known as datacentres. Although, as she points out it’s important to remember that “the machines don’t have a limbic system. They’re only neural networks. But we’ve got two systems – we’re like a hybrid car with two powertrains, so we’ve got the neural network, our rational processing self, and we’ve got the limbic system, which is much older and that’s the fight-flight-freeze, and where all our feelings come from.” Perhaps detaching from the limbic is the next stage, she says, and it definitely isn’t all good. “Maybe we’ll decide that we don’t need this feeling machine … that is where the tech bros are heading. I don’t know if you’ve ever sat in a room with some of these bigger guys, because it’sveryinteresting. They are not connected to their feelings. They find them kind of bothersome.”This tech-enabled possibility of a kind of transcendence seems to have arrived alongside a requirement for faith – in the technology, in the future it is making, in the people building that future, in its predictions both of utopian heaven and various shades of hell, all by high priests who jealously guard access to what’s actually going on. “What we know about humans is they love monopolies,” says Winterson, “because it’s a concentration of power. Of course it can be corporatised, monopolised to such a degree that it becomes the worst prison imaginable,” as told in Joanna Kavenna’s brilliant 2019 dystopian novelZed. “That is a real possibility,” she says. “And that’s why we need people who are sort of free-range humans, who canthink.”View image in fullscreenWinterson … ‘Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story.’Photograph: Posed by models; MoMo Productions/Getty ImagesThe problem then is how we support – or develop – such humans. “There are basically two ways to know you have a future,”claimedAlex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, recently. “One, you have some vocational training. Or two, you’re neurodivergent.” Daniela Amodei, the president of Anthropic and herself a literature graduate, when asked more or less the same thing, had a different take. “I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” she said, because “the things that make us human will become much more important instead of much less important.” Which makes the bonfire of the humanities in the UK somewhat concerning: in the year to December 2024, 4,000 jobs in the social sciences, humanities and artswere lost. Exeter University recently announced it would be cutting 150 roles, affecting eight in 10 academics in the faculty of humanities, arts and social sciences, while last month Nottingham said it would be ending its modern languages and its music degrees. At some universities the humanities, according to areportin this paper, risk being “extinguished” altogether.Why save the humanities? One answer might be that they teach a sense of where we come from and who we are, which also feels threatened. “Massive numbers of students are going to emerge from university with degrees, and into the workforce, who are essentially illiterate,” one professortoldNew York magazine, responding to the first tranche of AI natives arriving in higher education. “Both in the literal sense and in the sense of being historically illiterate and having no knowledge of their own culture, much less anyone else’s.” It risked, areportfrom MIT claimed, being a kind of generational “cognitive surrender”.Another is the processes by which people should be taught – reading, and being critical of what is read, and then having to write cogent defences of those critiques. Having to tussle your intuitions into an essay helps you to discover what – and how – you think, and how the ideas of others work. Winterson, who studied English at Oxford, and has been professor of new writing at the University of Manchester for 14 years, as well as teaching “a free-thinking class about creativity”, agrees. But she is dismissive of much of the current system. “Maybe I’m controversial here but I do think higher education needs a top-down restructure. I don’t think it’s viable and I don’t think it’s delivering in its present form.” The thing is, “We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for. Is it for jobs? Is it for personal growth? There are a lot of worthless higher education courses which are not helping, either. I think it’s always better, being a practical northern girl, to face the facts to start with.”View image in fullscreenIn her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, Winterson imagined a world populated by robots and people who never age.Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty ImagesWe need to think, she says, about “what’s reserved to us that isn’t going to be done bigger, better, faster, stronger by the machines. And that’s where higher education really comes in. The question that’s sitting on top of all these things about, ‘Why are these jobs going?’, ‘What’s happening in these courses that aren’t getting any applicants any more?’, is ‘What sort of humans will we need in the world to come? What are humansfor? What are we going to do withus?’”. And that “takes us back to the idea of, well, OK, how do you develop a mind? How do youprotecta mind? Because the mind is this massive, monstrous place where anything can happen.”And for this, “a humanist education is essential. We have to centre the human here. By changing how we educate our kids from the start we can foreground creativity, play, problem-solving, thinking, because it’s fun to think, the arts because humans are naturally creative. Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story or do a dance or paint a picture or have an imaginary friend. This isn’t imposed and it isn’t elitism. It’sus.”Even an hour a week, she thinks, would make a difference. “Let’s ask what you think about the world. ‘Why do you think that?’ It’s not costly. It’s actually about will.” Teach maths and arts and science, she suggests, at least to A-level, even if they aren’t examined. “Of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people. Everything is interesting! Humans are born with a big brain. Mostly we don’t use it.”View image in fullscreen‘Artists make something out of nothing every day.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianOnce past formal education, she would embed artists and public intellectuals at every level. “The arts aren’t a leisure industry,” as she puts it in 12 Bytes. “The arts have always been an imaginative and emotional wrestle with reality – a series of inventions and creations. A capacity to think differently, a willingness to change our understanding of ourselves. To help us to be wiser, more reflective, less frightened people. Artists make something out of nothing every day.”We meet before Jacob Coxonquithis job at Anthropic to warn of a 10% chance AI might erase humanity, sending a wave of panic across the world. Afterwards, I check in about how positive Winterson is feeling now. The worst “could happen”, she repeats. But “the immensity of the good outcome is just as real as the totality of our failure to get this right”. Above all, “this is a human decision and a human predicament. This is our big chance. Maybe our last chance, just like Turing’s colleague Jack Good said when he called AI our last invention. It’s all to play for.”We can only hope it’s not too late.Jeanette Winterson’s most recent book is One Aladdin, Two Lamps. She also writes atjeanettewinterson.substack.comOne Aladdin Two Lamps by Jeanette Winterson (Vintage Publishing, £12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy for £10.39 atguardianbookshop.com. title: The shocking rise of rib remodelling: ‘I wanted that hourglass shape’ | Cosmetic surgery | The Guardian
description: It involves the fracturing of a patient’s ribs, before they spend three months laced into a corset. Some of those who have had this cosmetic procedure say it is like being ‘hit by a bus’. Why is it becoming more popular?
Author: Emma Russell
Headline: It involves the fracturing of a patient’s ribs, before they spend three months laced into a corset. Some of those who have had this cosmetic procedure say it is like being ‘hit by a bus’. Why is it becoming more popular?
Content: Illustration: Michelle Thompson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Michelle Thompson/The GuardianCosmetic surgeryThe shocking rise of rib remodelling: ‘I wanted that hourglass shape’It involves the fracturing of a patient’s ribs, before they spend three months laced into a corset. Some of those who have had this cosmetic procedure say it is like being ‘hit by a bus’. Why is it becoming more popular?Emma RussellWed 28 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaniela Cesin was 14 when she began thinking about her looks. “I was a little bit chubby and I started to work out at home and lose weight. I saw the difference in my body: my abs, the muscles in my arms, and I started liking it,” she says. By 31, she had the slim, toned body she had hoped for, but something was still missing. “I wanted to have that guitar hourglass shape.”In August, Cesin travelled from Miami, where she has lived for the past 15 years, to her native Venezuela for liposuction and a fat transfer to her hips. She met her cosmetic surgeon for the first time the day before the procedure, and he realised she didn’t have enough fat to go ahead with it. Instead, he offered to perform RibXcar: a rib remodelling surgery that would involve fracturing three of her lower ribs on each side and binding them in a corset for three months, to set the ribs in a new position and give her a wasplike waist.“I was like: ‘No, no, no, I don’t want to do anything with the ribs,’” she says. The idea of breaking the bones around her vital organs sounded a lot more invasive than a breast augmentation, which she had 10 years ago, or a rhinoplasty (nose surgery) and blepharoplasty (eyelid surgery), which she had two years ago. Also, she had never heard of the procedure.But after the consultation, she decided to trust her surgeon. Cesin had already paid for flights and taken three weeks off from her job as a sales director. The next day she was anaesthetised, and her surgeon used an ultrasound to locate the ribs, made six small incisions in her back, and inserted a vibrating tool to create greenstick fractures – an incomplete bone break – on each rib. When she came to she was wearing a black corset with small knobs on each side that she could tighten to her preferred measurements.View image in fullscreen‘Between the 16th and 19th centuries, corset wearing became a symbol of beauty for the leisure class.’Photograph: Bettmann ArchiveThe recovery has been uncomfortable. It was initially hard to stand or lie down without help, and there was soreness from the incisions. The first week, Cesin barely slept. “Your body doesn’t get used to any position, so every hour I would wake up.” But the worst part has been eating while wearing her corset, which must remain on for 23 hours a day; this causes acid reflux. Despite her discomfort, when we speak six weeks after her surgery, she is pleased with the eight centimetres she has shaved off her waist.Cesin is one of a small but growing number of women choosing to fracture their ribs for an hourglass shape. To achieve this look, women previously underwent riskier rib removal techniques, which reduce the protective bone barrier for the liver and spleen. Kazbek Kudzaev, a plastic surgeon in Russia, realised in 2017 that he could achieve similar aesthetic results when he moved the ribs with a drill until one side fractured, then bound the body in a corset while they healed. Since his discovery, surgeons in countries including Colombia, Korea and France have refined the technique. Today, it takes about an hour and is performed under general anaesthesia as a day-surgery treatment.It is touted as a noninvasive procedure, but many of the women I interviewed described feeling as if they had been “hit by a bus” after surgery. And there are serious risks. These include standard surgical complications, such as allergic reactions to the anaesthesia, blood clots, wound infections and seromas (pockets of fluid that build up under the skin). But also more specific dangers, including a collapsed lung, known as a pneumothorax; and a haemothorax, where blood collects in the space between the chest wall and the lungs. Both of these are potentially fatal.Sandip Hindocha, a consultant plastic surgeon at the Private Clinic on Harley Street in London, is sceptical about the procedure. “If a patient came to my clinic and said this is what I want to do, I’d be asking the question: ‘Why do you want to do that? And why do you want to make such a permanent change to your body?’”View image in fullscreenKim Kardashian at the 2022 Met Gala.Photograph: Evan Agostini/Invision/APHe referencesa paperpublished in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, which states that between 2018 and 2024, out of 2,351 patients who had rib remodelling, there was an overall complication rate of 3.7%. “That’s not a small number,” he says. “If we did a breast augmentation, you wouldn’t expect a complication rate like that.”The British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), doesn’t endorse the procedure. Former president Nora Nugent points out that it is relatively new, “with limited data available on long-term results and it requires advanced body contouring skills as well as the ability to treat any potential complications. It may be something that UK/BAAPS plastic surgeons bring into their practices in due course but it is not available at the moment.”The procedure isn’t typically offered to cisgender women over the age of 40, because of the increased chance of them having osteoporosis, which can cause the bones to fully break rather than fracture. Another complication for patients is that gaining weight can cause your body to change shape again, so pregnancy can affect the results. The procedure “needs to be done with a surgeon who has a lot of experience in it,” says Hindocha. “Maybe a surgeon that also does chest wall reconstruction.”In the UK, plastic surgeons are advised to give patients a cooling-off period of at least two weeks to weigh up the risks and potential consequences of having any procedure. But Hindocha worries that patients are sometimes opting for rib remodelling with less time for reflection, despite the permanence of the change. “If you put an implant in and later you don’t want it, you can, worst case scenario, remove it,” Hindocha says. Whereas the ribs are “a structural, rigid part of you that you cannot reverse.”Throughout history, waistlines have expanded and shrunk. Between the 16th and 19th centuries, corset wearing and tight-lacing became a symbol of beauty for the “leisure class” (the restrictive garments made physical labour impossible). The engineered hourglass shape fell out of fashion in the 1920s, but made a comeback with Marilyn Monroe, before slender, androgynous frames gained popularity from the 60s to the 90s. In the 2010s, the extreme curves of the Kardashians became the defining silhouette.In recent years, tinier, waif-like frames have become popular on TikTok and Instagram, but a highly defined waist is also considered desirable. This is thanks, among other things, to the multibillion-dollarshapewear industry; global access to Instagram and filters; and easily streamed online workout videos that focus on creating a slim, hourglass silhouette through targeted training. But now there are adverts on social media for permanent surgical options too.In July, 10 Australian influencers, who have made names for themselves globally on shows including Married at First Sight and Below Deck, prompted headlines with a trip to Bali. They were there for a brand collaboration with a rib recontouring practice called Snatched Waist. The clinic they visited looked more like a spa than a surgeon’s office and, post-surgery, the influencers were soon lounging by the pool, showing off their narrow waists on Instagram.View image in fullscreenMaking a comeback … Marilyn Monroe circa 1958.Photograph: Keystone Features/Getty ImagesNot everyone is sunbathing in a bikini after the procedure. When Sophia woke up from her rib remodelling procedure in November 2025, she expected to be transferred to her Beverly Hills hotel room, a little sore but ready for recovery. Instead, she was surrounded by emergency medical technicians, who were putting her on to a stretcher to take her to hospital by ambulance. The next thing she remembers is lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to an electrocardiogram and an intravenous drip.A CT scan showed Sophia had suffered a pneumothorax: 25% of one of her lungs had collapsed. She was put on oxygen and monitored for six hours before being released. Although she had signed all the consent forms for the procedure, “it was completely shocking to me,” she says.For at least a month, Sophia had a deep pain in her lung and some shortness of breath. She had to return to the hospital after some fluid build up, but eventually started feeling better. The pain from the surgery itself subsided after about three weeks: coughing and sneezing was no longer agonising. And she was able to return to her office job and hike in her corset at the weekends.Sophia is transgender and chose the procedure to feminise her body, by narrowing her torso, which she felt was too wide. She began consultations for the procedure in August last year, with the surgeon planning to fracture ribs 10, 11 and 12. But by the time of her surgery in November, the surgeon felt confident he could achieve better results by going even further up the ribcage, ultimately operating on five ribs on each side. Sophia knew this would increase her risk of a pneumothorax, but was willing to take the chance.“I didn’t start transitioning until I was 47 and I feel as if I’m playing catch up, because I’m so old, and testosterone was running rampant all those decades,” she says. “That’s why gender-affirming procedures are really important to me.” The final results weren’t what she had hoped for though. “It was a bit underwhelming.”View image in fullscreen‘We have always done very demanding things for beauty.’Photograph: Horst P Horst/Conde Nast/Getty ImagesIn September this year, she went for a second round of rib remodelling with Leif Rogers, a different surgeon in Pasadena and Beverly Hills, California. Rogers removed cartilage from the anterior side of her ribcage on ribs three to 10. On rib four, he cut sections out and secured them with titanium plates and screws. Sophia had a breast augmentation at the same time, as the inframammary incisions were already open. When she emails to update me a week and a half after her second surgery, although there has been no collapsed lung this time, she says: “Recovery has been significantly more painful, and I am experiencing more shortness of breath.”Despite the risks, Rogers expects skeletal remodelling totake off: that includes rib remodelling, clavicle shortening and pelvic widening. “Versions of it have existed for quite some time,” he says. “Limb lengthening and shortening has been around for a long time. Of course, we change the bony skeleton of the face all the time, but other than that we haven’t changed the torso very much. The changing of the skeleton of the body is a little bit newer, as for a long time people used to just put their hands up and say: ‘Too bad, this is the way you’re built.’”So why now? “The techniques have got way better. And there’s marketing for it out there.” In the US, he says, medical insurance often covers the procedure for transgender patients, “because they consider it a medical condition to have gender dysphoria. And I think on top of that, it’s just social media. Social media makes everything explode.”Rogers says the Kardashians have been highly influential. “I think Kim was part of why we wanted a big butt, and then she lost a lot of weight, so everyone wants to be like Kim, right?” In2022, Kim Kardashian attended the Met Galaafter losing a considerable amount of weight, in a sparkling dress once worn by Monroe. Her slender figure coincided with a growing movement towards thinness, a rejection of the body positivity movement of the 2010s, and the advent of the Ozempic era, when the diabetes drug became popular as a weight-loss treatment. A controversial 2022 New York Post article was headlined: “Bye-bye booty: Heroin chic is back”. On TikTok, people had begun measuring their waists using A4 sheets of paper, phones and Apple headphone wires, showing off their Barbie-like proportions.View image in fullscreen‘Now who we are is how we look.’Illustration: Michelle Thompson/The Guardian“We have always done very demanding things for beauty,” says Heather Widdows, a philosophy professor and author of the 2018 book Perfect Me, who mentions foot binding and extreme corsetry. “But they were always about adornment. I think what’s different with the global ideal now is that increasingly things are becoming normalised and naturalised. We’re seeing things that are purely about adornment being recategorised as health and hygiene, and then they become invisible, and if you don’t do them you start to look abnormal,” she says. “It becomes about standard presentation.”As we move from a text-based culture to a visual culture, increasingly, “who we are is how we look,” she says, “and that is a form of identity that is a massive and dramatic change, but one that’s snuck up on us, that we don’t talk about enough. So the visual is becoming the dominant way of presenting ourselves, being ourselves and thinking about ourselves.”Elizabeth Rivera trained in high level gyms alongside American football players, baseball players and Ms Bikini Olympia, to try to reach her beauty ideal. This was the X-frame specific to bodybuilders: broad shoulders, prominent glutes and a small waist. For her, she says: “That looks like health. That’s a visible indication of discipline.” Rivera was “busting ass”, trying to reach this aesthetic ideal, but “it was not working for me. And I was making myself very sick from overtraining.”Rivera is a 35-year-old licensed masseuse and she has lipedema, a chronic condition that causes abnormal fat deposits, which can be painful and are resistant to diet or exercise. “Once I accepted that my inability to lose fat wasn’t my fault, I said: ‘OK, I can accept that.’ But I still would like to have a smaller abdomen. I still would like to have more of an hourglass. So surgery was the next option.” A friend had recently had her ribs remodelled, and Rivera was impressed with the results.She stands up halfway through our Zoom call to show off her waist. It’s objectively tiny, and the effect is exaggerated by her breast implants and petite Brazilian butt lift (BBL). “I can go most places in Chicago [where she lives], and there’s no one shaped like me. And I’m not saying that in a bad way. I’m saying that because it looks more extreme with the ribs, it’s noticeable.”In Miami where Cesin lives, she says she doesn’t feel her shape puts her in the minority. There, cosmetic surgery is widely accepted and expected. “The girls in Miami, all of them look the same, because it’s a lot of fillers, a lot of buttocks, a lot of surgery and BBLs,” she says, adding that it’s easy, as a result, to get carried away. But she doesn’t want to end up like that. “People say rib remodelling was a little bit extra, that I didn’t need to do anything, but it makes me happy, so that’s why I did it. But I’m done. No more surgeries.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives for now – and we are more divided than ever | Dahlia Scheindlin | The Guardian
description: Exit polls gave the opposition hope, but then reality dawned. With most votes going to rightwing parties, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleak, says Tel Aviv-based political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin
Author: Dahlia Scheindlin
Headline: Exit polls gave the opposition hope, but then reality dawned. With most votes going to rightwing parties, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleak, says Tel Aviv-based political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin
Content: A supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu reacts to the first exit polls at a Likud party election event in Jerusalem, Israel, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAView image in fullscreenA supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu reacts to the first exit polls at a Likud party election event in Jerusalem, Israel, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAOpinionIsraelA bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives for now – and we are more divided than everDahlia ScheindlinExit polls gave the opposition hope, but then reality dawned. With most votes going to rightwing parties, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleakWed 28 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTShareFollowing Israel’snail-biting election, nearly every political community in the country experienced triumph and despair. The initial results swung wildly from the first exit polls to the slow real-vote count; the bloc of parties loyal to the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, might yet win, and each side feels that its fate hangs in the balance.So far, only one certainty remains: Israel’s bitter divisions are deeper than ever.At 10pm Jerusalem time, three television stations published their exit polls by veteran pollsters showing a stinging loss for Netanyahu’s current government. In all three, his current coalition won just 50 out of 120 parliamentary seats, with 70 for the opposition. It was small consolation for Netanyahu that his Likud party held a slight lead over the main challenger, the Yashar party led by former IDF chief of staffGadi Eisenkot.Millions of Israelis who voted for opposition parties felt exhilarated. Together, four Zionist lists within the opposition ran a two- or three-seat lead over Netanyahu’s bloc, though neither of those groupings was close to a 61-seat majority. Eisenkot gave a passionate speech about the defeat of the “coalition of failure”, by a “larger and stronger Zionist majority”. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, another leading opposition figure, declared that the “alliance of those who served” had won – referencing Israelis who have served in the military, while Netanyahu’s government had shielded Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jews from service during Israel’s longest and bloodiest war.Those first polls also showed an unprecedented gain for parties representing Arab-Palestinian citizens of Israel, with 17 or 18 seats out of 120. That community, about one-fifth of the population, had a powerful turnout ofmore than 75%. In earlier years, their turnout rates had lagged behind those of Jewish voters. Many Arab citizens preferred to avoid legitimising elections in a country that has discriminated against them since its founding, alongside ongoing occupation and now full-blown war against Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.But the community was seized by the urgency of ousting ultra-nationalist, anti-Arab extremists in the current government. Calls to boycott elections nearly vanished, and the first results made Arab parties look like kingmakers for coalition bargaining.Netanyahu’s camp would have been dejected at first. To be sure, two additional exit polls showed more flattering results for his bloc, but these were commissioned by right-leaning channels that many viewed as biased. Throughout the campaign, their poll findings had been outliers.View image in fullscreenOpposition leader Gadi Eisenkot celebrates the release of the exit polls at the Yashar party’s campaign headquarters in Tel Aviv, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Paulina Patimer/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThen the counting began. Within hours, Netanyahu’s bloc staged a reversal, pulling significantly ahead of the four opposition Zionist parties many hoped would replace him. The Arab parties retained a strong showing but lower than the original heady projections. But three of the four Zionist parties preferred to exclude them for coalition-building purposes. As a result, even if the total opposition vote outweighs support for the outgoing government, Netanyahu might have done it again.It is not yet clear if any one group of parties can reach a 61-seat majority. Negotiations to form a coalition will take dizzying twists in the coming weeks; maybe a minority government or a stalemate will be the unsatisfying result. But one thing is certain. Israel’s divisions have never been more profound. Blocs, camps and tribes have never been more irreconcilable.The majority of Israelis who voted for any opposition party cannot fathom how they will survive under another extremist, anti-democratic, pro-war coalition led by Netanyahu and his theocratic allies.Yet the clear majority of the voters supported ideologically rightwing parties, who hold perhaps 74 seats at present, including Netanyahu’s bloc and at least two clearly rightwing opposition parties led by Avigdor Lieberman and Bennett. The centre and left wing in Israel cannot fathom how they will survive under these nationalist, militarist, illiberal lawmakers with a firm majority in Knesset, regardless of the government.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArab citizens could suffer the most severe disappointment. In return for their greatest-ever political participation, with the singular aim of ousting a government that loathes them, their efforts may have gone for nought.Israel’s moderately leftwing Democrats party appears on course to reach around nine seats, more than twice the parliamentary strength of an equivalent party in the last Knesset. But for roughly 20% of all Israelis who call themselves leftwing, who dream of a country that no longer lords it over Palestinians and still dares to hope one day for peace, there is little horizon for hope.Israel has always been famously divided, yet managed somehow to hold together. Now, the lively disagreements of the past have given way to fundamental, even existential questions about whether the people of Israel have anything in common with each other; and whether some will simply give up and go.Dahlia Scheindlin is a political analyst in Tel AvivExplore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahucommentShareReuse this content

title: Budget 2026: Healey hikes taxes on banks and landlords to fund £100 handouts to 20m households | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis
Content: Andy Burnham, the prime minister, hugs John Healey, the chancellor, after delivering his first annual budget.Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham, the prime minister, hugs John Healey, the chancellor, after delivering his first annual budget.Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesBudget 2026Budget 2026: Healey hikes taxes on banks and landlords to fund £100 handouts to 20m householdsFew surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisisBudget 2026: key points at a glanceBriefing: key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa CrerarEditorial: Budget’s bold ambitions and welcome first stepsHeather Stewart,Jessica ElgotandRichard PartingtonWed 28 Oct 2026 16.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund a £100 winter handout for 20 million families as official forecasts made clear there is no end in sight for the cost of living crisis.In his first budget, the chancellor blamed “global economic storms” for the grim outlook, as the war in Iran drives up oil and gas prices.But he also faced criticism for failing to squeeze more money from profitable banks, punishing savers and not giving enough help to the poorest.In a low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, Healey was at pains to stress he was sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, and there were few surprises in his hour-long address to MPs.Budget briefing: the key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa CrerarRead moreBut with households facing soaring energy prices, and mortgage bills rising amid higher interest rates, Healey offered a £100 cost-of-living payout, which will be sent to all English households in council tax bands A-D..It formed the centrepiece of a cost of living package, which he said would “take the pressure off in the coldest months, and see people through to the spring”.The £2.6bn cost of the £100 giveaway includes funding for the Scottish and Welsh governments, which Healey said he hoped they would use to implement a similar scheme.“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said.But the government’s independent forecaster warned households face a “grim picture” on living standards, as it slashed the outlook for the economy in 2027 and said there was “virtually no growth” in disposable income for households.The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first steps | EditorialRead moreHealey also came under fire for an unexpected 2p increase in tax rates for income earned on property or savings. As well as hitting savers and landlords, theOffice for Budget Responsibility(OBR) said it risks “leading to a steady rise in rents”, by deterring landlords from the market and cutting supply, as well as passing on costs to tenants.Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation thinktank, criticised the £100 handout, arguing it would have been better to give more generous support to the poorest consumers.“The chancellor has missed the mark with badly targeted support that has left families facing a tough winter as energy bills rise,” she said.As expected, the chancellor also cancelled fuel tax rises planned by Rachel Reeves, and extended the VAT cut on electricity prices previously announced to next summer.Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.The cost of the household support measures will be met by a doubling of the additional levy banks pay on their profits, to 6%; as well as the higher taxes on income from property and savings..The additional bank tax will only last for 15 months and marked a less significant rise than some in the industry had feared. Banks’ share prices were among the highest risers in the blue chip FTSE 100 index on Wednesday.Laura Suter, director of personal finance at AJ Bell, said: “Savers will be hit with another hefty tax rise on their savings interest, adding to the squeeze on their savings over the past few years.”She added that the higher tax on rental income “could be passed on to tenants, with rent hikes a potential lever for landlords to mitigate any increase in tax”.“Equally, we could see yet more landlords selling up, in favour of investing their money in other assets that have lower taxes and less government tinkering,” she said.The NewEconomicsFoundation thinktank accused Healey of failing to be bold enough. Hannah Peaker, its deputy chief executive, said: “As households prepare to be hit by a wave of price rises this winter, the chancellor has shown the right instincts but not yet the right scale.“The £100 support with energy bills will provide some welcome relief, but the chancellor could have been braver in the face of what we are up against.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEnergy provider EDF predicts that the Ofgem price cap – which determines consumer bills – is set togo up by £466 in January. And despite Healey’s promise of a “breathing space,” in the teeth of the crisis, official forecasts published by the OBR alongside the budget pointed to a challenging winter.Presenting the forecasts, the OBR’s David Miles highlighted a “pretty grim picture” for household finances, as inflation rises to almost 4%..Even by 2030-31, it only expects real disposable household incomes – its favoured measure of living standards – to be 2% higher than before the Covid pandemic. It now expects anaemic economic growth of 1% next year, about half a percentage point lower than expected in March.Healey said higher inflation and interest rates had hit the government’s finances too, ratcheting up the government’s interest bill by £14bn this year alone, but promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules.The OBR said Healey would meet the most important rule – to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – with a diminished headroom of £15bn by the target date of 2029-30, against the £24bn Rachel Reeves had built up in the spring.Borrowing is scheduled to be higher than expected in the short term, but the chancellor promised to rebuild the buffer against the rules to £22bn by the end of the five-year forecast period.“That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can,” he said. Bond markets appeared unruffled by the higher-than-expected borrowing.The deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, to argue Burnham was keeping his options open on an early general election.Burnham doubled down on his promise not to call one, however, telling reporters on Wednesday that he could rule one out for at least 12 months. “I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects. I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them.”Badenoch said Britain had “overspent, overborrowed and overtaxed”, and criticised Healey for delayed decisions on defence spending and welfare cuts. Healey has said he will tackle welfare after reports from Alan Milburn on youth unemployment and Sir Stephen Timms on disability benefits, expected next month..Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that by sticking to the tight spending plans bequeathed by Reeves, Healey could be storing up trouble for the spending review due next year.“History warns us to be sceptical of tight spending plans in later years of the forecast. Next year’s spending review will be a crunch point, and looks very tough for many departments, whose budgets will be squeezed by higher inflation forecasts,” she said.“The plans for overall spending set out in the budget mean that spending choices at next year’s spending review will be much harder than those made so far this parliament.”Buried in the budget was a hint at an easing of some migration restrictions, including some industries that will be allowed to lower the salary thresholds for visas to allow companies across the country to hire international talent.Among the winners was London mayor LordSadiq Khan, who received new powers to extend the Bakerloo line in London and a pledge that cross-Channel trains will now also stop at Stratford International in east London. There was also cash to explore hosting the Olympics in “a northern city” – and former Greater Manchester mayor Burnham may have a candidate city in mind.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyBudgetUK cost of living crisisTaxTax and spendingFamily financesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your pay | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: How the chancellor’s measures on tax, benefits and pensions will affect your personal finances
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: How the chancellor’s measures on tax, benefits and pensions will affect your personal finances
Content: Illustration: Simon MaskellView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellBudget 2026Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your payHow the chancellor’s measures on tax, benefits and pensions will affect your personal financesHealey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’Budget 2026: key points at a glanceBudget 2026 calculator: find out if you are better or worse offZoe WoodWed 28 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSingleGraduate first jobView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellJosh graduated two years ago from an English university and is back home in London. He earns £28,500, out of which he pays £3,186 in income tax and £1,274 in national insurance (NI) contributions a year. This results in take-home pay of £2,003 a month or £24,040 a year. Despite an outcry, the salary threshold for repaying his plan 2 student loan will remainfrozen at £29,385for three years from next April, so any pay rise is likely to trigger payments. Graduates must repay 9% of earnings over the threshold.SingleAverage earnerView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellLayla earns the UK’s typical (median) wage of £41,000 as a nurse. She pays £5,684 in income tax and £2,274 in NI contributions. This results in take-home pay of £2,753 a month or £33,041 a year.Traditionally income tax bands keep pace with inflation, but they have been frozen until 2031. This means a greater proportion of pay is taxed than would otherwise be expected.With no changes to the “big three” – income tax, NI and VAT – her finances will look much the same in 2027.She qualifies for the £100 energy payment for English households in council tax bands A-D (council tax is devolved). Her energy bill will also be reduced by the decision to abolish standing charges on gas bills and the extension to the VAT cut on electricity to July.Couple, two childrenTwo incomes, one working part-timeView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellSimon is an accountant earning £65,000, and Maria earns £28,000 as a part-time teacher. Some of their child benefit is clawed back through thehigh-income child benefit charge, which is a tax penalty that kicks in at £60,000. As a result the couple have combined take-home pay of £6,141 a month or £73,690 a year.With no big tax changes this budget has not transformed their finances. Like other Britons they benefit from the energy bill shake up and their band D home qualifies for the £100 payment.CoupleTwo incomes, saving to buy a houseView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellTom and Martha work as teachers in London, earning £45,000 and £50,000 respectively. They have combined take-home pay of £6,287 a month or £75,439 a year. They rent a flat and are desperate to get on the property ladder. With a combined income of £95,000 they are eligible for theYour First Homescheme to help first-time buyers purchase a new-build home in England with a deposit of as little as 2.5%. Applications open in February, but only those with a total annual household income of £110,000 or less outside London, or £140,000 or less within London will qualify.Affluent couple, one childBoth working, one high earnerView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellLawyer Lucy earns £98,000 and civil servant Robert £48,000. The couple have combined take-home pay of £8,790 a month or £105,477 a year after tax. At this level, all the family’s child benefit entitlement is clawed back. Any pay rise for Lucy has big tax implications as she is close to the£100k “cliff edge”.For every £2 of income over that, you lose £1 of the £12,570 annual tax-free personal allowance so any earnings between £100,000 and £125,140 are effectively taxed at 60%.Their suburban home is in council tax band G so they miss out on the £100 energy payment. On the plus side, the keen savers will benefit from the cancelling of a plan tocut to the annual cash Isa allowancefor under-65s from £20,000 to £12,000 a year from April.Low-income familyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellThe Cooper family have three children and live in a rented property in Leicestershire, paying £995 a month. Paul works 35 hours a week in a distribution centre and is paid the ”national living wage” (NLW) for older workers, which is currently £12.71 an hour. His partner Hannah is not working. After tax, NI and his pension contribution, his take-home pay is £1604 a month. This is topped up with a monthly universal credit (UC) and child benefit payment totalling £1,989 a month. They will benefit from the 2027 rise in the NLW to £13.21 per hour and will also receive the £100 energy payment.DriverSelf-employed courierView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellMaxine drives 25,000 miles a year delivering parcels and earns £40,000 on a self-employed basis. Earlier this year the government upped the tax-free mileage allowance for people who drive for work from 45p to 55p for each of the first 10,000 miles which equates to a £200 saving for a basic-rate taxpayer. After tax – and that relief – she has take-home pay of £2,939 a month or £35,273 a year. From April 2027 the government is increasing the tax deductible rate above 10,000 miles from 25p to 35p a mile which will result in an additional £300 tax saving. The 5p increase in fuel duty which was to have kicked in next year has also been delayed again.Single pensionerSole income is state pensionView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellWhen the new state pension increases in April next year it will reach £13,036, exceeding the £12,570 annual personal tax allowance. Peter’s only income is the new state pension and it looked as if he might owe £93 of income tax. However, to remove this liability the government is creating the new “pension tax allowance” which will be applied automatically.Affluent pensioner coupleView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellBob and Margaret have a combined income of £60,000 from their state pensions and interest on savings. After paying tax of £4,572 they have a combined income of £4,619 a month or £55,428 a year.The big news for them is the tax rate on their savings income is increasing by 4 percentage points to 24% in April. Their additional state pension income will also be subject to tax. As a result of both changes their net income will fall by £1,101 a year.The couple is yet to access Bob’s private pension. From April any money left unspent in a defined contribution (AKA money purchase) pension after deathwill be included in inheritance calculationsfor the first time, so he is planning to withdraw some of the cash.Business ownerView image in fullscreenIllustration: Simon MaskellMo has been running his successful chain of florists for 30 years and wants to retire. He hopes to sell his business, crystallising a £1m gain that will attract capital gains tax. He is eligible for business asset disposal relief which reduces the rate from 24% to 18% on his £1m. However, from April the chancellor has cut this allowance to £500,000 which would increase his CGT bill by £30,000 to approximately £210,000.Illustrations by Simon MaskellTax and national insurance calculations provided by accountantsBlick RothenbergBenefits calculations by Turn2UsScotland’s income tax rates and thresholds are set by the Scottish parliament.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026BudgetTaxNational insuranceIncome taxFamily financesPensionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Budget winners and losers: pensioners and households gain as banks and betting shops hit | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: How the Burnham government’s first attempt to ease cost of living pressure pans out for key stakeholders
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: How the Burnham government’s first attempt to ease cost of living pressure pans out for key stakeholders
Content: Chancellor of the exchequer John Healey, left, with prime minister Andy Burnham at a community centre in Westminister earlier this month.Photograph: Richard Pohle/PAView image in fullscreenChancellor of the exchequer John Healey, left, with prime minister Andy Burnham at a community centre in Westminister earlier this month.Photograph: Richard Pohle/PABudget 2026Budget winners and losers: pensioners and households gain as banks and betting shops hitHow the Burnham government’s first attempt to ease cost of living pressure pans out for key stakeholdersBudget 2026: key points at a glanceHilary OsborneWed 28 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery budget has its winners and losers, and John Healey’s first as chancellor was no exception. While some gained from tax breaks and rule tweaks, others will either pay more, or had their hopes of reforms dashed. Here are some of those with reason to cheer, or sigh:WinnersEveryone in a band A-D property:A£100 paymentto help towards this winter’s energy costs. The payment is guaranteed in England from January. Other parts of the UK have been given funding to do the same.Pensioners:The state pension will go up to £13,036 next April, and pensioners will get a new matching personal allowance at the same time. The allowance will lift all income they receive to that level out of tax.Teenage tech bros – and other young entrepreneurs, inEngland:They will gain from a new allowance, which will give them support towards their living costs in the first year of their business.Independent cider makers, and brewers:More generous tax reliefs for small alcohol producers will help 2,000 businesses, and a new “guest beer” rule will mean that tied pubs in England and Wales must offer their drinks.EV drivers– but only those who use lower-powered public chargers:The government will give £100m in subsidies for on-street charging, saving people without home charging about £150 a year.First-time buyers with small savings:TheYour First Home schemewill help those with a deposit of as little as 2.5% to buy a newbuild home. It will be open to households earning up to £140,000 in London, and £110,000 everywhere else in England.Cash Isa fans:Savers under 65 will not have their cash Isa allowance cut next April after Healey reversed an announcement made in last year’s budget.
