They will, however, be encouraged to try their hand at investing with a new, yet to be announced, incentive for those buying stocks and shares for the first time.Self-employed fathers:Two weeks of paternity pay, currently worth up to £194 a week, will be available from April 2029 to those who work for themselves.Paddington Bear:The small bear from Peru is a well-known consumer of marmalade and could see the cost of his favourite spread fall by 20% as a result of the removal of tariffs from more than a 100 products, which also included gherkins and garlic.Budget 2026 calculator: find out if you are better or worse offRead moreLosersBanks:A temporary increase in the bank corporation tax surcharge, from 3% to 6% for 15 months, will mean they pay a combined £1.5bn extra to the Treasury over the period. But it had been suggested thatthe levy would be raised to 8%and bank shares rose after the budget, so maybe they are actually winners.Betting shops:Tax on slot machines with stakes of £1 or more will increase from 20% to 25% from April 2027. Shares in gambling companies also rose, as investors had feared the hike may be bigger.Students:They may have hoped for a change in the repayment thresholds to ease thepain felt by those on plan 2 loans, but there was no movement. Instead the thresholds are set to be frozen from next April.Savers who have money outside Isas:The tax on interest was set to go up next April and Healey added another two percentage points to the rates that had already been announced. Once a basic-rate saver has used up their tax-free allowance on interest they will pay 24% on returns, while a higher rate taxpayer will pay 44% and an additional rate payer 49%.Buy-to-let landlords:Taxes on property income will also go up by more than had been expected, and to the rates outlined for savers. For this, however, there are different rates in Scotland.Private renters:The increase in taxes on landlords could lead to a steady rise in rents, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility. It says, together with other measures introduced in recent years, the extra cost means landlords may leave the market and potential new investors stay out.Poor families in bands E and above:The £100 energy rebate is being distributed using council tax bands, but this means 1.4 million of the poorest families miss out, according to the Resolution Foundation.People in urban communities hoping to access nature:The budget included exemptions for biodiversity net gain (BNG) on brownfield sites. BNG requires developers to build in nature gains when developing plots but Healey is removing this requirement for plots up to 1.5 hectares (3.7 acres) in England.Additional reporting by Jasper Jolly and Sandra Laville10:59Bills, banks, ‘breathing space’: what was in Burnham’s first budget? - The LatestExplore more on these topicsBudget 2026Economic policyEnergy billsConsumer affairsHousehold billsFirst-time buyersEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel responds | Polly Toynbee, Hettie O'Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik and John McDonnell | The Guardian
description: Amid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Amid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP/REX/ShutterstockThe panelBudget 2026Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel respondsPolly Toynbee,Hettie O'Brien,Rohan Sathyamoorthy,Kevin Cashman,NikandJohn McDonnellAmid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?Wed 28 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShare‘Growth in every postcode’? Not yet, but hope at lastPolly ToynbeeGuardian columnistFirst, he did no harm. Then he scattered sprinkles of feel-goods. He told the truth about the state we’re in, deep in anextra £14bn of expensive debt, and, though he put it politely, at the mercy of the monster in the White House’s whims on Iran and tariffs.The losers were popular targets: the banks and gambling companies. But plainly bank threats to decamp partly paid off. Their shares leapt up on the news that their surcharge would rise to only 6%, not its original 8% before Tory reductions. They expected to pay more, and indeed they should. Gambling company shares jumped up too, with Rank up more than 10% on the day when the companies were only hit with five percentage points more tax on high-stakes machines, a missed chance, but better than nothing. The Treasury makes£4bn from gambling. Time to ban their advertising next.The chancellor gave a gracious nod to his predecessor. He should be grateful, as she took the pain and he takes the gain for her £66.6bn in tax rises, in NI for employers andfrozen income tax thresholdsthat slide by unseen, but yield mightily until 2031.The publicexpected more personal taxes, according to Ipsos. It didn’t happen. Labour can take comfort that they think the Conservatives and Reform would both raise tax and cut public services.Instead, help comes for their energy costs, one of the greatest causes of household debt, with bills set to rise brutally in January. Homes in council tax bands A-D get £100 and the VAT reduction has been extended until July, while abolished standing charges leave 60% of homes better off. But the rumbling discontent that has upended our politics since Brexit is easily explained by the unprecedented long fall inmedian household income, only in the last year rising back to levels six years ago.Yet people’s priorities remain perverse: immigration stays top of their concerns, above inflation and the economy. Spending more on tougher border controls is second only to the NHS as the most popular expenditure. What do you do? Give in and let Shabana Mahmood be her harshest – or start telling people about the trade-off? Visas for work for another 200,000 migrantswould bring the Treasury £18bn, says the Office for Budget Responsibility. Think what people could have for that.Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.Voters might have been hoping for something bolder than thisHettie O'BrienWriter on the Guardian’s morning newsletter First Edition, the Guardian Long Read, and the author ofThe Asset ClassWhile Keir Starmer promised to tread more “lightly” on voters’ lives, interpreting political disaffection as a sign that people wanted to hear less from their politicians, Andy Burnham has interpreted this loss of faith as a demand for more political action. But there was always a risk that without a theory of power, his premiership would come to resemble the Downing Street equivalent of the TV show Rip-Off Britain, giving voters “everyday fixes”, starter ISAs and cheaper gherkins while failing to change the economy or society as a whole.The charitable reading of John Healey’s budget is that it was better than it could have been (and better than the Treasury, which briefed this as a “low-key” event, wanted us to expect). His energy package, including a £100 cut to bills for houses in council tax brackets A-D, will help ease the cost of living and should lower inflation. He also proposed a series of changes that should help to bring down energy bills in future. But there was no help for low-income renters, nor any plans for funding public services that are facingreal-terms cuts. Bankers, meanwhile, will be breathing a sigh of relief after Healey imposed a temporary 6% tax on bank profits, below the pre-crisis level of 8%.For a government that has promised to turn back 40 years of neoliberalism, you might have been hoping for something much more radical than this. Small, short-term fixes and making it easier to cancel your Netflix subscription don’t equate to a political philosophy, let alone a programme capable of convincing voters that difficult trade-offs – whether on defence spending or the costs of an ageing society – will be worth it. Governing, as Mark McVitiewrote recently, requires political imagination and a sense of where you want to end up. Let’s hope that Andy Burnham has more to offer than this.Budget cuts to fund military spending will lead to job losses and lower growthKevin CashmanResearcher at Transition Security Project, a centre founded by Common Wealth and Climate and Community InstituteJust last month, the prime minister made the significant promise to “break with the direction of the past 40 years” and “build a new economy and a new politics”. John Healey’s budget, unfortunately, doesn’t do enough of either.Department budgets were alreadyslashed this summerto help finance the Ministry of Defence’s demand for an extra £15bn. Now, this budget adds £3bn more in cuts.In July,Transition Security Projectestimated that the defence investment plan, funded partly through £6.8bn in cuts, would result in more than 10,000 net job losses. With a further £3bn in cuts, those losses are now likely to exceed 15,000.The reason is simply that military spending is a weaker driver of growth than the investment being sacrificed to fund it. Too much of the money leaves the country – flowing, especially, to the United States.These cuts also undermine programmes that would help bring down the cost of living. The budget confirms a £1bn cut to Warm Homes, which supports heat pump grants. The additional help with household energy bills is welcome. But directing up to £5bn from the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank towards defence reinforces the same misplaced priorities when these resources could have been invested in areas that help with living standards.Burnham does not have to accept these constraints. Healey has left the detailed funding route to the Nato spending targets until next year’s spending review. These targets – pushed by the US – imply a colossal transfer of wealth from the public to the military sector. Burnham should abandon these targets he inherited, which will steal more investment from every other department.Healey was right that wars are driving up our energy bills and making Britain less safe. But let’s be honest about the role the government is playing. The US used British bases in its unprovoked attack on Iran, and our government is now backing Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen. Diplomacy and de-escalation are part of a serious cost of living strategy – not bombing.Welcome news on apprenticeships, but otherwise little cheer for young peopleRohan SathyamoorthyWriter from south-west LondonLook hard enough at this budget, and there are some signs that the chancellor is serious about bridging the age divide: an increase in tax for Britain’s banks, increased investment in apprenticeships and a new scheme for first-time buyers will be a welcome relief for many young and working people who are tired of bearing a disproportionate share of Britain’s economic burden. However, the limitations of even these mild reforms are already apparent:bank stocks roseconspicuously this morning on news that the rise would be temporary and only a mere three percentage points. And although the first-time buyer ISA will help young savers in the immediate term, in the long run it is only continuing to subsidise the housing crisis at the expense of the taxpayer, rather than intervening directly in the market to bring prices back down to an affordable level.Furthermore, while pensioners, businesses, workers, women, carers, families and even nightclubs all received explicit support from Healey, outrageously absent was any real help for young people, nor any mention of the student loan crisis. The only mention of young people not in employment, education or training was made in the context of reforming welfare. Instead of addressing the problems facing young people and making clear that he would tackle intergenerational fairness, Healey made his priority clear, with “the biggest increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war”.Ultimately, it will be impossible to fully judge this budget until we see the one that succeeds it. This “breathing space” budget will be beneficial only if it really is just that – buying time for the government to solve the painful, unignorable issues still crippling Britain’s young people: jobs, student loans, soaring rents. If the mixed rhetoric today is anything to go by, I won’t be holding my breath.I wish more had been done to help us pay our rent and fill our fridgesNikParticipant in theChanging RealitiesprojectThe chancellor said “hope starts with a home”, but for me, it’s the cost of my home that keeps me in poverty. I work multiple jobs just to pay my rent, and nothing in today’s budget will make that situation better. Where is the “breathing space” for families like mine, or hope for the future?Families struggling through the storms of living on a low income deserve more than modest, micro-policies and everyday fixes to protect them from the incessant headwinds.Extending the removal of VAT from electricity bills to next summer is being presented as help for households, but for rural families like mine, it offers little (or no) meaningful relief. I have no access to mains gas and can’t afford heating oil, so I depend on electricity to heat my home. Yet this measure does nothing to address the reality of living rurally without affordable alternatives. A record number of people now live in very deep poverty, with incomes that don’t cover the basics of food, housing or energy. We need meaningful, targeted support, not policies that offer some households a small saving while leaving others struggling to keep warm. In Cornwall, many homes rely on heating oil, and removing the kerosene tariff may help, but any savings depend on supplies holding up and suppliers passing them on.The chancellor promised a distinctly Labour approach to welfare but I know many will feel incredibly fearful about the white papers to come later this year, afterAlan MilburnandStephen Timmsdeliver their reports on youth unemployment and disability benefits.What we know from this budget is that families will be able to save about 40p on the weekly shop, assuming toffees and caramels are a part of your weekly essentials. Food poverty directly impacts health, productivity and social inclusion. I wish more had been done to help fill our fridges.This budget buys time to go bigger and bolder in next year’s spending reviewJohn McDonnellLabour MP for Hayes and Harlington. He was shadow chancellor for Labour from 2015 to 2020The chancellor has called his budget a “breathing space” budget and that’s exactly what it is. It’s less a break with Keir Starmer, but hopefully the start of a step away.The range of small-scale cost of living assistance offered on energy and food costs are all welcome elements of relief, but the harsh reality is that they provide an extremely limited breathing space.The government has to be extremely careful that the goodwill that Andy Burnham’s arrival has generated does not degenerate into disappointment and disillusionment. Reform UK may have dipped in the polls but the rise of the far right in Germany, France and Italy demonstrates all too clearly where that disappointment can lead to.This budget indicates to people that the government appreciates their concerns and is on their side, but it is absolutely critical that the time this budget may buy is used to demonstrate that it also has the plan needed to tackle the financial pressures people are under.Next year’s spending review provides that opportunity.The government has committed to the large-scale capital investment programme in council housing, home insulation and alternative energy that can stimulate the growth promised in every postcode.But there has to be demand in the economy too. That means putting money to spend in people’s pockets by modernising our taxation system to redistribute wealth and tackle the underinvestment in our public services, low pay and poverty that have held our economy back.Nobody doubts the pressure John Healey has been under as a result of the crass geopolitical nightmares caused by Donald Trump’s attacks on Iran. Both Benjamin Netanyahu and Vladimir Putin have played Trump like a fiddle to their own advantage, and we are all now paying the economic price. With the potential change in the midterms, perhaps it’s also time for leaders to start talking less about defence spending and more about peace making.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026The panelTax and spendingJohn HealeyHousingMilitarycommentShareReuse this content

title: Spain’s Sánchez declares three days of mourning after at least 68 killed in Toledo train crash | Spain | The Guardian
description: High-speed service travelling from Madrid to Seville ran into back of another, knocking two carriages off track
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: High-speed service travelling from Madrid to Seville ran into back of another, knocking two carriages off track
Content: 0:39On the ground footage shows scene of fatal rail crash in Spain – videoSpainSpain’s Sánchez declares three days of mourning after at least 68 killed in Toledo train crashHigh-speed service travelling from Madrid to Seville ran into back of another, knocking two carriages off trackSam Jonesin Urda andAshifa Kassamin MadridWed 28 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 05.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Spanish prime minister has declared three days of mourning after at least 68 people were killed and dozens more injured in a collision between two high-speed trains that officials suggested was caused by an “inexplicable” error at the central command centre.The trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling on Wednesday morning in the same direction on the line that stretches from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to the southern region of Andalusia. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near the town of Urda.The tragedy was the second major deadly high-speed train accident this year in Spain, rattling a country where the extensive rail network has long been a point of pride. “Today all of Spain is grieving,” the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said.0:46Aerial footage shows aftermath of deadly Spain train collision – videoIn January, 46people were killedand dozens more injured after two trains – again, one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía. On Wednesday Sánchez said it was “unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in the same year, as we have”.The causes of the accident were under investigation, he added. If it emerged that it was due to failures in the security system or negligence, these shortcomings would be addressed with the “utmost severity”, he said.The Urda crash, which ranks as one of Europe’s deadliest such disasters this century, comes weeks beforegeneral electionsin which Sánchez is waging an uphill battle for re-election. The crash in January left his Socialist partyfending off criticismsthat it had not done enough to maintain the safety of the high-speed rail line, suggesting that this latest crash would add to the fractious political climate.Images from the scene showed a derailed train with at least one carriage remaining on an elevated section of track. Twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the rail line. Officials said the trains had been carrying 544 people.Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, said that rear-end collisions like that which had taken place on Wednesday were “highly unlikely” and suggested that the accident may have been caused by human error made in “inexplicable” circumstances.He said the LZB signalling system, which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied, had gone down at about 8.30am local time due to a computer malfunction. As a result, an estimated six trains had been halted along a stretch of around 63km of track, he said.View image in fullscreenPassengers check departure boards at Santa Justa station in Seville after the crash.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesThe task of monitoring the rail lines then fell to a 24-hour command centre in Madrid. Minutes after the computer malfunction, the centre instructed at least two of the trains to continue as normal, despite the fact that there was still a “stop signal” in place, said Puente.“It was the control centre, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he said. “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said on Wednesday afternoon that the death toll had risen to 68 as rescue teams continued to ⁠search through the wreckage of the derailed carriages. Castilla-La Mancha’s leader, Emiliano García-Page, told reporters that more victims were likely as “it has not yet been possible to reach the bottom of the carriages”.Officials said another 107 people had needed medical treatment in hospital, including 15 who were in a serious condition.Miguel, ‌a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described the moment of the accident to Cope radio. “We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were ‌about to derail,” he said. “Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been the other one.”The crash turned the municipality of Urda, surrounded by olive groves and vineyards, into a hub for the rescue effort. A local sports centre became a triage centre for those with minor injuries, while a nearby hall was repurposed into a space for those scrambling to find their missing loved ones.A constant flow of vehicles from local, regional and national emergency services headed in and out of the town, while locals pitched in by bringing food and bottles of water to those waiting anxiously for news of their relatives.Giving initial details about the crash, Puente said the Iryo train had been travelling ahead on the tracks and had been sitting stationary when the Renfe train was instructed by the command centre to resume its journey. The Renfe train then travelled approximately 25km before colliding with the Iryo train about 17 minutes later.The speed at which the Renfe train had been travelling remains unknown, the transport minister told reporters, though the section of rail on which it was travelling allows for speeds of up to 200km/hour.The control centre “had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it”, Puente added. “I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts.”Puente said that similar erroneous instructions had been given to at least one other train on Wednesday morning. “And it was the engineer of one of the trains who corrected the command centre and told them he can’t resume normal operation – it has to be [an] on-sight operation,” Puente said, citing a protocol that allows trains to advance but at a greatly reduced speed in order to ensure that there are not other trains sitting on the tracks ahead. “The operator said: ‘OK, on-sight operation.’”Amid growing anger over the crash, the prime minister said there was little to suggest that the two high speed rail collisions Spain has suffered this year had shared any kind of similar cause.“Everything strongly suggests that the causes of the two accidents are completely unrelated, but it is not up to me to say so,” he said. “But what is clear is that, if we need – as we certainly do – to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, it will be done.”Across the country, people held moments of silence for those who were killed, while Spain’s football federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday.The first victims to be named included a 31-year-old Guardia civil agent, José Manuel Chacón.The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues. Spanish media said the missing included a former minister for the People’s party and several foreigners who were likely on holiday in the country.The opposition People’s party leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsSpainTrain crashesRail transportEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in jail after being found guilty of harassing journalists | Tommy Robinson | The Guardian
description: Judge says he will consider all options to sentence far-right activist who trial heard deployed ‘bullyboy, intimidatory tactics’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Judge says he will consider all options to sentence far-right activist who trial heard deployed ‘bullyboy, intimidatory tactics’
Content: Tommy Robinson leaving Southwark crown court on Wednesday after being found guilty.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson leaving Southwark crown court on Wednesday after being found guilty.Photograph: Yui Mok/PATommy RobinsonTommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in jail after being found guilty of harassing journalistsJudge says he will consider all options to sentence far-right activist who trial heard deployed ‘bullyboy, intimidatory tactics’Ben QuinnWed 28 Oct 2026 12.04 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of harassing two journalists to the point it caused them fear of violence.Journalists from theDaily Mailand their family members fled their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, his trial was told.Robinson had shared pictures of the family of one of the journalists online and said he had “tagged and bagged” all three reporters who worked on an article about his alleged role influencing unrest that broke out after the 2024 Southport murders. The charges related to two of the journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.Dirnhuber and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after an allegedcampaign of intimidationthat also included a call to the editor of the Daily Mail in which Robinson said he would make the journalists and their families “famous”.Robinson was found guilty on both counts against him on Wednesday at Southwark crown court. The jury had deliberated for two days and had to be directed by the judge that they could return a majority verdict rather than a unanimous one.View image in fullscreenRobinson attended court each day with a large number of supporters.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAJournalists were given an escort out of the courtroom by security after one of them was threatened inside the court by one of Robinson’s supporters. The man was ejected from the press gallery and later from the courtroom.Robinson, a former member of the British National party and co-founder of the English Defence League, had said before the trial that his legal bills were being paid for by the billionaire tech mogul and owner of X, Elon Musk.He was accused of harassment causing fear of violence through posts shared with his hundreds of thousands of followers on X and by direct messages. He called Young on 5 August 2024 and told him that he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”Robinson, who attended court each day with a large number of supporters, was said to have become enraged after the Mail tracked him down to a hotelin Cyprus, where he was commenting on events in the UK after the Southport murders, and published a story about him with the headline “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.Dirnhuber said in a witness statement he did not know how Robinson had obtained his address, or who he had shared it with, adding: “I was concerned about the risk of being intercepted on my way to work, either by Robinson for a livestreamed interview or by an unpredictable supporter of his hoping to cause me or my partner physical harm.”Young said he felt his family was under threat and he was fearful of what might happen next. “It was clear to me that Tommy Robinson was following through on his threats. My main concern was that while he may not physically harm me, he had 800,000 followers on X at the time who might have been tempted to seek revenge on me, or my home, or my family for what I had written.”A third Daily Mail journalist, George Odling, said in a witness statement that he, his wife and young child had to leave their home through a neighbour’s house because they feared being followed by Robinson’s supporters.The trial heard that Robinson’s “angry” and “retaliatory” posts began on 5 August 2024, as he questioned the Daily Mail’s decision to photograph and write the story about him in Cyprus.In a post on X, which has been viewed 244,000 times and made reference to the newspaper’s front page headline “Stoking riots from his sunbed”, he wrote: “Quick question, these lies have a direct result on threats to my family.“Is it ok if I track down the journalists addresses + families details + dox them. Would that be journalism. This has been coordinated from the top down because my latest documentary humiliates their lies.“They have purposely doxxed where my children are is it fair for me to do the same to them.”Robinson said in evidence he had been in “a panic” after the Mail had in effect identified the hotel in Cyprus where he had gone with family and friends and published a photo of his ex-wife, which he said put her at risk. He said he had only wanted to question the journalists and claimed they knew he was “not coming to beat them up”.After he was found guilty, the Crown Prosecution Service said Robinson had “weaponised social media”. Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Nobody should be made to fear violence because of the work they do. Journalists play an important role in a democratic society and should be able to carry out their professional duties without being subjected to harassment.“We will always seek to work with the police to prosecute those who break the law and I hope these convictions provide reassurance that such behaviour will be treated seriously by the criminal justice system.”Welcoming the verdict, a spokesperson for the Daily Mail said: “Yaxley-Lennon’s behaviour was reprehensible, and had grave consequences for our reporters and their families. Through his actions, Yaxley-Lennon sought to undermine our right to hold him to account. We stand by our journalists and their freedom to report legitimately in the public interest.”Robinson is due back in court on 16 December for a sentencing hearing. Mr Justice Cavanagh said after the verdict he would be considering all options, including a custodial sentence, whether in full or suspended. Harassment causing fear of violence can carry a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.Explore more on these topicsTommy RobinsonJournalist safetyDaily MailFar rightCrimeNational newspapersNewspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand tells trial it was wrong to use fame to ‘facilitate’ sex with women  | UK news | The Guardian
description: Former comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, says he misused position but ‘consent is more important than sex itself’
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Former comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, says he misused position but ‘consent is more important than sex itself’
Content: Russell Brand gave evidence at Southwark crown court for four hours on Wednesday.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRussell Brand gave evidence at Southwark crown court for four hours on Wednesday.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockUK newsRussell Brand tells trial it was wrong to use fame to ‘facilitate’ sex with womenFormer comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, says he misused position but ‘consent is more important than sex itself’Emine SinmazWed 28 Oct 2026 17.28 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand has told a court that he was wrong to have used his fame and success to “facilitate” sexual activity with women.The 51-year-old comedian said he had “misused” his position “very selfishly” and dedicated his life to “reckless philandering and idiocy”.But he insisted that “consent is more important than sex itself” and that the criminal case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life.Brand is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Wearing a dark suit, white shirt and tie, he appeared in the witness box for four hours on Wednesday as he gave evidence at Southwark crown court.He said he had achieved “staggering fame” after marrying the US pop star Katy Perry in 2010 but that now nobody would “touch him with a bargepole”.View image in fullscreenRussell Brand denies all the charges. At the start of his evidence, he repeatedly said ‘no’ when the individual claims were put to him.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAHe blamed his downfall on “devastating” 2023 media reports about his alleged sexual misconduct, which he said had led to him being barred from visiting his baby son when he was having open heart surgery at Great Ormond Street hospital.He also said he had failed to persuade a single person with relevant information to give evidence on his behalf at his criminal trial. “Would they touch you with a bargepole?” his barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked. Brand replied: “No.”The TV personality gave confident answers in a booming voice to Winter, issuing a series of terse “no” replies when asked if he had raped women in a hotel room, at his home and in a bar toilet, and sexually assaulted radio and TV workers.He told the court he was “innocent” of all the charges and said: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself.”He later added: “Consent is an ongoing process and at any point anybody can withdraw their consent.”During the course of his evidence, Brand told the court he does not remember some of the incidents in the charges and remembers only consensual sexual encounters in others.He admitted saving the telephone number of a woman who accuses him of anal rape in 2009 with the letter “T” next to her name, meaning “tart”.The woman alleges Brand raped her at his north London townhouse, a few days after she had willingly engaged in a threesome with the star backstage at the Hammersmith Apollo venue in London.When Winter asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups.”He also put two asterisks next to the woman’s name, which he told the jury meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.”Brand used colourful language to describe some of his accusers. He described a woman who alleges he raped her at the Labour party conference in 1999 as “vivacious and loquacious” and an MTV worker who accuses him of oral rape in 2004 as having “prominent eyes”. “She was lithe, elfin, pixieish, energetic,” he said.But there were tense moments during cross-examination in which Brand stared at the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, in silence for several seconds. Occasionally he could be seen moving his lips before speaking out loud.The prosecutor probed him about alleged inconsistencies in his previous statements and what he has told the jury with regards to the woman who accused him of anal rape. Brand said: “Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree. Since these events occurred there’s been escalating recollection.“It’s been a deeply traumatic episode of my life I’ve focused on at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I ask your forgiveness, well, not your forgiveness.“I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that.”And when asked if the young fan was “just another sexual conquest” in his attempt to sleep with 5,000 women, Brand told the court: “I really don’t know the number, but it’s difficult to dispute that’s how I conducted myself in the pursuit of willing sexual partners.”As he came to the end of his cross-examination, Karmy-Jones challenged Brand on what he had done to upset the woman so much. “I think I was in a position of fame, a successful person who was admired and I misused that commodity very selfishly,” he said.“You were in a position of power in respect of each of these women,” the prosecutor continued, to which Brand replied: “As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong.”Karmy-Jones also confronted him with extracts from his 2007 book, My Booky Wook, in which Brand said he “would never have relented until I received my birthright orgasm”. Responding to one of the passages, Brand said: “I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.“With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy.”The prosecutor said that Brand’s book included a picture of himself as a seven-year-old with the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took fifteen years to produce results.”View image in fullscreenExtracts from Brand’s My Booky Wook were read to the court on Wednesday.Photograph: Metropolitan policeThe first alleged rape victim has told the court she believed Brand was gay when they first met at a Labour party conference fringe event, which led to her agreeing for him to come to her hotel room.The prosecutor asked Brand: “That’s something you would do, wasn’t it? That was something you would do to make girls trust you?”“No,” Brand replied.Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Mr Justice Bennathan told jurors they should find Brand not guilty of the indecent assault allegation after he concluded “there was insufficient evidence” to support the charge.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Coalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majority | Israel | The Guardian
description: Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that drew highest turnout in decades
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that drew highest turnout in decades
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu claimed without evidence that Arab Israeli parties had ‘stolen the election’, while Gadi Eisenkot appeared to rule out a coalition with Palestinian parties.Composite: AFP and Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu claimed without evidence that Arab Israeli parties had ‘stolen the election’, while Gadi Eisenkot appeared to rule out a coalition with Palestinian parties.Composite: AFP and Getty ImagesIsraelCoalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majorityProjections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that drew highest turnout in decadesIsrael election: what we know so farAnalysis: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscapeJulian Borgerin JerusalemWed 28 Oct 2026 15.58 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 01.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s future hung in the balance on Wednesday as it became clear thatBenjamin Netanyahuhad lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot’s bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister’s bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots – about 14% of the total electorate –yet to be fully counted.With the remaining 86% of the votes tallied,both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.On Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and the success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming they had “stolen the election”. He did not offer evidence, butsaid on Xthat his Likud party had sent “hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence” to the central elections committee and the Shin Bet internal security agency.Both those agencies have been politicised under Netanyahu’s government. The elections committee had sought to ban Arab Israeli parties before the poll, but the attempt to exclude them was overturned by the country’s supreme court.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu at an election night event for his Likud party in Jerusalem.Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesDonald Trump took credit for Netanyahu’s better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am (the United Arab List).“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid. And if we don’t put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscapeRead more“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.Noa Landau, a commenterwriting in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can’t be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu’s government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot at an election night rally in Tel Aviv.Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to their rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other’s camps.Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.View image in fullscreenThe scene outside the Knesset in Jerusalem on Wednesday.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAThe Palestinian parties and Jewish centre-left have been urging the opposition to focus on finding common cause in the Knesset, replacing the speaker and pursuing legislation that the factions can agree on, such as ordering an independent review into the security failures that led to the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023.On Wednesday, Herzog urged all parties to keep an “open mind” in trying to build a new government coalition.“We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said.The election happened in the midst of Israel’s war in Gaza – barely mentioned in the course of the campaign, despite the fact that Israel has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and Netanyahu is wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.View image in fullscreenProtesters take part in an anti-government demonstration calling for an end to the war in Gaza near Netnayahu’s residence in Jerusalem on Wednesday.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesA UN commission of human rights expertsreported on Mondaythat Israel had continued to commit genocidal acts against Palestinian civilians in Gaza after a ceasefire was declared in October 2025. Since then 1,431 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military, including 300 children.The report, by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said: “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Daniel Meron, rejected the report as an “attempt to destroy the Jewish state” and “to undermine Israel’s ​legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself”.Eisenkot and much of his bloc support the war in Gaza, and sought to make the election a referendum on Netanyahu. The turnout was nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting.View image in fullscreenNetanyahu supporters celebrate in the early hours of Wednesday.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesPolitical deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, he and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war alongside the US against Iran.Explore more on these topicsIsraelBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks | European Union | The Guardian
description: Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’
Content: Mark Carney and the European Parliament president, Roberta Metsola, in Strasbourg last month.Photograph: Ahmet Sel/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Carney and the European Parliament president, Roberta Metsola, in Strasbourg last month.Photograph: Ahmet Sel/Anadolu/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionEU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talksWatered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’Lisa O’Carrollin Brussels andLeyland Ceccoin TorontoWed 28 Oct 2026 17.27 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU has backed away from its offer toCanadato start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.The issue was triggered after the European Commission president,Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister,Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economicssaid.Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionCanadaAmericasEuropeMark CarneyUrsula von der LeyennewsShareReuse this content

title: Knifeman on LNER train ‘caused terror and fear on unimaginable scale’, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder passengers and staff on board a London-bound train last November
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder passengers and staff on board a London-bound train last November
Content: A photo of Anthony Williams, 33, on an LNER train  last year, which was shown to the jury at Cambridge crown court.Photograph: British Transport Police/PAView image in fullscreenA photo of Anthony Williams, 33, on an LNER train  last year, which was shown to the jury at Cambridge crown court.Photograph: British Transport Police/PAUK newsKnifeman on LNER train ‘caused terror and fear on unimaginable scale’, court hearsAnthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder passengers and staff on board a London-bound train last NovemberNeha Gohil and press agencyWed 28 Oct 2026 15.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA knifeman “caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale” to passengers when he stabbed 10 people on a London-bound train, a court has heard.Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on an LNER train on 1 November last year and stabbing four people in the 24 hours before.Christopher Paxton KC told jurors at Cambridge crown court on Wednesday: “The defendant, Mr Williams, armed with a knife, caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale, moving up and down a busy train from which there was no escape, stabbing several people as he did so.”During his opening statement, Paxton showed a CCTV clip of a passenger, Stephen Crean, attempting to wrestle a knife from Williams. He said Williams asked Crean: “Do you want to die?”“We say, clear evidence of the defendant’s intention to kill, as was the use of the knife to stab so many, and to stab and cut Mr Crean in his hand, head and lower back,” Paxton said.Paxton described the “terror” of the attack, which led some train passengers to run “for their lives” and hide away in toilets, store cabinets and under seats.The prosecutor also praised the “extraordinary bravery” of the passengers who tried to wrestle the knife off Williams.This included Scott Green, who was stabbed while he attempted to grab the knife from Williams. A member of the train crew, Samir Zitouni, was also stabbed multiple times as he tried to use a frying pan to stop Williams, jurors heard.“In the face of that threat and the defendant’s sheer brutality some stood tall to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage, defending themselves and putting themselves in harm’s way to protect strangers,” Paxton said.Paxton also praised the train driver for his decision to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon.Williams, of no fixed abode, previously admitted a series of offences, including the wounding of 12 people, but denies 14 counts of attempted murder.Paxton told the court Williams posed a “dangerous threat” to the people he encountered before the train attack on the evening of 1 November.Jurors heard Williams had approached a 17-year-old boy on the Docklands Light Railway in London in the early hours of 1 November and asked him if he was “beefing the devil” before he knifed him in the face and hand.Williams also attacked three people in Peterborough on the evening of 31 October, the court heard, including a 14-year-old boy.“Across the Halloween weekend last year, to the many people he encountered, the defendant, Anthony Williams, posed a dangerous threat, marauding through towns and cities, on streets and trains alike, armed with a knife,” he said.“He stabbed many, seeking to end their lives with deadly intention, striking out at them when they were defenceless and in fear.”The trial continues on Thursday.Explore more on these topicsUK newsCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of Starlink | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine
Content: Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk during a summit with African leaders in Moscow.Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/ReutersView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin praised Elon Musk during a summit with African leaders in Moscow.Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/ReutersUkrainePutin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of StarlinkRussia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack UkraineDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 28 Oct 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’sSpaceXwith Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US andUkraineearlier this month.A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.View image in fullscreenElon Musk is a controlling shareholder in Starlink and an ally of Donald Trump.Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.Starlink does not work inRussiaand its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaElon MuskVladimir PutinSpaceXEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Guardian and ITN have ‘duty to public and sources’ to publish sexual allegations against well-known figure, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Individual known in court as PPT is seeking a permanent injunction, with lawyers citing his risk of suicide
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Individual known in court as PPT is seeking a permanent injunction, with lawyers citing his risk of suicide
Content: Gavin Millar KC told the high court on Wednesday that the Guardian and ITN had ‘not just the responsibility, but the duty to publish information we believe to be in the public interest’.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenGavin Millar KC told the high court on Wednesday that the Guardian and ITN had ‘not just the responsibility, but the duty to publish information we believe to be in the public interest’.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersUK newsGuardian and ITN have ‘duty to public and sources’ to publish sexual allegations against well-known figure, court hearsIndividual known in court as PPT is seeking a permanent injunction, with lawyers citing his risk of suicideMichael SavageMedia editorWed 28 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo news organisations have a duty to the public and their sources to publish allegations of exploitative sexual behaviour by a well-known figure despite claims he is “highly likely” to attempt suicide, the high court has heard.The anonymous individual, known in court simply as PPT, is seeking an injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing the allegations, which he denies.His legal team have argued that publishing would be likely to lead to his death, after two previous attempts to take his own life.However, the legal team for the media groups told the high court there were powerful “countervailing” considerations compelling them to publish the claims.Gavin Millar KC, the lead barrister for the media outlets, said they had “not just the responsibility, but the duty to publish information we believe to be in the public interest”.He argued the claimant had not taken the impact on the sources involved in the investigation “sufficiently into account”.“They have made a substantial commitment to being contributors, and were extremely anxious for the publication and the broadcast to go ahead as soon as possible,” Millar said.Many of the women making the allegations have been traumatised by PPT’s alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result, according to a written submission from the media groups.It states: “They believe that it is important that their allegations are publicly aired so that other women are protected and the full nature of his conduct is disclosed, and in order to assist the sources to recover from their own experiences.”It said the media outlets had credible evidence of seriously improper conduct “towards a large number of women over a prolonged period”, including potential criminal conduct.Millar said if publication of the allegations were blocked, “our women contributors and others we are aware of” were likely to find “other ways to make their stories known publicly”.He added that proceeding with publication through the Guardian and ITN would be the “best way to put the information into the public domain”.The well-known figure is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life; article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”; and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.However, the media companies argue that the European court of human rights, which enforces the ECHR, has never ruled in such a way that would cause these articles to apply in this case. They also argue countervailing rights under article 10, which protects the right to freedom of expression.Millar said the investigation into PPT had spoken to more than 100 people, including 30 who gave first-hand accounts.He told that court that since the Guardian and ITN first contacted PPT in May so he could respond to the allegations, deadlines had been repeatedly extended and unusual measures put in place in order to act responsibly, given PPT’s medical issues.Millar said that “recognising the difficult and unusual nature of the case”, the media companies had then agreed to delay publication so that PPT could seek an injunction and have his case heard before a judge.PPT’s legal team has previously told that court there was evidence his life would be endangered should the allegations be published.A summary of an assessment of the claimant’s current wellbeing by an independent expert stated that he could not conclude either that suicide was inevitable if publication went ahead, or that psychiatric treatment could eliminate all risk.The expert said that the risks could be lowered should the allegations be published while PPT was in an inpatient psychiatric setting.The trial has now concluded, with Mr Justice Nicklin retiring to come to a ruling.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsUK newsInjunctionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Allison Pearson said to be negotiating exit from Daily Telegraph amid job cull  | Telegraph Media Group | The Guardian
description: Columnist’s relations with some senior editorial figures said to be strained over subjects she raised in her columns
Author: Tara Conlan
Headline: Columnist’s relations with some senior editorial figures said to be strained over subjects she raised in her columns
Content: Allison Pearson, left, greets Lucy Connolly at Reform UK’s annual conference last year. Connolly was jailed in 2024 after calling for hotels housing asylum seekers to be set on fire after the Southport attacks.Photograph: Jacob King/PAView image in fullscreenAllison Pearson, left, greets Lucy Connolly at Reform UK’s annual conference last year. Connolly was jailed in 2024 after calling for hotels housing asylum seekers to be set on fire after the Southport attacks.Photograph: Jacob King/PATelegraph Media GroupAllison Pearson said to be negotiating exit from Daily Telegraph amid job cullColumnist’s relations with some senior editorial figures said to be strained over subjects she raised in her columnsTara ConlanWed 28 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe controversialDaily Telegraphcolumnist Allison Pearson is understood to be in negotiations about leaving the broadsheet as the newspaper’s new owner makes significant newsroom cuts.Sources told the Guardian that Pearson – firmly on the right of the Telegraph’s roster – is preparing to announce her exit imminently and is crafting a statement about her future plans.Telegraph cuts up to 100 jobs as new owner promises to turn paper into ‘AI-powered’ global businessRead moreThe news comes after the German media companyAxel Springer, which completed a £575m takeover in June, warned that as many as 100 journalists’ roles were at risk of redundancy as it transitioned into being “a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.One insider said the Brexit-backing columnist had been “in some sort of negotiation to make an elegant departure” after discussions with management about her future at the title.But they said rumours of her expected exit had been circulating within the newsroom for a number of days, and were not a surprise after a column she wrote in September had raised some eyebrows internally, particularly among senior management.Pearson wrote in an opinion piece that the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, had “the rough-diamond charisma to pull a large, enthusiastic crowd”.She also wrote: “Every single person who marched in the rain to Unite the Kingdom, every decent person hanging our beautiful flags from lamp-posts and motorway bridges and on village greens, is making patriotism respectable again. Step by step, inch by inch, we are taking our country back from those who hate it.”View image in fullscreenThe Telegraph is cutting up to 100 jobs as it transitions into ‘a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business’.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Getty ImagesPearson has been the Telegraph’s chief interviewer and a columnistsince 2010.But her relations with some senior editorial figures were said to be strained over a number of subjects she raised in her columns, particularly around immigration.Other managers did not welcome the attention she brought to the title when she was investigated by police in Essex in 2024 forallegedly stirring up racial hatredwith a social media post.The force was criticised by Pearson and her supporters when officers knocked on her door on Remembrance Sunday over a photograph she retweeted amid heightened tensions over the policing of Gaza protests. Pearson deleted the post andthe police investigation was dropped, but a review concluded the force was right to look into the allegations.When the Telegraph’s purchase was announced – ending three years of uncertainty over its future – Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer’s chief executive and controlling shareholder, said he planned to invest in the title as he wanted to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.The Telegraph will also focus on increasing its audience globally, “particularly in foreign affairs, defence and business”, according to an email to staff from the chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe added: “To deliver on this ambition, we need to change how we are organised, how decisions are made, where we focus our resources and create efficiencies. We need clearer accountability, faster decision-making and a simpler, more effective organisation.”View image in fullscreenMathias Döpfner, the CEO of Axel Springer SE, has said he wants the Telegraph to become the ‘leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world’.Photograph: Sebastian Gollnow/Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamySome staff at the Telegraph said that in the difficult period since the cuts were announced, the newsroom had felt like “a morgue”.Proposed changes include folding separate departments such as health and travel into one features department.A spokesperson for the Telegraph declined to comment, saying they could not discuss the employment status of individual staff members.Pearson has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsTelegraph Media GroupNational newspapersAxel SpringerNewspapers & magazinesNewspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain | Spain | The Guardian
description: Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives
Content: The small town of Urda, near where the crash occurred, was swiftly transformed into a frantic emergency response centre.Photograph: Andrea Comas/APView image in fullscreenThe small town of Urda, near where the crash occurred, was swiftly transformed into a frantic emergency response centre.Photograph: Andrea Comas/APSpain‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in SpainPassengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 livesAt least 68 killed in Toledo train crash – full reportSam Jonesin UrdaWed 28 Oct 2026 14.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”View image in fullscreenJosimar Medina and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, from Peru and Brazil respectively, were thrown across their carriage of the fast train from Madrid to Seville after it collided with another train on the track.Photograph: Sam Jones/The GuardianThe Peruvian stood recounting the details ofWednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south ofSpain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.View image in fullscreenA member of the Spanish Red Cross embraces a woman as they wait for news of passengers on the two high-speed trains that collided near Urda.Photograph: Susana Vera/ReutersFredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.“One guy was shouting: ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”View image in fullscreenFrederich and Arabella Barilea, originally from the Philippines but currently living in Dubai, were passengers on the Iryo train that the fast train from Madrid hit from behind.Photograph: Sam JonesAround the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending.
