Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second major rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of theAdamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.View image in fullscreenMedical staff converted a nearby sports centres into a temporary medical facility.Photograph: Andrea Comas/APBut, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly collisions that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With asnap general electionjust a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly and thoroughly as possible.For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.“Mejor no verlo,”she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.Explore more on these topicsSpainTrain crashesRail travelRail transportEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars glory | Movies | The Guardian
description: Oozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it up
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: Oozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it up
Content: Spanish civil war meets Grindr … singer Guitarricadelafuente makes his acting debut in La Bola Negra.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyView image in fullscreenSpanish civil war meets Grindr … singer Guitarricadelafuente makes his acting debut in La Bola Negra.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyMoviesInterview‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars gloryRyan GilbeyOozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it upWed 28 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – the directing duo known in their nativeSpainas “Los Javis” – began writing their queer epic La Bola Negra, they weren’t thinking about whether it would be stylish (which it is) or win numerous awards (which it has) or capture what they refer to as “the anti-fascist zeitgeist” (which it does). Instead, they thought only of scale. “I’m done with LGBTQ+ movies being niche,” says Ambrossi. “I was like, ‘Let’s make the biggest, gayest war movieever.’” Job done.At Cannes this year, the best director prize was awarded jointly to them and to Paweł Pawlikowski, who made the Thomas Mann road trip filmFatherland. La Bola Negra is now an Oscars frontrunner, with best picture and best director nominations all but guaranteed. Brimming with panache, the movie darts back and forth between three stories set in Spain: in 1932, a young man applying for membership of an exclusive casino is rejected on the grounds of his suspected homosexuality; in 1937, a callow nationalist soldier develops tender feelings for the injured republican prisoner under his watch; and in 2017, a queer historian inherits an unfinished story by Federico García Lorca. That story lends the movie its title and provides the thread that sews its strands together.double quotation markPeople are videoing themselves before watching it – then afterwards when they’re crying and huggingThrow in spectacular set pieces, Ken Russell-style visual flair, cameos from a blond-wiggedPenélope Cruzand a Spanish-speaking Glenn Close, and the result is a maximalist collage where the Spanish civil war sits side-by-side with Grindr hook-ups. “We loved imagining scenes that you don’t usually have in queer movies,” says Ambrossi, citing the spectacular opening sequence in which a Spanish village is bombed by Italian fascists. “A lot of people have said they’ve been missing something like this. They want to buy popcorn and be given a big movie like Titanic.” His eyes widen. “This is the gay Titanic!”View image in fullscreenBeating Scorsese … Penélope Cruz entertains the troops in the film.Photograph: Carla Oset/Netflix/AltitudeRelaxing at a corner table in the restaurant of a London hotel, Los Javis represent a study in contrasts. Ambrossi is 42, dinky and loquacious, his impish face crowned with a laurel of curls. He leans forward as he talks, arms folded on the white tablecloth. The taller, taciturn Calvo, 35, is gravely handsome. Battling jet lag, he repeatedly stretches his limbs like a cat, sneaking a glance at himself in the mirror next to the table as he does so. Both men have black caterpillar eyebrows, as well as cheekbones that could double as clothing rails.On this chilly autumn morning, Los Javis could do with some extra layers. They rub their bare arms furiously until an assistant arrives bearing hoodies. Then again, maybe the three of us have goosebumps not from the cold but from discussing their film. Ambrossi approves of this theory: “There’s a trend on TikTok where people video themselves – ‘This is usbeforewatching La Bola Negra’ – and then it cuts to afterwards when they’re crying and hugging. All this togetherness from the cinematic experience is beautiful.” No wonder Los Javis insisted on an extended theatrical window for their film before selling the US rights to Netflix. La Bola Negra will remain in US cinemas for 47 days, a record for the streaming platform. Even Scorsese didn’t get that.The movie also marks a personal breakthrough for the pair, who first met when they were actors. “Friends who read the script said to us, ‘Oh, you’re goingthere?’” recalls Ambrossi. “We’ve been writing together for 13 years about LGBTQ+ characters but it has always been, like, lesbians, trans women …” Previous collaborations include their 2017 debut film, Holy Camp!, which they adapted from La Llamada, their stage musical about a summer camp staffed by nuns. In one scene, God materialises to sing I Will Always Love You. Their 2023 series La Mesías (nowstreaming on Mubi) is a hypnotically bizarre tale of Christian pop stars, extraterrestrials and bad parenting. But no gay men.View image in fullscreen‘I was told to cut my hair, not paint my nails’ … Javier Ambrossi, Guitarricadelafuente and Javier Calvo on set.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWhat took them so long? “Sometimes you don’t want to talk about yourself,” offers Calvo, speaking up at last. “Many queer creators have projected themselves into other characters. Pedro Almodóvar, Lorca with The House of Bernarda Alba, Michael Patrick King with Sex and the City.” He flashes a rare smile. “Good show.”Ambrossi identifies a psychological dimension to the delay: “It’s true you don’t want to be too on-the-nose. But you start wondering if there is also another reason.” In the 1932 strand of the film, the elite casino members use a system of black and white balls to vote on admitting newcomers. The black ball for no–la bola negra– becomes a symbol of queer generational shame and rejection that must be wrestled with. Is it shame, then, that kept Ambrossi from addressing his own sexuality in his work? “In my case, yes. I wasn’t ready to talk about desire or sex because I felt ashamed in some way.”He and Calvo were already friends with their compatriot and hero Almodóvar, whose company El Deseo, meaning Desire, co-produced La Bola Negra. “I told Pedro, ‘I don’t deal well with desire.’ He looked at me and said, ‘You need to start.’ That’s when it clicked: if you don’t deal explicitly with desire, you are missing life.”View image in fullscreenLorca scholar … Glenn Close and Carlos González discuss the great Spanish writer.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyPerhaps that is why the word “explicit” crops up several times in Ambrossi’s conversation today: having been out as a gay man but under the radar in his work, he is eager now to emphasise the ways in which La Bola Negra is defiant or unequivocal. One aspect is the casting of gay actors in gay roles, most notably the Bambi-eyed singer Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his screen debut as the lovestruck soldier.“It’s not that straight actors can’t play gay,” says Calvo. “There are no rules in art. But …” Ambrossi jumps in: “We like to do it this way. When I was 10, I watched Rupert Everett in My Best Friend’s Wedding. I wasn’t sure I was gay, but I knew he was like me. There was a truth in his eyes that I want to get in my movies.” He sighs. “Rupert Everett was so brave. He should have been James Bond.”La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people’s choice awardRead moreCalvo had an unhappy experience as a young gay actor. “I was a teenager playing a gay role on TV,” he says. “When it finished, I didn’t get many auditions. I was advised to cut my hair, not paint my nails.” A short back and sides didn’t help, though. “I guess people could still tell. So I decided to write roles for actors who don’t have space in the industry.”Once the pair began dating as well as working together, the two-headed queer celebrity phenomenon of Los Javis was born. They were playwrights, film-makers, actors and reality TV participants, including regular judges on the Spanish version of Ru Paul’s Drag Race. Being an indispensable part of Spanish cultural life came at a price. Calvo points to this now as one of the reasons he and Ambrossi separated during the making of La Bola Negra. “People would talk to me in the plural all the time, ‘It was nice to meet you guys.’ I’d be like, ‘Huh? I’m standing alone here.’ I felt I’d lost my individuality.”View image in fullscreenMeet the judges … Ambrossi and Calvo (far right) in Drag Race España All Stars, 2024.Photograph: AtresplayerSpain didn’t cope well with the breakup. “It was a big deal,” Calvo admits. “There were cameras outside my door for a month.” Keen to move on, Ambrossi displays a flicker of irritation: “I think we’ve passed through this conversation. Imagine everyone talking about your ex forever! We love to write and direct together and we’re going to keep doing that.” The matter is closed.After all the diversifying and cross-platforming, Los Javis have reached their Pokémon-style final evolution. “From now on, we want to focus on movies,” says Calvo. No regrets, though. “The other things were important in making a statement,” Ambrossi points out. “I grew up thinking directors should be serious and monolithic. We represented a new way.” Calvo lifts a finger: “A non-binary way,” he says. “We don’t see life as stiff. We mix genres. A more flexible time is coming. Take the work seriously but not yourself.”La Bola Negra review – the complicated secrets of gay sexuality in Spain are brilliantly toldRead moreBefore they go, there is a line in La Bola Negra that I ask them to unpack. When the modern-day researcher Alberto asks the Lorca scholar played byGlenn Closefor advice on what he should do with the pages of that incomplete story, she tells him: “You’ve inherited something and you don’t know what to do with it. You are truly a Spaniard.”Calvo is happy to help. “In Spain, we always have to be reminded by foreigners that we have a rich, interesting culture and history,” he says. Ambrossi elaborates: “It is as if pride is shameful. When someone is doing well and winning awards all over Spain, people are like, ‘Hmm. That’s not very Spanish.’ Unless it’s football.” Where does that attitude come from? “Maybe religion,” muses Calvo. “Maybe dictatorship.”Does it apply to them? Are they destined to underplay their triumphs for ever? They offer their best you’ve-got-to-be-kidding looks, then answer in unison: “Not us.”La Bola Negra is in UK cinemas from 6 November.Explore more on these topicsFilmPeriod and historical filmsPenélope CruzGlenn CloseFederico García LorcaSexualityLGBTQ+ rightsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice review – a family’s astonishing bravery helped make history | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: When Robert McCartney was killed in a bar brawl involving members of the Provisional IRA in Belfast in 2005, his five sisters refused to be intimidated. They took their story to the White House and it accelerated the peace process
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: When Robert McCartney was killed in a bar brawl involving members of the Provisional IRA in Belfast in 2005, his five sisters refused to be intimidated. They took their story to the White House and it accelerated the peace process
Content: Inspiring … Robert McCartney’s sister Paula in Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenInspiring … Robert McCartney’s sister Paula in Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice.Photograph: BBCTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewMurder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice review – a family’s astonishing bravery helped make historyWhen Robert McCartney was killed in a bar brawl involving members of the Provisional IRA in Belfast in 2005, his five sisters refused to be intimidated. They took their story to the White House and it accelerated the peace processLucy ManganWed 28 Oct 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe documentary Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice, about the McCartney siblings’ fight to bring their brother’s killers to justice, makes you wonder. As it outlines the five women’s ceaseless, fearless actions over the last 20 years, you can’t help but ask: when did the IRA and Sinn Féin realise they had picked on the wrong family to cross?Robert McCartney, a Catholic father of two, was 33 when he was killed in 2005. He was trying to extricate his friend Brendan Devine from a brawl involving members of the local Provisional IRA at Magennis’s bar in the nationalist Short Strand area of Belfast, where the McCartney family had lived for five generations. Devine was seriously injured. Robert was stabbed, brutally beaten and had an eye gouged out. “I’m not going to make it,” he told Devine as they tried to escape the alleyway in which they had been attacked. “Our Gerard needs me. I have to go.” (Gerard McCartney was Robert’s brother, who had killed himself a few years earlier after struggling with mental illness.)Soon after uttering those words, Robert died in hospital. “Utter disbelief,” says Gemma, the eldest of the sisters, as she remembers realising that she would have to tell their parents another son was gone. “The two most tragic ways to die – and we’ve got both?”There were about 70 people in Magennis’s that night and – thanks to a campaign of intimidation by the IRA – no witnesses. Apparently, they had all been in the toilet at the time. Instead, the bar was cleared of all forensic evidence – glass swept up, bloodstains bleached, CCTV tapes removed – and a wall of silence erected. “Like a bloody cult,” says Donna, one of Robert’s sisters. Everyone knew what had happened – “the dogs in the street knew who was involved”, as Bertie Ahern, Ireland’s prime minister at the time, puts it – and names were gathered by the family, but without physical evidence or witnesses nothing could be done.The first hour of this three-part series concentrates largely on the impact on Robert’s family – sisters Gemma, Paula, Donna, Catherine and Claire, and his cousin Gerard Quinn all appear – and friends, including Devine. The remaining two episodes chart the sisters’ refusal to give in to the IRA’s wishes, the Police Service of Northern Ireland’s frustrated investigations as Sinn Féin refused to allow its members to confess to involvement or come forward as witnesses to the police (such is the tentacular reach and power of the party in a place where religion, politics and history are so enmeshed). We see what the family’s astonishing determination and bravery eventuallymeant for the peace process in Northern Ireland.View image in fullscreen‘I was too angry to be afraid of the IRA’ … Catherine McCartney.Photograph: BBCA few weeks after the murder, Sinn Féin invited the sisters to its annual conference. The sisters knew it was in the hope of placating them (“It’s like being lovebombed,” says Claire. “Meant to get swept away, aren’t you?”) and of getting a propaganda coup from appearing to have their support as its leader Gerry Adams paid lip service to the idea of witnesses coming forward. What the party got instead was a televised shot of the sisters lined up in the front row refusing to join in the applause that greeted his speech.The usual playbook wasn’t working. Just as the sisters refused to be intimidated, they also refused to be charmed. They stepped up the publicity. “I was too angry to be afraid of the IRA,” says Catherine. “I still am.” A few months after the murder,they went to the US to meet PresidentGeorge Bush and senators including Hillary Clinton and Ted Kennedy, while Adams was refused an invitation to the White House. It was a signal to the party that the US required them to start doing more to move towards genuine conciliation and power-sharing with the British government.On and on through the years it went, with the IRA and Sinn Féin gradually having to cede enough ground to enable a court case to be brought against three men in 2008, although it fell apart due to the continuing flimsiness of the physical evidence and flawed witness testimony.The sisters still look shattered by their ordeal. They are clearly mired in many kinds of grief – for their brother, for the homes they had to move out of after the killing, for the community they had once believed in unquestioningly – although they say they still gain comfort from the memory of the vigils held and the rallies attended following Robert’s death.The McCartney sisters are inspiring, but Murder in Belfast is not a heartening story. It is a reminder of the undemocratic, unaccountable powers still at work across the Irish Sea and how long the evil that men do – British, Irish, Protestant, Catholic – lives after them.Murder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice is on BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionDocumentaryNorthern IrelandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bone of contention: why dog trainers are at war | Dogs | The Guardian
description: It’s the canine equivalent of gentle v tough parenting – and there is no sign of a ceasefire. So what is the correct way to get man’s best friend to behave?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It’s the canine equivalent of gentle v tough parenting – and there is no sign of a ceasefire. So what is the correct way to get man’s best friend to behave?
Content: In-person dog training can cost £150 an hour.Photograph: Chalabala/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenIn-person dog training can cost £150 an hour.Photograph: Chalabala/Getty Images/iStockphotoPass notesDogsBone of contention: why dog trainers are at warIt’s the canine equivalent of gentle v tough parenting – and there is no sign of a ceasefire. So what is the correct way to get man’s best friend to behave?Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Dog training wars.Age:Puppy to 14 months, and beyond.Appearance:Aggressive.Is this about dogs fighting?No, it’s the trainers who are fighting.What are they fighting about?There are two camps: “positive” trainers, and “balanced” trainers. The former rely on rewards, the latter on a range of disciplinary stimuli, which might extend to prong collars that dig into a dog’s neck when it pulls.What do the balanced ones say about the positive ones?“It’s all treats, treats, treats, so help me God,” the dog trainer Brian Lee told the Wall Street Journal. “It’s no different than giving your kid a BMW on his 16th birthday.”And how do positive trainers address these allegations?“I kind of laugh at this whole idea that using treats in training is somehow going to spoil dogs,” says another dog trainer Victoria Stilwell.I don’t see this getting resolved any time soon.Rewarding dogs with too many treats is “the biggest problem with dog training at the moment,” says the animal behaviourist Dr Ian Dunbar, despite standing in the positive camp.If I’m honest this war of words doesn’t sound that heated.But it’s getting worse thanks to social media.To be fair, everything is getting worse thanks to social media.Positive trainers call balanced trainers cruel; balanced trainers call positive trainers “treat-slinging wieners”.Is this the dog version of the“gentle parenting” vFafoparenting debate fromearlier this year?It’s similar, but I don’t think anybody was recommending prong collars in that instance.Is treat-slinging v discipline the only issue?There’s also a parallel war about the virtues of online training versus in-person training.Which is best?Some say in-person is the only way. “You can’t resolve temperament issues over the phone,” Dunbartold the Timesrecently. “It’s insane.”I seeDunbar has more than one dog in this fight.But Siobhan Dunn, who runs online courses, disagrees. “We’re working with owners all over the UK, many of whom would never have been able to reach us in person,” she says.I’m confused – who’s right?It may help you to know that in-person training can cost £150 an hour.Any signs of a ceasefire in the training wars?Lee has already called for calm on Instagram. “The criticising culture has been exhausted,” he wrote. “It’s time to put down the ‘dog training approach’ pitchforks.”Did people respond positively to his message of calm?Not so far. “There is literally NOTHING in your bio that tells me you actually have an education in canine behaviour,” wrote another trainer.Do say:“Dog rewards don’t have to be food-based – what about a trip to the theatre?”Don’t say:“DOWN BOY.”Explore more on these topicsDogsPass notesPetsAnimalsSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I am mother, leader, warrior of the Amazon’: Nemonte Nenquimo on why the west needs to be rescued  | Indigenous peoples | The Guardian
description: The Waorani leader says millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights into the consumerist west
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Waorani leader says millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights into the consumerist west
Content: Nemonte Nenquimo, from the Amazonian region of Ecuador, takes part in the Restore Nature Now protest in London on 22 June 2024.Photograph: Benjamin Cremel/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNemonte Nenquimo, from the Amazonian region of Ecuador, takes part in the Restore Nature Now protest in London on 22 June 2024.Photograph: Benjamin Cremel/AFP/Getty ImagesSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanIndigenous peoples‘I am mother, leader, warrior of the Amazon’: Nemonte Nenquimo on why the west needs to be rescuedThe Waorani leader says millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights into the consumerist westSupported byAbout this contentOliver BalchWed 28 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery Waorani child knows the story of the boa’s mouth. How the snake inches forward, watching, its movements almost imperceptible, before it strikes, swallowing its victim whole.Nemonte Nenquimo knows the boa’s bite. Beguiled as a young girl by the blue eyes and bright dresses of an American missionary child in her Amazon village inEcuador, she consented to be baptised and left home to study at a church school.“My grandfather used to tell me that the global system of money and material things is like the boa. It attracts people, it bewitches,” the 41-year-old Indigenous activist says. “It’s a fact, I’ve lived it.”The Nenquimo of today has travelled far from her teenage self. Feted by Time magazine as one of theworld’s 100 most influential people, this vocal activist for Indigenous rights proudly identifies as a “mother, leader, and warrior of the Amazon”.View image in fullscreenNemonte Nenquimo leading a successful legal action against oil extraction in the Amazon rainforest.Photograph: Sophie Pinchetti/The Goldman Environmental Prize 2020Dressed in ceremonial dress, her eyes masked behind an achiote-seed red dye and with a sacred palm-fibre band around her head, she was in Europe in September to collect the €1mGulbenkian prize for humanity.The prize recognises her leadership of theCeibo Alliance, a coalition of four forest peoples spanning Ecuador, Peru and Colombia that she helped co-found back in 2014 and that fights to defend Amazonian lands and cultures.Born into a Waorani community in the southern Ecuadorian Amazon, Nenquimo first grabbed international headlines when she issuedan open letter to global leadersin which, among other stinging truths, she denounced the “white man that knows too little for the power that he wields”.The viral letter was prompted by the Covid-19 pandemic, which claimed the lives of thousands of forest peoples across the Amazon, including that of theprominent Kayapó chief Paulinho Paiakan.“The outside world comes with beautiful words, ‘We save, we bring a project of salvation’, [but] you’re not saving; you’re really killing my people, my ancestors, my territory,” she says.Through the Ceibo Alliance, Nenquimo has done much to resist the outside world’s encroachment. The “pillaging” of the Amazon rainforest, a magnet for loggers, oil companies, cattle ranchers and goldminers over recent decades. Years ago, she spearheaded a successful legal case against theEcuadorian government’s decisionto license a 202,000-hectare (500,000-acre) plot of Waorani historic lands for oil exploration.View image in fullscreenNenquimo co-founded the Ceibo Alliance in 2014 to protect the AmazonPhotograph: Mitch Anderson/The Goldman Environmental Prize 2020Other tactics deployed by the alliance includean “Indigenous guard” system, where volunteer patrols use drones, camera traps and other monitoring equipment to track illegal incursions into their land.But opposition is fierce. Last year, followinga nationwide protestorganised by Ecuador’s main Indigenous group (Conaie), the Ceibo Alliance had itsbank accounts frozenwithout warning.Violence from drug gangs and illegal miners is also spilling over into Indigenous territories, Nenquimo warns. In neighbouring Colombia, for example – which includes territories of two of the Alliance’s people groups, the A’i Cofán and Siona –39 land activistswere murdered last year, almost one-third of all such killings globally.Her fight extends beyond land protection. The incursion ofcowori(the Waorani word for “white man”) is also undermining the rich linguistic, cultural and spiritual traditions of the forest peoples, she argues.“Through their ‘salvation’, they make us disconnect from our own connection with the plants, with the spirit of the jaguar, with healing,” she says. “The Waorani people have even begun to stop taking ayahuasca, which is a sacred medicine for all Amazonian peoples.”Yet, Nenquimo vehemently rejects any narrative of victimhood. She says that it’s the west that really needs rescuing. Moreover, the rainforest defender believes people groups like hers have answers to hand.First, the west has an imperative to reconnect with Mother Earth. The forest, as Nenquimo is fond of saying, is her community’s “market, pharmacy, hardware store and place of worship”. To destroy it, therefore, is to jeopardise their survival.“We are not destroyers. We do not pollute the river. Gold is what we have to leave. Petroleum is the blood of our ancestors,” she says. “The water you drink, the air you breathe – asIndigenous peoples, we are protecting it.”View image in fullscreenNenquimo with her grandmother beside the Puyo river in the Omaere ethnobotanical park in Ecuador.Photograph: Virginie Clavieres/Paris Match/Getty ImagesConnecting with nature extends to connecting with those who inhabit and guard it, she adds. Millennia of living in harmony with their surroundings give Indigenous groups unique insights that the consumerist west would gain by rediscovering them. Hence her antipathy to international charities and other well-meaning groups that impose sustainability solutions born of their own market mentality, such as carbon credit schemes and “sustainable” commercial agriculture.In her recent memoir,We Will Not Be Saved, Nenquimo goes further, arguing that “connectedness involves responsibilities”; not least for those in industrial economies to beware the boa and question their pursuit of relentless economic growth.Learning to overcome the barriers that divide us is also critical, she maintains. As a union of distinct peoples with a history of inter-tribal conflict, the Ceibo Alliance demonstrates in microcosm what is possible when old enmities are left behind.That journey begins with empathy, she says. In her memoir, she recalls realising that for the judges in her landmark court case to “truly see” her, she must also see them: “Not as enemies … not as caricatures of conquest but rather as people.”View image in fullscreen‘When we die, we will go with a peaceful spirit’: Nenquimo in Nemompare village on the banks of the Curaray river, Ecuador.Photograph: Rodrigo Buendía/AFP/Getty ImagesLast, and arguably hardest, is finding the humility to genuinely listen and the strength to truly love. This Waorani leader has every reason to hate the cowori: under their hand, disease, pollution, deforestation and, in her own lived experience, sexual abuse have been inflicted upon her people.If the world’s “developed” countries are to be saved – from the desire to take, to own, to control – then acknowledging that the planet’s last remaining “primitive” peoples might have something valuable to impart merits consideration, she suggests.“If you don’t have a mind or heart to love, then what’s the point? It’s just being angry, wanting to devour, wanting to accumulate,” she says. “When we die, we will go with a light, peaceful spirit. We won’t have to suffer in our spirit.”Explore more on these topicsIndigenous peoplesSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanEcuadorAmazon rainforestConservation and indigenous peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory’: how did the restaurant end up in a Maga fight over ‘elitism’? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Obama has been accused of ‘snobbery’ over his Trump diss, as people rush to defend the restaurant chain’s ‘affordable opulence’
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: Obama has been accused of ‘snobbery’ over his Trump diss, as people rush to defend the restaurant chain’s ‘affordable opulence’
Content: The Cheesecake Factory signage at a restaurant in Denver, Colorado.Photograph: Matthew Staver/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Cheesecake Factory signage at a restaurant in Denver, Colorado.Photograph: Matthew Staver/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesLife and style‘Like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory’: how did the restaurant end up in a Maga fight over ‘elitism’?Obama has been accused of ‘snobbery’ over his Trump diss, as people rush to defend the restaurant chain’s ‘affordable opulence’Matthew Cantorin Los AngelesWed 28 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAround lunchtime on Tuesday, a Rolls-Royce stopped at the intersection of Beverly Drive and Dayton Way in Beverly Hills, California. Local people in athleisure walked past Balenciaga, Dior and Prada boutiques, as visitors on Hollywood bus tours ogled nearby Rodeo Drive, where Burberry and Louis Vuitton shops meet at a celebrated street corner.Up the street, across from the upmarket Erewhon grocery store – home to $21 smoothies – a few diners sat outside an American landmark: the Cheesecake Factory.The beloved restaurant chain began here in Beverly Hills in 1978; now it has hundreds of locations across the US and Canada. And this week, it’s become the US’s latest surreal culture-war touchstone.It started when Barack Obama, campaigning for Democrats in Ohio, made a joke that hitDonald Trumpright in the real estate. Referring to his successor’s remodeling obsession, the former president said: “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”The joke was about maximalism: Saddam had100 palacesand loved gold plating, and the Cheesecake Factory, while affordable for many, offers swanky surroundings that a curmudgeon might describe as over the top. While the Beverly Hills restaurant has a fairly staid interior, a nearby location at Los Angeles’s Grove mall has a grand staircase, floral paintings on the ceilings and an ornate balcony.Obama’s comments got a laugh at the rally – which surely contained many Cheesecake Factory customers – and went viral. It’s likely the former president knew he would touch a nerve, given Trump’s twin fixations on remodeling and on Obama himself.Then the backlash began.View image in fullscreenBarack Obama speaks during a campaign rally in Cleveland, Ohio, for Democratic Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown on Saturday.Photograph: Sue Ogrocki/APAsked by a reporter whether he had a response to Obama, “who made fun of the Cheesecake Factory, comparing it to the White House”, Trump spentnearly two full minutesexplaining that the work had been done by the “finest artisans”, that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” – a racist trope – and that Trump himself only spends “five minutes a day, 10 minutes a day” addressing the problem. (Later that day, he spent another 10 minutes talking about it.)But the framing of the question – posed by a reporter for LindellTV, founded by the Trump-supporting My Pillow founder Mike Lindell – pointed to what has become a rightwing talking point: the out-of-touch Obama, these critics claim, was mocking restaurant for regular people. The Cheesecake Factory isn’t cheap – a burger will run you about $20 – but it’s positioned as a treat that won’t break the bank.The conservative political strategist Corinne Clark Barrontweeted: “KEEP THE CHEESECAKE FACTORY OUT OF YOUR ELITIST MOUTH.”On CNN, the New York Post columnist Lydia Moynihan said the remarks showed “how elitist he and the party that he continues to lead has become”. On Fox News,a chyron announced: “Obama criticized for Cheesecake Factory ‘snobbery’.”This seems to deliberately misconstrue the joke’s primary target, which was the president, not the restaurant. It also conveniently forgets the first half, about Saddam Hussein, who was not known for minimalist taste. Nevertheless, the pitchforks were out, and the Trump administration deployed a true man of the people – the treasury secretary and hedge fund founder Scott Bessent – to dine there.In fact, he “always” does, as he wasat great pains to point out. “I had a great meal, always have a great meal,” he told a Fox Business reporter. He ordered “what I always have: the French Dip Cheeseburger”. Bessent, whose net worth isroughly $600m, said he would “tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try”.View image in fullscreenSaddam Hussein’s palace on 13 April 2003.Photograph: Alain Buu/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesThe median home price in Beverly Hills, home to the first Cheesecake Factory, is $4m; the restaurant itself is far more affordable than the 90210 zip code might suggest. But as Bessent himself proved, the restaurant’s clientele includes plenty of elites:Jennifer Lawrence, Miley Cyrus and Drakeare all reportedly fans. It’s a stretch to suggest Obama was punching down here.That said, given the fierce devotion the restaurant inspires, Obama was perhaps taking a risk even mentioning it – especially at a time when the cost of living is on the ballot. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that soundbite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” Rick McCormack, who helped create the restaurant’s decor, told CNN’s David Mack. Odes to the restaurant and its “affordable opulence”, as Mack puts it, abound.Inthe Atlantic, Elaine Godfrey praises its “sumptuousness: the orange, inviting glow from the knobbly chandeliers; the floral frescoes and painted columns; the generous fountain pops and the dense wedges of cake”.A Redditorputs it more simply: “I can eat the whole plate of food like a savage and waddle to my car afterward with a piece of cheesecake to go.” The food is indeed good, and plentiful: the chain is known for its enormous and diverse menu, with items ranging from fried mac and cheese to avocado egg rolls to vegan cobb salad. There’s also, of course, lots of cheesecake, including but not limited to the mind-boggling Oreo Dream Extreme. On Tuesday, the chainreported third-quarter revenueof $1.03bn, up from $907.2m a year before. It’sroutinely namedamong Fortune’s 100 best companies to work for.In short, everyone loves the Cheesecake Factory, from Birmingham, Alabama, to Des Moines, Iowa, to Beverly Hills, where the autumn sun shone this week over warm baskets of complimentary bread. Surely it can take a joke.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleRestaurantsFoodBarack ObamaDonald TrumpUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best LED face masks in the UK, tested: 12 light therapy devices that are worth the hype | Skincare | The Guardian
description: They claim to reduce fine lines, blemishes and redness – but which stand up to scrutiny? After consulting dermatologists and putting them to the test, we have crowned a brand new number one
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: They claim to reduce fine lines, blemishes and redness – but which stand up to scrutiny? After consulting dermatologists and putting them to the test, we have crowned a brand new number one
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSkincareReviewThe best LED face masks in the UK, tested: 12 light therapy devices that are worth the hypeThey claim to reduce fine lines, blemishes and redness – but which stand up to scrutiny? After consulting dermatologists and putting them to the test, we have crowned a brand new number oneThe best anti-ageing creams, serums and treatmentsSarah MatthewsUpdatedWed 28 Oct 202611.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLED face masks are booming in popularity – despite being one of the most expensive at-home beauty products to hit the market. They claim to reduce the appearance of fine lines, stop spots and calm redness, with some even combining different types of light to enhance the benefits.However, it’s wise to be sceptical about new treatments that are costly and non-invasive, and to do your research before you buy. With this in mind, I interviewed doctors and dermatologists to find out whether these light therapy devices work.They’re not a miracle cure for deep-set wrinkles, but experts say the best light therapy masks can promote collagen production, improve elasticity and help smooth skin with sustained use. And while it may seem like a new technology,research from the 1990sshows the efficacy of light therapy in wound healing, acne treatment and skin rejuvenation.Red and infrared light are safe to use on all skin types, but be warned that blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones.I’ve tested some of the most popular devices on the market – including infrared masks – to narrow down my favourite LED face masks for treating a range of skin concerns.At a glanceBest LED mask overallCurrentBodySeries 3£499.99 at CurrentBodyBest budget LED face maskSilk’nLED face mask 100£99.99 at LookfantasticBest LED mask for full facial coverageTherabodyTheraFace mask Glo£299 at Space NKBest LED device for acne-prone skinLustreSolo£60 at LustreBest LED mask for quick treatmentsDr Dennis GrossSpectraLite FaceWare Pro£465 at Space NKBest LED mask for travelSilk’nLED face mask Pro£259 at LookfantasticWhy you should trust meI’ve been reviewing health and beauty tech for the past five years. During this time I’ve witnessed many beauty fads come and go. Naturally tight-fisted and a sceptic, I was initially struck by the cost of these masks. How on earth can an elaborate LED light strip set you back more than £300?But after testing multiple light therapy masks, I’ve come to understand the technology behind them – and, sadly, you won’t be able to engineer your own light therapy system with a costume mask and a set of LED string lights.I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles to test on, but I can comment on how blue-light treatment affects acne because I’ve suffered from it since I was a teenager – despite my mum’s assurances that it would clear up after puberty. The experts I spoke to agreed on the efficacy of red and infrared light for anti-ageing.Are LED face masks worth it?Light therapy masks are fantastic additions to a skincare routine, helping to smooth, firm and reduce blemishes. Since I started using one almost two years ago, my skin is calmer, less prone to redness, and has a more even tone.However, LED masks can be expensive, and if you’re not disciplined enough to use one regularly, you won’t see results. You could also incorporate targeted skincare serums, such asretinolandvitamin C, to help firm and brighten the skin without the need for an expensive light therapy mask.How I testedView image in fullscreen‘I tested the fit, comfort levels and usability of 18 of the most popular light therapy masks.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianSince LED treatments take a while to show visible results, it’s difficult to test multiple light therapy masks at once (at least, without spending a few years testing them), so I enlisted the help of dermatologists who were familiar with light therapy treatments long before they were commercially available.I spoke to Dr Barbara Kubicka, an expert in aesthetic medicine; Dr Derrick Phillips, a consultant dermatologist and spokesperson for the British Skin Foundation; and aesthetic doctor Dr Priya Verma, an authority on the science of skin ageing.I asked these experts to identify which light therapy mask features – such as bulb quality and quantity, light wavelength and treatment time – matter the most, to inform my choices. Believe me, I wanted this mask to be a winner, but its solid plastic structure, with no eye shielding or padding, made it so wildly uncomfortable to wear that it was an almost instant write-off. The straps are another problem; they come together around the bottom part of your head, causing the mask to constantly fall. It also seems built for very small faces, so it constantly slipped down my face, pinching my nose and making it difficult to breathe properly – even if I used it without the straps and lay flat during treatment. Throw in fewer LED bulbs than average and dim lights, and this mask is impossible to recommend.A high price tag doesn’t guarantee how good the mask is either, as evidenced by theForeo FAQ 202 LED mask, £719 at full price. Its light weight and comfort level, along with an array of treatment options via its app-based controls, meant it impressed initially. However, its silicone design felt incredibly flimsy, and after a week of use, it had already started peeling away from the central battery pack.This might be forgivable if Foreo offered a full warranty and repair service. There’s atwo-year warrantycovering defects and faulty workmanship, but this does not cover “cosmetic deterioration caused by fair wear and tear, or damage caused by accident, misuse or neglect”. To access accidental damage coverage, you have to pay Foreo’s £9.99/month subscription. Even if you’re happy to risk it, at the time of testing in June 2026, you still had to shell out £4.99/month to access the mask’s full suite of preset treatments. Add to this the scale of advertising you’re bombarded with in the app – some of it unskippable. When you consider its price, this brazen money-grubbing leaves a very bad taste.Through testing this family of devices, I had also been hoping to find an undereye brightening LED patch to usurp the Peep Club wand, which requires constant movement across the eye area. I had hoped that theLustre GoGlowbrightening and de-puffing patches would fit the bill. They come in a handy headphone-like charging case and have a clever wireless design. However, when positioned under the eyes as advertised, the light was incredibly bright, which made it tricky to see. The sticky pads, although small, were uncomfortable to remove, and my skin was left feeling irritated for a day afterwards. The search for the perfect undereye LED patch continues …What you need to knowView image in fullscreenRed light is just one of several LED wavelengths used to target different skin concerns.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianWhat is LED therapy, and how does it work?“LED (light-emitting diode) therapy is a non-invasive treatment that uses specific wavelengths of light to stimulate various cellular processes in the skin,” says aesthetic medicine expert Kubicka. “Depending on the colour or wavelength, LED light can target inflammation, promote collagen production, accelerate healing and even kill bacteria.”Light therapy is a great addition to your skincare routine – for me, it’s helped reduce breakouts, improve healing and reduce the appearance of my acne scars. LED face masks are quick, gentle and non-invasive, and suitable for most skin types (although as mentioned above, blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones, according to the experts I spoke with). The masks are effective and foolproof to use, and the daily treatments also force you to take a little time for yourself – perfect for a morning pick-me-up or an evening wind-down.Does red light help with anti-ageing?“Red-light therapy can reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles through a process called photobiomodulation,” says consultant dermatologist Phillips. “It energises mitochondria, which are the batteries of the cells, powering the production of collagen and elastin by fibroblasts, the factories of the skin.”Elastin and collagen are “the building blocks of firm, youthful skin”, says Kubicka. Stimulating the production of these molecules can “improve skin density, elasticity and overall smoothness” as long as you complete treatments regularly.I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles, but I’m keen to avoid more by using red-light therapy for “preventive ageing”. However, “most of the clinical evidencefocuses on treating visible signs of ageing or repairing damaged skin, rather than long-term prevention in younger skin”, as aesthetic doctor Verma explains.Still, Verma reassured me my efforts wouldn’t be in vain. “Using LED light consistently and appropriately may help support overall skin health […] especially when combined with sun protection and a good skincare routine.”For more, readdo you really need an LED face mask?What different colours of light therapy are available?Several colours are available, with each wavelength said to target a different skin concern. These colours correlate to the visible light spectrum, and each can have a different effect on the skin.Red light has a wavelength of between 630 and 700nm and is the most widely known form of light therapy, loved for its non-invasive potential anti-ageing benefits. Near-infrared light above 700nm “penetrates the skin more deeply to support tissue repair and reduce inflammation”, according to Kubicka. Blue-light therapy (415nm), on the other hand, has been proven to target acne-causing bacteria, leading to a reduction in breakouts over time. Kubicka also says blue light can help regulate oil production – another common problem for those with acne.The effects of some types of light on the skin are better researched than others.Near-infrared,red lightandblue lightare backed by scientific studies that identify the biological processes that each type of light triggers in the body.Meanwhile, research into green and yellow light is more limited. One study questions theefficacy of yellow-lighttherapy and claims that a previous study may have been influenced by the placebo effect. Similarly, a study ongreen light therapysuggests that more research is needed to provide a solid recommendation for use as an anti-ageing treatment.How and when would you recommend using light therapy?The “how” is simple: always use light therapy masks on freshly washed, dry skin, before applying serums and creams. This will give the light the most direct access to the skin.Despite what some instruction manuals advise, don’t jump into daily treatments straight away – you may end up with slightly irritated skin. Start by introducing treatments two to three times a week, and monitoring the impact on your skin. If you don’t notice any sensitivity, you can incorporate more treatments, if permitted by the manufacturer’s guidelines.Once your skin is used to the treatment, “home devices should be used three to five times a week, for 10-20 minutes a session,” says Phillips. But treatment times vary between devices, so always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, and don’t expect instant results. If you’re hoping to reduce breakouts, you should “see a reduction in redness and the frequency of acne breakouts within two to four weeks”. Those using red light for anti-ageing benefits will need to wait a little longer: “It typically takes six to eight weeks to see visible changes.”Is light therapy safe for all skin tones?“LED light therapy is generally very safe when used correctly,” says Verma. This is because, unlike laser hair removal, it only uses low-level, non-thermal light. “The most common side effects are mild and temporary, such as slight redness, dryness or irritation.”“People with known photosensitive disorders or taking medications that make them more sensitive to light (eg certain antibiotics) should consult their doctor,” says Phillips. He also warns that those with darker skin tones should exercise caution when using blue light, since “some blue wavelengths have been associated with hyperpigmentation”. The Lustre Solo patches recommended above offer exclusively blue light, but the other masks in this roundup have blue-light-free settings if you do find that it causes sensitivity.How much should I spend on an LED therapy mask?There are hundreds of light therapy masks available at different prices, but the quality varies wildly. You may see results from a budget-friendly mask, such as theSilk’n LED face mask 100reviewed above, but spending more will generally get you a larger quantity of bulbs that offer a greater range of wavelengths. You’re also more likely to get a mask with a better fit and coverage.The best mask for you will depend on your skin concerns and budget. Those hoping to invest in a mask with anti-acne properties will be able to spend less, since blue light is more widely available, but if you’re looking for the best anti-ageing deep near-infrared light therapy, you will need to part with more cash.High-end red-light therapy masks can cost upwards of £500; if you spend that much, just make sure you use it regularly, or you won’t see results.How to clean an LED face maskCleaning instructions for LED masks will differ slightly from brand to brand, based on the different materials used. As a general rule, you want to steer clear of using chemical or alcohol-based cleansers since these can damage a mask’s delicate silicone and padded components. Always check the instructions for your specific mask before jumping into cleaning.The usual best practice is to use a non-abrasive cloth, such asmicrofibre, dampened with water to wipe down your mask after every use. Try not to use too much water and never submerge the mask, as doing so will damage the electrical components. Always make sure your mask is unplugged and switched off before cleaning, and wait for the mask to dry completely before storing, charging or switching it on.For more:The best concealers for camouflaging blemishesThe best retinol and retinal serums for smoother, firmer skinThe best eye creams for banishing bags, puffiness and fine linesShark FacialPro Glow + DePuffi reviewSarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, andcan sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’sdisciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)This article was originally published on 19 September 2025. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. title: Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget | Aditya Chakrabortty | The Guardian
description: The financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent moment, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Author: Aditya Chakrabortty
Headline: The financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent moment, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionBudget 2026Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budgetAditya ChakraborttyThe financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent momentWed 28 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.50 EDTShareWas this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of neoliberalism”? Fat chance. Was it John Healey’s budget – the repair job of a cautious chancellor fretting about record-high taxes, £3tn of public debt and an economy stuck in first gear? Little sign of that.This budget was cast in the image of a man who isn’t in Burnham’s government or even a Labour politician – but who appears almost every day on TV, on podcasts and is probably better known than 649 of the MPs at Westminster. Today’s budget was theMartin Lewisbudget.Lewis is theMoneySavingExpert, whose weekly Money Tipsemail advises 10 million British subscribers on cheap mortgages, Black Friday deals and how to score two pizzas for £10. Tips and tricks to stave off rising prices and make the most of the money you have. Given that the Bayeux tapestry is French, and the Koh-i-noor is Indian, Lewis may be the closest thing Britain has to a genuine national treasure.Over the past four years, since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine and sent energy prices soaring, Lewis has become more political and wielded greater influence in Westminster. His fingerprints were all over this “red book”. This morning, before the cabinet had even had its traditional pre-budget pep talk, Lewis had gone to Downing Street for a personal briefing from the chancellor on its key measures. On Radio 4’s Today programme, he was the big budget interview, rather than any politician or BBC editor.No wonder, because the most eye-catching of thebudget’s measureshad been written by the money saving expert. Scrapping standing charges on gas bills, shielding more pensioners from income tax and fixing energy bill credit against council tax bands – all of these came from Lewis’s wishlist. Beyond policies, he has also informed Burnham’s politics. At last year’s Labour conference, Lewisadvised any new prime ministerto “pick a hundred things that piss people off and fix them at one a day for the first hundred days”.Et voilà! The King of the North has vowed to end loudcasting on public transport, crack down on unfair parking fines and introducemore drop boxesfor the post … and more and more.ForLabourministers, government by MoneySavingExpert may seem a no-brainer. After a wretched couple of years under Keir Starmer, they can pose as the people’s champion, for ever on your side. Best of all, all these micro-policies cost micro-money. Today’s budget had 98 measures – more than any I can remember in decades of covering fiscal events, yet they all cost trifling sums.Which brings us to the killer problem: Lewis is one of the most trusted people in Britain. But he’s not a politician. He’s never claimed to be. He speaks the language of terms and conditions, not financialisation – and he knows his limits. To quote aNew Statesman essaylast week on the new MoneySavingPolitics: “As governments have embraced retail policies and suggestion-box-style politics in his image, Lewis has been raising the alarm that there are too many people who can no longer help themselves and it is time for structural change.”The difference was clear today. In her first budget, Rachel Reeves announcedextra spendingworth £74bn by the end of the period. By comparison, Healey announced agrand totalof £380m. For all Burnham’s grand ambition and soaring rhetoric, his first budget was only 0.5% of Starmer’s first budget.This is obviously not how the King of the North wants you to see him. Listen to Burnham speak, and you hear a changemaker, an ideas man, a leader with a 10-year plan. But does he put his money where his mouth is? Does he heck. The anxiety I have heard for months from so many of his advisers and MPs was borne out in this budget: he’s big talk and small stick.The best line of the day came from Kemi Badenoch. “The prime minister came to power promising to end 40 years of neoliberalism, and instead we got 4p off gherkins,”the Tory leader said, while Burnham and Healey frowned like men caught bang to rights. What’s the point of cut-price marmalade when a few months ago you promised to nationalise Thames Water?Why, for that matter, chuck out the old boss when the new one is less ambitious? Whacking banks with a tax in order to cut energy costs is good politics, but this new government should have been much more ambitious. A hundred pounds is a token saving when the typical household’s fuel bill is about to top £2,000. Given how harsh thisEl Niño winteris likely to be, I imagine the government will have to cobble together another intervention before the new year.Ministers are now caught in a pincer movement between Badenoch to their right, who can argue they aren’t tackling the really big problems and, to their left, the Greens and Plaid, as well as the Scottish nationalists, who will keep on saying they aren’t doing enough for their own voters. In a day of grim economic forecasts, perhaps the worst was from the Office for Budget Responsibility,which said thatin the face of high inflation, earnings willnot rise at all next year– while 2030 would see households with take-home pay just 2% above where it was before Covid struck in 2020. Put those two figures together and – despite all the Westminster chat – you can forget about a snap election that delivers Labour a new majority.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf ministers can’t offer any protection against an economic outlook that bleak, they will face an angry and mutinous public. If the Labour party wants to be re-elected, it needs to give people a reason to go out and vote for it. Pointing to bond markets isn’t a defence, because markets aren’t in open rebellion. Yes, government borrowing is a lot more expensive than it was in the post-crash years of cheap money and the interest bill on the nation’s debt is high. But no one thinks Britain is France. Gilt traders today looked at a government running down its financial buffer and were completely unruffled. Had Healey borrowed much more to invest in social and cheap housing, he could have argued that such spending would soon enough bring down benefit bills – and markets would have believed him.I write this as someone who wants Burnham to do well – and certainly to do better than today’s tiny raft of tweaks. Unlike many Labour politicians, he can talk sincerely about where disastrous rightwing politics have led this country. When he promises a new economic and political model, I – and many others – am up for it. In contrast to Starmer he doesn’t act as if he hates 80% of his own party members. Unlike Starmer’s advisers, his team doesn’t subsist on a diet of received wisdom and petty vindictiveness. But at some point, the grand rhetoric and the romantic notions need to cash out into a programme of change. Otherwise, voters will draw the conclusion that this summer’s coup against a recently elected prime minister had no grand motivation apart from saving the skins of Labour MPs and fanning a few egos.A Martin Lewis budget is fine, but Labour chose Andy Burnham as its leader and the public were promised a Burnham budget. They’re still waiting.Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist and the Guardian’s senior economics commentatorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I’ve been watching the 7 Up TV series. One change in our behaviour really struck me | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: Before mobile phones, being filmed was very rare – and if you were, you acted naturally. Today, our relationship to the camera is very, very different, writes Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: Before mobile phones, being filmed was very rare – and if you were, you acted naturally. Today, our relationship to the camera is very, very different, writes Adrian Chiles
Content: She’s a natural …Photograph: Reka Olga/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenShe’s a natural …Photograph: Reka Olga/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionTelevisionI’ve been watching the 7 Up TV series. One change in our behaviour really struck meAdrian ChilesBefore mobile phones, being filmed was very rare – and if you were, you acted naturally. Today, our relationship to the camera is very, very differentWed 28 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTShareNot for the first time, I got something wrong. As someone who made a living being on camera, I developed theories about what it takes to be yourself on screen. My main thought was that everyone in the world would soon be able to do it, because they’d be getting so much practice.Once upon a time, hardly anybody was filmed or videoed. When the head of my middle school announced in assembly one morning that there would be television cameras in the dinner hall at lunchtime, every child woke up. For once the headteacher had our full and undivided attention. Consternation was in the air. This would have been about 1979. Regional television news probably needed pictures to cover a story about school dinners or something. Nobody, but nobody, in the school that day missed that evening’s edition of Midlands Today. It was a big deal. I saw the back of my head, and was agog.In the home, being filmed was just as rare. Before smartphones, before camcorders, moving pictures of domestic life were few and far between. Growing up in the last decades of the last century I was aware of the existence of cine cameras but knew of no one who owned such an exotic, perhaps even vaguely sinister piece of kit.By the time I first appeared on television in the mid-90s, the dam was starting to burst. Not only did I stand as proof that any Tom, Dick or Harry could have a go at TV presenting, but camcorders were proliferating. Babies bawling, toddlers toddling, kiddies doing “shows”, teenagers sulking, grandads snoozing – all were preserved for posterity, or at least until the tapes were lost for ever in some dark corner. Now there can’t be a human being in the UK of whom there isn’t some video footage on a smartphone, in the cloud, or wherever these things exist.View image in fullscreen70 Up.Photograph: MultiStory Media/ITVThe ubiquity of video cameras surely means we’re more natural in front of them. But looking natural is different tobeingnatural. It might even be the opposite.This dawned on me when talking to the remarkable Tony Walker, who 63 years ago was one of the seven-year-olds featured on the longitudinal documentary series which started with Seven Up! and has nowconcluded with 70 Up. From the back of Tony’s black cab I listened as he told me how this little East End rascal had barely seen a TV, let alone a TV camera, before the day Michael Apted’s crew came bowling into his life. I went back and binge-watched the series from the beginning – 7, 14, 21 Up and so on – and, while this group obviously gained experience of television every seven years, from the outset it’s striking how naturally everyone speaks. This is not despite, but because of, their lack of practice. They’re blisteringly honest and are being – dread phrase – their authentic selves. They’ve yet to learn how to be anything else.The same thought is provoked byChris Terrill’s seminal BBC series, Soho Stories, now repeated 30 years after it first went out. Chris, embedded in the Soho area of central London for a year, mines a rich seam of characters: Gwen the student/burlesque dancer, Mark the tailor, Danny the wannabe actor and so on. Even as recently as 1996 it’s noticeable that they don’t have enough of a grasp of the grammar of television to be able to do anything other than reveal an unvarnished, unmediated version of themselves. The lack of guile is at the heart of their honesty.Fast forward to 2026 and it’s guile galore. Influencers, vloggers, clever dicks, dicks, whoever – all are talking to camera with disarming competence, entirely at home with the form and quite coruscatingly natural. Yet natural is the last thing they are. To see what natural really looks like, examine people’s expressions on very old black and white photographs, back before they’d worked out what faces to pull. Compare and contrast with today, in which everyone’s acquired the knack of presenting a carefully, if unconsciously, curated version of themselves. The level of naturalness is a lot of things, but the one thing it isn’t is natural. If you want natural, go back to the days before folks had worked out how to pretend to be natural.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
