title: I’ve mailed off my vote in the US midterms. It will be a nail-biting watch, but easier from outside Trump’s America | Eleanor Limprecht | The Guardian
description: I’m hopeful these elections will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris
Author: Eleanor Limprecht
Headline: I’m hopeful these elections will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris
Content: Virginians cast their ballots during early midterm voting in Alexandria on 27 October. The 2026 US midterm elections are on 3 November.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenVirginians cast their ballots during early midterm voting in Alexandria on 27 October. The 2026 US midterm elections are on 3 November.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAOpinionUS midterm elections 2026I’ve mailed off my vote in the US midterms. It will be a nail-biting watch, but easier from outside Trump’s AmericaEleanor LimprechtI’m hopeful these elections will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubrisWed 28 Oct 2026 18.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTShareRecently I made my own envelope out of a sheet of paper and sticky tape, signed it and affixed a sticker. Then I took it to my nearest Australia Post shop in Sydney and mailed it.In other words, I voted from abroad in the US midterm elections. Because my last place of residence in the US was the state of Virginia, I can register to vote and request a ballot online, but the ballot still needs to be printed, signed, sealed in an envelope made of folded paper, signed again, placed inside another (store-bought) envelope and mailed in. There was nosausage sizzleor cake stall to reward me for my civic duty, and no spectre of a fine if I didn’t complete it.I give a wide berth to anything resembling a craft project (haunted by the ghosts of Easter hat parades past) but I would cross-stitch a ballot if it lessened the power that President Trump wields over my country of birth. Hell, I would papier-mache an airplane and decoupage a pilot’s licence to deliver my vote in person.What are the races to watch in the US midterm elections and why do they matter?Read moreUnfortunately, not everyone is as fervent: voter turnout in the midterm elections in the US is typically less than half the eligible voting population. The midterms are viewed as less important; in-person voting is arduous and inconvenient (with long queues, on a weekday rather than a Saturday) and some voters view state-based elections as secondary to the presidential election.3:38US midterms: what are they and why do presidents dread them? – explainerThe current administration is trying to reduce voter turnout even more because things are not looking good for Republican candidates. They have gerrymandered, sued the state of California for refusing to disenfranchise 20,000 voters, tried to restrict mail-in voting (this wasblocked by the supreme court)and alreadymade a challengeto Alaska’s Senate election results if the incumbent Republican senator Dan Sullivan does not win.Can you smell it from here? That’s not raw sewage overflow from the recent heavy rains, that’s Trump’s fear.Democrats only need three seats to gain majority in the House of Representatives and four to gain majority in the Senate. If theDemocratscontrol Congress it will be far more difficult for Trump to get his laws through. They could create committees to investigate the president and even begin an impeachment trial.Trump’s egregiously named Operation Epic Fury has caused the price of fuel to skyrocket and most Americans (two-thirds) now view the ongoing war against Iran as a mistake. As the price of fuel goes up, Trump’s approval rating sinks. (His dismantling of democracy and campaign of disinformation didn’t seem to disturb voters in the same way that this hit to the hip pocket does.)I am cautiously hopeful. I’ve spent the past two years wishing I was Canadian and rushing to turn off the radio or television at the sound of Trump’s hyperbole. Perfecting my simultaneous sigh and shrug when people hear my accent and ask me to explainhowandwhythe bully-in-chief was re-elected.Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must change | Kathryn SikkinkRead moreBut I keep recalling the awful events of 6 January 2021, when in the wake of a Trump rally, an angry rightwing mob attacked the US Capitol building after his defeat in the 2020 elections. Five people died and 174 police officers were injured while the rest of the world watched in horror. As a child in Arlington, Virginia, I visited those rotundas and chambers on field trips. As an adult here in Australia, I worried over friends and family who live and work in Washington DC. If the Republican candidates are defeated in these elections, will the administration accept the results?4:10The key Capitol attack footage shown on day two of Trump’s impeachment trial – videoThere are three million Americans who live abroad and more than 110,000 here in Australia (around 60% of us have Australian citizenship). It will be nail-biting to watch the 3 November midterm elections, but easier from afar than from within Trump’s America: a country where immigrants are endangered, abortion rights have been eroded, artificial intelligence has grown without regulation and foreign aid, environmental protections and domestic social services have been gutted. Even Trump’s tariffs are backfiring for the United States, uniting the countries they are aimed against, such as Canada. Elbows up!These midterms, I am hopeful it will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris.Just please, whatever happens, don’t ask me to explain theelectoral collegecome 2028.Eleanor Limprecht is the author ofCul de Sac,What Was Left,Long Bay,The PassengersandThe CoastExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsTrump administrationRepublicansDemocratscommentShareReuse this content

title: Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: The chancellor is right to focus on pure affordability, but £100 handouts and delayed decisions won’t shield consumers from the next wave of price hikes
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: The chancellor is right to focus on pure affordability, but £100 handouts and delayed decisions won’t shield consumers from the next wave of price hikes
Content: A wind farm near Hartlepool. The chancellor announced the government ‘will only buy and build new projects when they lower bills and when they can connect to the grid’.Photograph: Caroline WalkerView image in fullscreenA wind farm near Hartlepool. The chancellor announced the government ‘will only buy and build new projects when they lower bills and when they can connect to the grid’.Photograph: Caroline WalkerEnergy billsLabour is still searching for an energy fix for a new worldNils PratleyThe chancellor is right to focus on pure affordability, but £100 handouts and delayed decisions won’t shield consumers from the next wave of price hikesWed 28 Oct 2026 15.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 15.58 EDTShareAmid the myriad of small measures, virtually everything in John Healey’s budget came back to the cost of energy. The higher energy prices that have resulted from the Iran war have pushed up inflation, are eating into households’ incomes, are a drag on businesses – and are the main reason why the forecast for GDP growth next year was cut from 1.6% to just 1%.And energy was the focus of Healey’s sole surprise in his consumer-facing policies –the £100 paymentto 20m households in A-D council tax bands to help with fuel bills this winter. It will be funded, in effect, by tapping the banks for a few quid for 15 months via the bank surcharge.But the chancellor will know that £100 won’t look generous when the bills land. Gas prices are still rising, and leading supplier EDF’slatest predictionis that the regulator’s price cap will be hiked by £466 in January, pushing the annual rate for an average household to £2,189. When Labour took office in July 2024,talking naively about taking £300 off bills over the life of the parliament, the cap was £1,568.No surprise, then, that the messaging on energy is shifting. Here is the passage in Healey’s speech that hinted at big changes ahead: “Today I’m setting a new course on energy: to get UK energy costs down in line with Europe. From this point, our Labour government’s priority is first and foremost cheaper energy, with clean power key to achieving this.”.Thank goodness for the reset towards affordability. It is long overdue. The biggest impediment to economic growth, including the prime minister’s longed-for “reindustrialisation”, is the cost of energy in the UK. There is little Healey can do about international gas prices, but he can do “deep reform of our energy system”, as he put it. So what’s the plan?That, unfortunately, is where the “new course” turned blurry. Take the promise to introduce “a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills”. The ambition is laudable, because energy bills have become littered with levies and charges – everything from socialising unpaid consumer energy debt to funding Sizewell C – that should more naturally be funded from general taxation. It’s about time the Treasury took an interest in such hidden taxes.But the costs don’t disappear just because they are placed within a new framework. The tough question is how much a chancellor is willing to fund from Treasury coffers in the interest of lower upfront bills for consumers and business. It is not a small question, because wide-ranging definitions of levies can produce figures as high as £15bn.It’s good that Healey is demanding no new levies (unless they bring down bills), but that’s not the same as hacking into the existing thicket. Funding for green hydrogen projects is being taken on by the Treasury, which is a start. But come back in next year’s spending review, it seems, to discover the size of Healey’s scythe. More urgency is needed.There was a bit more clarity on the electricity generation side. “This government will only buy and build new projects when they lower bills and when they can connect to the grid,” said Healey. That reads as a strong hint that offshore wind commissions will be slowed until prices fall (which probably requires a fall in borrowing costs for developers) and the upgrade of the grid is more advanced. Very sensible: sequencing matters, asthe alarming costs of “wasted wind”demonstrate regularly.But Healey’s ambition to “break the grip of international gas prices” by switching older renewables projects on to lower fixed-price contracts is not new. Ed Miliband, when energy secretary,said the same. The test is how hard ministers are willing to twist the arms of renewables owners, who are very attached to arrangements that give them jackpot revenues when gas prices are high. The basic tension remains: for consumers to win, somebody has to be paid less than they were expecting.So, yes, one can applaud the change of tone and direction. A reset in energy policy to prioritise affordability was bound to arrive eventually. The drive to clean power also had to be a drive to cheap power. But one cannot yet say the new approach is joined-up. Policies to drive the electrification of homes and transport were not turbo-charged, which they need to be to reduce long-term dependency on gas and oil. And “deep reforms” to the electricity market are, to put it gently, a work in progress. More urgency needed.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsBudget 2026Household billsConsumer affairscommentShareReuse this content

title: We are seeing the rise of psychopatriarchy everywhere | V (formerly Eve Ensler) | The Guardian
description: Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalism
Author: V (formerly Eve Ensler)
Headline: Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalism
Content: ‘It is propelled by its own mad trajectory.’Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘It is propelled by its own mad trajectory.’Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersOpinionUS newsWe are seeing the rise of psychopatriarchy everywhereV (formerly Eve Ensler)Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalismWed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.25 EDTShareFor those of us who have spent our lives trying to dismantle this endlessly destructive paradigm of patriarchy, it has become increasingly clear in recent months that something more terrifying is afoot.The wheels are off the cart. We are in the midst of a chaotic, demented acceleration of the most violent and cruel aspects of this system which has evolved into what I am calling Psychopatriarchy.Psychopatriarchy is a reaction, a backlash against the progress we have made on all fronts: women’s rights, civil rights, immigrant rights, workers rights, trans rights etc.It has birthed an authoritarian fascist reality, poisoning our social and psychological environment with terrorizing violence, cruelty and precarity. It has consolidated the billionaire class who are driven by the mindset summed up in the slogan “move fast and break things.” Or, one might say, grab things, rape things.Psychopatriarchy is found in the 120 people who own more money than half the population on Earth, in the systems of oppression, surveillance and violence which become more and more sophisticated and widespread, in the few mainly white men with extreme wealth and power who are now merged with the government and own the systems of communication, AI, police or state militias like ICE.America must reverse Trump’s moral squalor | Robert ReichRead morePsychopatriarchy is a sanctioning of extreme hatred and violence against women from the top, many of whom are rapists, batterers, pedophiles and abusers or men who openly support them.The president of the US is a civilly adjudicated sex abuser and has not only flippantlydismissed allegationsof sexual violencemade against othersin his orbit, but made it fashionable and popular attitude for the men in his delusional cult.He has created a suffocating atmosphere of misogyny and predation. We only have to look to the manosphere, or the rape academies online where millions of men exchange best practices for drugging and raping their wives, girlfriends, sisters or deepfake pornography which is destroying thousands of women’s lives or sex robots.Orrape islandswhere some of the most powerful men in the world are alleged to have raped underage girls and not one has been prosecuted. Or universities where young men allegedly gang-rape an incapacitated woman or where young women can’t put down a drink at a party without fear of being drugged, where they are blamed for being assaulted.Psychopatriarchy is women dying preventable deaths because abortion care is denied or delayed or the introduction of extreme constitutional amendments such asNorth Carolina House Bill 1232, where menmight belegally allowed to kill women who have abortions. This bill will hopefully not pass, but the fact that it is even being considered is an example of how deeply far we have fallen.Psychopatriachy is the open and unapologetic death of compassion; asElon Musk said: “Empathy is the fundamental weakness of western civilization.” This means a kind of contempt for anything that appears to be emotional, alive, feminine, caring.Strength in the form of dissociation is revered. When you feel nothing, no guilt, no shame, no horror at your actions, you can better serve your goals and the state. When you are ruled by your blind devotion to the president, the boss, the father, you become capable of doing anything in his name.Psychopatriachy is renaming the Department of Defense the “Department of War”, well, the “High-T Department of War”,as Hegseth calls it, wanting all military personnel aged 30 and over to “have the right testosterone levels” to operate at their “absolute best” and to optimize “natural capabilities”, “longevity”, and “readiness”. Preparing a psycho army driven by chemicals beyond their control.Psychopatriarchy iswanting to livestreama firing squad. It’s the endless genocide in Gaza, the outright murdering of babies, toddlers, mothers, fathers, journalists, doctors. It’s the US bombing a girls school in Iran and murdering 120 girl children and 26 teachers, and no one ever taking responsibility for one of the worst war crimes since Vietnam.It’s illegally kidnapping presidents and randomly murdering people by bombing them in boats in the middle of the sea. It’s masked men dragging away wailing children from their parents.It’s killing activists in the streets: Renee Good and Alex Pretti. It’s intimidating and threatening deportation to those who disagree with you: Ilhan Omar. It’s creating the conditions for the lynching of Black people across the United States.It’s tearing down ancient grandmother trees to build walls to keep suffering people out or to landscape a golf course. It’s the coldhearted, discompassionate billionaire class taking everything, erasing everyone.Psychopatriarchy is the decimation of all forms of accountability. Infinite impunity. No supreme court, no Department of Justice, no leaders, no Congress. Withdrawing or refusing to be part of any international courts or abiding by international law. When there is no accountability, when there is no place to turn for justice, a society loses its moral footing and begins to fall.Psychopatriachy is not just a political notion. It’s a state of existence, a blight on the condition of humanity locking us into daily terror, cruelty, depression, malaise, a manufactured sense of powerlessness, alienation and a desire to disappear.It is a kind of low-level anxiety, an ongoing foreshadowing or feeling of imminent destruction coming from multiple directions at once, and rather than reducing these threats (AI, nuclear weapons, climate catastrophes, pandemics), the psychopatriarchs are accelerating all these things. AI is charging forward with no regulation, escalating the nuclear arms race, increasing drilling of oil at breakneck speed.Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to all the other -isms: racism, colonialism, imperialism, capitalism.It is propelled by its own mad trajectory. We can try to block it (courts); we can starve it (strikes); we can remove it (vote and get them out office). We can name and shame it (speaking out, marches and rallies), refuse to normalize it (write about it, make art about it); we can prosecute it.We can create a parallel world that is so inviting, generous and caring that even those who are still struggling to break out of the cult will eventually be emboldened.But what we cannot do is go to sleep, become small and still, with the childlike fantasy that they will not find us. What we cannot do is succumb to it or become them – numb, selfish, hollow and cruel.Our feelings, our pain, our empathy, our rage, our love, our refusal to turn away will be our salvation. Psychosis is the inability to tell what is real from unreal. Our work is to say what we see and trust what we know, to keep speaking truth to power and go to any lengths to stay connected to reality and each other.V (formerly Eve Ensler) is a playwright and activist and the founder of V-Day, a global movement to end violence against women and girlsExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Donald TrumpUS politicsAbortionReproductive rightsRape and sexual assaultcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first steps | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Banks, landlords and gambling firms will pay more as the chancellor begins building a fairer economy and a more active state in a cost of living crisis
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Banks, landlords and gambling firms will pay more as the chancellor begins building a fairer economy and a more active state in a cost of living crisis
Content: A Rorschach test inkblot is open to interpretation – just like John Healey’s budget.Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenA Rorschach test inkblot is open to interpretation – just like John Healey’s budget.Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoOpinionBudget 2026The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first stepsEditorialBanks, landlords and gambling firms will pay more as the chancellor begins building a fairer economy and a more active state in a cost of living crisisWed 28 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.54 EDTShareJohn Healey’s first budget was a Rorschach test. Supporters saw dozens of measures offering “breathing space”to a public worn down by rising prices. Critics admitted to a slew of announcements but countered that each wasmodest in value. Underlying both views is that the budget was more ambitious on how a state can do more to protect the public than on how much it spends. The chancellor has taken a small step in the right direction – a tricky feat in a turbulent world. But an economy marked by entrenched inequality and more than a decade of stagnation will need a bigger stride.The Office for Budget Responsibility’s “pretty grim picture” of living standards exposes the budget’s central weakness: its relief is temporary, while the squeeze on households persists. As the government deficit shrinks and company profits recover, households are expected to move from saving roughly £50bn in 2026 to borrowing roughly the same amount in 2031. By then,mortgage repaymentsare expected to reach 4.25% of household disposable income – the highest level since 2009. The OBR expects growth to recover from 1% in 2027 to 1.8% in 2029, while weak worker “bargaining power” allows firms to rebuild profit margins. That sits uneasily with Mr Healey’s promises to working people.View image in fullscreenJohn Healey.Photograph: House of Commons/PAAdmittedly, the budget’s ambitions – shaping energy markets,ending rough sleeping, devolving tax and spend decisions – go beyond its winter relief package. Mr Healey is also right to ask banks, gambling companies andlandlordsto contribute more. Preventing hardship is better than repeatedly paying for its consequences. In ringfencing homelessness prevention in local government spending, even though the savings are experienced in the NHS, he is making both moral and financial sense.The problem, however, is not that Mr Healey’s budget lacks ambition, but that it lacks firepower. The bank tax raises just £1.5bn over 15 months, against the projected £11bn that a Thatcher-style levy oninterest-free depositscould have yielded. The Resolution Foundation has a point when it says that 80% of homes get a £100 energy payment, while 1.4 million poor families miss out. Relying on revenues from the giantRosebankoilfield before its approval is settled would be reckless. So would treating the export of its oil as an answer to the climate damage caused by burning it.The choices that Mr Healey makes all too often reflect the fiscal constraints he opted to retain. Is it really “credible” to claim that there will be £11bn of cuts to “unprotected” budgets (those that aren’t defence, the NHS, schools or international aid) in 2031-32? Many expertsthink not. Should the defence budget be funded by “reprioritising” other departments’ capital spend? Mr Healey thinks so. The prime minister called the 2009Marmot review his bibleon reducing inequalities – it advocates for widescale economic rebalancing. But devolving tax revenues without adequate redistribution risks giving the wealthiest places the most to spend, rather than giving the poorest the help they need. Mr Healey has yet to explain how he will prevent that.Global events could make Mr Healey’s life much tougher. Prolonged disruption in thestrait of Hormuzwould further squeeze real incomes. But the chancellor has in his budget sketched the outline of a social-democratic active state: taxing rentiers, protecting vulnerable people and investing in prevention. The question is whether those commitments have enough resources to succeed.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Israel’s elections: Netanyahu lost his mandate. If opponents unite, he’ll lose power too | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: His chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work withPalestinian Israeli parties
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: His chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work withPalestinian Israeli parties
Content: ‘Mr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine”.’Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Mr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine”.’Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/GettyOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuThe Guardian view on Israel’s elections: Netanyahu lost his mandate. If opponents unite, he’ll lose power tooEditorialHis chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work with Palestinian Israeli partiesWed 28 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.55 EDTShareBenjamin Netanyahu haslost his mandatebut not, so far, power. While final votes are still being tallied, most voters picked his opponents on Tuesday. His bloc’s share of seats remains the largest, but appears to have slumped by around 10, leaving it below the 61 needed for a majority in the Knesset. Palestinian Israeli parties surged, and are projected to almost double the 10 seats they held. The result is that Mr Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the military, now faces a choice: fall into line with Mr Netanyahu’s racist fearmongering or work with Arab-led parties.The prime minister who oversaw shocking security failures ahead of the Hamas atrocities of 7 October 2023 still pitches himself as “Mr Security”.On trial for corruption, he has persistently attacked democratic institutions, especially the judiciary. He embraced and then indulged the ultra-right as they cheered onbrutal settler violencein the occupied West Bank. (Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich lost ground in these polls, but perhaps due to their vision’s permeation of mainstream politics more than a revolt against it.) Mr Netanyahu’s war on Iran has destabilised the region. The tens of thousands of Palestinians killed by his government’s genocidal war on Gaza have barely featured in the election campaign, butits cost for Israeli hostagesand international support for Israel have been noted by voters.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot.Photograph: JNA/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockMr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine” andaccusingPalestinian citizens of Israel, around a fifth of its population, of trying to “steal the election”. They haveoften boycotted their democratic right, in a system stacked against them, with politics moving rightwards. Mr Eisenkot’s bloc gives themlittle reason for optimism; Tuesday’s turnout testifies totheir desperation to see an endto the most extreme government in Israel’s history. Millions of Palestinians living under illegal Israeli occupation got no vote at all.Mr Netanyahu, the consummate survivor, maypin his hopes on another election. For now, as incumbent, he holds extra cards. The greatest danger is that he pushes Donald Trump into a renewed offensive on Iran after the midterms, seeing perma-war as political salvation.Mr Eisenkot, one of many burned by their dealings with the prime minister, is unlikely to risk a “unity government”. His bloc could remove Mr Netanyahu “if it is brave enough”,observed Ahmad Tibiof the Joint List ticket of Palestinian parties. In campaigning, most opposition Israeli politicians ruled out a coalition with the Joint List or Ra’am (the United Arab List) – except on termsthat they will not accept. But the Palestinian parties have made clear that they are open to cooperation and there is precedent. Mr Netanyahu himself reportedlymade overturesto Ra’am in 2021; instead it joined the coalition that unseated him.“We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,”wrote Yair Golan, head of the centre-left Democrats – noting that Mr Netanyahu talks of a Zionist majority but relies on the support of non-Zionist Harediparties. Mr Eisenkot may fear that supporters will not tolerate a deal but they will not thank him for failing to boot out Mr Netanyahu when given the chance. That would also allow the prime minister to turn this result into an ideological victory. Israel defines itself as Jewish and democratic. Mr Eisenkot and his partners should accept every vote and citizen as equal.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Ensuring prisoners can’t refuse to attend court | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letter: One prison officer says existing rules on offenders making court appearances should be enforced rather than introducing fresh sanctions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: One prison officer says existing rules on offenders making court appearances should be enforced rather than introducing fresh sanctions
Content: ‘Few prisoners refused, because they knew their refusal would not prevent them from appearing.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Few prisoners refused, because they knew their refusal would not prevent them from appearing.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyPrisons and probationLettersEnsuring prisoners can’t refuse to attend courtOne prison officer says existing rules on offenders making court appearances should be enforced rather than introducing fresh sanctionsWed 28 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTShareThe report on judges being given powers to punish prisoners who refuse to attend court raises a question about why we appear to have abandoned a straightforward approach that once worked (Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing face losing prison privileges under new rules, 22 October).When I joined the Prison Service as an officer more than 30 years ago, prisoners were not permitted to decide whether they would attend court. If they refused to go voluntarily, they could be escorted under restraint where necessary.The result was predictable: few prisoners refused, because they knew their refusal would not prevent them from appearing.There is a wider lesson here for the administration of justice. When noncompliance becomes a means of delaying or obstructing the system, introducing additional punishments may be less effective than ensuring that lawful instructions are carried out in the first place. Prisoners have rights, and the use of restraint must always be lawful, proportionate and justified. But those rights do not extend to exercising a veto over the judicial process.After more than three decades, I find it difficult to understand why a principle that was once routine now appears to require a fresh solution. Sometimes, effective public administration is not about creating new sanctions but about having the resolve and resources to enforce existing rules.Name and address suppliedExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justicelettersShareReuse this content

title: Support unpaid carers so they aren’t pushed to the brink of suicide  | Carers | The Guardian
description: Letter:With almost half of parent-carers contemplating taking their lives, Dr Louise Lawson calls for urgent action by the government
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter:With almost half of parent-carers contemplating taking their lives, Dr Louise Lawson calls for urgent action by the government
Content: ‘Campaigning by Ed Davey, alongside the Guardian’s investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal, have exposed the extent to which unpaid carers have been failed by the state.’Photograph: Aire Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Campaigning by Ed Davey, alongside the Guardian’s investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal, have exposed the extent to which unpaid carers have been failed by the state.’Photograph: Aire Images/Getty ImagesCarersLettersSupport unpaid carers so they aren’t pushed to the brink of suicideWith almost half of parent-carers contemplating taking their lives,Dr Louise Lawsoncalls for urgent action by the governmentWed 28 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTShareReading the report on Matilda Davis’s death was heartbreaking (Burnham backs mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after parent-carer Matilda Davis’s death, 21 October). That someone already under immense pressure could leave a meeting with social workers feeling so distressed, and that the professionals had received no suicide-prevention training, is an indictment of the system. It is reassuring to hear Andy Burnham’s support for mandatory training for social workers. But there is an even more troubling issue at the heart of this story – the finding that 41% of parent-carers have contemplated suicide should prompt outrage and immediate action.Campaigning by Ed Davey, alongside theGuardian’s investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal, have exposed the extent to which unpaid carers have been failed by the state. For years they have been described as inspirational and selfless. They give up careers, sacrifice income and provide care that saves the state billions of pounds. Yet the reality revealed by this figure is that many feel so overwhelmed and unsupported that they have contemplated ending their lives.Mandatory suicide-prevention training may help professionals identify those in crisis. But the real scandal is that so many are being pushed to this point in the first place. It is time for the government to provide the practical, emotional and financial support that unpaid carers desperately need.Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy,University of GlasgowIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123.In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsCarersMental healthHealthSocial careCarer's allowanceBenefitslettersShareReuse this content

title: The Jackdaw gasfield, net zero and climate adaptation | Green economy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article in which the prime minister said the government’s gasfield approval was part of its commitment to a greener future
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article in which the prime minister said the government’s gasfield approval was part of its commitment to a greener future
Content: (From left) Scotland secretary Douglas Alexander, energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and chancellor John Healey visit a gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAView image in fullscreen(From left) Scotland secretary Douglas Alexander, energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and chancellor John Healey visit a gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.Photograph: Paul Reid/PAGreen economyLettersThe Jackdaw gasfield, net zero and climate adaptationReaders respond to an article in which the prime minister said the government’s gasfield approval was part of its commitment to a greener futureWed 28 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTShareAndy Burnham writes that his determination to tackle the climate crisis is “unwavering” and that the transition must not leave communities behind (We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain – approving the Jackdaw gasfield is part of the plan, 22 October). Whatever one thinks of Jackdaw, the test of that pledge is whether people are also protected from climate impacts that are already here.The research that you reported on last week attributed two-thirds of the heat deaths that it estimated – 4,354 of them in the UK – to climate change.The numbers from that study were not available when the health secretary took questions in the Commons last Tuesday, but the signs were – stretched ambulance services, cancelled operations and overheated wards. Heat was barely mentioned.The prime minister says that he will not be “so careless with people’s lives” as oil and gas workers face the transition. He is right, and the same care is owed to older people in care homes, pregnant women, patients on hospital wards and outdoor workers facing the next heatwave.So the government must commit to practical action before next summer. That means effective cooling and heatwave plans in hospitals, maternity units and care homes, stronger early warnings, welfare checks for isolated older people, and protections for workers in dangerous temperatures. The Climate Change Committee has shown that the investment needed is manageable and the cost of inaction far greater.Net zero and adaptation are not alternatives. Mr Burnham should say what he will deliver, and when.Emma Howard BoydChair, National Heat Risk CommissionThe idea of using fossil fuels as a “bridge” to green energy has been touted by polluters and politicians since the 1980s. It’s mind-boggling that we’re still at this point.Energy security, national security and avoiding climate catastrophe all come with rapidly expanding green technologies such as heat pumps and renewables. The benefits there far outweigh those produced by gas drilling, and it’s these that should be Andy Burnham’s full focus when he talks of a green transition. After decades of delay, the world’s transition now needs to be fast.Thanks to the failure of the politicians who came before, we need heaps of gas to heat our homes this winter, but the idea of baking that in for more decades isn’t just stupid – to myself and my peers who look ahead with fear at an increasingly precarious future, this decision is an insult.Gwydion ElliottSheffieldAndy Burnham – “not a climate guy”, according to one of his MPs – argues in his opinion article that an increase in CO2emissions is required to bring down CO2emissions. George Orwell would appreciate that.Douglas CurrieEdinburghHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The BBC’s education editor role should not be scrapped | BBC | The Guardian
description: Letters: The broadcaster’s decision speaks volumes about BBC priorities and the state of public dialogue, says David Blunkett. Plus a letter by Richard Bourne
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The broadcaster’s decision speaks volumes about BBC priorities and the state of public dialogue, says David Blunkett. Plus a letter by Richard Bourne
Content: ‘Education needs sustained scrutiny by journalists … to hold to account government and educational institutions.’Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Education needs sustained scrutiny by journalists … to hold to account government and educational institutions.’Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersBBCLettersThe BBC’s education editor role should not be scrappedThe broadcaster’s decision speaks volumes about BBC priorities and the state of public dialogue, saysDavid Blunkett. Plus a letter byRichard BourneWed 28 Oct 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTShareCan I add my voice to the expression of considerable disquiet at the BBC’s proposal to eliminate the post of education editor, instead combining responsibility with that of social affairs (BBC News to axe education editor role in cost-cutting move, 22 October). These two distinct areas of public life are critical to our understanding – under the remit of the BBC charter – to educate and inform, as well as entertain.The requirement to take education seriously surely requires someone with deep understanding of this complex area, which affects every single person in the country: from the moment they’re born, all the way through lifelong learning and the current challenges of artificial intelligence and robotics.Some readers will remember the greatMike Baker, who was a practitioner as well as an informer; an experienced and extremely erudite broadcaster who brought alive the elements of the education debate which, when I was the education and employment secretary, were described as the then-government’s top three priorities: “Education, education, education.”The proposition to downgrade the standing and the acquired experience necessary to present to the public speaks volumes not only about BBC priorities, but about the state of our public dialogue.David BlunkettLabour, House of LordsIt is retrograde of theBBCto downgrade its education coverage. Educational changes and debates are news. They need nuanced analysis. While it is true that they fit into a wider spectrum of social issues, all electors deserve journalists devoted to this coverage.When I was the Guardian’s education correspondent from 1968 to 1972, when debates raged on comprehensive schools and there were student sit-ins and a teachers’ strike, it would have been inconceivable if there had not been a full-time BBC education correspondent.People as different as Margaret Thatcher, then education minister, and Jack Straw, then a student leader, became household names thanks to TV, radio and journalism. The BBC should think again.Richard BourneLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties yet again to secure Carabao Cup progress | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Liverpool won penalty shootout in which there were five failed kicks 6-5 after a 1-1 draw with Chelsea in the Carabao Cup at Anfield
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool won penalty shootout in which there were five failed kicks 6-5 after a 1-1 draw with Chelsea in the Carabao Cup at Anfield
Content: Wesley Fofana lifts his penalty over the bar and Liverpool go through.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWesley Fofana lifts his penalty over the bar and Liverpool go through.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesCarabao CupLiverpool beat Chelsea on penalties yet again to secure Carabao Cup progressAndy Hunterat AnfieldWed 28 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 20.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea must have been resigned to their fate as soon as the shootout arrived at Anfield. Four times they had faced Liverpool on penalties previously and four times they had lost. Number five was confirmed when Wesley Fofana’s wild effort sailed high into the Kop and sent Andoni Iraola’s side into aCarabao Cupquarter-final against his old club Bournemouth.Fofana was not the only culprit as Chelsea’s catalogue of penalty misery againstLiverpoolgained a new chapter alongside the 2007 Champions League semi-final, the 2019 Uefa Super Cup final and the FA and League Cup finals of 2022.Liverpool beat Chelsea 6-5 on penalties: Carabao Cup reaction and quarter-final draw – liveRead moreEmmanuel Emegha had the chance to win it for Xabi Alonso’s side in sudden death but was denied superbly by Giorgi Mamardashvili. Liverpool fluffed their lines with victory in sight too, Kostas Tsimikas blazing over and ruining the chance to reprise his match-winning role at Wembley four years ago. Ryan Gravenberch and Valentin Barco also failed to convert.It fell to Joe Gomez of all people to edge Liverpool ahead with the first shootout penalty of his Anfield career. The long-serving defender, who has never scored for Liverpool, found the top corner of Mike Penders’s goal in convincing style. Fofana could not repeat the trick and finally, after Morgan Rogers and Cody Gakpo had both scored penalties in normal time, the two adversaries were separated. It was another painful result for Alonso, fresh from the home defeat against Tottenham on Saturday, although theChelseadisplay was an improvement.The Chelsea manager said: “For sure it is not the outcome we wanted or expected but once you go to penalties there has to be a sad side. We played with courage, the game was close with not many chances for both sides. It is a small setback because it is probably the least important competition for us. As soon as we leave Anfield our focus will be on a very important game [against Manchester United] on Saturday.”If, as Alonso claimed, the Carabao Cup is not a priority for Chelsea this season then his decision to again overlook the merits of Estêvão, who was left kicking his heels on the bench all evening, was mystifying. With João Pedro injured and Cole Palmer suspended Chelsea started with Danny Welbeck in attack and the former Liverpool captain Jordan Henderson operating in an advanced midfield role. Liverpool contained them relatively comfortably.View image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola embraces his goalkeeper Giorgi Mamardashvili.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesThe Premier League rivals served up a fast-paced, committed cup tie that was lacking goalmouth incident before they exchanged penalties in the space of four minutes. Chelsea were awarded the first when Moisés Caicedo was released inside the Liverpool area by a cleverly disguised pass from Malo Gusto and clipped from behind by Gravenberch. The boos for Henderson intensified as he carried the ball to the spot with a wry smile on his face and handed it to Rogers, who sent Mamardashvili the wrong way with an emphatic penalty kick.Liverpool soon had a spot-kick of their own when Caicedo and Fofana challenged Virgil van Dijk at a Tsimikas corner and the ball struck the Chelsea defender’s raised hand. Gakpo converted confidently into the bottom corner. The referee, Darren England, called both penalties instantly and correctly, showing officials do not always have to rely on video assistance. The game benefited as a spectacle from the absence of a video assistant referee, although Iraola might well have disagreed had Rogers scored after appearing to control Pedro Neto’s chip with his arm. Mamardashvili’s save meant that controversy was avoided.Penders, keen to atone for his costly error against Spurs, took centre stage for Chelsea when saving a flying header from Ronald Araújo at close range. The Liverpool defender had been supplied by a fine cross from Gomez and, with two defenders pushed forwards, Rogers almost punished them on the counterattack. Gomez, however, worked tirelessly to chase back and block the forward’s eventual shot. Penders also saved impressively from Bradley Barcola when the France international cut inside from the right and his low shot was deflected towards the bottom corner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideCarabao Cup quarter-final drawShowFleetwood v Everton or NewcastleManchester City v Bradford CityCrystal Palace v SunderlandLiverpool v BournemouthTies will take place during the week commencing 14 DecemberWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Rogers was involved in several promising openings for Chelsea as Alonso’s team – improved more than Liverpool by their substitutes – finished strongly. Marco Palestra had the best of them when released by the England forward’s perfectly weighted pass but Mamardashvili produced an excellent save low to his right. Wirtz also had a late chance to seal victory but his attempt from Gakpo’s knock-down struck Levi Colwill and was eventually cleared. And so to penalties, and a familiar feeling for the side from Stamford Bridge.Iraola said: “I’m pleased for the players because they put in a big effort tonight. I can feel [togetherness within the squad] and I’m happy to feel it because it is very important. The players are feeling support from the crowd and now we have another big one on Sunday [against Arsenal] so let’s try to finish this four in a row in the best way.”Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupLiverpoolChelseamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Howe, Nagelsmann, Pochettino: can anyone end Manchester United’s doom loop? | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Even an elite coach would surely struggle at Old Trafford amid the executive chaos and with an unfit, uneven squad
Author: Daniel Harris
Headline: Even an elite coach would surely struggle at Old Trafford amid the executive chaos and with an unfit, uneven squad
Content: Fans of Manchester United let their feelings be known  in a protest outside Old Trafford before the Premier League match against Manchester City in September 2026.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans of Manchester United let their feelings be known  in a protest outside Old Trafford before the Premier League match against Manchester City in September 2026.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedHowe, Nagelsmann, Pochettino: can anyone end Manchester United’s doom loop?Daniel HarrisEven an elite coach would surely struggle at Old Trafford amid the executive chaos and with an unfit, uneven squadWed 28 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.49 EDTShareIn January 2014 the 13th series of Celebrity Big Brother aired in the UK, the show so popular that its run time was extended by five days before a public vote anointed Jim Davidson the winner. Then, two years later when Brexit happened, people wondered where their tolerant country had gone, lamenting the ephemeral spirit of London 2012 as though the 2011 riots were some kind of fever dream, not a desperate response to decades of structural and institutional racism exacerbated by the cruelty of unnecessary austerity.The truth is that if security is quickly upended, it was built on quicksand to begin with. Which brings us to Manchester United, easing effortlessly from an uplifting third-place finish tosome of the worst footballin their history.An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeurRead moreIt is entirely possible that Alex Ferguson made a deal with the devil to the effect that United would be great until he retired and hilariously dreadful thereafter. But assuming not, hisl’état, c’est moimentality was busy setting up the post-him fall even at the height of the success – itself a consequence of what had gone before.A day after the Munich air disaster, Louis Edwards – later a seller of condemned meat to schools – joined the board, eventually assuming control thanks to a dodgy rights issue. He bequeathed the club to Martin – his substellar son – who floated it for personal gain, turning an institution that sought to win, entertain and unify into a business legally compelled to return value to shareholders.This left United vulnerable to acquisition by anyone and, whenFerguson fell out with two directors– a horse, a horse, his kingdom for a horse’s ejaculate – they sold to the Glazers, who loaded the purchase price and accordant interest obligation on to the club, with government and football authorities waving through a move since outlawed. Ferguson, meanwhile, must have feared exactly what the takeover would entail and known that without his support the banks might not have lent the money, while thechief executive David Gill admitted opposition to it but stayed in his roleanyway, and so the pillaging began.View image in fullscreenManchester United fans let their feelings know about Malcolm Glazer’s proposed takeover of the club in May 2005.Photograph: John Peters/Manchester United/Getty ImagesThe English game then exploded, with investment in United left available only to those of wealth so extreme it necessarily casts aspersions over their character – such asarch polluterand anti‑immigration zealot, Jim Ratcliffe. Proclaiming inaccurate and divisive rhetoric contrary to the inclusive, cosmopolitan spirit of Manchester and United, jobs were culled and fights picked with fans, Old Trafford’s most desirable seats socially cleansed so the club could sell them to day-trippers for astronomical prices, with longstanding supporters banned aftertrumped-up charges of touting– a deeply principled stance the club fails to apply to itself.Not untypically for a billionaire, Ratcliffe seemingly believes that correct opinions reflect exchequer not expertise, giving himself final say on footballing decisions. And rather than the “best in class” executives he promised, his United operate according to what political analysts call the “Boris principle”, no‑marks in thrall to their own self‑image given jobs for which they lack the ability and character, the consequent chaos being effective sabotage.So the patterns continue: Champions League qualification is missed, insufficient funds are released; a new unsuitable manager spends heavily on players below requisite standard; Champions League qualification is achieved via unsustainably reactive style; the manager is denied necessary funds amounting to less than the bounty of Champions League qualification; the manager imposes a proactive style without the necessary materials; the manager is belatedly fired for a fee far exceeding that saved by cutting jobs; a new unsuitable manager, with entirely different requirements to his predecessor, is appointed; executive accountability is absent.View image in fullscreenEddie Howe is the preferred choice of director of football Jason Wilcox if there is a change of manager at Old Trafford.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersIt is thus no surprise thatMichael Carrick remains unfired, despite exuding the vibe of a man who’s mentally fired himself. Perhaps it’s a stay of execution, but more likely there’s bizarre hope of a turnaround, partly to save paying him off, partly because the relevant executives can’t achieve consensus on a replacement, and partly because surely even Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox accept that, following another catastrophe, after dismissing Carrick they are honour-bound to dismiss themselves.Except they and United don’t work like that.So, just as they failed Carrick bynot recruiting properly; failing to add experience to his coaching team; failing to replace outgoing fitness and set-piece coaches and failing to interrogate details of his new game-model, they are now failing him by having him continue in a job that is too much for him, destroying a season that remains salvageable. Meantime, the Glazers’ dividends continue unabated.As such, the question isn’t so much who should be United’s next manager as can anyone manage United? Increasingly, it looks like the answer is – to quote Don Logan in Sexy Beast – “No”.There are immediate on‑pitch issues: the team are unfit and their collective mentality weak; after years being lied to, the captain has finally broken; and the players hate the suits, the package toxic. Those are the minor problems.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRoughly, football management comprises five aspects: coaching, tactics, talent ID, pastoral care and presence. And, though no manager excels in every department, at this version of United surely they must. Moreover, given this is no job for a novice, track record is also important – and it might be here that Unai Emery’s candidature falls down, his brilliance in transforming mid‑ranking clubs undermined by failures at two high-profile basket cases.View image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino has recently signed a contract extension which puts him in charge of the USA men’s team until 2030.Photograph: Kirby Lee/Imagn Images/ReutersWhich brings us to pastoral care and presence. In the postwar era, onlyErik ten Hag has won a trophy at Unitedwithout tangible charisma, the size of the club now demanding it more than ever. This is not a quality associated with Eddie Howe, while Antonio Conte does not scream pastoral care and, brilliant though his career has been, he failed miserably at Spurs, the only environment he has inhabited that is remotely similar to United.Should United miss Champions League qualification, financial strictures will make an elite coach and tactician essential. But in any event, football has changed such that the alchemic art of combining players and personalities no longer guarantees success.Which leaves us with talent ID, player quality and intelligence being the best coaching and tactics there are. Of the 78 players purchased post-Ferguson, only Bruno Fernandes and perhaps Zlatan Ibrahimovic could be classed as cast-iron successes, so the next man – assuming United don’t target Emma Hayes, who embodies more of the right stuff than almost anyone else – must have a keen nose. Even Jürgen Klopp, the other manager who fulfils these criteria – and of all the damage Ed Woodward wreaked on United, turning him off was most costly – benefited from a department which delivered the greatest run of transfers ever.View image in fullscreenGermany’s coach at the 2026 World Cup, Julian Nagelsmann, speaks to his squad. He is believed to be admired by Manchester United’s executives.Photograph: Pilar Olivares/ReutersWhich leaves Mauricio Pochettino, who built something at Tottenham despite the environment, and Julian Nagelsmann. But had Pochettino not signed a new contract with the USA men’s team, the sense is that, as when Mourinho arrived at Old Trafford after years of speculation, he’s past his magical best, while Nagelsmann may be the free-thinking genius of his own imagination, just as he may be an emperor’s new clothes bluffer.All of which is to say that failure has many fathers and, once ingrained, is not easily eradicated. Yet just as society has too much going for it to ever move quite beyond the pale, so too doesManchester United. Even the longest journey starts with one step; but does anyone have the nous to ensure it’s taken in the correct direction?Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickJim RatcliffecommentShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal’s Slegers hails ‘role model’ Russo after historic hat-trick sinks Benfica | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Alessia Russo’s hat-trick made her the highest English goalscorer in the Women’s Champions League, as Arsenal cruised to a 3-0 win against Benfica
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Alessia Russo’s hat-trick made her the highest English goalscorer in the Women’s Champions League, as Arsenal cruised to a 3-0 win against Benfica
Content: Alessia Russo (No 23) celebrates with her teammates after making it 2-0 against Benfica.Photograph: David Cliff/EPAView image in fullscreenAlessia Russo (No 23) celebrates with her teammates after making it 2-0 against Benfica.Photograph: David Cliff/EPAWomen's Champions LeagueArsenal’s Slegers hails ‘role model’ Russo after historic hat-trick sinks BenficaSophie Downeyat Mangata Developments StadiumWed 28 Oct 2026 18.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 20.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlessia Russo wrote herself into the history books once more as she became the highest English goalscorer in the Women’s Champions League. Her hat-trick gave Arsenal a vital 3-0 win against Benfica to send the Gunners up to second in the league phase table.“I’m so happy. I think we’ve found a nice dynamic as well with the last two games,” Russo’s manager, Renée Slegers, said. “She’s one of the leaders and she does it her way. She cares for everyone around her and connects well with her teammates. She leads the way as a role model, doing the right things consistently.”It was a statement performance from the 27-year-old who has shaken off the early-season cobwebs. Her three goals at Meadow Park on Wednesday took her tally up to 10 in her past seven appearances for club and country, hitting a rich vein of form just when Arsenal have needed her most.Arsenal 3-0 Benfica: Women’s Champions League – as it happenedRead moreIt is safe to say Arsenal’s season has yet to fully burst into life. Struggles in front of goal and unforced errors have defined the opening two months but the grittynorth London derby winon Saturday did feel like it could be a springboard for momentum.There was no less pressure coming into this Champions League match against Benfica, another must-win game with Arsenal’s European form mirroring their domestic struggles. A last-ditchwin against HB Køgeand a heartbreaking draw against Paris FC (in which they surrendered a two‑goal lead) left them fifth in the league phase table before kick-off, with Barcelona and OL Lyonnes looming.Slegers made three changes to freshen things up. Ona Batlle returned to her more natural right‑back role while the summer signings Élisa De Almeida and Géraldine Reuteler made their full debuts.Ivan Baptista’s Benfica arrived in confident form on the back of consecutive wins domestically. Slegers was keen to highlight their strong identity pre-match, having had first‑hand experience of their resilience in last year’s league phase. So it proved once more in a first half in which Arsenal dominated, but struggled to break through against a well-structured opposition.View image in fullscreenThe Arsenal head coach, Renée Slegers, has eased pressure on herself with back-to-back wins over Spurs and Benfica.Photograph: David Cliff/EPAIt was the visitors, in fact, who had the best opportunity of the first half hour. Frøya Dorsin was left beating the turf in frustration after spurning a glorious opportunity to catch out a stranded Misa Rodríguez with a lob. It was a moment that jolted Arsenal into life as they upped the tempo and began to rain pressure on Benfica’s goal. First Olivia Smith set up Russo for a low shot that went narrowly wide before Smith herself forced Lena Pauels into a fine save.Arsenal found their breakthrough just before half-time when Russo produced a sublime finish after a well‑worked move down the left.It was like a switch had flipped for Arsenal after the break as they exuded confidence, zipping the ball around the turf with increasing ease. Smith looked more and more comfortable in her central role while Caitlin Foord came alive down the left, the latter denied a clear shot by a superb last-ditch challenge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe conductor behind them all was Russo as she pressed and stretched the play to her tune. The captain on the night was at the heart of things once more as the hosts doubled their lead, rising high to glance home a corner. She completed her hat-trick shortly afterwards, converting from the spot after Foord was brought down by Catarina Amado.Quick GuideRoundup: Chelsea roll past Roma, Bayern and Real drawShowChelsea maintained their strong start to this year’s Women’s Champions League campaign as second-half goals from Ellie Carpenter [pictured, centre] and Kadeisha Buchanan secured a 2-0 win over Roma at Plough Lane.After a goalless first half, substitute Carpenter combined with Wieke Kaptein to open the scoring in the 51st minute. The Australian made a powerful run, found Kaptein and then met her cross from the right with a low shot which took a deflection off Roma defender Winonah Heatley before going in.Central defender Buchanan wrapped up the win in the 89th minute, heading home to ensure a second win in three European matches for Sonia Bompastor’s unbeaten team. Roma were left to rue chances missed by Maya Doms and Alayah Pilgrim as they extended their scoreless Champions League start to three games.'I’m pleased with the fact we scored really early in the second half. We could probably have killed the game a little bit earlier,' said the Chelsea head coach, Sonia Bompastor. 'It’s important for us in these games to be able to be clinical and ruthless as early as possible. But we find different ways to impose ourselves in the game and to score goals. So it’s good.'Bayern Munichfought back from two goals down to draw 2-2 againstReal Madridand preserve their unbeaten home record in the pre-knockout phase. Last season’s semi-finalists have now not lost any of their 17 home games in the group stage or league phase thanks to Momoko Tanikawa's second-half equaliser.Athenea del Castillo pounced from Linda Caicedo’s cross in the seventh minute, before Lineth Beerensteyn headed in from close range to double Madrid’s lead midway through the first half. Edna Imade nodded in to reduce the deficit on the half-hour and Tanikawa levelled soon after the restart, before Sophie Proost hit the post for Bayern in stoppage time.Eight-time championsLyonnescruised to an emphatic 6-0 home victory overInternazionale, with Marie-Antoinette Katoto scoring twice before Lily Yohannes made it three on the hour mark. Vicki Bècho came off the bench shortly after and hit a hat-trick as the French giants went top of the table on goal difference.Swiss sideServetteclaimed a historic maiden Champions League win at the ninth attempt as they brushed aside OH Leuven 5-1 in Geneva. Paola Hernández and Gloria Marinelli both struck twice to leave the Belgian champions winless so far in this season’s league phase.Press AssociationPhotograph: Andrew Redington/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.It was a finish that marked the 200th goal of Slegers’s tenure and one that further eases the pressure on the head coach. With every minute that passed the hosts looked increasingly like themselves and could have added more to their tally.“It looks like there is something off our shoulders,” Slegers said. “We were playing like us tonight and I am so happy. The players enjoyed themselves – they connected, they expressed themselves and they played with intensity. We backed the last performance up. We need to do it again at the weekend.”There will no doubt be sterner tests to come in Europe, more immediately away to Barcelona in a fortnight’s time, but this was a victory that signified something more important than just climbing up the Champions League table.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueArsenal WomenBenfica womenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Prem and RFU commit to expanding with English clubs after report of Welsh sides joining | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: After a report claimed two Welsh sides could join the Prem, a statement from Prem Rugby and the RFU said their focus was on supporting English clubs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After a report claimed two Welsh sides could join the Prem, a statement from Prem Rugby and the RFU said their focus was on supporting English clubs
Content: Cardiff’s Johan Mulder is tackled in last month’s game at Scarlets. Last week the WRU announced losses of £18.1m.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCardiff’s Johan Mulder is tackled in last month’s game at Scarlets. Last week the WRU announced losses of £18.1m.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena/The GuardianPrem RugbyPrem and RFU commit to expanding with English clubs after report of Welsh sides joiningReport claimed two Welsh sides could join PremJoint statement said ‘resources focused on English clubs’Press AssociationWed 28 Oct 2026 13.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 15.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrem Rugby and the Rugby Football Union have stated they are committed to expanding the top flight with English clubs in response to a report claiming that two Welsh sides could soon join the competition.According to the report, the Welsh Rugby Union is in advanced discussions with Prem Rugby and the RFU over the possibility of turning the Prem into a cross-border competition.England’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blowRead moreIt comes as the WRU wrestles with a financial crisis that saw it announce a loss of £18.1m for 2025-26 last week, a figure that it says strengthens its case to reduce the number of regions from four to three.The Prem is aiming to expand from 10 to 12 sides in time for the 2029-2030 season and English rugby’s governing bodies insist their priority is to back domestic teams.“Resources are currently focused on supporting English clubs throughout the pyramid who aspire to join the league,” they said in a joint a statement. “The Prem is an attractive league and responsibility for its expansion sits with the Men’s Professional Rugby Board, which has established detailed entry criteria that any prospective club would need to satisfy.”Joining the Prem could cost an interested club up to £23.5m, made up of the P-share that secures a percentage of central income and voting rights and the requirement to fund a Premiership Women’s Rugby programme.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe RFU would have to approve Welsh teams moving into the league due to it becoming a cross-border competition.Explore more on these
