title: Fleetwood go their own way to down Arsenal and live Carabao Cup dream | Soccer | The Guardian
description: In today’s Football Daily: Fleetwood’s fairytale night, Kylian Mbappé and Kai Rooney
Author: Barry Glendenning
Headline: In today’s Football Daily: Fleetwood’s fairytale night, Kylian Mbappé and Kai Rooney
Content: Fleetwood’s Raffaele Cirino gets gripped by a fan after the win over Arsenal.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFleetwood’s Raffaele Cirino gets gripped by a fan after the win over Arsenal.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesFootball Daily newsletterSoccerFleetwood go their own way to down Arsenal and live Carabao Cup dreamSign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!Barry GlendenningWed 28 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCODSWALLOPPEDHaving made a passing reference to Mick Fleetwood in Tuesday’s thrilling edition of your favourite email, Football Daily genuinely wasn’t expecting to be repeatedly typing that particular F-word in our lead story in today’s edition. While we were aware Arsenal were in the coastal town of Fleetwood for a Fizzy Cup tie that could scarcely have been less glamorous than the previous evening’s Ballon d’Or ceremony at the Palladium, the needle on our patented Potential Shock-o-Meter had barely moved before a match pitting the Premier League champions against a side struggling in League Two. Even with the residual winds from Storm Boelo still buffeting the ground, we presumed Arsenal’s second string would have enough about them to record a comfortable win at Highbury, over 20 years after they left a London stadium of the same name to begin their residency at the Emirates. It was not to be and almost five months to the day since exiting a cup competition on penalties following a curiously flat and uninspired display, Mikel Arteta’s side exited a cup competition on penalties following etc, and so on.Considering their team came into this game on the back of consecutive defeats by Cheltenham and Exeter, Fleetwood’s Cod Army would almost certainly have settled for seeing their players avoid embarrassment but after watching them go ahead against a team of Fancy Dans who were visibly labouring in the miserable conditions expectations were duly raised. Arsenal equalised courtesy of a scrambled Viktor Gyökeres effort that is unlikely to trouble the Puskas Award jury, before all hell broke loose when young Max Dowman was sent off for retaliation following a Harrison Neal challenge that – depending entirely on what team you support – was a potential career-ender or wasn’t even a foul. While he is not yet old enough to drive, get a tattoo or vote, Dowman has apparently been around long enough to earn himself a stinging rebuke from his manager, whoconveyed the impression the 16-year-old could look forward to being sent to bed without any supperand having his screen-time vastly reduced.Max Dowman’s Fleetwood fracas leaves him, Arsenal and Arteta red-facedRead moreA penalty shootout in which yet another Brazilian missed a crucial spot-kick for the Gunners ended in victory for Fleetwood, when Conor Haughey fired past Illan Meslier to make it five successful kicks out of five for the hosts. The second teenager to disgrace himself on the night, the young man from Norn Iron proceeded to drop a different kind of F-bomb in a post-match interview with Sky Sports. Asked what had been going through his mind before he took his penalty, Haughey replied: “Hit the top corner and run like f**k.”Despite the post-watershed lateness of the hour, Sky’s pitchside reporter felt compelled to apologise to viewers for the youngster’s forthright response. While Arteta is left to focus on making sure his players get their act together ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool, Fleetwood head coach, Matt Lawlor, can look forward to tonight’s quarter-final draw. “I’ve got no preference whatsoever,” he said. “We’ve got a big game at home [against Bristol Rovers] on Saturday and I want to win it. I would absolutely love to make an amazing night into an amazing week.” For Arsenal, on a night when heroes were hard to find, the dream of a domestic treble went its own way.LIVE ON BIG WEBSITEThe MBM OGs are in tandem tonight for steaming hot live action. Join Scott Murray from 8pm GMT for Carling Cup fourth-round updates from Liverpool 3-2 Chelsea  while Rob Smyth will be on deck at the same time to talk us through Arsenal 1-1 Benfica in the Women’s Champions League.QUOTE OF THE DAY“Our club holds deep respect for China, its history, its culture, and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid. The club joins the public apology expressed by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself has conveyed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people” – Real Madrid are in crisis PR mode as Mbappé’s Chairman Mao comments reach the second day of saying sorry.View image in fullscreenFallen idol.Photograph: Wu Hao/EPAFOOTBALL DAILY LETTERSdouble quotation markYour headlineMbappé’s China Crisisleads me to point out he was born in Paris and is not one half of a synth pop duo from Kirkby, Merseyside – Kev The Poet, Tiverton (born in Kirkby).double quotation markSo pathetic Arsenal get knocked out of the Carabao Cup by plucky Fleetwood Town. I think that Michael Carrick should be sacked immediately! – Nigel Sanders.double quotation markThe Nevada in Florida storyreminded me of my coaching time with under-11s in Maryland in the 90s. The rule from the league was clear, if you’re leading by six goals at half-time, take off the star(s) for the second half. Football was designed to develop as well as to win. As for parents, I had them stand in an area I designated where during game-time they could encourage their scions but not encroach. This was unusual but they understood this strange Brit in a faraway land and it worked well for everyone. Happy times and no police needed, except welcomed as parents! – Jeremy Foxon.double quotation markRegarding the quote of the day from Wayne Rooney inyesterday’s Football Daily, he seems to be inferring that players from Brentford and Wolves are not good enough for Manchester United. This is from a man who signed for said United in the summer of 2004 from Everton, who (checks online encyclopaedia) finished 17th in the Premier League a couple of months earlier. Pot/kettle? – Tracey in Leicester.If you have any, please send letters tothe.boss@theguardian.com.Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Kev The Poet. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, arehere.This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version,just visit this page and follow the instructions.Explore more on these topicsFootballFootball Daily newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership: McInnes booed in Rangers draw at Hearts, Celtic held at home | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Derek McInnes was booed on his return to Tynecastle, where Rangers drew 2-2, which was also the score between Celtic and Dundee United
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Derek McInnes was booed on his return to Tynecastle, where Rangers drew 2-2, which was also the score between Celtic and Dundee United
Content: Olwethu Makhanya jumps between two Hearts defenders for Rangers’ second.Photograph: Zak Mauger/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOlwethu Makhanya jumps between two Hearts defenders for Rangers’ second.Photograph: Zak Mauger/Getty ImagesScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership: McInnes booed in Rangers draw at Hearts, Celtic held at homeDerek McInnes returns to Tynecastle for 2-2 drawMartin O’Neill ‘disappointed’ by Dundee United resultAgencies andGuardian sportWed 28 Oct 2026 19.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 20.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlwethu Makhanya scored a late equaliser asRangersearned a 2-2 draw withHeartson the much-hyped Tynecastle return for Derek McInnes.The Rangers manager was booed loudly by the home support as he emerged from the tunnel for his first match back since leaving for Ibrox in June, just weeks after the Edinburgh side were pipped to theScottish Premiershiptitle.Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties yet again to secure Carabao Cup progressRead moreHowever, his team silenced a pumped-up home crowd when Kevin Kelsy scored a 16th-minute opener after a lapse from Laurent Mendy.Hearts turned the game round with goals from Cláudio Braga and Calvin Miller early in the second half. But Makhanya’s 89th-minute header ensured the match ended all square, keeping second-placed Rangers four points behindCelticand four above Hearts.Celticshowed their mettle as they fought back to grab a 2-2 draw withDundee Unitedat Parkhead.The Colombian striker Camilo Durán put Martin O’Neill’s team ahead in the 18th minute with his 11th goal of the season. But the Australian forward Zac Sapsford levelled in the 28th minute with a header before the defender Neil Farrugia put the visitors in front three minutes later with his first goal for the club.Celtic piled forward in the second half and the defender Liam Scales equalised with a 64th-minute header. O’Neill said: “We cannot control anything that’s happening elsewhere. The disappointment and the frustration comes from not winning a home game.“That’s really it. But considering the trials and tribulations over the last number of weeks, yeah, I’m not totally dissatisfied. We conceded some poor goals, but we fought back and I just thought we were going to win it. But in the end we could have lost it too, on the break. I thought Dundee United were very dangerous and they played very well in the game.”View image in fullscreenCeltic’s Liam Scales rises highest to make it 2-2 against Dundee United.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAStephen Robinson, theAberdeenmanager, admitted his side were not good enough in the 1-0 defeat byFalkirk, but refused to shout and scream at his players in the aftermath.Ben Brauhaus, on as a substitute, scored the only goal of the game, side-footing into the bottom-left corner from the centre of the box after 73 minutes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRobinson, though, felt his side should have scored from at least one of their chances before then, saying: “Not good enough. We got what we deserved. We had four chances we should score. We had four great chances from inside the penalty spot, and we should score.“All four are very, very easy chances. We don’t do that, they take their one chance, and that’s why you don’t win football matches.”Ash Hay piled more pressure on theKilmarnockmanager, Neil McCann, after scoring a late double to earnDundeea 3-1 win at Dens Park. His strikes, in the 83rd minute and the fifth minute of added time, gave his side the win after Joe Hugill’s 75th-minute penalty.Hibernianmoved off the bottom of the table as they drew 1-1 atSt Mirrento secure Marink Reedijk’s first point as manager. Marko Ivezic put Hibs ahead but Jason Kerr’s own goal denied them a third league win this season.Motherwellended a six-match losing run but they were denied a victory as Josh Campbell’s 93rd-minute equaliser forSt Johnstoneearned them a 2-2 draw. Taylor Steven had given the home side the lead before Ibrahim Said and Tawanda Maswanhise turned the scoreline around. However, Campbell’s late header sealed a point.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipHeartsRangersCelticDundee UnitedAberdeenFalkirknewsShareReuse this content

title: British racing chief warns budget tax hike may have ‘devastating’ impact on sport | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Horse racing’s ruling body will ‘urgently engage with the government’ after the duty on the profits from fixed-odds gaming machines was raised in the budget
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Horse racing’s ruling body will ‘urgently engage with the government’ after the duty on the profits from fixed-odds gaming machines was raised in the budget
Content: The 5% increase in duty on fixed-odds gaming machines could close betting shops, which provide a third of British racing’s £350m annual income.Photograph: Daniel Hambury/PAView image in fullscreenThe 5% increase in duty on fixed-odds gaming machines could close betting shops, which provide a third of British racing’s £350m annual income.Photograph: Daniel Hambury/PAHorse racingBritish racing chief warns budget tax hike may have ‘devastating’ impact on sportCall for urgent talks after gaming machines tax increaseBrant Dunshea: ‘thousands’ of betting shops may closeGreg WoodWed 28 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrant Dunshea, chief executive of theBritish Horseracing Authority, said on Wednesday that the sport’s ruling body will “urgently engage with the government to establish how we can work together to reduce the impact” after John Healey, in his first budget as chancellor, raised the duty on the profits from fixed-odds gaming machines in betting shops from 20% to 25%.The widely expected rise in machine games duty (MGD) was well below the doubling of the rate, from 20% to 40%, recommended this year by the Social Market Foundation thinktank, but Dunshea warned that the move could “still prove devastating for our sport” since it presented a “clear risk” that “hundreds, if not thousands” of betting shops nationwide faced closure as a result.Bookies fear budget hit but gaming machine self-harm killed off the old-fashioned shopsRead moreThere are about 5,500 betting shops in the UK and the average shop contributes approximately £25,000 to racing annually via the levy and rights payments for live coverage and data.“British racing derives nearly a third of its £350m annual income from betting via high street shops,” Dunshea said, “[and] is now set to potentially lose £57m a year, based on independent modelling that was shared with the Treasury before today’s budget.“While the MGD rate increase is not as severe as some called for, this change could still prove devastating for the future of our sport, impacting prize money, the viability of racecourses, thousands of jobs and vital horse welfare projects and research.“[Closures] will also significantly impact a large part of the sport’s fanbase for whom a visit to their local bookie is the primary way they engage with horse racing.”Quick GuideGreg Wood's Thursday tipsShowBath: 12.42Silent Wisdom1.12Space Bob1.42Ground Force2.12Spirit Lead Me2.42The Dark Baron3.12Nogo’s Dream3.42Barnsnape Boy4.12Legendsoftheland title: Carey and Inglis counterpunch to put Australia on top in South Africa | Australia cricket team | The Guardian
description: Keepers rebuild the innings to reach 330 for four at the close Green sparkles but Labuschagne duck is ominous
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Keepers rebuild the innings to reach 330 for four at the close Green sparkles but Labuschagne duck is ominous
Content: Australia's Josh Inglis hits out on day two of the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town.Photograph: Halden Krog/APView image in fullscreenAustralia's Josh Inglis hits out on day two of the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town.Photograph: Halden Krog/APAustralia cricket teamCarey and Inglis counterpunch to put Australia on top in South AfricaKeepers rebuild the innings to reach 330-4 at the closeGreen sparkles but Labuschagne duck must be the endGeoff LemonWed 28 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Cape Town’s first daywas a rollercoaster, the second was some more sedate form of transport, though it continued with ups and downs fitting its mountainous backdrop. Twice, South Africa produced double strikes to stall promising Australian positions; twice the Australians rebuilt. Finally, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey pushed Australia in front, 330 for four to South Africa’s all out 329, ready to surge on through day three with those six wickets left in hand.While Travis Head was there, Australia’s first session threatened to match South Africa’s the day before, when Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman had piled on 140 against a bewildered attack. Head threw his hands at width, mixing luck with skill for seven boundaries. His new foil Matthew Renshaw showed contrasting temperament for the opening role, leaving and defending the new ball with the clarity he had shown in the middle order in Durban, underlining why he was the original candidate to replace Jake Weatherald at the top before the selectors’ brief and ill-fated Nic Maddinson excursion.Australia reach 330-4, one run ahead of South Africa on the second day of the third men’s Test – as it happenedRead moreHead’s contribution of 41 out of 58 will continue debate about his batting position. It’s clear at a glance, given an opener’s average of 49 is titanic by modern standards, but the detail is stark: that average breaks down to 23 in the first innings of a match, 43 in the second, 71 in the third, and 60 in the fourth. Head smashes up teams later in games set up to suit his approach, but hasn’t batted time when doing so is essential in tricky early conditions. Having more of a shield up top, leaving Head to plunder in the middle, may still be the best use of a precious resource.There is also his current problem with chopping on to his stumps, today via an awkward cut against Simon Harmer’s off-spin. That makes eight times bowled in his last 15 dismissals, up from 20 out of 66 before that span. Harmer struck again in the same over, teasing Marnus Labuschagne into a catch at slip on what must be Labuschagne’s last chance at Test cricket before the opportunity comes to blood a replacement during the Australian summer.Labuschagne’s problem is not so much the duck, which can happen to anyone, but its tentative provenance: a player who has trained so hard to move dynamically against spin had both feet in cement, poking uselessly at a ball that would have carried on past the stumps. In theory, he has one more innings left to save himself, but that was the shot of a player who is in no state to use it.Cameron Green arrived for a rebuild, but South Africa were fuming after the third umpire denied a catch from Gerald Coetzee’s bowling. Harmer at second slip was convinced, and replays looked identical to precedents where a player with fingers flat on the ground gets the ball to bounce up into their palms. This time it wasn’t given. Australia added 85 before the stand ended, including an explosive over when Green hooked the returning Rabada’s bouncer barrage, with some risk, for a consecutive six, six, and four.View image in fullscreenSouth Africa’s Simon Harmer celebrates after dismissing Australia’s Marnus Labuschagne.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesHarmer also had Renshaw given not out to a gorgeous ball that drifted across the left-hander, spun back past the edge, and hit his back pad, but was umpire’s call for height. It was Marco Jansen who ended the frustration, needing third-umpire recourse to prove that extra bounce had nicked the top edge of Renshaw’s half-hearted uppercut, then in Jansen’s next over, Harmer at slip inked in the Green catch that had been whited out. Just before tea, Australia’s set pair had been removed for 74 and 65. Still trailing South Africa by 144, at 185 for four, more was needed.It came from Inglis and Carey, both wicketkeeper-batters, though Inglis adopted the traditional counterpunching style of their kind, while Carey tended more to defence between moments of creative scoring. Again a partnership grew with both contributors heading towards half-centuries. Harmer was milked, Rabada remained ineffective, and as Inglis opened out after passing 50, he hit a six off both, and consecutive fours cutting Coetzee.There were moments of peril mixed in, like Harmer spinning one back to Inglis that almost took off-stump, and a couple of top edges that landed safe, but Australia’s scoring kept the field spread, and unlike Mitchell Starc’s demolition derby with the new ball the previous evening, South Africa’s use of it just sped up the scoring. By stumps the stand was 145, with Carey 51 and Inglis 85, and after captain Pat Cummins was sufficiently unsure of his batting that he chose to bowl on day one, the new configuration had come good on day two. Next is whether day three sees Australia move into a decisive lead, or whether South Africa can rein them in.Explore more on these topicsAustralia cricket teamSouth Africa cricket teamAustralia sportCricketmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: London Broncos to go without £1.3m RFL funding if they enter Super League next year  | Rugby league | The Guardian
description: London Broncos have agreed to a condition from the existing 14 Super League clubs that they must relinquish any rights to around £1.3m in central distribution funding if they are to enter the competition in 2027
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: London Broncos have agreed to a condition from the existing 14 Super League clubs that they must relinquish any rights to around £1.3m in central distribution funding if they are to enter the competition in 2027
Content: Sam Davis of London Broncos celebrates with the Championship Grand Final trophy earlier this month.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSam Davis of London Broncos celebrates with the Championship Grand Final trophy earlier this month.Photograph: Olly Hassell/SWpix.com/ShutterstockRugby leagueLondon Broncos to go without £1.3m RFL funding if they enter Super League next yearRugby Football League set to ratify elevation imminentlyPartnership with NRL not expected now till 2028Aaron BowerWed 28 Oct 2026 10.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon Broncos have agreed to a condition from the existing 14 Super League clubs that they must relinquish any rights to about £1.3m in central distribution funding if they are to enter the competition in 2027, with the Rugby Football League expected to ratify their elevation imminently.A partnership betweenSuper Leagueand Australia’s National Rugby League (NRL), which would mean the latter taking administrative control of the English game and injecting tens of millions of pounds of much-needed financial support, is now not expected to begin until 2028. Despite that, the expansion of Super League to 15 teams to include London has moved a step closer.London Broncos graded below Barrow but still set for Super League placeRead moreMany of the existing top-flight clubs were aware the NRL would insist on London’s inclusion in Super League when a partnership eventually starts. It was initially suspected that would be in 2027, but the two competitions have failed to agree a deal in time, though the NRL will assist in ensuring four Super League games per week are shown on Dazn next year.That partnership not beginning until 2028 appeared to have consigned London to another season in the Championship, which they won at a canter this year. But Super League clubs informed the Broncos they would still be willing to include them on the proviso they came in with zero distribution. The other 14 clubs currently get around £1.3m in central funding.It is understood that London have now accepted those terms. They were only due to get around £140,000 in distribution had they remained in the Championship, such is the harsh financial reality of life outside Super League. But London were also fearful they would lose their best playing talent if they decided against agreeing to the stringent financial conditions.York and Toulouse joined Super League with half the central distribution of the other teams, around £650,000, this year when the competition expanded to 14 teams. It will now grow again with London set to be included as a 15th team – with Super League clubs now ultimately expected to vote on expansion shortly.Super League clubs cannot handpick new teams though, only decide on the size of the league. That decision will then go to the RFL, who will launch a process to decide the 15th team. The governing body would probably use the IMG gradings system which decides the makeup of Super League as a metric for London’s elevation.Broncos actually finished 16th in this year’s gradings but the team that finished 15th, Barrow, have already saidthey are not ready for Super League. Their facilities also do not meet minimum standards – meaning the RFL can approach London as next in the pecking order and invite them into Super League.Explore more on these topicsRugby leagueLondon BroncosSuper LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: RFK Jr assailed over ‘wildly racist tirade’ about Arabs at Michigan campaign stop | Robert F Kennedy Jr | The Guardian
description: US health secretary falsely claims at Mike Rogers rally that Arabs have never won major prizes in science or literature
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: US health secretary falsely claims at Mike Rogers rally that Arabs have never won major prizes in science or literature
Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr speaks at a campaign rally on Friday at Alico Arena on the campus of Florida Gulf Coast University in Fort Myers, Florida.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr speaks at a campaign rally on Friday at Alico Arena on the campus of Florida Gulf Coast University in Fort Myers, Florida.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APRobert F Kennedy JrRFK Jr assailed over ‘wildly racist tirade’ about Arabs at Michigan campaign stopUS health secretary falsely claims at Mike Rogers rally that Arabs have never won major prizes in science or literatureRichard LuscombeWed 28 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, faced backlash on Wednesday for a “wildly racist tirade” during a campaign stop inMichiganin which he falsely asserted that Arabs never won leading awards in science or literature.Kennedy was speaking at the Monday night event in Grand Rapids in support of Mike Rogers, the Republican US Senate candidate trailing his Democratic midterms opponentAbdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, in polling.“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the ⁠Nobel prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf prize, they don’t produce literature,” Kennedy said.Afactcheckpublished on Tuesday by the Associated Press showed that Arabs have won, or been shortlisted, for all those awards in recent years.The ⁠Council on American-Islamic Relations called Kennedy’s Islamophobic remarks “a ⁠textbook display of ​unvarnished racism and bigotry”, and the US healthcare advocacy organization Protect Our Care condemned his “wildly racist tirade”.JD Vance steps up extreme attacks on Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-SayedRead moreHillary Scholten, a Democratic congresswoman representing west Michigan, whodeclined to endorseEl-Sayed this summer,said Kennedy’s comments were “disgraceful and have no place in public service”.In astatementposted to her Facebook page late Tuesday, Scholten said: “As secretary of health and human services, he has a responsibility to serve all Americans, not use his position to demean entire communities with bigoted and demonstrably false claims.“Arab Americans are our neighbors, colleagues, health care professionals, scientists, educators, and public servants. Their contributions to science, literature, medicine, and countless other fields are undeniable.“The last I checked, Secretary Kennedy has neither a medical degree nor a Nobel peace prize, and his rhetoric has undermined public confidence in health science. Maybe he should sit this one out.”Kennedy’s comments came as part of an attack on theMuslim Brotherhood, a global Islamic group with branches that have beendesignated terrorist organizationsby the US government.The rise of the group had “created stagnant societies”, Kennedy said, ending what he called “a golden age [in which] Islamic lands were the center, the foundation for art and literature and science and engineering, and they were highly tolerant and pluralistic and cosmopolitan”.Other Trump administration officials havetried to paintEl-Sayed as a supporter of Islamic radicalism, including the president himself, who at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan,on Sundaycalled the Democrat “a jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJD Vance, the vice-president,escalatedthe inflammatory attacks at an event in Howell, Michigan, on Tuesday, during which he sought to connect El-Sayed’s politics to violent leftwingprotestsin Paris that saw thousands arrested.“I guarantee you, if those rioters were burning down New York, or Detroit, the Hasan Pikers and El-Sayeds would be right there leading them and cheering them on,” Vance said, referring toPiker, an outspoken socialist commentator andinfluencer.Rogers has also spoken out against El-Sayed’s alleged links to the Muslim Brotherhood, despitequestionsover his own relationship with the group. In 2012, as chair of the House intelligence committee, he said the US should have talks with the movement after Mohamed Morsi, who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood, won the Egyptian election.El-Sayed hasrepeatedly deniedany ties to the group, and disavowed it in a town hall event in Michigan last week that went viral for aconfrontation over the issuewith a heckler whoturned outto be a former aide to Josh Hawley, the Republican US senator for Missouri.Chris Murphy, the US senator for Connecticut who joined other senior Democratic politicians canvassing for El-Sayed inMichiganlast week, also condemned Kennedy’s comments.“I really think ​everyone needs to pay ‌attention to this coordinated campaign ​to delegitimize Muslim Americans, ​not just as citizens but as humans,” he said,reportedby Reuters.Explore more on these topicsRobert F Kennedy JrMichiganTrump administrationRepublicansUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026IslamophobianewsShareReuse this content

title: Tory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy Burnham | Politics | The Guardian
description: Prime minister warns cabinet not to express opinions about future relationship with Brussels before review of options
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Prime minister warns cabinet not to express opinions about future relationship with Brussels before review of options
Content: Brexit was the main subject of Andy Burnham’s exchanges with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions today.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrexit was the main subject of Andy Burnham’s exchanges with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions today.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersPoliticsTory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy BurnhamPrime minister warns cabinet not to express opinions about future relationship with Brussels before review of optionsPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this.Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote.A Downing Street summary of the cabinet meeting put his comments about Brexit above even those concerning the budget, which the chancellor, John Healey, was to deliver soon afterwards.“The prime minister opened by setting out how he would shortly write to cabinet on the UK’s relationship with the EU,” it said, adding: “He said the Brexit deal left by the last government had been bad for the UK and had led to a harder Brexit than had been promised at the referendum.”View image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among ministers said to be concerned about the implications of a revised Brexit deal.Photograph: James McCauley/ShutterstockThe letter to ministers made similar points, and ended with a warning from Burnham that they should not express opinions about the future shape of relations with the EU before a review of longer-term options.“It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period,” he said. “It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.”It follows reportsthat some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the idea of a revised deal potentially bringing back the free movement of people to and from the EU, something Burnhamhas talked upas a possibility.The letter set out Burnham’s two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will stay within Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement – a process that will formally kick off when the prime minister attends a European summit next month.Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail.“I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain,” he said in the letter. “It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We hope the summit will lead to some important, concrete steps. Beyond it, we will need to consider the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan. I will set out the next steps for this process around the summit.“Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.”Any fundamental changes in the relationship “would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament”, he wrote, adding: “This is government policy to which cabinet collective responsibility applies.”Challenged by Badenoch atPMQsabout his Brexit plans, Burnham reiterated his criticism of the current deal, saying the UK “was paralysed by the party opposite” in the wake of the referendum.In response, Badenoch said that Burnham had been using freedoms allowed under Brexit, for example, the ability to remove VAT from energy bills: “What he should be saying is: ‘Thank you.’”Explore more on these topicsPoliticsEuropeAndy BurnhamLabourBrexitEuropean UnionForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC allegations cost Tory and Reform donor a peerage, defamation trial told | BBC | The Guardian
description: Mohamed Amersi is suing over Panorama episode that made claims of his suspected involvement in corruption
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Mohamed Amersi is suing over Panorama episode that made claims of his suspected involvement in corruption
Content: Mohamed Amersi donated £25,000 to Reform UK last year and has previously donated to the Conservatives.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMohamed Amersi donated £25,000 to Reform UK last year and has previously donated to the Conservatives.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesBBCBBC allegations cost Tory and Reform donor a peerage, defamation trial toldMohamed Amersi is suing over Panorama episode that made claims of his suspected involvement in corruptionDaniel BoffeyChief reporterWed 28 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Conservative andReform UKdonor lost out on a knighthood and a peerage amid claims of his involvement in corruption, the high court has heard at the start of his defamation case against the BBC.An episode of Panorama in 2021 and aBBCarticle caused “very serious harm” to Mohamed Amersi, his barrister, Oliver Powell, said on Wednesday.The programme and article alleged strong grounds for suspecting that during Amersi’s work for the Swedish telecoms company Telia he was involved in deals that he knew or should have known were corrupt or involved corrupt payments.In an opening statement to the high court at the start of a seven-week defamation trial, Powell said the claims made by the BBC went to the heart of Amersi’s reputation and integrity.The barrister read a witness statement from Amersi, who donated £25,000 to Reform UK last year and who previously donated hundreds of thousands of pounds to theConservatives. The businessman claimed in the statement he had been forced by the publicity to step aside from what he described as his educational philanthropy.Amersi said the “scandal cost me a knighthood and a peerage” and that he was debanked by Union Bancaire Privée of Switzerland.The BBC, which is defending its content on the grounds of truth and public interest, claimed there was no evidence that Amersi suffered serious reputational harm either from its programme – Pandora Papers: Political Donors Exposed – or the article, which remains online.In its skeleton defence, the BBC said “no corroborating documentary evidence to support Mr Amersi’s assertions has been disclosed” and suggested there were factual inaccuracies in his statement.The focus of the BBC’s reporting in 2021 was Amersi’s work as an adviser to Telia, then known as TeliaSonera, in Uzbekistan along with a payment of $220m (£165m) made in January 2010 to a Gibraltar company called Takilant.Powell told the court: “The BBC’s case is that the real beneficial owner of Takilant was actually Gulnara Karimova, the eldest daughter of the president of Uzbekistan. And it is their case that she is said to have had influence over the regulator of the Uzbek telecommunications sector.“Mr Amersi will say that neither he nor Telia knew or suspected that Ms Karimova was the ultimate beneficial owner of Takilant and there was no basis for saying that he should have known.”Powell said the BBC was relying on admissions by Telia to the US Department of Justice in 2017 in a deferred prosecution agreement. The BBC was suggesting that this offered evidence that the $220m was a bribe, Powell said. He said any such admissions were untested “hearsay” and the court should give them “little or no weight”.Powell pointed to a legal review commissioned by Telia, which did interview Amersi, and was “unable to determine with any certainty that there was any legal or financial connection between Takilant and Gulnara Karimova”.In its defence, the BBC has claimed that Telia “entered into a whole series of corrupt deals and payments for the benefit of its businesses in (variously) Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Nepal”.Amersi claims that the BBC has failed to provide any evidence of his knowledge or involvement in corruption in any of those countries, claiming that his “work for Telia in Uzbekistan was very limited in scope during a very short period of fewer than six weeks in December 2009 and 2010”.Amersi further claims there is “no contemporaneous (or other) evidence to suggest that [he] knew or should have known that Takilant was secretly owned (as the defendant claims) by Karimova”.He has claimed that the BBC “seriously misled its readers and viewers by suggesting that [he] had been centrally involved in the payment of a ‘bribe’ to Karimova”.The court heard from Amersi’s barrister that the BBC was offering “inference and generalised suspicion rather than any evidential foundation” in seeking to defend its reporting.Amersi is seeking damages, “including aggravated damages”, and an injunction to prevent further publication of the statements he argues are defamatory. He will give evidence for six days from 11 November.The case continues.Explore more on these topicsBBCConservativesReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to Miami | Flávio Bolsonaro | The Guardian
description: Far-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via Ecuador
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Far-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via Ecuador
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro steps off a plane after arriving at the Miami-Opa Locka airport in Florida on Wednesday.Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro steps off a plane after arriving at the Miami-Opa Locka airport in Florida on Wednesday.Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty ImagesFlávio BolsonaroFlávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to MiamiFar-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via EcuadorTiago Rogeroin Brasília andJoseph Contrerasin MiamiWed 28 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonarodeclared himself the “true president” ofBrazilafter losing last Sunday’s presidential election and fleeing to the United States.After landing on a private jet with his family in Miami,Florida, on Wednesday morning, the far-right senator published the claim in a letter – even though his own party has recognised the legitimate victory ofLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, as have all of Brazil’s institutions, and international observers who monitored and endorsed the vote.Brazil’s three main newspapers – Folha de S.Paulo, O Globo and O Estado de S.Paulo – all described Bolsonaro’s declaration as “coup-mongering”.The senator later deleted the letter and published a new one in which, instead of calling himself the “true president”, he described himself as “the leader of Brazil”.Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in picturesRead moreAfter losingSunday’s runoff voteto Lula, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.From there he boarded a Gulfstream IV, registered LV-JQW, which had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian presidentJair Bolsonaro, took off on the jet with his wife and two teenage daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil in Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador and continued on to the Miami-Opa Locka airport, a private aviation hub about 11 miles north of downtown Miami catering to corporate executives and wealthy travelers.Bolsonaro, wearing a black bulletproof vest and looking somber, and his family emerged from the plane into a postcard-perfect sunny southFloridamorning at 9.24am. They briefly remained inside the airport before leaving, shielded by black umbrellas, climbing into a dark gray Ford Expedition Max and speeding away under police escort.Bolsonaro said nothing to reporters before boarding the vehicle and the mood was low-key, without any supporters present to welcome him and only two dozen journalists who were kept at a distance by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents.In the letter, published about seven hours after his arrival, Bolsonaro also thanked Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, “for his courage, sense of justice and legality”, and Donald Trump “and the wonderful American people for welcoming me”.He again repeated, without evidence, his claim that there had been “electoral fraud” – a claim rejected by Brazil’s electoral court and supreme court, as well as the presidents of the lower house and senate. Bolsonaro’s party said on Monday: “We recognise the presidential result.”At least three different versions of the letter were published by Bolsonaro and his allies, including one that used the country’s pre-1968 name and the English spelling “Brazil” rather than the Portuguese “Brasil” – which some saw as another sign of the Bolsonaro clan’s subservience to the US.Brazilian newspapers reported that Bolsonaro and his family had been granted humanitarian visas in the US. On Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.View image in fullscreenLula greets supporters while celebrating his birthday and re-election on 27 October 2026.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty Images“They’re fine people. … I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flávio a little bit. I know the father very well,” the US president said.On Wednesday, however, when asked about Bolsonaro’s claim, Trump said he would stay out of Brazil’s post-election turmoil.“Well, I’m not going to make a comment about that, but I know that we gave him a pass to come into the country, so we’ll see,” he said. “But I won’t get involved. It was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan to go through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him from leaving the country.There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies, at about 6pm on Monday, and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.The Argentinian newspaper Página/12reportedthat the aircraft belonged to the businessman Sergio Daniel Mastropietro, who was investigated by local police in one of the biggest scandals of Javier Milei’s administration, involving the allegedpayment of bribeslinked to the purchase of medicines for people with disabilities.Bolsonaro is under investigation in at least two criminal cases, one of them examining suspicions that the senator was involved in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.It was in connection with that case that, shortly after the election result, Brazilian police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.O Globo newspaperreportedthat the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.Fleeing Brazil has almost become standard practice among Bolsonaro supporters facing criminal charges or convictions in the country: about a dozen politicians or influencers closely aligned with Jair Bolsonaro havedone the samein recent years.The former president himself spent three months in Florida shortly after losing the 2022 election. He later returned to Brazil and, while facing trial over the attempted coup,spent two nightsat the Hungarian embassy in Brasília, then run by his ally Viktor Orbán.While under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison, the patriarch of the Bolsonaro clan used asoldering ironin an attempt to destroy his electronic ankle monitor.Explore more on these topicsFlávio BolsonaroBrazilMiamiFloridaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman woke up to see stranger invited into bedroom by husband, court hears | England | The Guardian
description: Jury at Winchester crown court sees video evidence by Joanne Young in trial of four men accused of sexual assault
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Jury at Winchester crown court sees video evidence by Joanne Young in trial of four men accused of sexual assault
Content: From left, top: Connor Sanderson Doyle, 32, and Norman Macksoni, 48; bottom, from left: Mohammed Hassan, 38, and Richard Wilkins, 62.Composite: PAView image in fullscreenFrom left, top: Connor Sanderson Doyle, 32, and Norman Macksoni, 48; bottom, from left: Mohammed Hassan, 38, and Richard Wilkins, 62.Composite: PAEnglandWoman woke up to see stranger invited into bedroom by husband, court hearsJury at Winchester crown court sees video evidence by Joanne Young in trial of four men accused of sexual assaultSteven MorrisWed 28 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman who was allegedly sexually assaulted by men invited by her ex-husband into their family home described how she would wake in the middle of the night restrained and blindfolded and feeling “hazy”.Joanne Young said that on one occasion she managed to remove her blindfold and was shocked to glimpse a stranger in her bedroom whom her then husband, Philip Young, had allegedly arranged to have sex with her.On another occasion she came around feeling “terrified”, with her husband asking her: “Wouldn’t you like it if somebody else was here?”Philip Young, 50, “advertised” Joanne Young on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court has heard.He has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of abuse, but four men who allegedly sexually assaulted Joanne Young, having been invited into the couple’s home by Philip Young, are on trial.Recorded video interviews of Joanne Young, 49, telling her story to the police were watched by the jury on Wednesday.Joanne Young said she and her husband had been married for 20 years and had three children. She said they were a straight, monogamous couple. “It was always just the two of us,” she said.On one occasion early on in their marriage, he “joked” about watching her when she was having sex with someone else but she “laughed it off”. She said: “That was never part of our relationship and was never going to be.”He liked to restrain and blindfold her during sex. “I didn’t object – it was fine,” she said.But she said she would wake up not knowing how she had come to be restrained. “I’d wake up and there would be a blindfold on and restraints and I wouldn’t always remember them going on. It was a bit like, when did that happen?” She described feeling “hazy” when she woke.View image in fullscreenPhilip Young, 50, will be sentenced after the four men’s trial.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAOn a night in February 2023, Joanne Young woke up and removed the blindfold and restraints. “I wasn’t comfortable,” she said. “I don’t know what was bothering me.”When she got the blindfold off, she realised there was a stranger in her room. Philip Young told the second person to “get down” and he ducked out of sight.“I was in shock,” said Joanne Young. “There was this man in my house and I was naked.” She hid in a bathroom and the next day asked her husband: “What was that?”He told her he had invited someone to watch them have sex. “I was shocked someone had been there. It was so intrusive.” He claimed it had not happened before. “I thought it was a one-off,” Joanne Young said.She said she decided to “stick my head in the sand” and carry on. “You can’t forgive. You have to hope it won’t happen again.”Joanne Young said that on the day of his arrest, her husband admitted to her that he had shared explicit images of her. “That was totally out of the blue. It was a kick in the stomach. How could he do that to me? That is so intimate. It’s not allowed.”She asked him if the incident in February was the only time such a thing had happened. Joanne Young said: “He stood there and looked at me and said: ‘No.’”After the arrest, Joanne Young recalled a “vague” incident some years before when she had woken up feeling “terrified” and saying: “No, no.”She said: “I remember him [Philip] saying: ‘Wouldn’t you like it if somebody else was here?’ I was scared.” The next day she put it down to a nightmare.Joanne Young briefly gave evidence in person on Wednesday afternoon, glancing occasionally towards the defendants in the dock. At one point Mr Justice Saini asked her to keep her voice up.When Tom Godfrey, the barrister for Mohammed Hassan, one of the defendants, asked about the incident in February 2023, she said that there were two people other than herself in the room, one who was touching her wrist and the other performing a sex act on her.Godfrey suggested the touch on her wrist may have been bedclothes. She replied: “I disagree – it was a hand around my wrist.”In statements read out in court, friends of the Youngs said the pair ran a business together and he was a school governor. Philip Young was described as opinionated and arrogant but had not shown misogynistic behaviour. During nights out he would often be on his mobile phone and some of them would wonder why.Jurors were also shown videos recorded by Philip Young allegedly showing three of the defendants allegedly sexually assaulting his wife. Some members of the panel looked distressed. Before the videos were played, the public gallery was cleared.Four men are charged with sexually assaulting Joanne Young jointly with Philip Young.Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, Wiltshire, denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016. Richard Wilkins, 62, of Toothill, Swindon, has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration in July 2016.Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. Hassan, 38, of Swindon, has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching in February 2023.Young will be sentenced after the trial.Explore more on these topicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Record-breaking high tides spark chaos – and kayak commutes – across California | California | The Guardian
description: Seawater surges into low-lying communities from San Diego to San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, homes and businesses
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: Seawater surges into low-lying communities from San Diego to San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, homes and businesses
Content: A resident walks through flood waters in Huntington Beach, California, on 28 October.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreenA resident walks through flood waters in Huntington Beach, California, on 28 October.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APCaliforniaRecord-breaking high tides spark chaos – and kayak commutes – across CaliforniaSeawater surges into low-lying communities from San Diego to San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, homes and businessesGabrielle Canonin San FranciscoWed 28 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHistoric high tides have caused chaos up and down theCaliforniacoast this week, as parts of the state were inundated by record-breaking water levels. Seawater surged into low-lying communities from San Diego to the San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, flooding homes and businesses, and jamming important transportation corridors and train routes.Trump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warnRead moreKayakers and paddle boarders could be seen gliding through typically busy thoroughfares in Marin county, north of San Francisco, on Monday and Tuesday. Several drivers had to be rescued from floating cars in the area, while cyclists who had attempted to cross the temporary lagoon that had formed quickly found themselves waist-deep. Further south, in cities such as Newport Beach, waterpounded the emergency infrastructureset up to keep out the swelling sea, which seeped through berms, seawalls and sandbag blockades along the shoreline.Up and down the state,all-time records were smashed. Near Los Angeles and San Diego, tides rose above 8ft. San Francisco registered its highest reading for the month of October on Wednesday, breaking a record set the day before.0:53Aerial video shows California flooding amid ‘record-breaking tides’ – videoThe National Weather Service has issued aswathe of flood advisories and warningsthat will last for days.In San Diego and Orange counties, forecasters said significant coastal flooding was expected during high tides through Thursday. “Numerous roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses, and some critical infrastructure will be inundated,” they said in a Wednesday outlook. In Los Angeles, moderate flood risks extended into the weekend, though tides would begin to drop after Thursday. Shoreline erosion is expected across the California coast.The repeated onslaught from the rising sea has made for a tumultuous autumn, especially in southern California, which has been hammered several times over the last two months. Los Angeleshas already logged 12 coastal flood daysin 2026, according to records from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) –outpacing any year in the last 50 – with months left to go.View image in fullscreenThe closed Pacific Coast Highway in the Sunset Beach community of Huntington Beach, California, on 27 October.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesBut the dangers won’t recede when the tides do, and the newly set records won’t be held for long. The worst flooding may be to come as severe impacts from an exceptionally strong and still-strengthening El Niño unfold in the months ahead, experts warned, with the potential to raise tides several feet above the levels recorded this week.“What we are seeing now could be the beginning of what could be significantly more disruptive conditions later this year,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said during an online briefing Tuesday.The sharply rising waters are the result of thermal expansion from a record-breaking oceanic heatwave layered on top of higher sea levels fueled by the human-caused climate crisis, Swain explained.A coastally trapped Kelvin wave– a massive underwater band of warm water that has crept across the Pacific and up the North American shoreline – has also added to the fray, and the California coast could see plenty more of them through the winter and into early next year. “I would expect these water levels to be exceeded multiple times this winter,” Swain said.View image in fullscreenPeople disembark from the Balboa Island ferry into a flooded street in Newport Beach, California, on 27 October.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersSan Diego, La Jolla, Los Angeles and Santa Monica all have abovean 80% chance of high tide flooding in Decemberaccording to a Noaa outlook. Most of the stations near coastal communities to the north, going all the way to the Canadian border, were in the 60-80% category.The floods seen this week were not so-called king tides, which are the highest predicted tides for the year.Those will show up right in time for busy holiday weekends, around Thanksgiving and Christmas this year, and around 20-23 January next year.King tides can add an additional foot or two to water levels, which are already elevated by roughly a foot due to human-caused warming, the effects from El Niño and Kelvin waves. If each of these layers align as they are expected to, they will create up to 5ft of sea level rise above average, in many places at once.View image in fullscreenFlood waters cover roads in Marin county as residents kayak on the bike trail between Sausalito and Mill Valley in California, on 27 October.Photograph: Tayfun Coşkun/Anadolu/Getty Images“We are well into extreme territory – and really in record-breaking territory,” Swain said. That will set the stage for disastrous flooding, should a storm arrive when waters are high.” Swain said that’s when things “get really hairy”.The historic El Niño brewing in the Pacific has the power to unleash extreme weather around the world, and in California that could mean supercharged storms. Southern California especially tends to get doused during the El Niños, and this year the climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer-than-average equatorial sea surface temperatures, could pack an extraordinary punch.Should a strong storm occur during the windows when the tides are highest, flooding could be disastrous. “There’s at least a 30-40% chance we stack all of these this winter, and potentially more than once,” Swain said.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaExtreme weatherOceansFloodingEl Niño southern oscillationWest CoastUS weatherShareReuse this content

title: How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon | Europe | The Guardian
description: Scientists uncover ancient hills and swamps that disappeared as sea levels rose across northern Adriatic
Author: Kate Ravilious
Headline: Scientists uncover ancient hills and swamps that disappeared as sea levels rose across northern Adriatic
Content: Gondolas wending through a canal in Venice, Italy.Photograph: Paulo Amorim/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGondolas wending through a canal in Venice, Italy.Photograph: Paulo Amorim/Getty ImagesTerrawatchEuropeHow rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoonScientists uncover ancient hills and swamps that disappeared as sea levels rose across northern AdriaticKate RaviliousWed 28 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVenice is famed for being a floating city, but research shows the land it sits on once lay many miles inland. Dramatic changes in sea level over 10,000 years have reshaped the northern Adriatic coastline, with much of the land that our ancestors roamed now lying beneath the waves.Samuele Ongaro, at the University of Southampton, and colleagues combined seismic data with sedimentary cores from the coastal basins of northernItaly, Slovenia and northern Croatia to model changes in sea level across the region and reconstruct past landscapes over the past 10,000 years.View image in fullscreenPicturesque canals and colourful rooftops in Murano, a historic old town in Venice.Photograph: Amazing Aerial/AlamyTheir results, published inQuaternary Science Reviews, show that the present-day Venice lagoon was once dry land extending more than 30 miles from the coast, and that Trieste was previously an area of hills overlooking swamps and lagoons.Starting just over 10,000 years ago, sea level rose in fits and starts, sometimes by up to 25mm a year, forcing Mesolithic hunter-gatherer populations to shift their hunting and fishing activities as they adapted to a rapidly changing environment. The most dramatic changes occurred in three distinct phases, followed by a period of relative stability over the past 6,000 years, which supported the formation of settlements and the advent of farming in the landscape we are familiar with today.Explore more on these topicsEuropeTerrawatchGeologyVeniceItalyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bafta trustees may have broken charity law by accepting free guest tickets | Awards and prizes | The Guardian
description: Chair of membership council says legal advice obtained at own expense suggests offences could have been committed
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Chair of membership council says legal advice obtained at own expense suggests offences could have been committed
Content: Bafta is an independent arts charity famous for its annual film, television and games awards.Photograph: London Entertainment/AlamyView image in fullscreenBafta is an independent arts charity famous for its annual film, television and games awards.Photograph: London Entertainment/AlamyAwards and prizesBafta trustees may have broken charity law by accepting free guest ticketsChair of membership council says legal advice obtained at own expense suggests offences could have been committedNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 07.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBafta trustees may have breached charity and company law by accepting free tickets for guests at the organisation’s awards ceremonies, the chair of its membership council has claimed.Michael Pritchett told members at Bafta’s annual general meeting that legal advice obtained at his own expense suggested offences could have been committed by trustees who approved the charity’s accounts, which stated that no trustees had received remuneration or benefits.“I did not go looking for what I found,” Pritchett said. “I found it doing the job that you gave me.”He claimed trustees had received complimentary tickets for themselves and a guest at the film, television and games awards, potentially for as long as 20 years. The guest tickets were top-table seats, he said, with a second ticket at the film awards selling for £2,000.Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson to watch Bafta Scotland awards in separate ‘relaxed’ spaceRead moreBafta’s governing document states that trustees may not receive remuneration or other benefits from the academy. Pritchett said the charity’s 2024 and 2025 accounts stated that no trustees had received remuneration for their services, while its public register said trustees received no remuneration, payments or benefits.“Counsel advises that offences under theCharitiesAct and Companies Act are likely to have been committed by the trustees who approved those accounts,” he said. “I really wish I didn’t have to tell you this.”Pritchett, who is also a member of Bafta’s governance and appointments committee, also raised questions about possible tax liabilities, saying benefits of this kind were likely to have been taxable since 2016, with national insurance potentially payable by Bafta. He said he could not establish whether the arrangements had been reported to the relevant authorities.Bafta’s outgoing chair, Sara Putt, said the board had decided to end the practice of giving trustees a guest ticket to awards ceremonies in 2025, after a recommendation from its governance committee.“The separate guest ticket and accounting matters are being examined by an independent review group,” Putt said, adding that the board would update members in due course.Bafta trustees are volunteers, and it is understood they are invited to awards ceremonies in a working capacity, hosting tables and acting as ambassadors for the academy. It is also understood that guest tickets were a longstanding custom dating back to a time when demand for awards tickets was lower.Pritchett also criticised the refusal of a senior Bafta executive to provide records of who had received complimentary tickets, despite the committee’s terms of reference stating it could seek any information required from academy employees.“The records belong to the charity that you subscribe to,” he told members, noting that they had paid £4.7m in membership fees the previous year.Twelve-year-old wins Australian slam competition prize with poem about ChatGPT: ‘It’s totally unnecessary’Read morePritchett called on trustees to pay any taxes found to be due, repay any money owed and correct the accounts. Putt responded: “If we were told we had to pay those taxes, we would absolutely pay those taxes.”Putt said the legal advice obtained by Pritchett and fellow committee member Sara Curran was based on the information available to them, while Bafta’s own legal counsel had access to a fuller picture of the charity’s circumstances.A Bafta spokesperson said: “Trustees of Bafta are invited to attend events in a working capacity, representing the academy in an ambassadorial role, and prior to 2025 they could also bring a ‘plus one’ guest to accompany them.“In 2025 Bafta decided to review its guest tickets arrangements and discontinued the longstanding custom and practice of trustees inviting a plus one. The board has since established an independent review group to consider the historic guest ticket arrangement – the review is under way.”Explore more on these topicsAwards and prizesBaftasCharitiesVoluntary sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Give UK workers right to know colleagues’ pay to prevent disparities, says watchdog  | Pay | The Guardian
description: EHRC says transparency needed to prevent pay discrimination, particularly against women
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: EHRC says transparency needed to prevent pay discrimination, particularly against women
Content: The EHRC also said bosses should be banned from asking about applicants’ existing salaries when recruiting staff.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenThe EHRC also said bosses should be banned from asking about applicants’ existing salaries when recruiting staff.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyPayGive UK workers right to know colleagues’ pay to prevent disparities, says watchdogEHRC says transparency needed to prevent pay discrimination, particularly against womenKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 09.58 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorkers should have a legal right to know their colleagues’ pay to help prevent pay discrimination, particularly against women, the UK’s human rights watchdog has said.The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) made the recommendationin response to government proposalsto overhaul equal pay laws, saying workers deserved a right to transparency if they suspected other staff were being paid more for similar work.The watchdog also said bosses should be banned from asking about applicants’ existing salaries when recruiting staff. Companies are currently allowed to request that information, but potential recruits do not have to respond.Ministers are considering forcing bosses to respond to staff questionnaires about their colleagues’ pay, reintroducing a right that was abolished in 2014 as part of a drive to cut bureaucracy for businesses.The EHRC said those forms should allow staff to request information about a colleague doing similar work, including annual salary and hours worked, as well as bonuses, overtime and their job description.They should also be able to ask for details on any job evaluations carried out by bosses, revealing job grades, salary benchmarks, internal “scores” and a copy of any final job evaluation records.They should also be able to ask for a ranking of each worker in a similar team, based on annual basic pay and hours, and have the right to push bosses for more information in cases where the data they receive is believed to be inaccurate or incomplete.Crucially, the watchdog said bosses should be forced to respond within a “specified timeframe”.The EHRC said: “Without such a requirement, employers may delay, provide evasive responses or avoid responding. We suggest this should be introduced as a mandatory measure, rather than an ‘optional’ one, to adequately meet the policy aims of this consultation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK’s gender pay gap ‘won’t close for 30 years’ at current ratesRead moreUltimately, boosting pay transparency could help companies avoid employment tribunals, resulting in “early resolution of pay disputes”, and help tackle the UK’s gender pay gap where women historically earn less than men, the EHRC said.The median gender pay gap, as of April this year, shows that women in full-time work earned 6.8% less, on average, than men in the UK,according tothe Office for National Statistics. However, that figure is wider across areas such asthe finance industry, where the mean and median pay gaps, at 24% and 22% respectively, are double the national average for UK companies.The EHRC said: “Introducing a requirement that prevents employers from asking about salary history or expectations, alongside the proposed pay transparency measures in this consultation, will likely reduce pay gaps and discrimination against women.”Explore more on these topicsPayGender pay gapEquality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC)Work & careersEqual payEmployment lawWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: Yvette Cooper drops plans to abolish NHS patient champion after outcry | NHS | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Health secretary to extend role of watchdog, which backers say helps hold service in England to account
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Exclusive: Health secretary to extend role of watchdog, which backers say helps hold service in England to account
Content: Healthwatch England and Local Healthwatch will be strengthened to ensure patient voices are heard.Photograph: SolStock/GettyView image in fullscreenHealthwatch England and Local Healthwatch will be strengthened to ensure patient voices are heard.Photograph: SolStock/GettyNHSYvette Cooper drops plans to abolish NHS patient champion after outcryExclusive: Health secretary to extend role of watchdog, which backers say helps hold service in England to accountDenis CampbellHealth policy editorWed 28 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYvette Cooper has abandoned plans to abolish the NHS’s independent patient champion after an outcry from MPs across the political spectrum.The health secretary has decided to keep and extend the role ofHealthwatch England, which was due to be axed as part of the government’s reorganisation of the health service in England.The move is the latest in a series of U-turns by ministers on core elements of the health bill since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.Sources at the Department ofHealthand Social Care (DHSC) said her decision to retain and strengthen Healthwatch and its network of branches illustrated her strong belief – which Burnham shares – in public and local accountability.The rethink means HealthwatchEnglandand its 150 branches will continue to collect and analyse feedback from patients about their experiences of the NHS and where its services need to improve. Its many supporters in parliament say the statutory body helps to identify areas where NHS care is lagging behind patient needs and hold the service to account.Cooper told the Guardian: “Patients need a voice in ourNHS. I’ve always been clear on the importance of people and communities having a say in local services and that’s why I said I would review all reforms in this area.“We will retain Healthwatch England and Local Healthwatch, while strengthening them to ensure patient voices are heard and can influence real change across health and care services.”Gillian Merron, the health minister in the Lords, will confirm the change of plan when peers debate the health bill .Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parliamentarians had criticised the planned abolition.Healthwatch has gained respect for publishing reports highlighting issues such as declining patient access to NHS-funded dental treatment and years-long waiting times for ADHD assessments. It has also exposed flaws in the way the service communicates with patients, for example telling some of them about appointments after the date has already passed.Cooper reprieved Healthwatch after MPs and peers from all sides in parliament raised serious concern that scrapping it would mean the loss of important oversight of the NHS.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in NovemberRead moreThea Stein, the chief executive of the Nuffield Trust thinktank and a former head of an NHS trust in Leeds, said: “Abolishing Healthwatch would have thrown away the independence that gave it credibility, without doing anything to address the reasons the NHS often don’t listen.“It was the wrong solution to a real problem. Healthwatch has played a valuable role in making it more difficult for the NHS to ignore patients’ often frustrating experience of using it.”Until now, the government had planned to transfer Healthwatch’s functions into NHS regional integrated care boards (ICBs) and local councils. But Healthwatch will now play a greater role in identifying recurring concerns and highlighting where action is needed to improve quality, safety and patient experience.The Local Government Association had warned that abolishing Healthwatch “risks [NHS] organisations being seen to mark their own homework” and could create “confusion” for patients.Other recent government climbdowns on the health bill include ministers dropping plans to:axe the Health Services Safety Investigations Body.end councils’ automatic representation on the boards of ICBs.remove the requirement for a nurse on every NHS foundation trust board.The U-turns show Cooper is closely examining the legacy bequeathed to her by her predecessor, Wes Streeting, and tearing up elements of the bill she thinks are misguided.Stein said: “This retreat needs to be followed by a cultural shift away from a health service where patients’ voices are all too often at the bottom of a long and impossible list.”Explore more on these topicsNHSHealth policyYvette CooperLabourHealthHospitalsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volunteer, 78, says Reform official likened her to Nazi collaborator for teaching asylum seekers English | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Mair Godley claims Essex councillor Carl Johnson told her she was ‘facilitating the invasion’ by giving language lessons
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Mair Godley claims Essex councillor Carl Johnson told her she was ‘facilitating the invasion’ by giving language lessons
