Content: Mair Godley with her husband, Nick, near the disused Wethersfield military base where asylum seekers are being housed.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMair Godley with her husband, Nick, near the disused Wethersfield military base where asylum seekers are being housed.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianReform UKVolunteer, 78, says Reform official likened her to Nazi collaborator for teaching asylum seekers EnglishMair Godley claims Essex councillor Carl Johnson told her she was ‘facilitating the invasion’ by giving language lessonsDiane TaylorWed 28 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 78-year-old volunteer has claimed aReform UKcouncillor accused her of “facilitating the invasion” and being akin to a Nazi collaborator during the second world war because she has helped asylum seekers learn English.Mair Godley and her husband, Nick, 77, a former chair of Wethersfield parish council, live near the former Wethersfield military base inEssex, where the Home Office accommodates hundreds of asylum seekers.The couple said the accusations were made against Mair Godley at a parish council meeting on 14 October.View image in fullscreenThe former Wethersfield military base.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianReform took over control of Essex county council after the elections in May 2026, ending 25 years of Conservative control. The Reform councillor, Carl Johnson, attended the meeting to update members of the parish council about local issues for which it has responsibility, including repairing potholes and “Operation Vanguard”, which involves private security guards patrolling Essex town centres.Wethersfield is the larger of two former military sites the Home Office uses to provide mass accommodation for asylum seekers. The other is at Crowborough in Sussex.Nick Godley challenged Johnson at the meeting about the potholes and whether Operation Vanguard was needed to protect local people against asylum seekers. He said crime and antisocial behaviour incidents in nearby Braintree, where asylum seekers sometimes go to, were low.View image in fullscreenTemporary housing units at the former Wethersfield military base.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn response, Johnson asked if anyone in the room had been helping the migrants at Wethersfield and “facilitating the invasion”. Mair Godley said she had previously volunteered to help teach English to the asylum seekers at the facility.Johnson then reportedly said that by doing so she might as well have been helping Germany during second world war. He said he didn’t want to bring his daughter up to be raped and murdered by asylum seekers.In a Facebook post the week before the parish council meeting, Johnson had written that people who enter the country “illegally” received things including clothing and accommodation for free while “the rest of us” had to pay for items. “I have never known a country to actively facilitate its own invasion and population replacement,” he wrote. “This is treason.”According to the draft minutes of the parish council meeting seen by the Guardian the discussion became heated and Johnson was asked to leave the meeting to “restore order”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of part of the former Wethersfield military base.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMair Godley said: “I’m nearly 79 years old. I felt violated by his comments. How dare he say that to me? I certainly told him at the meeting, ‘you are not wanted here’. He has left a really bad taste.”Nick Godley said he had had a “fairly challenging” discussion with Johnson about Operation Vanguard. It was after he had raised concerns that it had been introduced without consultation that Johnson accused Mair Godley of being akin to a Nazi collaborator by helping asylum seekers to learn English.“It was a member of the public who attended the meeting who suggested forcibly that he should leave. Cllr Johnson’s behaviour was shocking,” said Nick Godley.He has lodged a formal complaint about Johnson’s comments at the meeting with Essex county council.A spokesperson for the council said: “We comment on complaints made at a point where they have been investigated and a finding of a breach has been made, but not before that point.”Reform UK and Johnson have not responded to repeated requests for comment.Explore more on these topicsReform UKImmigration and asylumEssexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Medak, veteran director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88 | Movies | The Guardian
description: The film-maker enjoyed a long and varied film and TV career, from horror movies and true-crime thrillers to Cannibal and Breaking Bad
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The film-maker enjoyed a long and varied film and TV career, from horror movies and true-crime thrillers to Cannibal and Breaking Bad
Content: Peter Medak directing A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972).Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyView image in fullscreenPeter Medak directing A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972).Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyMoviesPeter Medak, veteran director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88The film-maker enjoyed a long and varied film and TV career, from horror movies and true-crime thrillers to Cannibal and Breaking BadAndrew PulverWed 28 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 15.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Medak, the British-Hungarian director of The Changeling, The Krays and Let Him Have It, has died aged 88. Medak’s family announced he died peacefully in Los Angeles on Tuesday.Medak enjoyed a long and varied career across film and TV, which included spirit-of-the-times classics A Day in the Death of Joe Egg and The Ruling Class (both from 1972), cult horror The Changeling with George C Scott, and The Krays and Let Him Have It, period true crime films made in the early 1990s. He also directed numerous episodes of high-profile TV drama, including the 80s revival of The Twilight Zone, Homicide: Life on the Street, and Hannibal.View image in fullscreenGary Kemp, left with Martin Kemp, right, and Billie Whitelaw in Medak’s biopic of the Kray twinsPhotograph: Warner Bros./Sportsphoto/AllstarBorn in Hungary in 1937, Medak was forced into hiding along with his Jewish family during the second world war, and then escaped the country during the Hungarian uprising. He came to London, where his aunt Lotte Medák was an internationally renowned opera singer and through her contacts Medak wastaken on as a traineeat newsreel producers Associated British-Pathé, working his way up through the studio departments, including a spell working in the editing room with future Chariots of Fire director Hugh Hudson. Medak then worked as assistant director to Joan Littlewood on Sparrows Can’t Sing and Guy Hamilton on Funeral in Berlin before making his own feature directing debut in 1968 with erotic thriller Negatives, starring Peter McEnery and Glenda Jackson.Medak then followed this up with two adaptations of celebrated plays: Peter Nichols’ A Day in the Death of Joe Egg, with Alan Bates, and Peter Barnes’ The Ruling Class, starring Peter O’Toole. Both were well received on their release in 1972, with O’Toole nominated for the best actor Oscar, but Medak would swiftly hit trouble two years later with Ghost in the Noonday Sun,a still-notorious Peter Sellers vehiclethat went vastly over budget, partly due to Sellers’ erratic behaviour, and which was only released on home video more than a decade later. (Calling it the “biggest disaster of my life”, Medak would later make a documentary about the experience, which screened at the Venice film festival in 2018.)Following the Graham Chapman comedy The Odd Job, Medak re-established his credibility with The Changeling, the creepy 1980 George C Scott horror about a composer who rents a haunted house. Calling it “filled with sadness and dread”, it was named by Martin Scorsese asone of his favourite horror movies. After spells on Shelley Duvall’s anthology series Faerie Tale Theatre and The Twilight Zone, Medak returned to features with two high-profile British crime thrillers. The Krays, released in 1990, cast Spandau Ballet’s Gary and Martin Kemp as the twin-brother gangsters, followed by Let Him Have It, about a controversial case which saw 19-year-old Derek Bentley hanged in 1953 for the murder of a policeman despite not pulling the trigger. Medak then returned to Hollywood with the Gary Oldman thriller Romeo Is Bleeding in 1993.View image in fullscreenPeter O’Toole in The Ruling ClassPhotograph: RONALD GRANTMedak pivoted back to TV and, starting in 1994, directed six episodes of acclaimed cop series Homicide: Life on the Street, and followed it up by directing an episode of The Wire in 2002. Later TV work included episodes of high-profile shows such as House,Breaking Badand Cannibal.Skyfall and No Time to Die writers Neal Purvis and Robert Wade, who worked with Medak on their first produced script Let Him Have It, told the Guardian: “Peter directed our first film and we couldn’t have hoped for a kinder, more respectful collaborator. It was wonderful to be treated as equals by this very experienced film-maker, who was enjoying a resurgence in his film career after the exciting and surprising The Krays. He was a good friend and we will miss the lunches and the talk of all the future projects he still burned to make.”Medak was married three times, to Katherine La Kermance between 1963 and 1972, Carolyn Seymour between 1973 and 1984, and Julia Migenes between 1988 and 2003.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsCrime filmsDrama filmsPeter BarnesPeter NicholsPeter SellersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence | Jafar Panahi | The Guardian
description: Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’
Content: The Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that authorities were cracking down on cultural figures.Photograph: Carlos Álvarez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that authorities were cracking down on cultural figures.Photograph: Carlos Álvarez/Getty ImagesJafar PanahiIranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentenceCharges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’Deepa ParentWed 28 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Iranian court has handed the award-winning film directorJafar Panahia new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.The 66-year-old, whowon the Palme d’Orat Cannes last year forIt Was Just an Accident, was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned toIranin March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said the sentencing, and the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, could violate Iran’s constitution, unless the authorities establish a clear legal basis linking the property to an alleged offence.Speaking to the Guardian while in the US earlier this year,Panahi warnedthat the current “cycle of violence” in Iran could continue.“What I have been depicting in this film is when the cycle of violence continues, then it becomes very difficult to stop it,” Panahi said. “Unfortunately, because of the savagery that is being carried out by the state, the fear is that this cycle of violence will continue.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I think of those I left behind in prison’: Iran’s Jafar Panahi on life as a banned film-makerRead moreThe latest sentence has raised concerns among fellow artists over the risks facing those who continue to work independently in Iran.The Iranian actor Setareh Maleki, who was forced into exile after starring in Mohammad Rasoulof’s Oscar-nominated filmThe Seed of the Sacred Fig, told the Guardian: “One of the greatest fears of a dictatorship is losing control over the stories people tell. When those stories cross borders and reach the world, they become impossible to silence. Jafar Panahi has told his stories too, and his sentence proves once again just how deeply the Islamic Republic fears even the act of storytelling.”Inside Iran, a film-maker currently shooting a film in secret expressed support for Panahi. “We all support him, who brings us great pride. He hasn’t remained silent and instead voices demands of the Iranian people,” said the film-maker, who did not want to give her name.She said she believed Panahi’s latest sentence was linked to his calls for unity during the January protests and his support for diverse voices inside Iran, including supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s former shah.The Iranian-British actor Nazanin Boniadi also condemned the ruling, saying: “Jafar Panahi has spent decades turning censorship into cinematic resistance, bearing witness to the suffering and resilience of the Iranian people. His latest draconian prison sentence is yet another attempt to silence a courageous artist whose work exposes the realities of repression in Iran.”In a recent report, the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that Iranian authorities are intensifying their crackdown on artists, writers, poets, musicians and other cultural figures, “pulling peaceful voices into the same coercive security and judicial apparatus used to suppress dissent across Iran”.Explore more on these topicsJafar PanahiIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Investors turn on Google owner Alphabet after profit miss, ad slowdown and high spending | Technology | The Guardian
description: Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bn
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bn
Content: Google logo is displayed at its headquarters in New York City.Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/ReutersView image in fullscreenGoogle logo is displayed at its headquarters in New York City.Photograph: Aleksandra Michalska/ReutersTechnologyInvestors turn on Google owner Alphabet after profit miss, ad slowdown and high spendingNet profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn, well short of expectations, though revenue rose to $127.6bnAgence France-PresseWed 28 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShares in Google parentAlphabetfell more than 10% in after-hours trading Wednesday, erasing tens of billions of dollars in stock market value from the $4tn tech giant. The company had reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn in the July-to-September period, or $2.12 a share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.Alphabet booked an $8.7bn loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentreRead moreRevenue, however, rose 25% to an enormous $127.6bn. The figure was slightly below the roughly $128bn analysts had forecast.Advertising revenue grew 11% to $82bn, short of expectations. Revenue from Google’s search business, still the company’s largest source of income, rose 12% to $63.4bn, slowing from 17% growth in the previous quarter.YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow 9% to $11.2bn, down from 13% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103% to $30.7bn, ahead of analyst expectations.The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to $11.1bn.Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI reportedly plans to buy some of the chips.Alphabet’s “Other Bets” division, which includes robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of $372m and an operating loss of $2bn.Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach 1m weekly rides by the end of the year.Alphabet spent $51.4bn on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on datacenters and AI chips, more than double the $24bn a year earlier.Its latest forecast for capex spending is between $195bn to $205bn in spending for 2026.The company said it would continue to increase capex spending significantly in 2027.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise,” Sundar Pichai, the Google CEO, told analysts of the company’s investment splurge.The company’s spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet’s businesses for a second straight quarter, leaving a $9.1bn gap.During the quarter Alphabet raised $28.7bn by selling bonds and $12.4bn by issuing new shares to help pay for its AI ambitions.Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.The Gemini app has reached 1bn users. Google’s AI models now process nearly 32bn tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google’s largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyGoogleAlphabetQuarterly resultsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Microsoft posts $92.3bn quarterly revenue after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees | Microsoft | The Guardian
description: Software giant reports $36.6bn in profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as Azure cloud computing division grows 48%
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Software giant reports $36.6bn in profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as Azure cloud computing division grows 48%
Content: The Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersMicrosoftMicrosoft posts $92.3bn quarterly revenue after offering buyouts to 60,000 employeesSoftware giant reports $36.6bn in profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as Azure cloud computing division grows 48%Agence France-PresseWed 28 Oct 2026 18.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMicrosoft gained billions of dollars in stock market value Wednesday afternoon after it reported better than expected revenue and profit, just days after it offered voluntary buyouts to some 60,000 employees.The office software giant’s growth was fueled by its Azure cloud computing division, which grew by 48% in the September quarter.Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cutsRead more“We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost-efficiency for customers across our entire stack,” Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said in a statement.The technology giant recorded $92.3bn in total revenue and more than $36.6bn in profit, the company said in a securities filing Wednesday. Analysts had expected around $90.6bn in revenue and $35.1bn in profit, according to FactSet.The quarterly earnings report comes two days after Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence investments.It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year, after giving seven percent of its US workforce the option to retire early in April.Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.Earlier this month, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips and will cost more than $2,500. Apple announced a similar touchscreen Macbook this week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud datacenters, where running AI is slower and more expensive.Explore more on these topicsMicrosoftComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms  | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%
Content: Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference in Washington DC on 29 July 2026.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh speaks during a news conference in Washington DC on 29 July 2026.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesFederal ReserveFed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midtermsFed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%Gaya GuptaWed 28 Oct 2026 15.26 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USFederal Reserveleft interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%.Inflationhas hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, thepause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, whosaidthat “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.Warsh declined to comment on a remark fromDonald Trumpthat, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists arepredictingone more rate hike before the end of the year.“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Wallersaidearlier this month.The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveUS politicsDonald TrumpUS economyInflationUS interest ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Business secretary writes to Poundland owner as administration fears build | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Jonathan Reynolds’ team has written to Gordon Brothers, which bought retailer for £1 last summer, to ‘establish the facts’
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Jonathan Reynolds’ team has written to Gordon Brothers, which bought retailer for £1 last summer, to ‘establish the facts’
Content: Poundland has 600 stores across the UK and employs 12,000 staff.Photograph: Paula  Solloway/AlamyView image in fullscreenPoundland has 600 stores across the UK and employs 12,000 staff.Photograph: Paula  Solloway/AlamyRetail industryBusiness secretary writes to Poundland owner as administration fears buildJonathan Reynolds’ team has written to Gordon Brothers, which bought retailer for £1 last summer, to ‘establish the facts’Sarah ButlerWed 28 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe business secretary’s team has written to the owner ofPoundlandamid fears that the cut-price retailer could collapse into administration, threatening to overshadow John Healey’s budget.Sources said that Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm that bought the 600-store Poundland chain for £1 last summer, looks set to appoint administrators to the struggling retailer.Jonathan Reynolds has written to Gordon Brothers to establish the latest situation at the company, which employs 12,000 staff.The company rejected the only bid to take on the group – which includes the 50-store Dealz chain in Ireland – as a solvent company in its entirety, from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group, earlier this week.It is understood Gordon Brothers is poised to file a notice of intention to appoint the advisory firm AlixPartners as administrator, potentially as early as Wednesday. This legal measure would protect Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought.Three independent directors appointed to help oversee a sale have quit amid disquiet over the move towards insolvency.The timing of the move threatened to overshadow Healey’sfirst budget as chancellor, amidlongstanding complaintsfrom companies over costs imposed by the government on businesses.Barry Williams, the boss of Poundland, wrote to workers saying the rejection of the bid from Martin Property Group was “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”.An improved bid from the Northern Irish firm has not been ruled out.View image in fullscreenJonathan Reynolds has instructed his team to get answers as the situation threatens to overshadow the chancellor’s budget.Photograph: Martin Dalton/ShutterstockHowever, sources said that Martin’s bid fell well short of Gordon Brothers’ hopes to recoup the £30m in debts it took on with Poundland. The bid is understood to be worth more than £15m, with only a portion upfront.One industry source said that suppliers to Poundland were already beginning to hold back on deliveries, making it tougher for the group to secure a rescue bid.Industry insiders said Gordon Brothers wanted to move quickly as Poundland was flush with stock ahead of the busy Christmas period. A quick break-up of the chain, with parcels of stores and stock sold off, would lead to a maximum return for the restructuring specialist, sources said.“Gordon Brothers has a simple choice. It can accept an offer from Martin Group, worth at least half of the £30m which it secured for £1, or get significantly more than that by busting the business,” a source said. “The only thing that can change this is if they feel the moral or public relations duty.”Reynolds has instructed his chief strategic business adviser, David Bickerton, to “establish the facts” regarding Poundland’s potential collapse, as first reported by the Financial Times. He is understood to have contacted Gordon Brothers but not Poundland’s management team, which had backed the Martin Property Group bid.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA business department spokesperson said:“We know this will be a concerning time for Poundland employees, their families and communities across the UK.“This is a commercial process and ultimately a decision for Poundland’s owners, so it would not be appropriate for the government to comment further.”Gordon Brothers is understood to believe that it can raise more cash – up to £30m – and keep more jobs in place long-term by breaking up Poundland and selling off the stock and stores to a variety of retailers.There could be as many as eight interested parties, including the US investment firm Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and the owner of The Range. B&M is thought to be interested in taking on at least some outlets.However, one industry insider said: “Who is going to take on 600 high street stores?” He predicted that up to 500 could be left without a buyer in the event of a break-up, leading to significant job losses.The general secretary of the Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers, Joanne Thomas, said: “I am calling on the government to do everything it can to save 11,000 jobs, which are mainly done by women and part-time workers.“Over the past five years, around 250,000 jobs have been lost in the retail sector. Job security is a key priority for a successful economy; therefore, I urge the government to grant the retail sector the same priority and strategic support it provides to other vital industries.”Gordon Brothers was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryPoundlandJonathan ReynoldsPrivate equitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Their orchestra is not a sacred object but a tool for struggle – Paris’s musicians join the frontline  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: L’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s young musicians went viral for their defiant performances during the last week’s protests in France. They belong to a fine tradition of radical orchestras. Also, today, what music should soundtrack the Traitors?
Author: Tom Service
Headline: L’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s young musicians went viral for their defiant performances during the last week’s protests in France. They belong to a fine tradition of radical orchestras. Also, today, what music should soundtrack the Traitors?
Content: Conductor Etienne Jarrier (centre) and the ONM perform during protests over the rising cost of living in Paris, France on 17 October 2026Photograph: Sipa US/AlamyView image in fullscreenConductor Etienne Jarrier (centre) and the ONM perform during protests over the rising cost of living in Paris, France on 17 October 2026Photograph: Sipa US/AlamyTom Service on musicClassical musicTheir orchestra is not a sacred object but a tool for struggle – Paris’s musicians join the frontlineTom ServiceL’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s young musicians went viral for their defiant performances during the last week’s protests in France. They belong to a fine tradition of radical orchestras. Also, today, what music should soundtrack the Traitors?Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTShareThey were the last people standing – or rather playing – during last week’s student protests in France, as gas canisters landed in double-bass cases. L’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde, co-founded by young conductor Étienne Jarrier and his friends when they were still teenagers, aren’t a typical orchestra. With theirmanifesto of activism and social justice, the orchestra is not “a sacred object of beauty, but a tool for struggle”, through civil disobedience, outreach in schools, demonstrations and concerts, all to “present a different kind of classical music – one reconnected to reality”.The new world Jarrier and his group dream of is “anti-racist, anti-capitalist, feminist, environmentalist and committed to de-growth”, and their way of working is deliberately provocative, not only to so many of the dominant directions of travel in the political world, but also to the institutions of classical music. They play scrappily passionate performances of La Marseillaise, of music from The Avengers, of Dvořák’s New World Symphony and protest songs but the ONM judge the quality of their performances not by playing the right notes in the right order, but by their consciousness-raising impact, whether they’re staging performances at Place de la République inParisor at the foot of a glacier.double quotation markThey don’t want their audiences to listen in silence but to sing with them, move with them and shout with them.This is not an orchestra trying to find hermetically sealed concert halls to perform in perfect acoustics. It’s a group that wants to be out on the streets, outside television studios and the headquarters of corporations, institutions or industries they choose to protest against. They don’t want their audiences to listen in silence but to sing with them, move with them, shout with them.All of this seems like a radical overturning of the way that orchestras usually function – and the ONM is arguably the most self-consciously radical orchestral assembly right now in how it fuses its political purpose to its musical ideals.But it’s not the first. In its political idealism and aesthetic radicalism, the ONM is a contemporary cousin of two British orchestras founded in 1969 and 1970: the Scratch Orchestra and the Portsmouth Sinfonia. Composers Cornelius Cardew, Howard Skempton and Michael Parsons founded theScratch Orchestra in 1969. Cardew’sThe Great Learning, based on texts by Confucius, is the Scratch Orchestra’s magnum opus, its notation and performance realised the Scratch Orchestra’s goals: to make music as open as possible to participants of all abilities and backgrounds. Instead of classical music’s polished perfection, the Scratch Orchestra’s experimentalism was an aesthetic of radical inclusion – socially, musically and aesthetically. The Great Learning’s greatest learning of all was that music of this ambition and scale belongs to anyone who wants to play it. The Scratchers went on to be welcome by the very institutions they critiqued,playing the Proms in 1972; but Cardew’s increasingly devoted leftwing activism took his music down a different course and the orchestra disbanded in 1974.View image in fullscreenBreaking convention … the Scratch Orchestra’s Cornelius Cardew listening to a man operating a jackhammer in 1969.Photograph: Tony Barette/Daily Mail/RexFor the Portsmouth Sinfonia, the self-styled “world’s worst orchestra”, the point was to try to play the classics – piano concertos, symphonies, orchestral hits – on instruments that the musicians, which included Gavin Bryars, Brian Eno and Michael Nyman, didn’t actually know how to play. The delirious, joyous and utterly deliberate cacophony that resulted remade everything from Beethoven’s symphonies toHandeland Hooked on Classics. (The Portsmouth Sinfonia’s attempt to disco-ify the classical repertoire parodied the Royal Philharmonic’s chart-topping kitschorama, and reached no 38 in the charts in 1981: Classical Muddly.Listen to it here, and enjoy.And even if the anarchy of the Portsmouth Sinfonia is no more, plenty of UK groups today are leading even more serious missions to reorient the priorities of orchestras towards social and political engagement. Here’s just a few: theMulti-Story Orchestra in Peckham, which amplifies the voices of the pupils and students it works with in south London as performers, composers and administrators; inclusive ensembles led by disabled musicians such as theNational Open Youth Orchestra,RNS Movesand theParaorchestraare all examples where social activism meets orchestral possibility, making the sounds of social change; whileContemporary Music for All (CoMA)continues a message of radical inclusion for new music, creating a repertoire of hundreds of pieces for non-professionals to play.View image in fullscreenThe Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s concert in Place de la Republique on 17 October was disrupted when police used tear gas as broader demonstrations over living costs, education and public services drew large crowds.Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Even so, the ONM’s commitment to direct political action makes them stand out in today’s musical world – but their manifesto has a clue to an even deeper history: they want classical music to be “reconnected to reality”. That’s the point: classical music only exists across the world today because of its often-problematic connections to conceptions of nationhood and political orthodoxy, from the courts of Vienna in Beethoven’s time to the concert halls of Shostakovich’s era in Soviet Russia. You can’t have the power of all that music without the complicated and compromised politics that produced it. The attempt to pretend that these connections don’t exist in the later decades of the 20th century and beyond is part of the problem with classical music’s often self-inflicted irrelevance, as if the art form were untethered to the world around it, existing only in glitzy concert halls and glossy programmes. The ONM’s performances and protests, and the police’s reaction to them, is a wake-up call to remind classical music where it comes from – and yes, to reconnect it to today’s realities.With Celebrity Traitors– the latest series ofthe most successful TV franchiseon the planet – drawing to a close this week, here’sthe BBC’s Mark Savage analysinghow the deliberate duplicities and misdirections of the show’s music are made, not leastthe “Braaams”of the composer Sam Watts’s opening titles. But is it just me or is there less of the Lacrimosa from Mozart’s Requiem, and less classical as a whole, in the soundtrack for the death marches and backstabbing this time round? I have a challenge to the music supervisors: next series, why not use only classical to soundtrack it all? There’s vast reserves of dark and doomy tunes and arias of treachery and treason to choose from after all –the Traitors Promthe summer before last was a mere drop in the ocean of classical melodramas. My choice for the opening titles? The opening ofWagner’s Walküre, which has enough storm, threat and malice in its opening minutes to dramatise any celebrity face-off. What would you suggest?View image in fullscreenHow to soundtrack the treachery? Maya Jama, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Professor Hannah Fry, on the current season of Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAThis week Tom has been listening to:I can’t get past The Portsmouth Sinfonia’s Classical Muddly, because who doesn’t need more joy and chaos in their lives? Also it’s not on the streamers, which only adds to the joy. If ever there was music made that the algorithms can’t touch, it’s this.See also:Tom Service on Stephen KovacevichExplore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicParisProtestFranceExperimental musiccommentShareReuse this content

title: Castle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared mess | Television | The Guardian
description: Billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’
Content: ‘Another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces’ … Castle Walls is the first fully AI-generated series to premiere on a major streaming platform.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video / YouTubeView image in fullscreen‘Another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces’ … Castle Walls is the first fully AI-generated series to premiere on a major streaming platform.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video / YouTubeTelevisionReviewCastle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared messBilled as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’Luke BuckmasterWed 28 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 21.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust as the world reels from Elon Musk’s AI-poweredThe Odyssey remake– though “remake” feels rather generous for a seven-minute splat of synthetic sludge – another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces. For Prime Video’s AI-generated TV series Castle Walls, produced by Turkish production studio Ay Yapım using a melange of generative video tools, has arrived, billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series to premiere on a major streaming platform.‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey filmRead moreIt’s certainly more epic than Musk’s production, consisting of two 17-minute episodes. Set in the 11th century, the show revolves around the historic Alamut Castle, although it’s entirely absent of any real sense of time or place. I was briefly intrigued by the opening images, with their bold palette of blues and mustard browns and yellows – but as soon as the “people” appeared, looking like Vaseline-smeared Madame Tussauds creations slowly melting in the sun, everything came crashing down.View image in fullscreen‘Like Vaseline-smeared Madame Tussauds creations slowly melting in the sun’: Castle Walls.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeThere are lots of heady moments across the first two episodes of this oddly paced show, with cranky-looking men aplenty and over-milked visual metaphors involving the likes of snakes, blood and fire. Everything looks like it was cooked up with the prompt: “Give me eye-watering visuals.” The opening shot depicts an eagle being transported across a desert in a cage (“make it look cinematic”), followed by a longshot of the castle (“make it more cinematic”), then an aerial shot of men arriving on horseback (“make it MORE MORE MORE cinematic”).View image in fullscreen‘Overloaded with grand and imposing imagery’: Castle Walls.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeWe learn of the arrival in Alamut of a “freak” who “doesn’t eat or drink” and is intent on claiming these sweet digs for himself. This is Hasan Sabbah, who is supposed to be charismatic but looks plasticky and spectral, with a complexion like wet glue. He has somehow inspired an army of followers and ventures into the castle’s dungeons to recruit one more: the notorious warrior Azazil.The frame is overloaded with grand and imposing imagery: when Azazil says goodbye to loved ones, of course the scene takes place in front of a milky sunset. When he fangs it across the desert on a horse at night, of course there’s a white full moon glowing resplendently above. When the doors of the mighty castle creak open, in the lead-up to a big moment in episode two, of course incandescent orange sunlight streams through the widening gap.View image in fullscreen‘Viewers understandably seem less interested in what the technology promises than in what it threatens to take away: art imbued with humanity.’Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeMake no mistake: the technology powering this is amazing and will profoundly alter the state of motion pictures. Productions such as Castle Walls are among the first out of the gates, and therefore prone to snarky commentary. Perhaps these early AI-generated workswill end up being broadly comparable to early silent films: revolutionary at the time, but quickly eclipsed by more sophisticated applications of the technology. But whereas the earliest motion pictures, famously dubbed the “cinema of attractions” by the historian Tom Gunning, provided some carnival-like wonder, these AI works tend to evoke a more cynical response from the general public. Viewers understandably seem less interested in what the technology promises than in what it threatens to take away: art imbued with humanity.The sensible path forward is surely for human and machine to enter into a reciprocal and carefully collaborative process, where artists only use algorithms and prompts to enhance, rather than replace, human creativity. On that front, Castle Walls did use human voice actors and was reportedly written by actual human screenwriters: Kerem Deren and Çisil Hazal Tenim. “This is not a production that bypassed human skill; it is one that used AI to amplify it,”Ay Yapım has said.But that’s hardly something to crow about, given how banal and chuckleheaded the writing is, puffed-up with lines like “I’ve stopped being a decent man” and “If I am the sheaf, you are the sword”. Were they really trying to make good art? Maybe that’s a question for ChatGPT.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTurkeyDramaAI (artificial intelligence)Amazon Prime VideoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Devils review – Ken Russell’s 1971 possessed-nuns tale is a frenzied aria of confrontation and hysteria | Movies | The Guardian
description: Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave put in the performances of their lives in this film originally banned for obscenity that highlights the violence of power
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave put in the performances of their lives in this film originally banned for obscenity that highlights the violence of power
Content: Amazing … Vanessa Redgrave in The DevilsPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenAmazing … Vanessa Redgrave in The DevilsPhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesReviewThe Devils review – Ken Russell’s 1971 possessed-nuns tale is a frenzied aria of confrontation and hysteriaOliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave put in the performances of their lives in this film originally banned for obscenity that highlights the violence of powerPeter BradshawWed 28 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Icould never be Satan’s boy. I haven’t the humility.” The speaker is Father Urbain Grandier, the 17th-century French priest accused of witchcraft, stylishly played by Oliver Reed, in Ken Russell’s scabrous 1971 classic; it is now restored and rereleased in its complete form after years of censorship. It comes from an era when movies, playing in high-street cinemas, still had the power to shock, to position that shock in the polite cultural mainstream and to compel serious discussion about whether that shock – or, conversely, a ban – was justified.The Devils is based on a true story of politically directed mass hysteria, adapted by Russell from two literary works:Aldous Huxley’s The Devils of LoudunandJohn Whiting’s stage play The Devils. Of course it is obscene; obscenity is the glowing sulphurous paint which Russell is applying to the canvas. It is about obscenity – but the obscenity does not reside in the sexualised images of the crucified Christ or naked nuns disporting themselves; it is the violence of authority that is shown to be obscene. The idea of martyrs or heretics being burned at the stake has long been an accepted fact recounted in U-certificate history lessons, and a punishment which survived well into the European enlightenment. Russell shows you what it might actually look like and that is to involve a confrontational assault on good taste.Reed is a revelation with his intelligent, focused, charismatic and dignified performance as the sensualist cleric who submits to injustice like a dissolute version of Thomas Becket. Grandier is a magnetically handsome man and de facto municipal leader of the town of Loudun in western France, bullishly promoting its independence, its walls and fortifications; this is to the rage of Cardinal Richelieu (Christopher Logue) and the Catholic church, who suspect that it will become a sanctuary and power-base for Huguenots and Protestants.Grandier is blandly tolerated by the equally decadent and vain Louis XIII (Graham Armitage); the king’s bizarre court masque is shown in the film’s stunning opening scene, with superb music by Peter Maxwell Davies, whose compositions do so much to give this film its crazed, dissonant fervour. Loudun’s Ursuline abbess Sister Jeanne Des Anges, played with radioactive certainty byVanessa Redgrave, is sexually frustrated like more or less every authority figure here – the displacement of sexuality into tyranny is, after all, part of the point – and tormented by her spinal-curvature disability; she is infatuated by Grandier and enraged by him marrying another woman, Madeline De Brou (played by Gemma Jones), and moreover declining her offer to be the order’s father confessor.View image in fullscreenDecadent and vain … Graham Armitage plays Louis XIII in The Devils.Photograph: Courtesy Warner Bros.So Sister Jeanne spitefully invents stories about his demonic hold over everyone, a tale cynically seized upon by agents of the state, who then fan the flames of hysteria – although Russell does not entirely endorse the theory that the nuns were themselves cynically putting on a show to incriminate Grandier. The priest’s persecutors are Baron de Laubardemont (Dudley Sutton) and the order’s Father-Canon Jean Mignon (Murray Melvin), a thin-faced disapproving ascetic who is to become this story’s contrite and despairing Judas to Grandier’s Jesus.Russell’s film allows us now to register what was perhaps not registered fully in 1971: the misogyny behind the publicising of her deformity over the centuries, turning it into a mark of villainy like that of Shakespeare’s Richard III, exaggerated or even invented by posterity’s myth-making. It is part of a tradition of monstrosity – perhaps even inaugurated by the self-flagellating abbess herself – that dramatised the penitent view that a woman’s sexuality was an ugly disorderly phenomenon.As well as everything else, The Devils is also about fascism; like upmarket psycho-sexual shockers of the same era such as Visconti’s The Damned in 1969, Cavani’s The Night Porter from 1974, or Pasolini’s Salò from 1975, it sees power licensing and permitting sexual decadence as a safety valve for discontented, frustrated energies that might otherwise be directed against the state. Yet it also uses that decadence as a pretext for moral panic and cracking down, and even rechannelling the mad sexual excitement into power worship.What comes across in the film is the cynicism of the religious authorities whose officers are quite well aware of more modern concepts of frustration and hysteria. Simply and importantly, the possessions and the “devils” are not real, or not real in the sense they are held to be by the church. How intriguing that just two years later, in Friedkin’s The Exorcist, we were offered a story of authentic possession, a plausibly conceived possession whose metaphorical properties can only be absorbed at one remove.The amazing, anachronistic set designs of the youngDerek Jarmanpresent to us the white-tiled nunnery, whose low arched ceilings mean everyone has to duck down in imitation of the abbess; it looks like a Victorian or Edwardian prison or public lavatory, while the giant, multi-storied library looks like the jailhouse in which Elvis Presley sang. The great brickwork walls of the city make it resemble the housing estate in Kubrick’s Clockwork Orange, released in the same year – and in fact Grandier’s torture scene is very Clockwork Orange.When the devils depart and the fever abates, what is left behind is a scorched and desolate landscape, like that after a plague or an apocalypse: a chilling final flourish to Ken Russell’s aria of angry pessimism.The Devils is in Australian cinemas on 29 October and UK and Irish cinemas from 30 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsFilm adaptationsAldous HuxleyTheatreVanessa RedgravereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Asher: Everywhere Man review – music-biz face from Beatles-buddy pop act to superstar producer  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Backstory of modest industry veteran who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Backstory of modest industry veteran who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt
Content: Peter Asher, right, with Gordon Waller on Ready Steady Go in 1966Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenPeter Asher, right, with Gordon Waller on Ready Steady Go in 1966Photograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewPeter Asher: Everywhere Man review – music-biz face from Beatles-buddy pop act to superstar producerBackstory of modest industry veteran who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda RonstadtAndrew PulverWed 28 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRock’n’roll is notorious for its tales of bad behaviour: throwing TVs out of the window, mountains of cocaine, parades of groupies … but you won’t find any of that here. Peter Asher, brother of Jane, one half of Peter and Gordon, and super-successful producer of acts such asJames Taylorand Linda Ronstadt, appears to be about as nerdish and clean-living as a 60s/70s music industry veteran could be. Although that might just be what he wants us to think; what are the chances Asher is a complete reprobate away from the camera, and is just brilliant at hiding it? That glasses and ruffled shirt front combo definitely reminds you of someone a tad more sleazy, even before Asher himself reminds you about it in the final credits.Peter Asher on being music’s incredible ‘Everywhere Man’: ‘The secret is simple’Read moreWhatever the truth, Asher by any standards carved an amazing path, making the absolute most of being in the right place at the right time. Smartly structured around Asher’s anecdotes-and-music live show, the film stitches together a collection of clips, audio and musical performances that gallops through his personal backstory. His luckiest break, of course, was that his early partnership with schoolfriend Gordon Waller (modelled, it turned out, on the Everly Brothers) benefited from cast-off songs handed over by his sister’s boyfriend, one Paul McCartney; there’s an amusing moment where we hear John Lennon’s sneer at the lyric of what would become Peter and Gordon’s first and biggest hit, A World Without Love: “Please lock me away …” “Yes”. While the film clearly acknowledges the debt to McCartney’s songwriting (which presumably Lennon vetoed for the Beatles), it’s perhaps not quite ready to admit that without this connection, none of what followed would have happened at all.At one point Asher says he wasn’t much of a pop star, and subsequent events suggest he was probably right. He appears to have been more comfortable away from the spotlight, thereby allowing him to become a ubiquitous figure in the Beatles’ orbit in swinging 60s London to which the title alludes. He was a co-owner of supercool art gallery Indica (where Lennon first met Yoko Ono), though given it only lasted two years, possibly he wasn’t all that great at that, either. It was the Beatles’ connection, though, that allowed him to really come into his own, when he was appointed head of A&R at the newly formed Apple Records, with his own top floor office in the Savile Row building.Asher’s big discovery was Taylor, who had relocated to London after failing to get anywhere at home in the US; after producing Taylor’s debut album (which with characteristic modesty he says he messed up with Beatles-style orchestration), Asher followed Taylor to Los Angeles and settled into a quietly impressive second act as a producer and manager. After producing Taylor’s breakthrough second album, Sweet Baby James, Asher became a key figure in 1970s Californian soft rock, overseeing acts including Andrew Gold, Kate Taylor, JD Souther and – most successful of all – Ronstadt. Admittedly, this now looks a tad middle of the road, a musical era since vanquished by punk and new wave, but Asher later got on board with credibility-stoking artists such as Cher, Diana Ross and 10,000 Maniacs, and even produced albums by Boyzone and Morrissey.Throughout this parade of achievement, Asher cuts an impressively self-possessed figure, unassuming in many ways but also not hiding his light under a bushel. The appreciation he gets from his big-name collaborators is clear enough, but he also gives houseroom to somewhat more tangential figures, with Carole King in particular coming across strongly. But it’s the interactions with late former partner Waller that are probably the most resonant, with the virtual duet Asher sets up being especially moving.Peter Asher: Everywhere Man is in UK cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMusic documentaryPop and rockJames TaylorPaul McCartneyJane AsherreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Everest: The Other Side review – couple’s climb on the mountain’s toughest face comes with tricky moral questions | Movies | The Guardian
description: Immersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest’s north face
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Immersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest’s north face
Content: Anxiety-inducing … Jim Morrison in Everest: The Other Side.Photograph: Jimmy Chin Productions/PAView image in fullscreenAnxiety-inducing … Jim Morrison in Everest: The Other Side.Photograph: Jimmy Chin Productions/PAMoviesReviewEverest: The Other Side review – couple’s climb on the mountain’s toughest face comes with tricky moral questionsImmersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest’s north faceLeslie FelperinWed 28 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith some of its showings in the huge Imax format, this National Geographic-backed documentary feels like a callback to the early, glory days of large-format cinema when it was all about spectacle and scale, turning footage of natural-world wonders into an immersive experience. Those with a fear of heights or prone to vertigo may find this all a bit too immersive, in fact. That’s even more the case considering the point of the movie appears to be to provoke anxiety in the viewer for nearly the entire running time as we watch the subjects scale the steeper, far less travelled north face ofMount Everestand then, for reasons never quite adequately explained, ski back down it again.Such was the mission ofexperienced mountaineer Jim Morrison, an amiable-seeming fellow who, like all of those who pursue extreme sports, seems to feel a compulsion to put himself in the kind of grave danger that, should things go wrong, would put other people in danger rescuing him. His partner Hilaree Nelson shares his passion, and the two of them set off to be the first people to ski down Everest’s north face, and the first third of the film tracks them as they plan and eventually do practice runs to achieve this goal. Neither seems able to adequately explain why they’ve chosen to take such a risk, although Nelson tries a bit to articulate her mountaineering life almost as if it’s a career choice that her two teenage sons should simply accept as her choice to make, and maybe even thank her for – even if that means that should she be injured or lost they and Morrison (who is not the boys’ biological father) would also have to deal with the aftermath.We don’t want to give away what happens, but these moral questions hang over this film in a much more obvious way than they do in most other mountain-climbing films. (Interestingly, this is also a work co-directed by another couple, Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, who appear on screen to thrash out their own feelings on risk and reward.) Meanwhile, there’s some thoughtful footage of the various Nepalese guides who assist in Jim and Hilaree’s adventures, local men who have been climbing these mountains all their lives because they have far fewer career choices than the western tourists who come through town with camera crews, swathed in brightly coloured, prominently logo-bearing sports equipment.The lurid palette of this kit does in fact become a bit distracting when we get back to the mountain climbing stuff, and if you want to just relax and look at the stunning landscape you need to train your eyes to ignore the fluorescent jackets obstructing the view. That’s not criticising the cinematography itself; it is pin-sharp thanks to the most advanced kinds of lens and drone technology. But it’s safe to say the ethics aired here are a far murkier affair.Everest: The Other Side is out on 29 October in Australia, and 30 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMount EverestExtreme sportsMountaineeringSkiingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I knead the audience, like a baker!’ House music legend Peven Everett on life after cancer and vanquishing the ‘Disco Sucks’ movement | Music | The Guardian
description: The prolific house and soul musician is the subject of a new documentary which follows him from child trumpet prodigy to becoming ‘everyone’s favourite artist, you just don’t know it yet’
Author: Kate Hutchinson
Headline: The prolific house and soul musician is the subject of a new documentary which follows him from child trumpet prodigy to becoming ‘everyone’s favourite artist, you just don’t know it yet’
Content: ‘Everyone’s favourite artist – you just don’t know it yet’ … Peven Everett.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘Everyone’s favourite artist – you just don’t know it yet’ … Peven Everett.Photograph: PRHouse musicMusicInterview‘I knead the audience, like a baker!’ House music legend Peven Everett on life after cancer and vanquishing the ‘Disco Sucks’ movementKate HutchinsonA new documentary follows the Chicagoan from child trumpet prodigy to Gabriel-singing icon and DIY maverick. ‘Not everybody wants to see musical genius’, he saysWed 28 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt We Out Here festival in Dorset in August, thousands of people could be heard singing a trumpet melody as if it was a giant brass-band karaoke session. On stage was Peven Everett, performing a rendition ofGabriel, one of the most celebrated anthems in dance-music history. Co-created with producer Roy Davis Jr, the best-known version, which blew up in UK clubs in the mid-90s, is a spiritual garage-house track about the “archangel of love” that can bring both punters and DJs to tears.But Everett is much more than one song. Damon Albarn ofGorillaztells me that “Peven has a once-in-a-generation voice … he’s a great inspiration to us all.” We Out Here founder, Gilles Peterson says that the Chicagoan is, alongside Detroit’s Moodymann and Amp Fiddler, “the closest thing dance music has to a Prince-type figure”. A prolific multi-instrumentalist and one-man cottage industry, Everett’s catalogue spans more than 500 tracks, across house, neo-soul, hip-hop, samba and more.As with Prince, Everett’s audience can expect something different with each performance; they’re often improvised and don’t have strict setlists. “I’m kneading the audience into position, like a baker,” says the 51-year-old. He claims the Prince-fluence goes both ways after the latter attended one of his shows in the mid-to-late 2000s. “He started going more into dance music at that exact time,” says Everett. “He knew what I was doing: he’d seen it for himself.”View image in fullscreenA still from Peven Everett: Voice of a Generation.Photograph: PRWhen we speak, Everett is preparing to join Gorillaz for the Chicago stop of their world tour. It’ll be the first time he’s been on stage with them since 2022, having contributed to their 2017 album Humanz. “It’s going to be one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to do,” he says. “I used to have some control over how much I gave emotionally, but tomorrow, I don’t think I’ll have that.” Two years ago, Everett was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer, just as his career was gathering pace. “A part of me feels like I let the people down by getting sick,” he says. “I missed a step.”He’s now completed treatment and his life and artistry is the subject of a new documentary by Denholm Hewlett (son of Jamie, the visual artist behind Gorillaz). “People always refer to him as a house music artist,” says Hewlett. “But he was a trumpet prodigy by the age of 12 and was raised by jazz royalty.” Before dance music, Everett gave up a scholarship at Boston’s Berklee College of Music to go on the road with his mentor, Betty Carter, and the Marsalis brothers, Wynton and Branford. When he was 21,a 1995 New York Times articleasked whether Everett was the next Miles Davis.But Everett returned to Chicago to look after his ailing mother, where he teamed up with the producer Roy Davis Jr. Out of those mid-90s sessions came 1999 deep house staple Watch Them Come, as well as Gabriel. The original version of Gabriel has more of a typical four-to-the-floor beat but it was its Live Garage Mix that resonated in the UK as DJs found that its swung drums matched the pace of the nascent UK garage scene.Roy Davis Jr: Gabriel ft Peven Everett – videoIt was rereleased in 1997, reaching No 22 in the charts. At the time, US dance music was often associated with a big “diva” vocal; in the documentary, producer Marc Cary claims that Everett “brought a richness to house music” that previously didn’t exist.Peterson says the song has become a dance-music standard, while Everett recalls dancing at Chicago’s Red Dog club in the early 2000s, when he claims that Thomas Bangalter of Daft Punk and vocalist Benjamin Diamond approached him. Two years earlier, they had a huge hit with Music Sounds Better With You under the name Stardust. “That was funny. They were like, ‘Yo,we made Stardustbecause of Gabriel, we used that as a template.’ I guess it’s kind of a compliment. At least they had the grace to tell me.”Though some early Gabriel promos did not mention his name, and some have knownthe song as a Roy Davis Jr track, Everett says he was not simply a hired hand (he also played that unmistakable trumpet part). “When I go into any studio,” says Everett, “I make the vocals: I arrange them, I sing them. I make the horn and keyboard parts: I arrange them, I play them.” In the past, Everett has raised the subject of his contributions to the track on social media; today he can only say “the situation itself is still pending”.Despite releasing other contemporary house classics such as 2007’s Stuck – and soundtracking theHermès catwalkat Paris fashion week last January – Everett is far from a household name. In an interview in the documentary, Moodymann says Everett is “everyone’s favourite artist, you just don’t know it yet”; elsewhere in the film, he is compared to Stevie Wonder and James Brown.View image in fullscreen‘Peven has a once-in-a-generation voice’.Photograph: Frazer Harrison/Getty Images for CoachellaYet Everett runs a DIY enterprise, and has self-released more than 50 albums on his Studio Confession Entertainment label. “He’d make an album in one week and then burn it on to CDs and sell them at record stores in Chicago,” says Hewlett. “People haven’t been able to keep up.”“For the majority of my career, I’ve been blacklisted,” Everett claims obliquely, citing his home town music industry in particular. Why? “For being a musical genius,” he replies. “Not everybody wants to see that.”‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating strokeRead moreEverett sees himself as following on from where musical greats such as Marvin Gaye and Barry White left off in the late 1970s, as disco’s name was being sullied by the racist, homophobic “Disco Sucks” movement. “That didn’t sit right with me, it was hateful,” Everett says. “It tarnished great music. So I said, guess what? I’m gonna make the records that I know should have happened right after.”The day after our interview,a videocirculates of Everett and Albarn at Gorillaz’s Chicago show, as an emotional Everett prepares to sing the late Bobby Womack’s part on the Gorillaz tune Stylo. Artists as varied as Shirley Manson of Garbage, Kelela and Honey Dijon commented on the video with words of support. Everett says that his time was always supposed to be now. “I’m glad that I did it this way,” he says. “I maintain control of my catalogue, I still have the enjoyment of making music, and I got through a huge disease. I feel blessed.”“He’s going to have his moment,” adds Hewlett. “It feels like he’s just getting started.”Peven Everett: Voice of a Generationpremieres on 30 October at the Barbican, London, as part of the2026 Doc’n Roll film festivalExplore more on these topicsMusicHouse musicBarbicanGorillazDance musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Kovacevich - a pianist who risked oblivion to know what it’s like out on the edge | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The death of Stephen Kovacevich, aged 86, was announced yesterday. Tom Service pays tribute to a pianist whose performances were full of beauty, clarity – and danger
Author: Tom Service
Headline: The death of Stephen Kovacevich, aged 86, was announced yesterday. Tom Service pays tribute to a pianist whose performances were full of beauty, clarity – and danger
Content: Intimacy and intensity: pianist Stephen Kovacevich rehearsing at London’s Queen Elizabeth Hall in March 2013.Photograph: Amy T Zielinski/Redferns/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIntimacy and intensity: pianist Stephen Kovacevich rehearsing at London’s Queen Elizabeth Hall in March 2013.Photograph: Amy T Zielinski/Redferns/Getty ImagesClassical musicStephen Kovacevich - a pianist who risked oblivion to know what it’s like out on the edgeThe death of Stephen Kovacevich, aged 86, was announced yesterday. Tom Service pays tribute to a pianist whose performances were full of beauty, clarity – and dangerAnd, here,in a piece published on Kovacevich’s 75th birthday, Andrew Clements picks his favourite recordings.Tom ServiceWed 28 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was just a couple of weeks ago that Stephen Kovacevich and I were last in contact. He was in hospital, recovering from a hip operation, and we were talking aboutHiromi, and where the latest generation of pianists were coming from. The players who had the brilliance, fire and commitment to the moment that his favourite players had: Vladimir Horowitz, Sergei Rachmaninov – his greatest of the greats – and his friend and occasional mentee, Yuja Wang.Among other things, he told me about a Charles Munch performance of Berlioz’sSymphonie Fantastique he had discovered on YouTubethat made him exclaim: “How the hell did he get an orchestra to play like that?” Conversation with Stephen was always like that: utterly intense, totally opinionated, with the feeling that the spirits he was talking about, whether performers or composers from Chopin to Beethoven to Brahms to Mozart to Bach, were in the room with you, conjured into being as real, passionate people and presences.Which was, of course, what you felt and heard in his playing. His long career devolved into name changes (Bishop, Bishop-Kovacevich, then Kovacevich) and relationship changes, as partnerships with conductors he loved to work with were intensely productive and then suddenly disappeared. Listen to any of the concerto recordings with Colin Davis to hear the adventure of what they made together, from Bartók to Mozart.View image in fullscreenStephen Kovacevich with cellist Jacqueline du Pré in London in 1964. The two made an acclaimed recording ofBeethoven’s Cello sonatas.Photograph: Erich Auerbach/Getty ImagesWhat was constant was a spirit of going to the edge of a performance to find the place where the music is most powerful and most vulnerable; risking oblivion to know what it’s like there, out on the edge. Stephen talked openly about how often his performances failed him, but he rejoiced in his successes, particularly the technical ones of the last decade or so of his life, whenhe recovered from a severe strokein his late 60s, and combatted nerves, to play Schubert and Rachmaninov with an intimacy and intensity that was breathtaking.He was driven by capturing the sensual spirit at the core of all the music he loved to play. This was a dangerous occupation, as it should be. Getting that close to the white-heat of Beethoven’s sonatas or Brahms’s concertos is all about being burnt and scarred, and plunging back in again to those cauldrons of extremity, the psychic and emotional places where music like that is made, and where performances like Stephen’s are born.One of his complaints about classical music right now was that performers often don’t take enough risks, that their music-making isn’t dangerous enough. I agree with him. His own playing was the perfectly imperfect response: that’s why his Beethoven sonatas are my favourite on record, because you’re with him in the moment of the attempt to reach the mountaintop, with everything on the line, throwing it all at the impossibility of the moment. In that struggle and that realisation, there’s more truth and more transcendence than most pianists will find in a lifetime. I’m going to miss him.More on Stephen Kovacevich“I don’t live in a subversive way. But I certainly believe in it” –a 2001 interviewTo celebrateKovacevich’s 75th birthday, Andrew Clements picked his favourite of his recordings.Wereview his 70th birthday concertat the Wigmore Hall, London, anda 2015 concertof music for two pianos with Martha Argerich.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We sold out tickets within 13 minutes’: new novel from romantasy author Sarah J Maas sparks fan mania | Books | The Guardian
description: Move over Oasis – 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets to a masquerade ball to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, while specialist bookshops catering for the genre report huge sales
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Move over Oasis – 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets to a masquerade ball to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, while specialist bookshops catering for the genre report huge sales
Content: The Spicy Librarian’s masquerade ball.Photograph: Beth MelvinView image in fullscreenThe Spicy Librarian’s masquerade ball.Photograph: Beth MelvinBooks‘We sold out tickets within 13 minutes’: new novel from romantasy author Sarah J Maas sparks fan maniaMove over Oasis – 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets to a masquerade ball to celebrate the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, while specialist bookshops catering for the genre report huge salesEmma LoffhagenWed 28 Oct 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen The Spicy Librarian, a romance bookshop in Leamington Spa, announced a masquerade ball to celebrate the newSarah J Maasnovel, 6,000 people tried to buy 220 tickets. “We sold out within 13 minutes,” says the shop’s co-founder Ali Maynard James. “As soon as tickets went on sale, our website crashed”.The shop was one of many across the UK marking the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, the first instalment of Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series in more than five years.
