On Monday night, bookshops threw parties and opened past midnight – and The Spicy Librarian hired a stately home to mark the occasion.The book, the sixth in the series known to fans as Acotar, went on sale at 12.01am on Tuesday. Few releases carry as much commercial weight – the first book, a dark retelling of Beauty and the Beast, was published in 2015, with later books following the adventures of Feyre across the faerie lands of Prythian. By 2021 the series had sold 13m copies, and across her three interlinked fantasy series, Maas hasnow sold more than 75 m booksin 40 languages.View image in fullscreenMaas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses.Photograph: Main Character BooksThe Spicy Librarian, which bills itself as Europe’s largest independent romance bookshop, held its ball at Ragley Hall in Warwickshire, where riders dressed as “fae warriors” carried torches on horseback. Tickets were £149 – the shop ran the event again the following night, which also sold out, and ordered about 750 copies to cover both balls and its pre-orders.“We gave everyone the books at midnight, and people started reading them immediately,” says Maynard James. “Some people stayed up and devoured the whole thing in a few hours.”Maas is the biggest name in romantasy, a genre combining fantasy and romancewhich has grown from an online nicheinto one of publishing’s most lucrative categories. Last year, Onyx Storm by Rebecca Yarros – another romantasy star –had the biggest first weekfor a hardback novel in the UK since Harper Lee’s Go Set a Watchman in 2015. In 2024, booming sales of romance and fantasy helped push UK fiction revenueabove £1bn for the first time. The genre’s readers are largely young women, and much of its growth has played out on TikTok.“It’s been such a long wait for this book, people are just itching to get their hands on it,” says Starlin Marot, owner of Bad Girl Books in Oxford,the UK’s first romantasy-only bookshop.“For so many of us, the series has been like a gateway drug into the genre, or into reading itself.”In Oxford, Marot had only planned to open Bad Girl Books for half an hour after midnight, for a couple of readers who had asked on Instagram. Instead, a queue formed outside. “It was just crazy, like a flurry of people came in,” she says. “I was honestly not expecting that many people just for half an hour. But it shows how popular these books are!”View image in fullscreenFaerie wine and “Tamlin’s Tears” blueberry lemonade.Photograph: Bad Girl BooksHer midnight release doubled as a pyjama party. “It was cute and cosy vibes,” Marot says. “We had Acotar-themed cakes and drinks.”In London, romance bookshop Main Character Books decided against a midnight opening, serving breakfast to readers collecting pre-orders instead and holding an evening party for 45 people. “We decorated the entire store,” says owner Cassie Simmons. “In early October we had more pre-orders than we expected … we doubled our order at the publisher.” After Tuesday’s sales, the shop ordered again. “We’re going through stock even faster than we expected.”The latest book is the first part of a four-part story. A Court of Forgotten Melody, out on 12 January, contains the next two parts, and the last is still being written.“I think it’s definitely the five-year wait and the hype that’s been going up online,” says Simmons.Maynard James, who says Acotar got her reading for pleasure again after becoming a mother, believes its heroines are a big part of the draw for its largely female fanbase. “They aren’t women that are damsels in distress that need rescuing or saving,” she says. “They almost prioritise themselves before they prioritise love. We want the women to be the centre of their own story.”For the specialist shops, the boom is showing up in the till. “Sales are so much higher than I even anticipated for the year already,” says Marot. “It’s so exciting.”While a Hulu adaptation of Acotar was announced in 2021, Maas has nowbought back rights. “I want to see everything adapted the way I envision it, and the way I know fans want it”, she said in March.Explore more on these topicsBooksRomance booksFantasy booksFictionSarah J MaasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? by Judi Dench review – whatever you do, don’t call her a ‘national treasure’ | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos and why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relic
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos and why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relic
Content: Judi Dench.Photograph: Paul StuartView image in fullscreenJudi Dench.Photograph: Paul StuartAutobiography and memoirReviewIs It Too Late to Make a Run for It? by Judi Dench review – whatever you do, don’t call her a ‘national treasure’The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos and why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relicFiona SturgesWed 28 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the late 1950s,Judi Denchwas invited to meet a major Hollywood producer about a possible career in the film business. The producer looked at her for a long time and said: “Very nice to meet you but you’ll never make a movie because you have every single thing wrong with your face.” As she left his office, Dench – who was 23 and about to make her professional debut as Ophelia in Hamlet at the Old Vic – breathed a sigh of relief and resolved to concentrate on theatre. Though she dabbled in film and TV, it wasn’t until the 1990s that she became a bona fide movie star, playing M in the Bond films and winning an Oscar for her portrayal of Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love. Yet, she notes: “Being onstage is where I feel safest. Yes, I’ve appeared in films, but I’d never consider myself a film actor.”Dench’s reflections on her working life form the backbone of Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, a memoir built around her conversations with the actor and theatre director Brendan O’Hea, Dench’s friend with whom she also collaborated on 2023’s Shakespeare: The Man Who Pays the Rent. This book confirms much of what is already known about Dench: that she is impishly funny, swears like a sailor, and that, despite that film producer’s unkind comments, she has “no hang-ups about what I look like on camera … Acting for me is not about looking glamorous. It’s whatever’s needed for the story.” We also learn that Dench, who is 91, can’t resist a prank: while playing Brecht’s Mother Courage at the Barbican in London, she replaced the drinks her character serves to two soldiers with cider vinegar – “It was a joy watching them knock it back, made even more glorious by the fact they had to ask for a top-up.”In keeping with her previous book, this one is delivered in a question-and‑answer format. The chapters are thematic and cover faith, animals, directors and directing, comedy, choosing a part, which means the chronology is all over the place. While the book starts quite reasonably with Dench’s early life in York as the daughter of a GP, it ends, oddly, with a chapter called Starting Out, in which we learn what she did after her A-levels. And while she has an easy chemistry with O’Hea, there are times when his line of questioning gets tediously granular, as in: “What’s your favourite dressing room?” Such are the perils of having an actor interview an actor.But despite the shoptalk and the haphazard structure, there are enough witty anecdotes and oddball facts to keep it clipping along. We learn that Dench has a waste-collection truck named after her: “Dame Foodie Dench”; that she had a cat called Bernard the Duck Fucker (though O’Hea neglects to ask how he earned his name); and that, on the opening night of Madame de Sade, Dench’s co-star Frances Barber gave her a double-ended, bendy dildo which she wore as a scarf when the company gathered for director’s notes. Elsewhere, Dench pays touching tribute to departed friends including the late Maggie Smith, whom she says was “a very complex person – intensely private, and I suspect quite lonely at times; she’d occasionally erect an electric fence around herself”.The whole project is kept afloat by Dench’s rare humour and warmth which long ago elevated her to national treasure status (an appellation she loathes as it makes her sound “like a dusty old relic”). Her eyesight is now poor, but her memories are pin-sharp, relayed through a prism of amused self-deprecation and passion for her job. The book’s title references Dench’s professional nerves, which lead her to keep her bag by the rehearsal room door in case she is compelled to do a runner. Learning lines may have become more difficult, but she has no intention of stopping work. “Take the keys out of the ignition and the car will conk out,” she cautions. “Don’t retire, do not go gentle, and don’t even think about going quietly.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak review – what Madame Bovary thought of Flaubert | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark times
Author: Lara Feigel
Headline: This audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark times
Content: Mia Wasikowska and Henry Lloyd-Hughes in the 2015 film of Madame Bovary.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyView image in fullscreenMia Wasikowska and Henry Lloyd-Hughes in the 2015 film of Madame Bovary.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyBook of the dayFictionReviewIn One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak review – what Madame Bovary thought of FlaubertThis audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark timesLara FeigelWed 28 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInFrantumaglia, her collection of essays on writing and reading, Elena Ferrante writes that she has sometimes dismissedGustave Flaubertas a “misogynist”, angered by his invention of as callous a mother as Emma Bovary. In other moods, however, she has wondered whether Flaubert allows his female characters to say what “women truly think and say and live but do not dare write”.Ferrante’s ambivalence is, I think, the most fitting feminist response to Flaubert’s novel. It’s tempting to castigate him as a male writer who kills his female character because he can’t imagine any other end for a transgressive woman; to reproach him for not giving Emma Bovary the profundity of emotion with which Tolstoy imbues Anna Karenina. But this isn’t the whole story, because Flaubert was so complex a figure: restlessly self-doubting even as he more than held his own in an age of cocksure egos; ecstatically happy in his solitary states of aesthetic creation precisely because they could throw him outwards into other people’s stories and minds.Elif Shafak’s audacious new novel is written out of this ambivalence. An opening chapter shows a devastated Flaubert killing what the narrator styles as “the only woman he has ever loved with heart, mind and soul”, by writing the end of Madame Bovary. The book then shifts briskly to Emma’s own voice, angry with her creator for denying her the freedom to learn from her mistakes (“Could it be because I am a woman?”). These two visions of Flaubert, teeming with creative passion for his own protagonist on the one hand and an exasperating misogynist on the other, become the twin poles of a vast 600-page novel exploring his life from every possible perspective. Thankfully, Shafak doesn’t attempt to ventriloquise Flaubert himself, master of themot juste. Instead, she has Emma summon the voices of 30 feminine figures, human or otherwise, encountered by Flaubert between birth and death, and alternates their accounts with that of the third-person narrator.This is the ideal vehicle for Shafak, who delights and often excels in giving voice to anyone and everyone, including, memorably, the tree protagonist inThe Island of Missing Trees. I have always admired Shafak’s storytelling verve while not quite falling for her whimsicality, and I balked slightly at the fancifulness of the chapters voiced by Opium (“Let me lighten up your load, ease the burden. I shall cradle you in my warm embrace”) and Syphilis (“I will damage your cells, burrow into your brain, penetrate your dreams”).double quotation markThis is the ideal vehicle for Shafak, who delights and often excels in giving voice to anyone and everyoneBut Flaubert himself might have been drawn to these extremes of literary inhabitation, which are a sort of extreme realisation of his own famous statement to Louise Colet: “It is a delicious thing to write. Today, for instance, as man and woman, both lover and mistress, I rode in a forest on an autumn afternoon under the yellow leaves, and I was also the horses, the leaves, the wind.” Certainly, I fell for Jamilah the camel (“I smile all the time. I cannot help it”), who comes at a point when the reader has either thrown the book aside in exasperation or been carried away by its abundance. “I saw those knives – and I smiled”: Shafak imbues Jamilah’s death with genuine tragedy, at a time when the inhabitants of defeated Paris are murdering zoo animals for restaurants to serve up as gourmet dishes.Throughout, Shafak powerfully evokes the minute-by-minute sensory experience of a sensitive child, and then of the adult still tragically caught up in his childhood world. She is astute and often moving on the main players in Flaubert’s life: the eventually overbearing mother who she suggests couldn’t quite bring herself to love him as an infant after losing several children before him; the sister whose death he never recovered from; the adored niece he allowed to be pushed into an unhappy marriage, despite understanding more profoundly than anyone in his century quite how unhappy such marriages could be; the lover who “thought I could help him, gently peeling off his loneliness like wallpaper lifted from a tired wall”.It’s with the invented minor characters that Shafak’s gift for storytelling finds its fullest expression. It’s as though she has tunnelled through Flaubert’s refined stylisation back into 19th-century chaos and exuberance, giving us a female murderer whose sister, passing as male, turns up to tutor the unteachable young Gustave; and the wife of the prosecutor who brought Madame Bovary to trial, laughing here at her husband’s secret hobby of writing pornographic poems. . By the end, Shafak’s powers of narrative invention become a kind of bravura performance, as unexpected, splendidly unlikely connections emerge between minor characters and disparate scenes.In an author’s note Shafak describes the novel as her “love letter to literature”. Certainly she shares Flaubert’s often idealistic sense that literature can help us even when everything else in our lives and world becomes bleak. “Without stories, without art, our descent into savagery would be even swifter,” she has Flaubert just about convincingly muse. Occasionally, I yearned for more of Flaubert’s cold analysis and sheer vitriol alongside the idealism. But this is unashamedly Shafak’s Flaubert, and I am glad of her faith in storytelling as a shaky light guiding us in dark times, even if I can’t always confidently share it.Lara Feigel is the author of Custody: The Secret History of Mothers (William Collins). title: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from? | Games | The Guardian
description: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry
Content: Oddly compelling or just slop? Minecraft and Fornite mashup.Photograph: @moreshiina/YouTubeView image in fullscreenOddly compelling or just slop? Minecraft and Fornite mashup.Photograph: @moreshiina/YouTubePushing Buttons newsletterGamesSocial media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industryDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 28 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarremashups of popular video games. Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from.Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube forthis informative video, which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more.Claude is now able to spit out a game’s source code from its compiled version overnight. Tell it to combine two games and it will help with that, too. There is not zero human involvement: from what I understand, the best of these mashups have needed significant human tweaking. But this has completely transformed video game modding because you now need drastically less time and computing knowledge to be able to pull off massive projects. It now takes an evening rather than months of work.View image in fullscreenSkateboards and swords … World of Warcraft and Skate 3 mashup.Photograph: @kimmo3223/YouTubeAs a person with zero coding knowledge, I was curious about how easy this was to do. I asked Claude how I’d go about making my own mashup, I picked one relatively obscure game and one extremely popular one, just to be annoying. Claude gave me comprehensive instructions and background on some modding and emulation tools, which was super interesting but ultimately of no use to me, because I had no idea what I was doing. So I just asked it if it could build me this in a browser.Four minutes later, it spat out a rubbish but playable game, with further instructions on how I could get the visual assets from the source games so that Claude could incorporate them for me and host it as a local file to avoid copyright issues. In half an hour, I had made something that’s still rubbish, but good enough for a 15-second TikTok. Except I haven’t made anything at all – the machine has done it for me. Istillhave no idea what I’m doing.This probably doesn’t seem that different from people using AI to create fake images of Jesus shaking hands with Trump to post on Facebook – and it isn’t, really. But people who DO know what they’re doing have gone much further with this AI-assisted source-code bonanza. I have seen relatively recent games such as Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom running in web browsers. Github is full of open-source code for Steam-like game launchers that draw from all the emulated codebases available, essentially giving you a vast library of retro games for free. Most consequentially, PlayStation 5 emulation has made an enormous jump: you can now run almost any PS5 game on a PC. For free.Much of this is obviously extremely illegal. Regarding the PlayStation 5 situation, I have seen a lot of angry videos describing this as a justified response to Sony’s abandonment of physical games: if you can’t buy a game anyway, how can you steal it? Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 emulation has also become astonishingly easy, thanks to AI-assisted launchers and mod hubs with beautifully clean interfaces. Speaking as a former prodigious teenage pirate (I wasn’t always so technically illiterate), you used to have to accumulate some secret knowledge to avail yourself of this stuff. That is no longer the case.There are enormous consequences here for any video game publisher that would rather nothave all of their game’s code freely available online for people to do what they want with. And that, presumably, is all video game publishers. AI is a technology built on the theft of creative work, as all writers and artists know – but up until now, it has not affected corporations to the same extent. Now that it does, will AI companies finally be forced to pump the brakes?What to playView image in fullscreenAll-consuming … Nintendo Switch Sports ResortPhotograph: NintendoMy house has been completely overtaken byNintendo Switch Sports Resort, which brings motion-controlled sports from skateboarding to thumb-wrestling to your living room, alongside more normal options such as tennis, golf and bowling. This is obviously a game in the Wii Sports lineage, and it fully embraces that landmark game’s accessible, fun-first philosophy, while also building on it to keep your interest going, from competitive leagues and online play to peaceful plane and jetski tours around the titular resort. My kids are obsessed with it. And because they’re up and moving, I felt perfectly fine about letting them play it for four straight hours while we were trapped in the house by Storm Boelo over the weekend.Available on:Nintendo SwitchEstimated playtime:anywhere from 20 minutes to 20 yearsWhat to readView image in fullscreenNight moves … Keith Stuart has investigated the best new horror games, such as The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionIf you’re looking forsomething to playfor a cosy Halloween night in, Keith Stuart has investigated the best newindie horror gamesfor spooky season.Microsofthas just offered voluntary redundancy to 60,000 people, including many working at Xbox game studios. AsVGC points out, that is a quarter of its entire staff. (The 1984-esque wording stood out to me – MS is calling this a “voluntary exit offer”.)The storied developer behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age and Knights of the Old Republic,BioWare, has been shuttered by EA. I could have written thousands of words on this – these were some of the defining games of the 00s and early 2010s, a hugely significant gaming period, and BioWare’s more recent history absolutely stinks of mismanagement – but I’ll leave it at this:it’s devastating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickLara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blundersEA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereftCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 – a thrilling airport novel of a game | ★★★★☆Nintendo Switch Sports Resort – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenGeographically accurate … Microsoft Flight Simulator.Photograph: gamespressReaderChrisasks:“I’m currently on a Field Trip in Iceland guiding a group of school students. It made me think whilelooking at the stunning volcanic scenery: what games are the most geographically accurate?”The boring answer to this is, of course,Microsoft Flight Simulator, which is 100% geographically accurate because it draws on satellite images of the entire Earth. I also played a strange experimental game last year calledPrologue: Go Wayback!, which a team in Amsterdam made – it procedurally generates accurate northern European wilderness for you to survive in, based on an impressively complex algorithm.Plenty of games have created architecturally accurate cities – all of the Assassin’s Creeds, Tom Clancy’s The Division, Yakuza/Like a Dragon and of course Grand Theft Auto – but fewer have made geographically accurate places that don’t have a volcanic lava-land in troublingly close proximity to a jungle. Forza Horizon’s versions of Mexico, Japan and the UK feelaccurate, but aren’t. ApparentlyKingdom Come: Deliveranceis based on a geographically accurate recreation of 15th-century Bohemia, which doesn’t surprise me at all given that game’s devotion to historical believability.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterAI (artificial intelligence)PiracyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Skulls, bulls and someone peeing in her own eye: four great exhibitions to see for free | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Andy Warhol’s skulls and Pierre Bonnard’s fruit have more in common than you might think. Plus: the world’s rudest cartoon character is up to dirty tricks again
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Andy Warhol’s skulls and Pierre Bonnard’s fruit have more in common than you might think. Plus: the world’s rudest cartoon character is up to dirty tricks again
Content: Head space … Andy Warhol’s Skull (1976) at the Still Life, Then and Now exhibition.Photograph: Courtesy RobilantView image in fullscreenHead space … Andy Warhol’s Skull (1976) at the Still Life, Then and Now exhibition.Photograph: Courtesy RobilantEddy Frankel's gallery crawlArt and designReviewSkulls, bulls and someone peeing in her own eye: four great exhibitions to see for freeAndy Warhol’s skulls and Pierre Bonnard’s fruit have more in common than you might think. Plus: the world’s rudest cartoon character is up to dirty tricks againEddy FrankelWed 28 Oct 2026 12.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStill Life, Then and Now★★★★☆Andy Warhol’s skull leers at Francisco de Zurbarán’s trussed-up little lamb from across the length of the gallery. Separated by hundreds of years – Warhol’s painting from the 1970s, Zurbarán’s from the 1630s – it’s an intergenerational conversation about still life’s staying power, and the inevitability of death.View image in fullscreenPierre Bonnard’s La Corbeille de Fruits (The Basket of Fruit), 1924.Photograph: Courtesy RobilantThis brilliant little show brings together still life paintings from way back in the past right up to the present day. There’s a gorgeous 1610-19 Dutch flower painting by Osaias Beert the Elder, and a vast vision of meats and cheeses with a pair of animal lungs hung grossly on a hook behind by Giovanni Battista Recco from the 1650s. There are piles of 19th-century French apples, vases of undulating 18th-century flowers. And then that little Zurbarán lamb – one of six he painted – glassy-eyed and morose, so laden with religious symbolism.When we hit the modern era, there’s a lovely Pierre Bonnard painting of grapes and apples in sickly yellow and orange, a genuinely amazing Nicolas de Staël composition of stark, blocky bottles, lumps of pink rock by Philip Guston that look like cheese. Ignore the crap Picasso and the lumpen Juan Gris, and you get to come face to face with Warhol’s grim, grinning neon orange skull.The whole show reinforces the idea that still life painting is terribly named. Because it’s not about life at all, it’s about death. Every fruit and vegetable in these works is about to rot, every flower is wilting, every animal carcass is about to go fetid. These are paintings of life’s fragility and precariousness. This is about how time is fleeting, how life is temporary. Mortality is written into every brush stroke.Is this the greatest still life show ever put on? Does it have a tight curatorial concept? Does it tell an important story about the history and evolution of the genre? No, no and no. It’s just a bunch of really good, historic paintings. See, still life isn’t all just flowers and fruit. And even when it is, it’s pretty good.Robilant, London, until 18 DecemberPaul Pfeiffer: Pasodoble★★★★☆View image in fullscreen‘Ritual and spectacle’ … a still from Paul Pfeiffer’s Pasodoble.Photograph: © Paul Pfeiffer. Courtesy the artist and Thomas Dane GalleryPanting, his grey tongue hanging out, blood streaming down his back, the bull is on the verge of death. Paul Pfeiffer’s newest film captures the moment a matador plunges a sword into that bull’s back, but with no fanfare, no drama, no judgment. This is a film about ritual and spectacle, not about animal cruelty or cultural violence.This isn’t Pfeiffer at his most attractive or impressive. Instead, this long, awkward, often ugly piece of art cinema zooms in on the faces of the crowd at a corrida, the hands of the saxophone players in the band, the colours of the walls, the patterns on the matadors’ clothing. It’s all the tiny details of this spectacle, the intricacies that make it tick.It is, essentially, a film about how humanity creates spectacles to lose ourselves in, and how we repeat actions, sounds and movements to create some kind of meaning. The film is outwardly about bullfighting, but more widely about all rituals, religious or cultural. Is the corrida any different from going to church or a concert or a football match? In the end, we’re all just trying to find meaning by taking part, by belonging, by coming together and cheering as one. Throughout the film, people cheer, drink and eat, the band plays, a bull dies. That’s life, I guess. Joy and sorrow with some snacks in between.Thomas Dane Gallery, London, until 19 DecemberFlip In: Ebecho Muslimova★★★★☆View image in fullscreenFatebe Blue Studio, 2026 (detail), by Ebecho Muslimova.Photograph: Courtesy the artsitEbecho Muslimova has gone through the looking-glass, and what she has found on the other side is more worrying and uncomfortable than any kind of horror fantasy land. She’s found reality.In every painting and installation here, Muslimova’s cartoon alter ego Fatebe is navigating a world turned upside down, spun on its head and inverted. Fatebe is a lewd, rude, nude comic book character, her naked body able to twist and contort, her face always plastered with a grin and her orifices always on display. One painting finds multiple Fatebes bent over, gleefully scrubbing parquet floors (a nod to a Gustave Caillebotte painting, this show is drowning in art history references) while another Fatebe makes a paper chain out of fabric she’s yoinking out of her nethers. Yet another work sees hundreds of Fatebes filing up the stairs of the gallery itself, but the plaster is crumbling and the print is peeling.Fatebe is trapped under a glass like a spider, or she’s turned herself into the legs of a table. In one drawing she has grown two heads, one peeing into the other’s eye, the other defecating back in return.All this gross-out weirdness and art historical density isn’t about fantasy and escape though. I think it’s about feeling pulled in endless directions, it’s about being stuck between the place you came from and the place you’re in now, it’s about discomfort and alienation. Or it’s about being able to wee in your own eye. Who knows, really. Either way, it works.Bernheim, London, until 28 NovemberRosalind Nashashibi: Gaza Apollo★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenGaza Apollo with Lemons, 2026, by Rosalind Nashashibi.Photograph: Courtesy of the Artist and GRIMM, Amsterdam | London | New YorkBack in 2013, a Palestinian fisherman found an ancient Greek statue of Apollo poking out of the sand. Thinking it was gold, they cut off a finger, but it was just beautiful, mottled green bronze. They tried to sell it on eBay, posting pictures of the sculpture laid carefully on Smurf bedsheets, but the authorities stepped in and confiscated the sculpture. No one knows where it is now, but Rosalind Nashashibi has painted it here, preserving its strange, almost magical history in hazy visions of green limbs on cartoon-covered sheets.Not all the works are good, and the images of nudes and landscapes feel either like a distraction or filler. But the Apollo images are great. They’re like paintings of an autopsy, stark and unsettling. They’re filled with narratives – a clash of ancient art and modern cartoon, a beleaguered people finding hope of salvation in a gift from the gods, an act of care as those people gently try to preserve this sculpture on their softest bedsheets. Hope and despair, history and the present, all colliding in some often beautiful, washed-out painting.Grimm, London, until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designEddy Frankel's gallery crawlreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Girls review – a story of friendship amidst extreme misogynist violence  | Stage | The Guardian
description:
Young Vic, London
Recalling Boko Haram’s abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok in 2014, Theresa Ikoko’s fierce and tender play reveals how three teenagers find hope and laughter under the most horrific circumstances
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Young Vic, LondonRecalling Boko Haram’s abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok in 2014, Theresa Ikoko’s fierce and tender play reveals how three teenagers find hope and laughter under the most horrific circumstances
Content: ‘Escape in fantasy’ … from left, Tara Tijani, Hannah Akhalu and Sewa Zamba in Girls.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreen‘Escape in fantasy’ … from left, Tara Tijani, Hannah Akhalu and Sewa Zamba in Girls.Photograph: Helen MurrayStageReviewGirls review – a story of friendship amidst extreme misogynist violenceYoung Vic, LondonRecalling Boko Haram’s abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok in 2014, Theresa Ikoko’s fierce and tender play reveals how three teenagers find hope and laughter under the most horrific circumstancesArifa AkbarWed 28 Oct 2026 09.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree girls huddle together, playing childish games to allay their fears from whatever terror stalks them. There are flashes of light and sounds, followed by sudden blackouts. At first, Theresa Ikoko’s play appears post-apocalyptic. Television screens line the back wall with radio frequencies tuning in and out. A strange structure looms overhead. Information about who they are, where they are hiding, who from, is parcelled out gradually.You learn that they are three Nigerian friends and schoolgirls living in a forest in 2015. Their captors are never named but you can infer they are part of theinsurgent Islamist group, Boko Haram, from the breadcrumbs of backstory. Director Ewa Dina makes this explicit in her programme note when she refers to the Chibok Girls, involving Boko Haram’s mass abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok, Borno State, in 2014.View image in fullscreenA new realiy … Girls.Photograph: Helen MurrayThese three girls, we realise, are being held hostage in a camp, forced to convert to Islam with rumours that they might be sent out as suicide bombers or fighters. They speak of not feeling like children any more, of seeing their homes destroyed, watching a woman being trampled to death, the smell of burning human flesh, and of the corpses lying in the well nearby. They tell each other childhood stories of a mythic forest god, yet feel the absence of such a deity in their damned corner of the forest. But they also laugh, play childish games of make-believe, talk about sex and fight, like any group of female friends.Each character is individuated and responds differently to the terror of the camp: Haleema (Tara Tijani) is belligerent and plans escape, Ruhab (Sewa Zamba) submits to this new reality and finds a version of love among her captors, and Tisana (Hannah Akhalu), flogged daily for refusing to attend Islamic prayers, finds escape in fantasy.This is certainly a play that reminds us of the fate of the Chibok girls, and violence against women at its most extreme, but it is also a story about female friendship, sometimes tender, other times mean and spiky, rather likeAva Pickett’s trio of friends in her Tudor-era drama, 1536. But it is also fierce and loyal to the last.There are a few too many breakouts with claps of stagecraft thunder and lighting, and some short scene changes that bring confusion. The final use of screens showing faces (presumably of real-life missing girls) is abrupt and unexplained. But those reservations aside, this play, a winner of the Alfred Fagon award in 2015 and joint winner of the George Devine award in 2016, is without doubt a gut-punch: imaginative, tender, shocking. Thataround 90 of the Chibok Girls are still believed to be missingmakes it all the more haunting, and infuriating.At Young Vic, London until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreNigeriaBoko HaramYoung VicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The bare-handed beekeeper who looks like something out of The Odyssey: Holly Lynton’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. “Should I put them on my face?” he said. “Sure!” I replied’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. “Should I put them on my face?” he said. “Sure!” I replied’
Content: ‘I got a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up’ … US photographer Holly Lynton’s Bare Handed Les, Honeybees.Photograph: Holly LyntonView image in fullscreen‘I got a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up’ … US photographer Holly Lynton’s Bare Handed Les, Honeybees.Photograph: Holly LyntonMy best shotPhotographyThe bare-handed beekeeper who looks like something out of The Odyssey: Holly Lynton’s best photograph‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. “Should I put them on my face?” he said. “Sure!” I replied’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 28 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe jumping-off point for myBare Handed serieswas a bird becoming trapped in the netting around the raspberry bushes in my backyard. It made me think of the problem humans have interacting with the natural world. How do we navigate obtaining food and the other things we need while still being good stewards of the land? I’d seen work by photographers demonstrating how Big Agriculture was destroying the environment. I wanted to find people who took a respectful approach, tried to work in tandem with it, but who might be in a fearful or dangerous situation.I approached Les, the man in this picture, after speaking to the director of an exhibition space in Albuquerque, New Mexico, who had hired him to remove a feral beehive from his tree. I’d already tried to photograph another beekeeper who wore a full protective suit, but he might as well have been an astronaut. With Les, I was able to stay nearby and work with him over three days. The first couple involved straightforward documentary pictures of him tending his hives. Then, on the third day, his apprentice Amber showed up to help.Les had the queen bee in a cage in his shirt pocket and asked Amber to take it out. Wherever the queen is, the rest of the colony will swarm. There’s a picture I made whereLes and Amber are joined together by bees, and that was my “ah ha!” moment. Amber took out the queen and placed her in Les’s hand, which is where the bees went next. He looked at me with his hands full of bees and said: “Should I put them on my face?” I said: “Sure!”Les slowly moved his hands up to his face.Beesdon’t like hair, which is why they’re not in his beard or the top of his head. He closed his eyes for a few minutes, and I photographed. Afterwards, he said: “You know, I couldn’t hear anything but the buzzing.” I don’t think he’d ever done that before. People sometimes have their own ideas, which I just go with. One of the reasons I like spending some time with them is that when they’re engaged in work, it’s almost like watching a dance and waiting for the right gesture.double quotation markThe bees were landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see themLes didn’t wear gloves when handling the bees. He said he needed to be able to feel them so he didn’t crush them, and that it was too hot to wear a suit. I wore a shirt that buttoned up tight at the wrists and tried wearing a beekeeper’s veil, too, but I abandoned that after finding it hard to focus through the mesh. I did get a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up.I was using a medium-format analogue camera, and the bees were also landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see them. That was disconcerting, but Les advised me just to move slowly, as he did. That worked: I didn’t get stung.A grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photographRead moreFor a while, the photograph of Amber and Les joined together by bees was the one I preferred. I was worried people would find the bees on his face over the top. The themes of the project were quickly reinforced when I photographed wolves in a sanctuary with their trainers, and then went out with a family of catfish noodlers in rural Oklahoma. “Noodling” involved them catching these fish with their bare hands – even though they can weigh 45kg and really fight back. I realised none of these people had any fear. They were all experts at whatever it was they were doing, and for them this was a spiritual, meditative practice. That became the focus for the series.Before I started taking photography classes, I planned to be a psychologist and a writer. But what I love about photography is that you can create ambiguous narratives, a multilayered story in a single frame. A lot of my work references cultural memory. Rather than straight documentary, I’m aiming for something more mythic, and gestures that happen spontaneously can sometimes seem to reference a certain myth or biblical allusion. This photograph leans more towards Greek mythology, even if it doesn’t directly reference an exact story. Les isn’t Odysseus but, like him, he elects to hear rather than protect himself, which makes him feel like he’s a part of The Odyssey, somehow.View image in fullscreenHolly Lynton.Photograph: Holly LyntonHolly Lynton’s CVBorn:Boulder, Colorado, 1972High point:High points occur when my photographs are both made and shown. When photographing, a high point is when everything aligns – the light, content, composition – and I create an unanticipated image that transcends the moment. One that elicits allusion, mystery and wonder. In terms of exhibitions or publications, it’s often what is recent. In the past few years, institutions as varied as the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City and Bristol Cathedral in England have exhibited my work. I’m thankful that institutions have enabled people from many different backgrounds and perspectives to see my photographs. Talking with viewers and hearing their reactions has been a real gift. My book Bare Handed, published by L’Artiere, was another high point.Top tip:Right now, the quest for authenticity instead of artifice feels crucial, and what I’d urge photographers to undertake. I’d also say there is no such thing as too much curiosity (even though some people might make you think so). Don’t be afraid to change your mind about what you are working on, the meaning behind it or how to go about it. Reframing is what I like to call it. Follow your intuition. And find the joy in the practice of making work and being creative. Difficult moments will occur, and ones that feel like failures, but it’s the journey, not the end goal.Holly Lynton’s exhibition,Beyond the Bounds, is at Bristol Cathedraluntil 15 November, part ofBristol photo festivalExplore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotBeesInsectsAnimalsFarmingArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Walter Koenig obituary | Star Trek | The Guardian
description: Actor beloved by Star Trek fans for his portrayal of the show’s baby-faced Russian navigator Pavel Chekov
Author: Anthony Hayward
Headline: Actor beloved by Star Trek fans for his portrayal of the show’s baby-faced Russian navigator Pavel Chekov
Content: Walter Koenig as Chekov in a 1967 Star Trek episode. He was cast after a search by the show’s creator, Gene Roddenberry, for an actor with boyish good looks to appeal to younger viewers.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWalter Koenig as Chekov in a 1967 Star Trek episode. He was cast after a search by the show’s creator, Gene Roddenberry, for an actor with boyish good looks to appeal to younger viewers.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesStar TrekObituaryWalter Koenig obituaryActor beloved by Star Trek fans for his portrayal of the show’s baby-faced Russian navigator Pavel ChekovAnthony HaywardWed 28 Oct 2026 08.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe American actorWalter Koenig, who has died aged 90, was unimpressed when, as a TV viewer, he caught a glimpse of Star Trek on its launch in 1966. “I’d flip through the channels,” he recalled, “and I’d see Styrofoam rocks – they were so obviously Styrofoam – and I said, ‘This has got to be phony.’ I didn’t give it a chance. I went past it.”A year later, he was cast in the programme as Ensign Pavel Chekov, the baby-faced navigator of Russian parentage on the bridge of the starship USS Enterprise. This followed a search by Star Trek’s creator,Gene Roddenberry, for a character to appeal to young viewers, someone with the boyish, pop-star good looks of the Monkees singerDavy Jones.View image in fullscreenWalter Koenig as Pavel Chekov in Star Trek.Photograph: John Springer Collection/Corbis/Getty ImagesWhile denying the move was in response to complaints from the Soviet Union’s Pravda newspaper that there were no Russian crew members inStar Trek, Roddenberry conceded that it should acknowledge their achievement in putting the first cosmonaut into space.Koenig (pronounced Kay-nig), the US-born son of Russian-Jewish immigrants from Lithuania, faked a Russian accent to take his place on the starship alongside William Shatner as Captain James T Kirk,Leonard Nimoyas the Vulcan science officer, Spock,DeForest Kelleyas Dr Leonard “Bones” McCoy and George Takei as Hikaru Sulu at the helm, battling Klingons, Romulans and other alien races.Fan mail poured in for Koenig as he relished playing a character in a programme that he had previously written off. Roddenberry suggested he ham up the accent to add a touch of comic relief, which meant Chekov would be seen looking at his monitor and warning Kirk of an imminent threat from an “enemy wessel”. Koenig said the accent was inspired by his father. “My dad inverted the Vs and the Ws,” he explained.A patriot for his ancestral country, Chekov falsely gives credit to Russia for various inventions and achievements. He tells his colleagues that the biblical Garden of Eden was “outside Moscow”, Cinderella emanated from a Russian epic and scotch whisky “was een-vented by leetle old lady in Leningrad”.Koenig appeared in 36 episodes throughout Star Trek’s second and third series (1967-69) before the programme was axed, having failed to attract a large enough audience on the US network NBC. But public interest in space missions after the 1969 moon landing, followed by syndicated re-runs across the US – and sales to more than 60 countries – turned it into a TV sci-fi classic.View image in fullscreenThe crew of the Starship Enterprise, from left, Leonard Nimoy as Spock, Koenig as Chekov, William Shatner as Captain Kirk, Nichelle Nichols as Uhura, George Takei as Sulu and James Doohan as “Scotty”, in a 1968 episode of Star Trek.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesKoenig also appeared in all six feature films (1979-91) spun off from the series, plus Star Trek: Generations (1994), a “passing of the torch” story featuring the original stars with those from TV’s Star Trek: The Next Generation.While he continued to land guest roles on TV, Koenig reached a sci-fi audience again in all five series of the 23rd-century “space opera” Babylon 5 (1993-98) as Alfred Bester, a manipulative senior cop with telepathic powers working for the Earth Alliance agency Psi Corps.Born inChicago, Illinois, Walter was the son of Sarah (nee Strauss) and Irving Koenig (born Isadore Naum Koenigsberg), who worked as a flautist, nightclub owner and translator after settling in the US and changing the family name.As a communist, Irving survived investigation by the FBI during the McCarthy witch-hunts era. “His beliefs were very, very ideological and philosophical,” explained Koenig. “He wasn’t encouraging the overthrow of the US government. He was just trying to create a better world and have people come together.” It was a sentiment echoed by Roddenberry in Star Trek.The family moved to Manhattan,New York, when Koenig was young, and he started acting at Fieldston high school. “I had a stutter until I took the lead in the school play and that killed the stutter,” he revealed.After graduating in psychology from UCLA (the University of California Los Angeles), where a professor encouraged him to act, from 1958 he trained at the Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in New York alongside fellow students such asJames Caan.View image in fullscreenKoenig in 2009 with his second wife, Judy Levitt, an actor who appeared in three Star Trek films.Photograph: Noel Vasquez/FilmMagicHis early television appearances included parts as a student in The Untouchables (in 1963), a teenage street-gang leader in The Alfred Hitchcock Hour (in 1964) and a Las Vegas entertainer in I Spy (1966). He also appeared in a 1964 episode of The Lieutenant, one of Roddenberry’s early creations, playing a US Marine Corps sergeant recommended for officer candidates school.After his run in Star Trek, Koenig voiced Pavel in spin-off video games and was a regular in front of Trekkies at fan conventions. He also popped up in other TV programmes in character roles and wrote for a handful of series, including Land of the Lost (1974) and The Powers of Matthew Star (1982), as well as an episode of Star Trek: The Animated Series (1973).Koenig wrote an autobiography, Warped Factors: A Neurotic’s Guide to the Universe (1998), and a sci-fi novel, Buck Alice and the Actor-Robot (1988), a post-apocalyptic story featuring an actor who believes he is the robot he once portrayed on TV, as well as creating the comic-book superhero Raver (1993).His first marriage, to the actor Anjanette Comer, ended in divorce. In 1965, Koenig married the actor Judy Levitt, who appeared in three Star Trek films; she died in 2022. Their son, Andrew, died in 2010. Koenig is survived by their daughter, Danielle.Walter Marvin Koenig, actor and writer, born 14 September 1936; died 25 October 2026Explore more on these topicsStar TrekTelevisionUS televisionChicagoNew YorkobituariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dear Charlie’: letter revealing move to snare future Rolling Stones drummer up for auction | The Rolling Stones | The Guardian
description: Brian Jones wrote to Charlie Watts in 1962 asking him to leave his R&B group and join his ‘far better’ band instead
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Brian Jones wrote to Charlie Watts in 1962 asking him to leave his R&B group and join his ‘far better’ band instead
Content: From centre clockwise: Brian Jones, Charlies Watts, Keith Richards, Mick Jagger and Bill Wyman.Photograph: Camerique/AlamyView image in fullscreenFrom centre clockwise: Brian Jones, Charlies Watts, Keith Richards, Mick Jagger and Bill Wyman.Photograph: Camerique/AlamyThe Rolling Stones‘Dear Charlie’: letter revealing move to snare future Rolling Stones drummer up for auctionBrian Jones wrote to Charlie Watts in 1962 asking him to leave his R&B group and join his ‘far better’ band insteadNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 06.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA handwritten letter from Brian Jones toCharlie Wattsin which he attempts to recruit the drummer to join the band that would soon become the Rolling Stones is being auctioned later this year.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Brian JonesThe 1962 letter, which comes directly from Watts’s sister and has remained in the family for more than six decades, will be revealed to the public for the first time.Watts was still working in advertising at the time while playing with Alexis Korner’s Blues Incorporated, one of the leading groups in London’s burgeoning rhythm and blues scene. He was initially reluctant to commit to Jones’s fledgling band, which had yet to be named.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Brian JonesThe letter comes with its original envelope and is addressed to “Mr. C. Watts” at his childhood home in Wembley. Jones begins: “Dear Charlie, if you consider this letter rather impertinent, please excuse me.”He goes on to enquire about Watts’s involvement with Blues Incorporated, before making his case for Watts to join his own band.“We are looking for a good drummer. Already we consider our band far better than Alex’s – we are getting a very tightly-knit sound.”In a particularly memorable postscript, Jones outlines the band’s existing lineup of two guitars, harmonica, piano and drums, noting their intention to eventually introduce a bass guitar, before offering a rather frank assessment of their current drummer: “Our present drummer is atrocious!”Despite Jones’s early overtures, it would take another seven months before Watts officially joined the Rolling Stones, in January 1963. By then, bassist Bill Wyman had also joined, completing the rhythm section that would become central to the band’s distinctive sound.On 2 February 1963, the Rolling Stones performed with their early six-member lineup of Watts, Wyman, Jones, Keith Richards, Mick Jagger and pianist Ian Stewart.The band’s desire to recruit Watts was later recalled by Richards in his autobiography Life, in which he described the lengths to which the musicians were prepared to go to bring him into the fold.Richards remembered that they had even cut back on food to afford the drummer, declaring: “We starved ourselves to pay for him!”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Brian JonesSotheby’s said the letter offered “a remarkable first-hand glimpse” into the band’s formative months and its determination to recruit Watts, who would become an integral part of their sound for nearly six decades.“Few documents bring us as close to the formation of a legendary band as this letter,” said Craig Inciardi, Sotheby’s music and pop culture specialist.“Written just weeks before the Rolling Stones’ first performance and months before Charlie Watts officially joined the group, it captures the excitement and ambition of a band on the cusp of history.“Having remained in the Watts family for more than six decades, it stands as an extraordinary first-hand record of the momentBrian Jonesset out to recruit the drummer whose distinctive sound would help shape one of the most influential bands in rock history.”The letter will be on public view at Sotheby’s New York from 2 December to 8 December, with online bidding open from 2 December until the Rock & Pop sale on 15 December. It is estimated to fetch between $70,000 and $80,000 (£52,000-£60,000).Watts would go on to remain the Rolling Stones’ drummer for nearly six decades, performing and recording with the band until his death in August 2021.Explore more on these topicsThe Rolling StonesCharlie WattsBrian JonesPop and rockShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: to nail this year’s British heritage look, just study Rivals | Women's coats and jackets | The Guardian
description: Thanks to Jilly Cooper, tartan and tweed, waxed jackets and wellies are a style vibe right now
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Thanks to Jilly Cooper, tartan and tweed, waxed jackets and wellies are a style vibe right now
Content: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionWomen's coats and jacketsJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: to nail this year’s British heritage look, just study RivalsThanks to Jilly Cooper, tartan and tweed, waxed jackets and wellies are a style vibe right nowJess Cartner-MorleyWed 28 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish heritage, in fashion terms, is a country where it is permanently October. A conker-brown and pleasant land, if you will. Brand Britain in the style sense comes into its own in autumn: roaring fires, muddy lanes, damp dogs. Waxed jackets and chunky knits, tartan and tweed, jaunty scarves to banish draughts. Clothes for going on a hearty walk, but with a hip flask in your pocket. Fashion has been mining this seam since long before Brideshead Revisited made battered evening dresses and Oxford bags look romantic, and it keeps returning, because trad British style is satisfyingly utilitarian while also being loaded with enough backstory (class, history, eccentricity) to be intriguing and reinventable.Also:Rivals. It has taken considerable restraint for me not to mention Rivals in the whole of the first paragraph, because it is now a matter of mere weeks until we get our next Jilly Cooper fix and I, for one, cannot wait. Cannot wait for Cameron stalking the corridors in her foxy power suits, for Taggie in her cute jeans and jumpers, for Valerie in head-to-toe tweed and an aggressive amount of blusher. The success of Rivals has done for old-school British dressing whatEmily in Parisdid for the beret, only with better jokes and more adultery. Jolly hockey sticks style is the new French girl chic. This fantasy is homegrown, which makes it both more embarrassing and harder to resist. Just as Emily and her friends and frenemies are a camp send-up of fashionable Paris, Rivals is a fond, nostalgic semi-parody of the British wardrobe. The show’s costume designer, Ray Holman, has drawn on original 1980s pieces from Dunhill and Mulberry for inspiration. With Liberty fabrics, nods to polo uniforms and sturdy waxed coats, he has brought the Sloane ranger back into the fashion conversation for the first time in years.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianBritish heritage is a style vibe right now. Barbour and Mulberry joined Burberry in stepping up to the style plate and taking part in London fashion week this season. Kate Moss is in her wellies forHunter’s latest advertising campaign, while Sienna Miller and Idris Elba star inBarbour’s. Barbour also features a cameo from some sheep, which says something about how countryside-coded the British heritage look is at heart. Fair Isle knits and Argyle diamond-pattern sweaters are worn draped over the shoulders, shown off as trophies. Waxed or tweedy jackets are taking over from urban puffer jackets. The neutral of the season is brown (mud) rather than black (asphalt).double quotation markThe twist? A touch of urban polish – a slick bun, a pointy shoe, or trousers with a crease down the frontThere is plenty of glamour, too. Pearls, silk scarves, jewel-toned velvets. Polka dots, which have broken out of the village fete and are now in their baddie era. The key is to let the fancy stuff rub up against the practical stuff. A waxed jacket over a party dress is a core British look, whether you are going to a rave, a festival or a hunt ball. There is something deeply British in the irreverence of putting a battered coat over a hot dress. A silk scarf is a retro touch that works equally well in a gale and a paparazzi shot. Tweed is surprisingly versatile, because it looks great out of context: with baggy jeans, or over a band T-shirt.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: how to wear a leather jacket so it doesn’t wear youRead moreOne of the best things about British heritage style is that – unlike the high maintenance of Emily in Paris – it is only improved by looking a little lived-in. A waxed jacket benefits from the creases it develops after a few adventures. Cashmere has more soul when the neckline is a little looser. Wellies are nothing without mud. It’s a style that often looks more appealing when you find it in a charity shop than when it’s box-fresh off the catwalk.The twist? One element of metropolitan polish. An urban girlie, slicked-back bun and a gold hoop. A pointy shoe, or trousers with a crease down the front. That way it works whether you have a labrador at your heel or a laptop on your knee.Styling: Melanie Wilkinson.Model: Imogen May at Milk.Hair and makeup: Sophie Higginson using Sam McKnight andMakeup by Mario.Blazer, £65,andtrousers£40, both Marks& Spencer.Trench, £269, andtop, £75, both Aligne.Shirt, £125, Me+Em.Heels, £99, Dune. Rings, model’s own.
