title: The best umbrellas in the UK for staying dry in the wind and rain – tested on a 517m hilltop | Accessories | The Guardian
description: Our reviewer braved Peak District downpours to see which brollies – from budget to mini to windproof – stayed standing
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Our reviewer braved Peak District downpours to see which brollies – from budget to mini to windproof – stayed standing
Content: Brolly good show: some umbrellas, such as the Davek Elite, pictured, sailed through the Mam Tor test.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBrolly good show: some umbrellas, such as the Davek Elite, pictured, sailed through the Mam Tor test.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterAccessoriesReviewThe best umbrellas in the UK for staying dry in the wind and rain – tested on a 517m hilltopOur reviewer braved Peak District downpours to see which brollies – from budget to mini to windproof – stayed standingThe best waterproof jackets for womenThe best waterproof jackets for menPete WiseUpdatedWed 28 Oct 202606.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe Britons have loved brollies since about the turn of the 19th century. Previously an aristocratic luxury, today they’re a broad tent covering tight budgets and expensive tastes alike. You’ll see them sprout like mushrooms whenever rain hits the high street.Most decent umbrellas will keep you dry(ish), but peek closer and you’ll find that not all are the same. Some have stronger, smoother mechanisms; others are lighter and more comfortable to hold. The best stand out for thoughtful details: from polished wooden handles to gleaming tips, a brolly’s aesthetic finish can often be a clue to how long it will last.At a glanceBest umbrella overallLondon UndercoverClassic£115 at London UndercoverBest budget umbrellaDopplerZero 99£21.61 at AmazonBest compact umbrellaBluntMetro£74.50 at AmazonBest-looking umbrellaOswin HydeJoseph£53 at DebenhamsBest windproof folding umbrellaShed RainVortex V2 windproof compact£30 at Shed RainBest mini umbrellaDavekMini£65 at DavekBest golf umbrellaFultonTitan 1£40 at AmazonBest fun umbrellaGillian KyleTunnock’s tea cake luxury umbrella£49.50 at Gillian KyleWhy you should trust meAs a regular umbrella carrier, I use mine to stay dry on my soggy travels around the north of England. The best models keep the rain off and are convenient to carry. I’m also selective about colourways, materials, design and construction.If I’m under a brolly, there’s a good chance I’m either on my way to field-test a product, or nipping to the library where I do much of my writing. I have extensive experience reviewing useful things, fromtravel pillowstoreusable cups, for titles including the Filter. For the past decade or so, I’ve devoted much of my time to working out what differentiates one product from another, and what really matters to the user.How I testedPete Wise stands on top of Mam Tor grinning as he holds a series of umbrellas blowing in the windTesting the brollies’ wind resistance on Mam Tor. Video: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianThroughout October 2025 – and again in September 2026 to test a second batch – I carried each umbrella daily and noted how effectively it sheltered me from rain and wind. Did it cover my head, shoulders and torso adequately? Was it comfortable to hold? And would a sudden gust of wind turn its canopy inside out?For a sterner test of resilience and wind resistance, I opened up the umbrellas in strong winds near the summit of Mam Tor, a highly exposed, 517-metre hill in the Peak District, which overlooks part of theSteel Cotton Rail Trail. To give the 2026 batch of brollies a comparable test, I used them in very windy weather in the West Yorkshire countryside. (Thanks to photographer Christian Hopewell for capturing the fun, and to Alice Ostapjuk-Wise for helping it run smoothly.)Of course, not all umbrellas are designed for use in extreme conditions. Each of the reviews below reflects the umbrella’s performance against the manufacturer’s claims, as well as how it fared during hilltop testing.I assessed 19 umbrellas in total and have featured the best selection here. After testing, I took the wind-buffeted brollies to my localMindcharity shop.The best umbrellas in 2026View image in fullscreenThe lineup: waiting to brave the elements.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianBest umbrella overall:London Undercover ClassicLondon UndercoverClassic£115£115 at London UndercoverWhat we loveExcellent craftspersonship and lovely materialsWhat we don’t loveIt’s an investmentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£115 at London UndercoverThe London Undercover Classic emerged as the top performer in both day-to-day use and hilltop testing.Why we love itIt’s a beautifully finished model, right down to the frilly orange rosette on the runner. Each design has a pleasant colour contrast on the underside to add some cheer to your under-brolly microclimate, which proved impressively dry here. I found the slim, elegant maple hook handle comfortable to hold.The canopy is made entirely from recycled polyethylene terephthalate fabric and comprises two layers – this is key to the Classic’s exceptional wind resistance. On the hilltop, it withstood strong gusts without inverting, and even when I held it high into the air, it inverted only slightly at one side.As the canopy is fairly deep, there’s decent coverage of the head and shoulders. For taller users, a wider model might be better for the torso and legs.It’s a shame that …at £115, this umbrella is a serious investment, although you get outstanding quality in return.Weight:500gLength (folded):91.5cmCanopy diameter:105cmWarranty:one year (and exceptional cases considered over a longer period)London UndercoverClassic£115£115 at London UndercoverWhat we loveExcellent craftspersonship and lovely materialsWhat we don’t loveIt’s an investmentBest budget umbrella:Doppler Zero 99DopplerZero 99from£21.61£24.99 at Debenhams£21.61 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to keep in a handbag or backpackWhat we don’t loveRelatively narrow coverageView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£24.99 at DebenhamsFrom £21.61 at AmazonAre you someone who ends up buying an ultra-cheap brolly on unexpectedly rainy days? I suspect many of us are.Why we love itThis fairly priced, pocket-sized brolly from Doppler is a better, eco-friendlier solution. Its weight and size mean you can happily keep it in your bag, ready for use whenever rain starts to fall. Using it on the sodden streets of Leeds, I foundit helpful during moderate showers, although the smallish canopy meant my legs received a dousing.It’s cleverly designed to minimise the heft, especially the small circular grip at the bottom of the pole. For the price, the design is outstanding.It’s a shame that …this umbrella is highly prone to inverting in the wind, and coverage is relatively limited. It’s fine in a light shower but not suitable for challenging weather.Weight:99gLength (folded):21cmCanopy diameter:90cmWarranty:three yearsDopplerZero 99from£21.61£24.99 at Debenhams£21.61 at AmazonWhat we loveEasy to keep in a handbag or backpackWhat we don’t loveRelatively narrow coverageBest compact umbrella:Blunt MetroBluntMetrofrom£74.50£74.95 at Wildbounds£74.50 at AmazonWhat we loveUplifting style and innovative designWhat we don’t loveSome water flicks back when you shake it outView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£74.95 at WildboundsFrom £74.50 at AmazonThe Blunt Metro is a statement piece that will bring sunshine to a rainy day – especially in the citrus yellow colour I was testing.Why we love itIt feels sturdy and durable, and the canopy proved broad enough to keep my head and shoulders dry. The automatic opening action is smooth, although the button for this in the handle was easy to press accidentally.Victorian Londoners were crying out for this brolly: an initial brake on their uptake was the risk of collisions on crowded streets – so argued William Sangster in his book of 1855, Umbrellas and Their History.The Metro’s solution for this continuing problem? It can spin freely through 360 degrees when open, so it rolls breezily away when knocked.Like every other folding umbrella I tested, it wasn’t long before the Metro inverted on the hilltop, but it popped back into shape easily. It stood up well against sudden gusts in day-to-day use, though.It’s a shame that …this umbrella tends to send a shower of droplets back towards you when you try to shake it dry.Weight:385gLength (folded):37.5cmCanopy diameter:100cmWarranty:two yearsBluntMetrofrom£74.50£74.95 at Wildbounds£74.50 at AmazonWhat we loveUplifting style and innovative designWhat we don’t loveSome water flicks back when you shake it outBest-looking umbrella:Oswin Hyde JosephOswin HydeJosephfrom£53£53 at Debenhams£53 at BurtonWhat we loveAttractive canopy with plenty of coverageWhat we don’t loveBuild quality is decent but not the bestView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£53 at Debenhams£53 at BurtonThis Oswin Hyde umbrella is a remarkable buy at its price of £53 (RRP £75) at the time of writing. It’s attractive, reminiscent of traditional Indian state umbrellas (calledchatra); the components feel of good quality; and the brolly rolls up neatly for carrying or storage inside its protective sleeve.Why we love itI found this a very pleasant umbrella to shelter under. It’s broad enough to prevent vertical or near-vertical rain from hitting most parts of the body, and wide enough for two.This umbrella did invert in the wind, without needing as much blustery coercion as some rivals, but I was impressed at how it bounced back. It’s clear that the ribs are highly flexible, which should help them to resist damage.It’s a shame that …this isn’t quite as robust as some of the higher-end brollies here. I found that the tip can be dented easily.Weight:658gLength (folded):92cmCanopy diameter:112cmWarranty:six monthsOswin HydeJosephfrom£53£53 at Debenhams£53 at BurtonWhat we loveAttractive canopy with plenty of coverageWhat we don’t loveBuild quality is decent but not the bestBest windproof folding umbrella:Shed Rain Vortex V2 windproof compactShed RainVortex V2 windproof compact£30£30 at Shed RainWhat we loveBest-of-breed wind resistanceWhat we don’t loveIt’s relatively heavyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£30 at Shed RainHere’s a novel thing: an umbrella that looks and feels like it hails from this century. It’s a folding model, with a canopy made up of two layers of material for inversion resistance. The US-based manufacturer Shed Rain is a newcomer to the UK in autumn 2026, and it claims this brolly can withstand winds of up to 75mph. Gusts only reached about 40mph during my testing, but the umbrella certainly didn’t invert.Why we love itThe Vortex V2’s construction quality is excellent. Even when folding the umbrella away, it snaps cleanly back into place. It feels solid and stable, so I’d be confident using it in pretty wretched weather. During testing in gusty autumn weather, it resisted wind more effectively than any other folding umbrella, and the canopy is broad enough to shelter a lone user from the rain.In the black colourway, neon yellow is used to highlight details, including the strong, ultra-thin cords reinforcing the frame and the barely there ferrule at the top, while the semi-transparent canvas improves outward visibility.It has a comfy bulb-shaped handle with a rubbery feel and scored lines towards the bottom for added grip.It’s a shame that …this brolly is quite heavy for its size and type.Weight:431gLength (folded):30.5cmCanopy width:109cmWarranty:conditional lifetime guarantee covering defects in materials or workmanshipShed RainVortex V2 windproof compact£30£30 at Shed RainWhat we loveBest-of-breed wind resistanceWhat we don’t loveIt’s relatively heavyBest mini umbrella:Davek MiniDavekMini£65£65 at DavekWhat we loveGreat wind and rain protection relative to its sizeWhat we don’t loveQuite costly for a mini-modelView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£65 at DavekThe Davek Mini is the finest miniature umbrella I’ve ever unfurled. Its elaborate frame (fibreglass reinforced for wind resistance) held up longer than other folding models at the summit of Mam Tor; however, I wouldn’t recommend it for use in blustery weather.Why we love itThis brolly feels incredibly light, and if you study the details, you’ll understand why. For instance, the handle is tiny and hollow, but surprisingly more comfortable to grasp than many of its more bulbous rivals. I’d suggest using the wrist strap at the same time, for a more secure hold.The canopy is broader than you might expect, with a diameter that rivals some mid-size umbrellas. It kept my head dry during rain showers, although the same can’t be said for my legs.It’s a shame that …it costs £65, which is steep for a mini-umbrella. However, factor in the lifetime guarantee, and this could be a prudent choice.Weight:225gLength (folded):17cmCanopy diameter:86cmWarranty:unconditional lifetime guaranteeDavekMini£65£65 at DavekWhat we loveGreat wind and rain protection relative to its sizeWhat we don’t loveQuite costly for a mini-modelBest golf umbrella:Fulton Titan 1FultonTitan 1£40£40 at AmazonWhat we loveAn effective, value-for-money optionWhat we don’t lovePersonally, I’m not keen on the straight handleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£40 at AmazonI’ll admit that golf umbrellas aren’t my favourite breed of brolly, but this model from Fulton won me over. The windproof vented canopy proved highly effective at resisting inversion in strong winds, even as I was beginning to lose my footing.Why we love itFulton describes this canopy as “supersize”, and at 136cm in diameter, it’s certainly the largest I’ve tested. There’s ample coverage for two people.The Titan 1’s construction is impressive, too, especially considering the affordable pricing. Its lightweight fibreglass frame has remarkable flexibility and gives the brolly a bouncy feel in hand.Rather than sporting a sleeve, the Titan comes in a carry case with a shoulder strap, allowing for easier, hands-free transportation.It’s a shame that …this umbrella can sometimes make your forearms ache. Holding it by the straight grip (which is undoubtedly comfy), I found it easy to rest back on my shoulder but quite strenuous to hold forwards into the wind.Weight:950gLength (folded):98cmCanopy diameter:136cmWarranty:all manufacturing faults consideredFultonTitan 1£40£40 at AmazonWhat we loveAn effective, value-for-money optionWhat we don’t lovePersonally, I’m not keen on the straight handleBest fun umbrella:Gillian Kyle Tunnock’s tea cake luxury umbrellaGillian KyleTunnock’s tea cake luxury umbrella£49.50£49.50 at Gillian KyleWhat we loveWell made with a fun designWhat we don’t loveNo crook-handled optionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£49.50 at Gillian KyleWhowouldn’twant to look like a Tunnock’s tea cake when viewed from above in rainy weather? This licensed print from designer Gillian Kyle makes the dream a reality.Why we love itFor a sweet-themed product, this umbrella hardly seems confected. The build quality is very good, and the brolly is beautifully designed with wooden ferrules on the end of each rib, a moulded wooden handle and a lozenge-shaped button to operate the opening mechanism.In terms of protection against the rain, the canopy is somewhere between mid-size and fairly large, with generous coverage for one person or just about enough for two slender folk. It’s a good size to carry when you’re ducking down snickets, or navigating your way through crowded city streets, and despite its decent coverage, the brolly is light enough to carry for extended periods without much effort.Of course, the main draw here is the Tunnock’s print, and this looks splendid across the canopy, with vivid reds that capture all the cheer of a chocolate teacake.It’s a shame that …there isn’t a crook-handled variant available for people like myself, who find straight handles a faff after a few miles pounding the pavements.Weight:548gLength (folded):90cmCanopy width:1mWarranty:60-day returns periodGillian KyleTunnock’s tea cake luxury umbrella£49.50£49.50 at Gillian KyleWhat we loveWell made with a fun designWhat we don’t loveNo crook-handled optionThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Resisted inversion impressively’: the Davek Elite.Photograph: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianV&A blue Japanese umbrellaV&ABlue Japanese umbrella£25£25 at V&A ShopWhat we loveBeautiful art print canopyWhat we don’t loveGeneric build qualityView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£25 at V&A ShopBest for:city dwellersAdorned with a 1930s Japanese art print, the canopy of this V&A brolly is surpassingly pretty. I love the rich, indigo background and the fine detail in yellows, reds and greens.The construction of this lightweight, folding umbrella is adequate for lighter showers and gentle breezes, and it just about resisted inverting during my trial walks. Its handle is a perfectly palm-sized cylinder, with a wrist loop to help you hold on to it.Considering the umbrella’s small folded size, the canopy is surprisingly wide, offering ample coverage for the head and shoulders, at least.Two other prints are available from the V&A collection: a May Morris honeysuckle print, and a French design featuring purple flowers.It didn’t make the final cut because…while the build quality is decent for the price you pay, it’s no match for some of the other folding brollies we’ve tested. Use this one to spread some beauty during lighter showers.Weight:285g;length (folded):28cm;canopy width:96cm;warranty:28-day returns periodV&ABlue Japanese umbrella£25£25 at V&A ShopWhat we loveBeautiful art print canopyWhat we don’t loveGeneric build qualityFulton Minilite 2FultonMinilite 2from£25£25 at Selfridges£25 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks cheerful and costs littleWhat we don’t loveLacks the refinement of higher-end brolliesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£25 at Selfridges£25 at AmazonBest for:a pocket umbrellaFulton makes this Minilite 2 style with various printed canopies, including retro stripes, art prints and the glitter bow version shown. The folded size is suitable for handbags and backpacks.It didn’t make the final cut because …it feels quite rickety compared with the other options here.Weight:236g;length (folded):25cm;canopy diameter:96cm;warranty:all manufacturing faults consideredFultonMinilite 2from£25£25 at Selfridges£25 at AmazonWhat we loveLooks cheerful and costs littleWhat we don’t loveLacks the refinement of higher-end brolliesPaul Smith compact umbrellaPaul SmithCompact umbrellafrom£87.50£87.50 at Liberty£125 at Paul SmithWhat we loveClassic style and compact proportionsWhat we don’t loveNot the most protective optionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£87.50 at Liberty£125 at Paul SmithBest for:a designer umbrellaWould you like an umbrella with ample coverage and a classic aesthetic or one that fits inside a rucksack? This Paul Smith covers both bases. Its canopy is wide and deep, and the telescopic pole allows it to fold down to a manageable size.My favourite touch is the wooden crook handle – a rarity in folding umbrellas.It didn’t make the final cut because …although it’s mid-size, this umbrella fared little better than smaller folding models in strong winds.Weight:433g;length (folded):47cm;canopy diameter:100cm;warranty:two yearsPaul SmithCompact umbrellafrom£87.50£87.50 at Liberty£125 at Paul SmithWhat we loveClassic style and compact proportionsWhat we don’t loveNot the most protective optionKnirps T200 DuomaticKnirpsT200 Duomatic£60.85£60.85 at AmazonWhat we loveSuper-slick opening mechanismWhat we don’t loveWhile it resists wind damage, it inverts easilyView image in fullscreen£60.85 at AmazonBest for:automatic opening and closingNot quite as small as some mini or pocket folding umbrellas, but this model from Knirps will fit comfortably inside a good-size backpack or handbag. So while it might not sustain damage in windy weather, it’s perhaps not the best brolly to use in these conditions.Weight:320g;length (folded):28cm;canopy diameter:98cm;warranty:five yearsKnirpsT200 Duomatic£60.85£60.85 at AmazonWhat we loveSuper-slick opening mechanismWhat we don’t loveWhile it resists wind damage, it inverts easilyLifeventure Medium TrekLifeventureMedium Trekfrom£21.99£21.99 at Liveventure£28.99 at Mountain WarehouseWhat we loveUV protective material for exposed treksWhat we don’t loveMiddling wind resistanceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Hopewell/The Guardian£21.99 at Liveventure£28.99 at Mountain WarehouseBest for:UV protectionBefore umbrellas were used to keep off rain, parasols shielded people from the sun. In black, it has a slightly “goth winter” feel to it, with a stitched leather handle and elongated rib tips.During tests in high winds, the Elite resisted inversion impressively, quickly returning to the desired shape. The fibreglass frame proved highly flexible and resilient to stress.It didn’t make the final cut because …personally, I preferred other umbrellas in a similar price range. That’s not to say this isn’t a great brolly, though.Weight:708g;length (folded):89cm;canopy diameter:112cm;warranty:unconditional lifetime guaranteeDavekElite£159£159 at DavekWhat we loveIt looks exceptionally smartWhat we don’t loveLess refined than certain similarly priced rivalsWhat you need to knowPete Wise stands on a rural hill holding a series of umbrellas, some turning inside out in the windStormproof umbrellas fared best in the hilltop tests. Video: Christian Hopewell/The GuardianFeatures to look out forAutomatic opening(and sometimes closure) makes using an umbrella easier. It’s common in golf umbrellas and even more so in folding umbrellas, which employ a telescopic pole (or shaft) for compact portability.Stormproofor windproof umbrellas have vents or dual layers of fabric to allow gusts through. These models performed best in high winds. Windproof models can also come with a double-ribbed frame, which makes the umbrella more resilient to the push and pull of high winds.What types of umbrellas are there?City umbrellasare the traditional choice in the UK, with a long, solid pole and a wide canopy. Most have a curved handle called a hook or crook.Sportier and often with brighter-coloured canopies,golf umbrellasare another large, non-folding option. Many have straight-grip handles.Folding umbrellas– also known as portable umbrellas or pocket umbrellas – have been around since the Victorian period. The best are made with super-lightweight materials and can endure blustery conditions without breaking. Their telescopic shafts make them easy to slip into a rucksack or handbag.Parasols– in the UK, using an umbrella for sun protection hasn’t been seen since Victorian times, but shielding you from the sun’s harmful UV rays is one of a parasol’s greatest strengths. There’s little difference between a regular umbrella and a parasol, but choose a model with a wide, deep canopy – ideally one made using UV-protective material, such as theLifeventure modelreviewed above.How to look after your umbrellaCare instructions for umbrellas vary from one brand to another, but there are some general rules to follow that will see your model last for as long as possible:Allow it to dry after use.Eschew superstition and leave your rain-sodden umbrella open indoors in a well-ventilated space, having given it a good shake outside. Leaving a brolly wet can lead to buildups of rust, mould and mildew, along with the accompanying smells.Clean it occasionally.Wipe it over with a mix of water and detergent to remove grime and germs. Dry it thoroughly after cleaning.Don’t store it in a car.Widely fluctuating temperatures inside a car, compared with in a home, can cause an umbrella’s materials to expand and contract, weakening them and causing the umbrella to deteriorate faster. Plus, a damp umbrella could harbour mould. Heat exposure can also damage an umbrella, so don’t leave yours by the radiator.Keep an eye on it.David McKie, formerly of this parish,once opinedthat “no object is so frequently lost” as an umbrella. To avoid this common misfortune while away from home, leave it with your coat or bag – or better still, keep it by your side.Choose a brandthat offers repairs.Certain brands, such asLondon Undercover, offer a repair service (at a cost for out-of-warranty items), covering issues with handles, canopies, ribs and other components – which means you’ll be able to use your brolly for many years to come.What to do with your old umbrellaCharity shops will often accept preloved umbrellas that are in good condition. Sadly, if your umbrella is damaged beyond repair, then you’ll need to take it to your local household waste recycling centre. Guidance on umbrellas varies among these facilities, so check with your localcentrebefore turning up.For more, read thebest waterproof jackets for menand thebest waterproof jackets for womenPete Wise is ajournalist from Leeds.Pete thoroughly enjoyed readingMarion Rankine’sbook Brolliologyas research for this article. His favourite umbrella is aBettys TeaRooms-branded one that once belonged to his mother. Beneath its canopy is the place where they can still have a chatThis article was originally published on 4 November 2025. title: Hold the lime! Could eating citrus zest and peel really be bad for your health? | Food | The Guardian
description: Food safety campaigners have long been concerned about pesticide residues on lemons, limes and oranges – and now a social media post about it has gone viral. How safe is it to eat lemon cake or drink a G&T with ice and a slice?
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: Food safety campaigners have long been concerned about pesticide residues on lemons, limes and oranges – and now a social media post about it has gone viral. How safe is it to eat lemon cake or drink a G&T with ice and a slice?
Content: If you want to avoid the pesticides used to preserve citrus fruit, buy organic produce.Photograph: Steve Lupton/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIf you want to avoid the pesticides used to preserve citrus fruit, buy organic produce.Photograph: Steve Lupton/Getty ImagesFoodHold the lime! Could eating citrus zest and peel really be bad for your health?Food safety campaigners have long been concerned about pesticide residues on lemons, limes and oranges – and now a social media post about it has gone viral. How safe is it to eat lemon cake or drink a G&T with ice and a slice?Rachel DixonWed 28 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you sprinkle citrus zest on to your cooking or drink hot water with a slice of lemon? According toan Instagram postthat went viral last week, you shouldn’t. “Select citrus fruits at Lidl now come with a ‘Peel unfit for consumption’ warning,” posts @wholefoodwarrior. She photographs some of the supermarket’s labels, which list the post-harvest chemicals used to conserve the fruit: azoxystrobin and fludioxonil (limes) and imazalil, 2-phenylphenol, thiabendazole, pyrimethanil and fludioxonil (easy peelers), plus E903 in the peel’s wax coating (both).The 10,500 comments on the post are largely appalled. So what are these substances? And how worried should consumers be?Sarah Compson, the head of policy and campaigns at the charityPesticide Action Network UK(Pan UK), says that many of them are fungicides and known or suspected carcinogens and endocrine disruptors. For example, “Imazalil is a post-harvest fungicide used extensively on citrus fruit during storage and transportation,” she says. “It is a suspected carcinogen and reproductive and developmental toxin. It mostly appears on the skin of citrus fruit, so can be consumed if the zest is used.” Nick Mole, a policy manager at Pan UK, adds thatthe EU considered a reductionin the maximum residue level for imazalil in 2018, but citrus got a reprieve andchanges made in 2019applied only to bananas, apples and pears.View image in fullscreenGrapefruit tops Pesticide Action Network UK’s  list of produce high in multiple pesticide residues.Photograph: DayDreamNative/Getty ImagesSo while the warning labels may be new, the use of these pesticides certainly isn’t. “Citrus fruit regularly tops our ‘Dirty Dozen’ list of produce found to be high in multiple pesticide residues,” says Compson. “This can include highly hazardous pesticides banned from use in the UK and Europe due to their toxic impact on people and the environment.” This year, grapefruit topped the list, with limes in third place. Over the past five years, soft citrus, oranges and lemons have always featured in the top seven.Supermarkets are advised, but not legally obliged, to declare the chemicals used in the production and preservation of fruit and vegetables, says Compson. “It’s great to see a supermarket being clear about it. Labelling of the chemicals on citrus at least allows consumers to make more informed choices, but they shouldn’t be exposed to these chemicals in the first place.” Pan UK surveys British supermarkets every two years and ranks them on their efforts to tackle pesticides. Inthe latest rankings, in 2024, Waitrose and M&S were “leading the way”.However, when the Guardian contactedLidlfor comment, it emerged that the labels were not a bid for greater transparency, but were apparently added in error. “We can assure our customers that these products have not changed and continue to fully comply with all UK safety standards,” said a spokesperson. “We are working with our supplier to have the packaging label updated to avoid confusion.’”The joy of veg-maxxing: how to eat many, many more plants – without really tryingRead moreWhile all the chemicals (accidentally) listed are classed as safe to use individually at certain levels, it is the “cocktail effect” that most concerns campaigners. “Safety testing isn’t carried out on real-life dietary exposure,” says Compson. As Lidl’s labels revealed, “People are exposed to more than one pesticide at a time. The regulations don’t do enough to protect public health.”Can’t we just give our oranges and lemons a good scrub when we get them home? “No, sadly not,” says Compson. “The pesticides are present in cells throughout the produce. They are designed to stick to the fruit. It’s not just a case of washing it off.” How about buying unwaxed fruit? “I don’t think it makes enough of a difference,” says Compson.The only way to cut out these chemicals altogether is to grow your own citrus – easier said than done in the UK – or to buy organic. “We all love a lemon drizzle cake or sticking lime in a gin and tonic,” says Sarah Hathaway, the head of technical at the Soil Assocation. “For people wanting to avoid these chemicals, they are not allowed in organic farming at all, either in production or post-harvest.”That is likely to mean paying more for your limes. If you would rather take the risk of pesticide exposure – most of us, of course, aren’t eating a huge amount of citrus zest – consider the farmers growing the fruit, who often don’t have the luxury of choice.A report last monthfound that 46% of farmers worldwide are being poisoned by pesticides every year.Explore more on these topicsFoodFruitHealth & wellbeingPesticidesLidlfeaturesShareReuse this content
