title: How to turn excess custard into a fruity treat – recipe | Dessert | The Guardian
description: A fool is absurdly simple – just fruit stirred through custard or yoghurt with. maybe a bit of cream – and you can then add whatever bits and bobs you fancy from the fridge
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A fool is absurdly simple – just fruit stirred through custard or yoghurt with. maybe a bit of cream – and you can then add whatever bits and bobs you fancy from the fridge
Content: Tom Hunt’s blackberry, apple and custard fool.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s blackberry, apple and custard fool.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notDessertHow to turn excess custard into a fruity treat – recipeA fool is absurdly simple – just fruit stirred through custard or yoghurt with. maybe a bit of cream – and you can then add whatever bits and bobs you fancy from the fridgeTom HuntWed 28 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFool is one of my go-to desserts for two reasons: first, its pure simplicity – it’s little more than custard or yoghurt mixed with whipped cream and pureed fruit – and, second, its adaptability to the seasons. Gooseberry, rhubarb and strawberry are traditionally the most foolish fruits, but just about any fruit goes. British blackberries are still available and apples are in their prime right now, so I’ve gone for those, but use whatever you’ve got in store.I usually make fool with yoghurt, not least because it’s much less work than making custard from scratch, but I’ve got lots of leftover custard fromthis week’s Food Filter taste test, so I’m going for a custard base here. I’m always looking for ways to use up small amounts of bits and pieces in the fridge, such as the end of a pot of custard or yoghurt, then add a few other ingredients to elevate remnants into regalia.Blackberry, apple and custard foolA seasonal fool is a firm British favourite, so I’m rather surprised not to have covered it here before. As I come up to my 10th year of writing this column, I feel it’s time to revisit the classics, frombanana bread last weekto fool today, but with a zero-waste twist. For this recipe, finely dice the apple, so you can leave the skin on, to save on waste and to add fibre and texture.Serves2-4100g blackberries, plus extra to garnish1 apple, finely diced¼ tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ginger(ground or freshly grated)Sea salt3 tbsp honey100ml double cream, chilled150ml custardor yoghurt, or a mix of bothPut the blackberries, apple, cinnamon, ginger and a pinch of sea salt in a small saucepan, then add a splash of water. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for about 10 minutes, until the fruit is soft enough to mash with a fork. Mash everything together, leave to cool, then stir in three tablespoons of honey and refrigerate.When the puree is cold, whip the cold cream to soft peaks. With a metal spoon, gently fold in the custard, then fold in two-thirds of the fruit puree, or just enough so it ripples through the custard and cream base. Spoon the mix into two to four glasses, and top each with a spoonful of the remaining puree and a blackberry or two to garnish. Enjoy immediately or chill for a firmer set.Explore more on these topicsDessertWaste notFoodAutumn food and drinkFood wasteFruitBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vegetarian coconut curry recipes: Maunika Gowardhan’s spicy aubergine baingan and spiced vegetable stew  | Vegetarian food and drink | The Guardian
description: Coconut flavours the base of both these hearty curries – one with aubergines, one with gingery vegetables
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Coconut flavours the base of both these hearty curries – one with aubergines, one with gingery vegetables
Content: Maunika Gowardhan’sbhagare baingan, or aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenMaunika Gowardhan’sbhagare baingan, or aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.Vegetarian food and drinkVegetarian coconut curry recipes: Maunika Gowardhan’s spicy aubergine baingan and spiced vegetable stewAubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves, and a gingery vegetable stew with coconut and green chilliesMaunika GowardhanWed 28 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoth these hearty curries use coconut as part of their base gravy. The region of Kutch in Gujarat is brimming with vegetable curries, and thebhagare bainganfeatures many classic Kutchi ingredients; it has several similarities to the Hyderabadi version, too. I’ve used baby aubergines, but if need be you can use regular diced aubergines instead.Avial, meanwhile, is often served at celebrations in south India, and this version is a Keralan recipe made with a flavourful coconut paste.Bhagare baingan, or aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves (pictured top)Prep15 minCook1 hr 30 minServes4For the paste1 tbsp poppy seeds2 tbsp vegetable oil90gfinely chopped white onion1 tbsp sesame seeds1 tbsp grated fresh coconutFor the gravy160g fresh tomatoes4 tbsp vegetable oil150g thinly sliced white onions5 garlic cloves, peeled and ground to a paste¼ tsp turmeric powder1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder2 tsp ground cuminSalt, to taste8-10 baby aubergines, slit open lengthways1½ tsp tamarind paste½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper2 mild dried red chillies12 fresh curry leavesCoriander, to garnishRice or roti, to serveFor the paste, soak the poppy seeds in 70ml warm water 20 minutes. Meanwhile, put the oil in a small frying pan on a medium heat, then fry the onions for eight or nine minutes, just until they start to change colour. Add the sesame seeds and grated fresh coconut, and fry, stirring, for two minutes. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature. Once cooled, stir in the poppy seeds and their soaking liquid, then blitz the lot to a smooth paste.Meanwhile, put the tomatoes in a blender and blitz to a smooth puree. In a large, heavy-based frying pan for which you have a lid, heat the oil over a medium heat, then add the onions and fry, stirring regularly, for 17-18 minutes, until softened and lightly browned. Add the garlic paste, fry for 20 seconds, then stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and cumin, and fry, stirring for a few seconds, until fragrant.Add the pureed tomatoes and fry, stirring, for five minutes, until the mix splits and the oil leaves the side of the pan. Add the ground poppy seed and onion paste and fry, stirring continuously, for four minutes. Pour in 350ml warm water, season with salt to taste, then stir in the aubergines, cover and simmer on a low heat for about 15 minutes, stirring once halfway through. Add the tamarind paste and simmer for a further five minutes.Take off the heat and stir in the black pepper, whole dried red chilliesand curry leaves. Garnish with coriander and serve warm with roti or rice.Avial, or vegetable stew with coconut, ginger, curry leaves and green chilliesView image in fullscreenMaunika Gowardhan’savial, or vegetable stew with coconut ginger curry leaves and green chillies.Prep20 minCook40 minServes4For the paste200ggrated fresh coconut2½cm x 2½cmpiece ginger, peeled and roughly chopped½ tsp cumin seeds1 green bird’s eye chilliFor the curry3 tbsp vegetable oil1 tsp black mustard seeds1 dried mild chilli, roughly broken into pieces7-8 fresh curry leaves70g finely chopped white onion1 tsp turmeric powder200g medium carrots, peeled and cut into 1cm dice150g potato(use a good all-rounder such as red rooster), peeled and cut into 1cm dice200gfrench beans, all topped and cut into three roughly equal pieces½ tsp coarsely ground black pepperSalt, to taste3 tbsp greek yoghurtCoriander, to garnishRice or paratha, to serveFor the paste, put the fresh coconut, ginger, cumin seeds and chilli in a blender, add 200ml water and blitz to a smooth paste.Put the oil in a heavy-based saucepan on a medium heat. Add the mustard seeds, dried chilli and curry leaves. After 15 or so seconds, when they start to splutter and pop, add the chopped onions and fry, stirring, for seven or eight minutes, until they start to soften. Add the turmeric and the chopped carrots and potatoes, fry, stirring, for just a few seconds, then pour in 200ml water, cover and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook gently for 10 minutes, then add the chopped green beans and cook for another eight minutes, until all the vegetables are tender.Add the coconut paste and the ground black pepper, season with salt to taste, then stir and simmer for another two minutes. Whisk the yoghurt, then stir it into the pan and simmer for a minute more. Garnish with coriander and serve at once with rice or paratha.Maunika Gowardhan’s most recent book, Curry: Recipes from Indian Home Kitchens, is published by Quadrille at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsVegetarian food and drinkCurryFoodVegetablesHerbs and spicesIndian food and drinkTomatoesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction? | Medical research | The Guardian
description: Experts say symptoms such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss can be a warning sign – but there are other factors too
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Experts say symptoms such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss can be a warning sign – but there are other factors too
Content: By measuring ferritin levels via a blood test it is possible to get a snapshot of the body’s iron reserves.Photograph: AegeanBlue/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBy measuring ferritin levels via a blood test it is possible to get a snapshot of the body’s iron reserves.Photograph: AegeanBlue/Getty ImagesMedical researchExplainer‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?Experts say symptoms such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss can be a warning sign – but there are other factors tooNicola DavisScience correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTikTok is rife with influencers warning of “ferritin face”, a term they use to describe the pallor, dark circles, dry skin, and hair loss claimed to indicate low iron stores. But is this based on fact or fiction, and when is it time to head to the GP?What is ferritin?Iron is not made in the body, so typically we consume it in our diet. Ferritin is the protein responsible for storing iron in the body, particularly in the liver, and releasing it in a controlled manner.By measuring ferritin levels, which can be checked via blood tests, it is possible to get an snapshot of the body’s iron reserves, although experts warn such levels are not always a reliable guide.Blood ferritin levels of less than 30 micrograms/L indicate an iron deficiency,according to guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.However “a level below 50 might be a pointer of iron deficiency,” said Sue Pavord, professor of practice in medical haematology at Oxford University hospitals.Can low ferritin change a person’s appearance?View image in fullscreenThe symptoms influencers describe include dark circles under the eyes.Photograph: Alamy/PAThe symptoms influencers describe, such as dark circles under the eyes, grey skin, cracked lips and hair loss, can be caused by a variety of factors, including genetics, stress and dehydration. But experts say low iron stores can have an effect.“Iron is needed for every single cell of the body. So if you are iron deficient, you will be very fatigued, have brain fog, your skin will look dull and saggy, you’ll look pale and tired,” said Pavord. “While we can’t diagnose iron deficiency from the face, it might be a suggestion that there is iron deficiency.”Prof Toby Richards of the University of East London and the Iron Clinic added such changes were particularly pronounced in people with very low iron stores. “They tend to be the really sick patients,” he said.Why might people have low ferritin?“Periods and pregnancies are the most common [causes],” said Pavord, but others include not getting enough iron – either from dietary choices or because of poor absorption, as can occur with coeliac disease.Low ferritin levels can also arise as a result of blood loss linked to gastrointestinal problems, such as gastritis or polyps.“We also sometimes see it in athletes because of the high demand for iron on their bodies,” she added.What should people who are worried they might have low ferritin do ?Richards said those who are at high risk of low ferritin – such as people who have heavy periods, are pregnant or have had children, or are vegetarian or vegan – should ask for a blood test, adding that should include a full blood count, ferritin level check, and test for levels of B12 and folate.“This is a proper disease, and to put it into perspective, it’s the leading cause of disability in women of reproductive ability,” he said.Pavord also said those who are concerned about their ferritin levels should ask for a blood test, adding it was important to understand the cause of iron deficiency.“Older people suspecting iron deficiency would need a proper clinical assessment and investigations to look for a source of bleeding from the bowel,” she said.Pavord said it is possible to buy iron tablets over the counter at a pharmacy.“Taking iron tablets without confirming iron deficiency is not really going to do you any harm, particularly if you’re a young woman, because you’re losing a lot of iron with periods,” she said.But Richards noted many products do not necessarily contain the appropriate dose. “If you are iron deficient, you need to be on a full treatment dose … and then repeat your blood results in three months’ time,” he said. “What’s marketed is normally the lower dose supplementsIs the social media focus helpful, or problematic?Pavord was positive about the increase in awareness.“We need to stop normalising iron deficiency,” she said. “Many women are just exhausted trying to cope with their periods, cope with their pregnancies, cope with their young children and their busy jobs, and we need to stop normalising fatigue.”Richards agreed. “ Anything that raises the plight of women in this area is a good thing,” he said.However Dr Asiya Maula, a GP from the private firm The Health Suite, was cautious. “The risk with social media trends is that people may see themselves in a list of symptoms and assume they have a deficiency without checking whether that is actually the cause,” she said.Explore more on these topicsMedical researchHealthSocial mediaexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: skincare for teens has had a glow-up | Skincare | The Guardian
description: From the packaging to the products, brands aimed at young people have come a long way
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: From the packaging to the products, brands aimed at young people have come a long way
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautySkincareSali Hughes on beauty: skincare for teens has had a glow-upFrom the packaging to the products, brands aimed at young people have come a long waySali HughesWed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s some great new skincare in town for teens – and none of it preys on insecurities.I really likeEquals Even, a British-made line for young people. The founders are two female doctors (and mothers), not dermatologists, which feels appropriate, since frontline physicians manage more routine, everyday teen skin struggles than specialist consultants tackling severe conditions and cutting out cancers.And their experience – pragmatic, moderate, realistic – can be seen across the small product lineup. There is an understandable focus on acne to the exclusion of other complaints, but there’s a pleasant soothing serum to restore comfort and moisture after the use of the exfoliating cleanser and toner. Overall, I think it’s a great, dependable choice. A full-routine bundle costs £100.double quotation markThe whole thing feels slightly like hiding healthy liquidised vegetables in some viral bubble teaMore fun perhaps isRocco, the teen skincare range from presenter and art director Laura Jackson. As a design specialist and a mother of three, Jackson was uninspired by tween-targeted branding, and alarmed by the great-looking but age-inappropriate and potentially damaging skincare young people are choosing instead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: will social media bans for teens mean the return of grownup skincare?Read moreRocco is smart, tapping the trends teens love – wellness messaging, vegan, plant ingredients, uplifting fragrances and so on – while grounding them in proper, dermatologist-approved formulations. As one might expect from Jackson, the packaging is strong and key to Rocco’s appeal. Bright and fun, but not babyish, the whole thing feels slightly like hiding healthy liquidised vegetables in some viral bubble tea, and I think it deserves to work. At 51, I loved theCloud Bouncemoisturiser (£18) and cheerfully use it myself.Byoma is not a teenage skincare line – it’s for everybody who wants noticeably effective products that don’t ravage their delicate skin barrier as penance for performance. But I frequently recommend the brand (excluding Byoma’s retinol – excellent, but for adults only) to young people, because it is honest, problem-solving, accessibly priced and kind to their developing skin.I’m not generally one to recommend a serum that does nothing more than hydrate, but Byoma’sHydrating Serum(£14) is especially good. Instead of doing what others do and flooding skin with cheap hyaluronic acid (impactful but often ephemeral in benefit), their serum includes glycerin, ceramides and squalane to keep skin comfortable, hydrated and glassy-looking for longer. The brand’sBlemish Clearing line, though, would be my first stop for spots.Explore more on these topicsSkincareSali Hughes on beautyYoung peopleBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cycling in the wild heart of the Netherlands: an autumnal break in the Veluwe | Netherlands holidays | The Guardian
description: The untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bike
Author: Suzanne Bearne
Headline: The untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bike
Content: A red deer in the Hoge Veluwe national park.Photograph: Laurens Verhoeven/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA red deer in the Hoge Veluwe national park.Photograph: Laurens Verhoeven/Getty ImagesNetherlands holidaysCycling in the wild heart of the Netherlands: an autumnal break in the VeluweThe untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bikeSuzanne BearneWed 28 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 03.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne minute I’m cycling through an expansive dusty pink stretch of heathland with sloping sand dunes in the distant horizon, the next I’m winding through a fragrant Scots pine forest as sunlight filters through the branches of red-barked trees to make a kaleidoscope of white shapes on the trail floor ahead.I’m in Hoge Veluwe National Park, a 5,400 hectare (13,000 acre) nature reserve in Gelderland, about an hour and a half from Amsterdam. It’s crisscrossed by 25 miles (40km) of cycling paths, and around 2,000 free-to-use white bikes are available for visitors to explore the ever-changing scenery.I’ve been flitting back and forth to the Netherlands for years and have lost count of the times friends there have raved about the park and the wider Veluwe region, a forest-rich ridge of hills and diverse landscapes, stretching 37 miles, north to south. Finally I’ve come to see for myself and explore on foot and on two wheels over a few days – adding in a dash of culture at some of its historic towns and museums too.My trip starts atNatuurcentrum De Ginkel, a charming nature and visitor centre near Ede outside Arnhem. Here I meet nature guide Hanna Pol who takes me into the forest. “Veluwe is very biodiverse,” says Pol quietly as we walk past verdant oak, pine and birch. Trees with autumnal tawny-coloured leaves line one side of the path and wildflowers, with pops of bright yellow sunflowers and vivid red poppies, the other. Pol reels off some of the wildlife here: roe deer, five types of woodpecker, beavers, wild boar and wolves. As we crunch through a carpet of fallen leaves, we spy a small brown frog on a log, a woodpecker dancing around a tree, and the outline of two rust-red deers in the distance.View image in fullscreenDeelense Veld flessen in Hoge Veluwe.Photograph: Henk RuselerWe make our way to the wildlife observation area, an enclosed building with curved windows and a theatre-style set of wooden chairs. “The deer pass this way every night to eat,” says Pol. “Once we saw a really big fight break out.” She’s seen wolves too – they returned to the country in 2015 after about 150 years and it’s a controversial topic, with farmers worried about their livestock. We don’t see the elusive creatures, just a solitary bright white buzzard perching on a tree. On the shelves behind us, an assortment of skeletal remains includes antlers, skulls, the teeth of a wild boar and the foot of a deer.That night I stay in a stylish and sleek cabin with floor-to-ceiling views of the forest atBuitenplaats Petersburgon the edge of the park. It’s a peaceful haven of lodges with fairy lights strung around the woods and an enchanting Italian restaurant, Il Lupo, with an outdoor terrace.Besides its unspoilt natural wonders, Veluwe has plenty of other attractions. I visitPaleis Het Loo, a 17th-century royal palace in Apeldoorn, once the summer residence and hunting lodge of William of Orange III and his wife Princess Mary II Stuart. It’s an impressive building with ornate rooms, a staircase with the second biggest mural in the Netherlands, formal symmetrical gardens and an underground museum which tells the story of the Dutch royal family.Hotel de Echoput, a family-run modern hotel nearby, surrounded by the forest, is my home for the night. Its Grand Bistro Echo is a treat, with a menu that focuses on local ingredients – I enjoy fried mushrooms with a creamy Dordogne sauce and a vegan cheesecake with basil and white chocolate.View image in fullscreenCyclists at Otterlo.The next morning, after a brisk walk in the woods with barely a soul around, I visit the historic Hanseactic city of Harderwijk, on the shores of Wolderwijd lake. I wander the narrow cobblestone streets, medieval city walls and Old Town Hall with guide Marianne van Limbeek. “Harderwijk means hiding place for shepherds,” she tells me. We bump into Hendrik Kaper, a local street organist wearing a flat cap who treats us to a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody on his portable wooden organ.But it’s in Hoge Veluwe national park that I find the greatest sense of serenity – though one day a small adder with a dark zigzag stripe stops me in my tracks. Come outside peak times, as I have, and you might have some of the trails to yourself.View image in fullscreenPaleis Het Loo, near Apeldoorn.Within the park liesKröller-Müller Museum, a revered national art museum and sculpture garden founded by art collector Helene Kröller-Müller, who along with her husband, shipping magnate Anton Kröller, bought vast amounts of land in Veluwe (their private estate was later donated to the state). My timing is great as all 88 of its Vincent van Gogh paintings are on show together for the first time since 1984 (until 3 January).The sculpture park is one of the largest in Europe, and I stroll around the surrounding open grass and into the forest and stumble across various artworks (there are about 200 pieces dotted around). A short cycle away isJachthuis Sint Hubertus, the former country residence of the Kröller-Müller family with a watchtower more than 30m tall (apparently Helene loved afternoon tea at such lofty heights) surrounded by a lake with a very athletic bunch of jumping carp.I stop at Restaurant De Hoge Veluwe at Park Paviljoen for an early pasta dinner on the terrace before the sky turns a moody grey and rain looks imminent. Fortunately it’s only a 15-minute cycle to Otterlo, a pretty village with clusters of fairy lights and bunting decorating red brick houses andVakantieoord Het Lorkenbos, a charming holiday park surrounded by trees. My bungalow is cute and, feeling as if I’m in a twinkling winter wonderland, I light a candle and look up the Dutch word for cosy. It’sgezellig– a perfect description of how I feel after my nourishing break in this wild and restorative part of the Netherlands.The trip was arranged byVisit Veluwe. Entrance toHoge Veluwe national park€13.85per adult. Cabins atBuitenplaats Petersburgfrom€110. Camping atHet Lorkenbosfrom€23 a night, bungalows from €320 for two nights. Double rooms atDe Echoputfrom€169.Omioprovided train travel:Eurostar runs from London to AmsterdamExplore more on these topicsNetherlands holidaysCycling holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Two years on from our first newsletter … how has the Long Wave evolved? | World news | The Guardian
description: From AI aunties to long diaspora Uber phone calls, here is a selection of our favourite editions to celebrate our second anniversary
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: From AI aunties to long diaspora Uber phone calls, here is a selection of our favourite editions to celebrate our second anniversary
Content: Space for manoeuvre … a large canvas of diasporic exchange.Illustration: Dakarai Akil/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSpace for manoeuvre … a large canvas of diasporic exchange.Illustration: Dakarai Akil/The GuardianThe Long WaveWorld newsTwo years on from our first newsletter … how has the Long Wave evolved?From AI aunties to long diaspora Uber phone calls, here is a selection of our favourite editions to celebrate our second anniversaryDon’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNesrine Malik,Micha Frazer-Carroll,Dipo FaloyinandMorgan OforiWed 28 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Long Wave is two! And over the past year, once again, it has surprised us with the breadth of stories and events in the diaspora.The Long Wave has also evolved into a large community, with many readers getting in touch and sharing their thoughts, tips and sometimes their polite disagreements. We welcome and relish all of it. Here is the team’s selection of our favourite editions.How to use the holidays to stop our ‘WhatsApp aunties’ falling for AIView image in fullscreenDisseminative power … aunties wield formidable authority and are entranced by AIPhotograph: Markus Mainka/AlamyIt’s wild that this has becomeeven *more* of a problem since this editionearlier in the year. Just in the past few weeks, social media has been inundated with memes about aunties and mums being duped and entranced by AI, but accompanied with little or no insight on grappling with that. This edition remains ahead of the curve and relevant.NesrineHow we eat and gather is central to who we are: the diaspora at ChristmasView image in fullscreenUnique customs … food at Christmas provides connective tissue.Photograph: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty Images/AlamyMorgan and I had so much fun putting together this edition whichexplored Christmas food traditionsfrom across the diaspora. Alongside customs that are unique and deeply personal sit traditions that transcend continents, from hibiscus-based beverages like sorrel, to side dishes that help connect families to their ancestral roots.Dipo Faloyin,guest editorHow did Arsenal become a home for Black players and fans?View image in fullscreenBlack Arsenal forever … joyous scenes erupted globally in May.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOne of the best things about working on this newsletter is that something can all of a sudden become the zeitgeist, and it’s never fully understood unless seen via the lens of a diasporan. When Arsenal ended a 22-year Premier League drought, and attention around the football club exploded,it was my pleasure to explain why Bukayo Saka, Jurrien Timber and Myles Lewis-Skellymean as much to those in Manor House, north London as they do to people in Mombasa, Kenya.Morgan Ofori, the Long Wave teamBraiding used to be low maintenance and budget-friendly. What happened?View image in fullscreenOn fire … Micha sports her newly done French curl braids and cornrows.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThis piece onthe skyrocketing price of box braidsdefinitely provoked the most fun, and the most furore, in my time writing for the Long Wave. Anna Gifty Opoku-Agyeman, economist, Harvard PhD student and author of The Double Tax: How Women of Color Are Overcharged and Underpaid, challenged some of my assumptions about why getting our hair done has become so expensive – pointing out that the economic pressures meaning that Black customers are overcharged are the same ones that cause braiders to be underpaid. The pieceset my social media on fire(my comments section is yet to recover). Ama Hair Salon in Tottenham also gave me some amazing French curl braids and cornrows for the piece, and the photos by Christian Sinibaldi were gorgeous.Micha Frazer-Carroll, Long Wave editorChasing Freedom: a poignant reflection on empire, education and parental expectationsView image in fullscreenDiversely gifted … Simukai Chigudu, the writer of Chasing Freedom.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty Images/PenguinI still think about this book. Writing about it and what ittriggered in realisationand homesickness felt like a second part of the reading process. I felt very lucky to have the space to do that for myself, as well as introduce the book to new readers.Nesrineskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuad Mooge on Ireland’s Rose of Tralee, navigating backlash and celebrating identityView image in fullscreenWhirlwind affair … Suad Mooge.Photograph: Dublin Rose CentreSpeaking of amazing pictures, I also loved Nesrine’s interview with Dublin Rose of Tralee contestant (and general ray of sunshine)Suad Mooge. Nesrine and Mooge delved into the online abuse Mooge faced during the traditional Irish festival. Their conversation built on our previous coverage of a kind ofexceptionalismthat crops up in Ireland around racism. “We just brush things under the rug,” Mooge said. “Yes, there is a lot of noise online and in person, everyone is lovely. In the same breath, there is an issue. We need to face it.” This edition also included a vibrant carnival cartoon by our regular contributor Sarah Akinterinwa, which linked our traditions across borders.MichaWho’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone callView image in fullscreenShooting the breeze … long distance conversations aid decompression.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty/ShutterstockStaying in touch with family and loved ones in the age of social media is quite easy. But keeping up with a more ritualistic form of communicating across continents is a laborious task; ask anyone who grew up using pre-paid international phone cards and a trusty landline. I loved howNesrine used the example of cab driversto explore the ways many of us and preceding generations navigate ‘the dislocations’ of immigrant life via a beefy, marathon phone call. Judging by the avalanche of responses in our inbox (more than we could humanly answer) and theonline reception, this was a hugely popular edition.MorganTo receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.CompetitionView image in fullscreenJason Okundaye’s book Revolutionary Acts: Love and Brotherhood in Black Gay Britain.Computer-generated: Guardian BookshopWe’ve extended the competition! What, to you, is the most memorable edition of the Long Wave? Perhaps there was a piece you deeply related to, or one that drew your attention to a shared diaspora experience?Send us your name, location, your chosen edition, and 3-5 sentences explaining why. Our favourite responses will receive a copy of former Long Wave editor Jason Okundaye’s book Revolutionary Acts: Love and Brotherhood in Black Gay Britain – part of the Guardian Bbookshop’sBlack History Month collection. They may also be published in a future edition of the Long Wave.Entries should be submitted tothelongwave@theguardian.comby 9am on Monday 2 November.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThe Long WaveAfricaCaribbeanBlack British cultureFoodWomen's hairBeautynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I was always a pushover – until I stood up to some teenagers | Life and style | The Guardian
description: On the eve of my 40th birthday, I was doused with cold water at a train station. Before, I would have shrugged it off. But suddenly I realised it was time to assert myself
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: On the eve of my 40th birthday, I was doused with cold water at a train station. Before, I would have shrugged it off. But suddenly I realised it was time to assert myself
Content: ‘Historically, my kneejerk reaction to being wronged would have been to pretend that I hadn’t been rattled’ … Ellie Violet Bramley on her 40th birthday.Photograph: Lexi PownerView image in fullscreen‘Historically, my kneejerk reaction to being wronged would have been to pretend that I hadn’t been rattled’ … Ellie Violet Bramley on her 40th birthday.Photograph: Lexi PownerA moment that changed meLife and styleA moment that changed me: I was always a pushover – until I stood up to some teenagersOn the eve of my 40th birthday, I was doused with cold water at a train station. Before, I would have shrugged it off. But suddenly I realised it was time to assert myselfEllie Violet BramleyWed 28 Oct 2026 02.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the evening before my 40th birthday – a freezing cold night in March – and I was travelling across London to meet some old school friends for dinner. As I walked down the stairs into the tube station, I spotted a few teens leaning over the balustrade above me. I thought nothing of it; teens hanging about aimlessly is as classic a combination as Archers and lemonade. That was, until they each threw a few KFC paper cups’ worth of icy water over my head.I noticed it in slow-motion and, at first, kept walking. Then I realised that my hair was wet and so was my back. Without thinking, I ran back up the stairs and followed the teens, who were marching off down the main road. People on the street were watching me, obviously intrigued to see what I was going to do.What was I going to do?A few people looked at me with pity and pointed me in the right direction.When I caught up with the teenagers, they pretended it wasn’t them. The two girls strode quickly ahead, but one of the boys hung back – perhaps also intrigued to hear what I was going to say. What was I going to say?Still drenched, I sputtered the kind of fangless inanity I might say to my five-year-old as she pours rice all over the floor or starts drawing on the walls.Why, I asked, had they done it? The boy said nothing. I asked again and he denied they’d done anything, all adolescent swagger and smirks.Eventually he changed tack, telling me that it was, to be fair, funny. He said it a few times, as if to hammer home his point. Eventually,after more back and forth,I remember saying, simply: “It’s upset me. You’ve upset me.” To my surprise, it prompted a mumbled but seemingly heartfelt: “Sorry, bro.”It might not sound like much, but I felt genuinely appreciative that this teen had uttered his low-key but nevertheless disarming apology. And after spending a lifetime as a pushover, this moment was a breakthrough for me.View image in fullscreenDamp but unbowed … Ellie Violet Bramley, pictured at dinner with friends on the night of her soaking.Photograph: Sehr Askari/Hind DahmashHistorically, my kneejerk reaction to being wronged would have been to pretend that all was well, that I hadn’t been rattled; the wind hadn’t been knocked out of my sails. All good! But here I was admitting to this stranger, who would no doubt have preferred that I had quietly scuttled off to the tube, that I was upset. I couldn’t simply shrug it off – I was too damp and too shocked. Plus, I had made a promise to myself that I wouldn’t be such a walking wet wipe.Previously, I would have done anything to avoid public confrontation, or even just discomfort. I would hide terrible food in a napkin and smuggle it out of restaurants rather than say anything to the waiting staff. I would allow myself to be overcharged, elbowed in the head on public transport,or worse, groped, and not say a thing.On one occasion I found myself saying yes to a flower subscription service in the street, despite being overdrawn and not in the market for weekly gladioli. All because it was less embarrassing than saying “no thanks”. With friends, I struggled with emotional honesty.When I’d turned 30, at a particularly low ebb, I had pledged to change my ways. But despite my determination at the time, the results were not instant and I’d spent another decade being broadly incapable of sticking up for myself – or others – in moments that mattered, and even in moments that didn’t.But that night something changed. In truth, it had been stirring for some time. As a new mum, I’d been forced to find my voice for the sake of my tiny baby, who was still without one of her own. I managed to stick up for her in a way that I wouldn’t have been able to do for myself,holding her place in the queue for the slide against bigger kids, or declining roughhousing from well-meaning toddlers at soft play – these were baby steps.Back outside the tube station, I thanked the boy for his apology and, in my mind’s eye at least, we shared a quick smile by way of closure. I made my way back to the tube, boarded my train, and a few tears of shock ran down my cheeks, as I messaged my friends to say that I was going to be late.When I arrived at dinner, they asked why I was so wet. I explained what had happened and felt a twinge of pride at their surprise. By the time I got to them I felt calm, but in a past life, I would have turned around and gone home, convinced that my soaking was evidence of something lacking in me – and the embarrassment would have stayed with me long after I’d changed into dry clothes. This, I realised, as I took a sip of victory wine, was progress.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsLife and styleA moment that changed meSocial etiquetteBullyingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A vial of water from the rivers, becks and springs of Yorkshire – but not without permission | Rivers | The Guardian
description: Wharram and York, North Yorkshire: It’s the nervy few days before a ceremony that will honour our local waterways, and I have work to do
Author: Amy-Jane Beer
Headline: Wharram and York, North Yorkshire: It’s the nervy few days before a ceremony that will honour our local waterways, and I have work to do
Content: A sample of water from the River Derwent, Yorkshire, collected for the Confluence of the Rivers ceremony.Photograph: Amy-Jane BeerView image in fullscreenA sample of water from the River Derwent, Yorkshire, collected for the Confluence of the Rivers ceremony.Photograph: Amy-Jane BeerCountry diaryRiversCountry diary: A vial of water from the rivers, becks and springs of Yorkshire – but not without permissionWharram and York, North Yorkshire:It’s the nervy few days before a ceremony that will honour our local waterways, and I have work to doAmy-Jane BeerWed 28 Oct 2026 01.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIvisit the source of the tiny stream called the Gypsey Race now and then, drawn by the everyday miracle of its water welling to catch sunlight like a plaything and alchemise it into colours and sparks. Today, though, is different, because I’ve come to ask for something. Something like permission, or approval maybe.I’ve been helping to organise a gathering of river advocates to co-draft a regional charter of river rights – making explicit our responsibilities towards them. We will be holding a ceremony to blend waters from across Yorkshire to make ink in which the charter will be written. I want to collect water from the Gypsey, but I also want some of its potent reputation. Its course is regarded as auspicious thanks to an extraordinary concentration of nearby prehistoric barrows, cursuses and henges, not to mention England’s tallest standing stone. Local folklore insists that its capricious flow holds the power of prophecy.View image in fullscreenThe Confluence of the Rivers ceremony.Photograph: Emilie FlowerI address my request to two sentinel trees rooted in the water – sister salixes, willow and sallow – then begin to walk around the spring. I’ve barely gone 10 steps when the clouds part and the recently tilled soil at my feet starts glimmering. I look up and the field is alight with what must be hundreds of miles of spider silk. Is this the answer I was hoping for?Early on the day of the ceremony, I meet my collaborators and we decide to swim at the confluence of the Ouse and the Foss. On the slipway, a gleam of colour reveals itself to be small lost brooch with an enamelled kingfisher. Minutes later, as we’re towelling off, a young lad comes hurrying along the path with a net containing a monstrous green, gold and russet pike, magnificent and terrible, with a judging eye and, as Ted Hughes put it, “the grin it was born with”.I choose to read the cobwebs, the kingfisher token and the pike as positive omens, but I remain nervous about the ceremony. Will the pragmatic Yorkshire folk we’ve invited get it? I soon relax: the first offering is a vial the woman says contains not only local rivers, but water from sacred springs around the world. I think this might just work.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsRiversCountry diaryRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closely | World news | The Guardian
description: A movement that began in outrage has delivered one of Europe’s most remarkable election upsets, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: A movement that began in outrage has delivered one of Europe’s most remarkable election upsets, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes next
Content: As people celebrate in Serbia, the rest of Europe is ready for change.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APView image in fullscreenAs people celebrate in Serbia, the rest of Europe is ready for change.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APThis Is EuropeWorld newsIn Serbia, a new type of democracy is taking hold, and Europe is watching closelyA movement that began in outrage has delivered remarkable election upset, showing that change is possible and prompting questions over what comes nextDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereAshifa KassamWed 28 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn April of last year, dozens of students set off fromSerbia, intent on making it to Strasbourg, France on bicycles. The aim of the arduous, 13-day transcontinental journey was simple: to make their voices heard in Europe and beyond.In their home city of Novi Sad, students had been holding near-daily protests after adeadly roof collapseat the city’s main railway station. As their push for accountability and justice spread across the country, it was met withbaton-wielding police,teargas and a political class that branded these young people as traitors.Their trek to Strasbourg was aimed at casting a spotlight on the deepening erosion of democratic values in their home country. “Serbia needs Europe’s support,” the studentsexplained in an open letterto the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as they arrived in Strasbourg and met with MEPs and officials. “We are not riding toward Europe to flee Serbia. We are riding to bring it back.”On Sunday, their movementmade headlinesacross the world as the students were catapulted from the streets of Serbia into the halls of power. In a ballot that saw the highest turnout since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992, over 50% of voters backed the students to oust the increasingly authoritarian leader, Aleksandar Vučić, and end his party’s 14 years in power.It was, as a Guardian editorialnoted,“one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history”.The students’ extraordinary feat came as Europe has been rocked by weeks of protests. From Porto to Paris and Madrid to Milan, analysts have pointed to thecommon threadthat weaves through the diverse protests: a view that the social contract has broken down, leaving younger generations bracing for a future in which they will be worse off than their parents.The election result in Serbia lays bare the power of these protests to reshape politics, postdoctoral researcher Aleksandar Matkovićnoted this week. Could it be, as WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange once told an interviewer in Belgrade, that Serbia is “a country where the future happens first”?Matković drew on hisinvolvement inside the student movement to offer a singular window into all that had gone into their win, citing discussions that had stretched as long as six hours as the students laid the groundwork for their entry into politics. “The world should be watching closely: it may be witnessing the start of a very different kind of politics,” he wrote.Their win sparked joy across Serbia, sending tens of thousands of jubilant revelers on to streets across the country. “It’s very strange that on the very streets where the police beat us, on the streets where we retreated countless times in the face of the gendarmerie, we are now standing here as the victors,” Sara, 24,told the Guardian.Hours later supporters of the movement appeared again, this timeto clean upafter a night of raucous celebrations.What happens now?View image in fullscreenWhen the celebrations are over, the question of government begins.Photograph: Aleksandar Jovicic/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe movement now faces a tremendous task – particularly given that it has no hierarchy or leader. For more than a decade, Vučić’s partyhad transformedthe state, tightening its grip on media, stuffing institutions with loyalists to the party and wielding ministries and Serbian institutions as political tools.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe movementwon140 of the 250 seats in parliament, giving a comfortable majority to a slate of candidates who range from academics to athletes, and who were chosenvia student assembliesin the lead-up to the election. As one candidate told my colleagues on Monday,the top prioritywas “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.Underpinning the movement is an 11-point plan, which includes ridding the country of corruption, reforming the judiciary and media and improving access to healthcare. “We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory,” one member of the movementwrote in the Guardian this week.“Rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.”And while their plans for power take shape, the impact of their bold experiment will certainly be felt far beyond Serbia. The countryappliedto join the European Union in 2009, but the process has largely stalled in recent years. Now, much like in neighbouring Hungary, the electionshave usheredin the possibility of a fresh start along with hope of a democratic resurgence in central Europe.As EU officials sent their congratulations this week to the students, whose policy platform promises to put the question of future EU membership to a referendum, a note of optimism laced their messages. “We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions and to work together to advance Serbia’s future in the European Union,” the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, said on social media.Marta Kos, the EU’s enlargement commissioner, was more direct. “A new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together,” she wrote on social media.It was a stunning reversal of fortunes for the students who last year felt they had to cycle more than 1,300km (780 miles) to make their voices heard. Now – after nearly two years of protests that were met with detentions on trumped-up evidence, illegal surveillance, threats and job losses – it seems they might have a chance to fulfil their wish of bringing Europe to Serbia.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeSerbiaActivismStudentsProtestnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr | Egypt | The Guardian
description: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website
Content: Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017.Photograph: Roger Anis/APView image in fullscreenLina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017.Photograph: Roger Anis/APEgyptEgypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada MasrWarnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed websitePeter BeaumontWed 28 Oct 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.The news website that’s keeping press freedom alive in Egypt | Leslie T ChangRead moreAttalahfounded Mada Masrin 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, shehas been arrestedon a number of occasions.Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – followsthe arrest of the entire six-person teamat the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.View image in fullscreenLina Attalah holds a meeting in the Mada Masr office in 2015.Photograph: Sabry Khaled/Sabry Khaled For The GuardianThe crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president,Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen Internationalissued a statementwith several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”Explore more on these topicsEgyptPress freedomMiddle East and north AfricaAfricaNewspapers & magazinesHuman rightsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official | Global development | The Guardian
description: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment
Author: Sarah Johnson
Headline: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment
Content: A map showing countries affected by active Ebola outbreaks at the headquarters of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention in Abuja.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersView image in fullscreenA map showing countries affected by active Ebola outbreaks at the headquarters of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention in Abuja.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersGlobal developmentAfrica’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health officialJean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatmentSupported byAbout this contentSarah JohnsonWed 28 Oct 2026 05.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe “unprecedented”spread of the Ebola outbreakmeans it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.As the current outbreak reached10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.View image in fullscreenJean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa CDC.Photograph: Ken Cedeno/ReutersKaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”This outbreak,the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congosince Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.Ebola is a highly contagious,severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.On 15 May,DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreakin Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmeda case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.France is the only non-African country to have confirmed acase of Ebola so far– a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.View image in fullscreenTravellers at a hand-washing station in Busia on the Kenya-Uganda border, where health officials screen for Ebola symptoms, 12 October.Photograph: Bright Emoja/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment,though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died inUganda, and two in Kenya.The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment andunpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.View image in fullscreenRed Cross staff simulate evacuating the remains of an Ebola victim in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, 22 October.Photograph: Tony Karumba/AFP/Getty ImagesAt a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentEbolaInfectious diseasesAfricaDemocratic Republic of the CongoKenyaUgandanewsShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to Miami | Flávio Bolsonaro | The Guardian
description: Far-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via Ecuador
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Far-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via Ecuador
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro steps off a plane after arriving at the Miami-Opa Locka airport in Florida on Wednesday.Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro steps off a plane after arriving at the Miami-Opa Locka airport in Florida on Wednesday.Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty ImagesFlávio BolsonaroFlávio Bolsonaro calls himself the ‘leader of Brazil’ after fleeing to MiamiFar-right senator and family land in US after crossing from Brazil into Argentina and then flying via EcuadorTiago Rogeroin Brasília andJoseph Contrerasin MiamiWed 28 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonarodeclared himself the “true president” ofBrazilafter losing last Sunday’s presidential election and fleeing to the United States.After landing on a private jet with his family in Miami,Florida, on Wednesday morning, the far-right senator published the claim in a letter – even though his own party has recognised the legitimate victory ofLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, as have all of Brazil’s institutions, and international observers who monitored and endorsed the vote.Brazil’s three main newspapers – Folha de S.Paulo, O Globo and O Estado de S.Paulo – all described Bolsonaro’s declaration as “coup-mongering”.The senator later deleted the letter and published a new one in which, instead of calling himself the “true president”, he described himself as “the leader of Brazil”.Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in picturesRead moreAfter losingSunday’s runoff voteto Lula, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.From there he boarded a Gulfstream IV, registered LV-JQW, which had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian presidentJair Bolsonaro, took off on the jet with his wife and two teenage daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil in Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador and continued on to the Miami-Opa Locka airport, a private aviation hub about 11 miles north of downtown Miami catering to corporate executives and wealthy travelers.Bolsonaro, wearing a black bulletproof vest and looking somber, and his family emerged from the plane into a postcard-perfect sunny southFloridamorning at 9.24am. They briefly remained inside the airport before leaving, shielded by black umbrellas, climbing into a dark gray Ford Expedition Max and speeding away under police escort.Bolsonaro said nothing to reporters before boarding the vehicle and the mood was low-key, without any supporters present to welcome him and only two dozen journalists who were kept at a distance by two Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents.In the letter, published about seven hours after his arrival, Bolsonaro also thanked Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, “for his courage, sense of justice and legality”, and Donald Trump “and the wonderful American people for welcoming me”.He again repeated, without evidence, his claim that there had been “electoral fraud” – a claim rejected by Brazil’s electoral court and supreme court, as well as the presidents of the lower house and senate. Bolsonaro’s party said on Monday: “We recognise the presidential result.”At least three different versions of the letter were published by Bolsonaro and his allies, including one that used the country’s pre-1968 name and the English spelling “Brazil” rather than the Portuguese “Brasil” – which some saw as another sign of the Bolsonaro clan’s subservience to the US.Brazilian newspapers reported that Bolsonaro and his family had been granted humanitarian visas in the US. On Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.View image in fullscreenLula greets supporters while celebrating his birthday and re-election on 27 October 2026.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty Images“They’re fine people. … I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flávio a little bit. I know the father very well,” the US president said.On Wednesday, however, when asked about Bolsonaro’s claim, Trump said he would stay out of Brazil’s post-election turmoil.“Well, I’m not going to make a comment about that, but I know that we gave him a pass to come into the country, so we’ll see,” he said. “But I won’t get involved. It was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan to go through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him from leaving the country.There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies, at about 6pm on Monday, and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.The Argentinian newspaper Página/12reportedthat the aircraft belonged to the businessman Sergio Daniel Mastropietro, who was investigated by local police in one of the biggest scandals of Javier Milei’s administration, involving the allegedpayment of bribeslinked to the purchase of medicines for people with disabilities.Bolsonaro is under investigation in at least two criminal cases, one of them examining suspicions that the senator was involved in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.It was in connection with that case that, shortly after the election result, Brazilian police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.O Globo newspaperreportedthat the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.Fleeing Brazil has almost become standard practice among Bolsonaro supporters facing criminal charges or convictions in the country: about a dozen politicians or influencers closely aligned with Jair Bolsonaro havedone the samein recent years.The former president himself spent three months in Florida shortly after losing the 2022 election. He later returned to Brazil and, while facing trial over the attempted coup,spent two nightsat the Hungarian embassy in Brasília, then run by his ally Viktor Orbán.While under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison, the patriarch of the Bolsonaro clan used asoldering ironin an attempt to destroy his electronic ankle monitor.Explore more on these topicsFlávio BolsonaroBrazilMiamiFloridaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks | European Union | The Guardian
description: Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Watered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’
Content: Mark Carney and the European Parliament president, Roberta Metsola, in Strasbourg last month.Photograph: Ahmet Sel/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Carney and the European Parliament president, Roberta Metsola, in Strasbourg last month.Photograph: Ahmet Sel/Anadolu/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionEU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talksWatered-down version of statement to be issued at end of Montreal summit instead offers ‘ever closer association’Lisa O’Carrollin Brussels andLeyland Ceccoin TorontoWed 28 Oct 2026 17.27 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU has backed away from its offer toCanadato start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.The issue was triggered after the European Commission president,Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister,Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economicssaid.Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionCanadaAmericasEuropeMark CarneyUrsula von der LeyennewsShareReuse this content

title: US ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his way | Canada | The Guardian
description: Pete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Pete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections
Content: Pete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada, speaks during a fireside chat at the SpaceBound 2026 conference in Gatineau, Quebec, on 20 October.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPete Hoekstra, the US ambassador to Canada, speaks during a fireside chat at the SpaceBound 2026 conference in Gatineau, Quebec, on 20 October.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockCanadaUS ambassador suggests Trump could blame Canada if midterms don’t go his wayPete Hoekstra, controversial US ambassador to Canada, has also accused Canadian officials of interfering in US electionsLeyland Ceccoin TorontoWed 28 Oct 2026 16.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US ambassador has suggested Canada could be blamed ifRepublicansperform poorly in next week’s midterm elections, the latest intervention from a controversial figure who has been accused of inflaming a bitter dispute that has angered and baffled residents of both countries.On Wednesday, CTV newsreportedthat Pete Hoekstra told business leaders at a closed door meeting that if a number of swing races – including Maine and Michigan – go to the Democrats, it could make things harder for Canada because Donald Trump might try to blame the loss on it.“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” the prime minister,Mark Carney, told reporters when asked about the allegations.For months,Canadaand the US have been locked in a bitter tariff war, with Ottawa retaliating against illegal US tariffs and targeting goods in states that rely heavily on trade with Canada.Carney said that Canada “will pursue” such a deal if it presents itself, but that Ottawa’s trade negotiators are “not in that position right now”.Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particular for his response to Trump’s rhetoric about making Canada the 51st US state. Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the threats as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”. He had previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election as “anti-American”.This year a House of Commonspetitionsigned by more than 225,000 Canadians called for his expulsion, suggesting his statements violated diplomatic protocols, including the prohibition on diplomats interfering in the internal affairs of a host country.More recently, Hoekstra has accused Canadian officials of interfering in US elections, pointing to Canadian politicians who have criticized the tariffs in US media, and the province of Ontario’s anti-tariff advertisement that ran on US television.“We see all of that. We are monitoring it. We are evaluating it.
