And if some of it becomes election interference, America will respond to it,” Hoekstra, who comes from Michigan, recentlytold a Canadian podcast, adding that Canadians should “keep your nose out of American politics”.Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, who was a target of Hoekstra’s comments, told reporters in Ottawa that her country “would never do that” and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada”.Carney, while in Turkey, told reporters there was “no merit” to the claims of interference and that he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the remarks were an “extraordinary thing” for a US ambassador to say about his host country and looked like an effort to “manufacture a pretext for the Trump administration’s own political difficulties”.“The job of an ambassador is to represent the interests of his country, but it’s also to maintain channels of communication and build relationships and manage disagreements,” he said.“His comments have repeatedly aggravated tensions instead of helping to manage them. I don’t think that he’s serving American interests very well. I’m not even sure that he’s serving the interests of his president.”Paris points to polling in the US that shows voters have increasingly linked tariffs, the war and cost of living. There is also widespread confusion over why the White House has chosen to treat Canada as a trade adversary.“It’s certainly not working in Canada. It’s on the contrary. It seems that every time Mr Hoekstra opens his mouth, the Canadians are more determined than before to stand up to the bullying of the Trump administration,” he said. “That’s not serving American interests.”The US embassy denied Hoekstra said Canada would face blame for a poor Republican showing, suggesting the remarks were “grossly taken out of context” from a broader discussion.“The ambassador has consistently said that the Canadian media is attempting to overstate the relevance of Canadian issues in American elections. As we have previously stated, Americans will decide American elections based on issues that are important to them,” the embassy said in a statement.At a Canadian American Business event last year, Hoekstra delivered what witnesses say wasan expletive-laden tiradeat Ontario’s trade representative after the province ran a series of anti-tariff ads in the US that featured Ronald Reagan. Ontario’s premier called the outburst “absolutely unacceptable” and “unbecoming of an ambassador”.Last week, Barack Obama noted the unusual choice to attack a longtime ally while speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit, mocking Trump’s fixation on Canada and jokingly referring to his northern neighbor as a “well-known evil empire”.“That historical adversary of ours: Canada,” the former US president said. “It’s your neighbor! It’s a few minutes drive over the bridge. These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup. They are the nicest people. And somehow we’ve gotten them so mad.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaTrump tariffsAmericasDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026Mark CarneyTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: A US woman feared dead was reported alive in Mexico. But police now say that isn’t true | Arizona | The Guardian
description: Mexican police had said they found Shayna Feinman in Tijuana, raising the hopes of missing Arizonan’s family
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Mexican police had said they found Shayna Feinman in Tijuana, raising the hopes of missing Arizonan’s family
Content: Shayna Feinman.Photograph: Yavapai county sheriff's officeView image in fullscreenShayna Feinman.Photograph: Yavapai county sheriff's officeArizonaA US woman feared dead was reported alive in Mexico. But police now say that isn’t trueMexican police had said they found Shayna Feinman in Tijuana, raising the hopes of missing Arizonan’s familyRamon Antonio VargasWed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArizonaauthorities say theirMexicancounterparts were resoundingly mistaken when they publicly claimed recently that they found alive a woman who was feared slain after disappearing in 2024 – a turn of events that her sister has called “turmoil” and “heartbreaking”.The case in question centers on Shayna Feinman, who was reported missing in rural Yavapai county,Arizona, in March 2024 at age 38.Authorities believe she was walking to an acquaintance’s home when she was last seen – but she never arrived or returned to her dog, as the Arizona news outlet KSAZreported. An ensuing search turned up Feinman’s car abandoned near where she had been staying with her boyfriend, Cavett Richards, according to the station.Her wallet and identification reportedly were inside the vehicle, and her cellphone was ultimately recovered on nearby land.Although Feinman had not been found, the Yavapai county sheriff’s office subsequently charged Richards as well as a man named William DalCerro with second-degree murder, conspiracy and concealing a corpse in connection with her disappearance. But the charges were dismissed, a $20,000 reward being offered for information as authorities kept investigating the case.View image in fullscreenThe person who Mexican officials thought was Shayna Feinman.Photograph: SSPCM TijuanaThe secretariat for security and citizen protection in the Mexican municipality of Tijuana thendeliveredwhat initially appeared to be a startling update in Feinman’s case on Saturday, saying in a statement that she had been located in the city’s Encino neighborhood the previous day.The statement from the secretariat had a picture of the woman sitting in front of a desk atop which was a missing poster with Feinman’s information. It asserted without elaborating that investigators had confirmed Feinman’s identity, noting that her physical characteristics matched those listed in her missing person report.The woman had been put in protective custody while Tijuana authorities arranged for her to speak with the Feinman family and US consular officials, the statement said. The agency went so far as to post a link to its Saturday statement on a social media page belonging to Feinman’s sister, Kara.But both Kara Feinman and the Yavapai’s sheriff’s office met the Tijuana officials’ statement with evident skepticism.Kara told KSAZ in a story published on Monday that she was waiting for the Yavapai sheriff’s office “to know for certain” that Shayna had been found.Though she acknowledged the woman in the picture released by Tijuana officials had “similar physical attributes” to Shayna, Kara struck a cautious tone, telling KSAZ: “I can only hope and pray [for] good news – but right now, we have to be realistic.”Alexander brothers each sentenced to 30 years for drugging and raping dozens of womenRead moreMeanwhile, a sheriff’s office spokesperson told KSAZ that the agency was “aware of reports indicating that Shayna Feinman may have been located in Mexico” – but “at this time, the information remains unconfirmed”.“There is insufficient evidence to verify her identity,” Paul Wick, a Yavapai sheriff’s office spokesperson, added to KSAZ. Wick said the sheriff’s office was “actively investigating the matter” and would provide an update as soon as one could be “confirmed and … released”.The Yavapai sheriff’s office published that update on Tuesday, when it said in a statement: “Today, US authorities confirmed to [office] detectives, utilizing physical evidence, that the individual located is not Shayna Feinman.”The sheriff’s office alluded to prior media reports “regarding the alleged discovery of Shayna Feinman” that “were published without official law enforcement confirmation” – before saying its “detectives continue to work diligently with [her] family during this stressful time”.Tijuana’s security and citizen protection secretariat did not immediately respond to a request for comment.In an interview with the Guardian on Tuesday, Kara Feinman said she believed the confusion about her sister possibly being in Tijuana initially stemmed from at least one concerned citizen who became convinced that she was there and made that known on social media.She described being guarded about that possibility, especially after previously having her hopes raised and crushed by numerous reported but unfounded sightings of Shayna. Yet she reluctantly opened her mind in light of the Tijuana secretariat’s confident claims – and then endured cyberbullying online by users who harshly judged her for not reacting effusively enough to the ultimately false news that Shayna had been found alive.As she processed the reality that the search for the truth about her sister’s disappearance continued, Kara Feinman said her hope now was for those passionate about such investigations to realize how harmful it can be “jumping to conclusions without having all of the information” and then directing harsh words at the people most affected by those cases.“Words are stronger than people think, and kindness can go so far,” Kara Feinman said. “It’s been turmoil going through this.“It’s heartbreaking. It’s terrible, and I don’t wish this on anybody.”Explore more on these topicsArizonaMexicoUS crimeAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit | Commonwealth summit | The Guardian
description: Royal tour of Caribbean comes as poll suggests majority support among younger Britons for dialogue on slavery reparations
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Royal tour of Caribbean comes as poll suggests majority support among younger Britons for dialogue on slavery reparations
Content: King Charles, pictured here in discussion with Philip Davis, prime minister of the Bahamas, acknowledged the ‘great suffering of the past in these lands and beyond’ as he began his tour of the Caribbean.Photograph: Ben Stansall/PAView image in fullscreenKing Charles, pictured here in discussion with Philip Davis, prime minister of the Bahamas, acknowledged the ‘great suffering of the past in these lands and beyond’ as he began his tour of the Caribbean.Photograph: Ben Stansall/PACommonwealth summitKing Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summitRoyal tour of Caribbean comes as poll suggests majority support among younger Britons for dialogue on slavery reparationsNatricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 02.55 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 20.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins hisCaribbeantour.The king arrived in theBahamason Tuesday to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.His arrival comes as a poll suggested strong support among young people and Labour voters in the UK for a dialogue on slavery reparations.The poll, conducted by More in Common last week and published by the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, found that 40% of Britons supported a meeting on reparatory justice, while 19% were undecided.But Repair Campaign elder and former St Vincent and the Grenadines prime minister Ralph Gonsalves pointed to disaggregated data showing that support was considerably higher among younger people, with 60% of those aged 18-24 and 51% of those aged 25-34 backing a meeting on reparatory justice.The poll also suggested that a majority of all ages who voted Labour (58%) and Liberal Democrat (57%) in the last election favoured a meeting.The findings come as the UK faces intensifying pressure from Caribbean leaders to apologise for its role in slavery and agree to a structured dialogue on reparations.“The bulk of the young people under the age of 35 are saying we have to have that conversation. This should prompt him, like the Dutch prime minister, to give a full formal apology,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.He also urged King Charles to apologise and help establish mechanisms for a dialogue, adding that he was disappointed with the King’s maiden speech in the Bahamas, which he described as “falling far short of what he had said before”.Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.A year later he described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to “deepen my own understanding of slavery’s enduring impact”, in a speech at the opening of aCommonwealth summithosted by Rwanda.In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”He said the leaders at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Chogm gathering, hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – afull and formal apology– and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summitRead moreThe chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.Charles is to travel to Guyana on Thursday where the president, Mohamed Irfaan Ali, recently called for the monarch to take the next step and offer to apologise.The king follows the guidance of his ministers, and it is understood the government has not advised him to offer an apology or reparations, in keeping with established policy.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will join Charles in Antigua for the gathering of Commonwealth leaders.A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “At the request of host governments, the king’s programme will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future that are having a transformative effect on the region, as it confronts the challenges of today.“For his majesty, this tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past. This will therefore also be reflected in differing ways and words during the tour, as you would expect.”Announcing the poll results, Repair Campaign founder Denis O’Brien called for a “time-lined commitment to holding talks with Caribbean states”.“To date, there have been too many unsubstantiated expressions of regret and sorrow about Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, coupled with empty promises – including at the last Chogm in Samoa – that some sort of dialogue would begin,” he said.Additional reporting by Press AssociationExplore more on these topicsCommonwealth summitReparations and reparative justiceKing Charles IIICaribbeanBahamasAmericasSlaverynewsShareReuse this content

title: Menindee Lakes water levels drop to lowest in five years as experts warn of mass fish deaths | Murray-Darling Basin | The Guardian
description: NSW government imposes water restrictions after Menindee water volumes fall below 2021 levels
Author: Lisa Cox
Headline: NSW government imposes water restrictions after Menindee water volumes fall below 2021 levels
Content: The combined storage at the Menindee Lakes has fallen below 480 gigalitres for the first time since 2021.Photograph: Google EarthView image in fullscreenThe combined storage at the Menindee Lakes has fallen below 480 gigalitres for the first time since 2021.Photograph: Google EarthMurray-Darling BasinMenindee Lakes water levels drop to lowest in five years as experts warn of mass fish deathsNSW government imposes water restrictions after Menindee water volumes fall below 2021 levelsSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereLisa CoxEnvironment and climate correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWater levels at the Menindee Lakes in westernNew South Waleshave fallen to their lowest point in five years, prompting the state government to impose upstream water use restrictions as experts warn of potential mass fish deaths over summer.Combined volume at the Menindee Lakes fell below 480 gigalitres earlier this month, the first time since 2021.In the upper Menindee Lakes, water volumes have dropped below 250GL, a level that triggers temporary state water restrictions across parts of the northern Murray-Darling basin.Mass fish deaths feared as Minns government promise to restore Murray-Darling rivers in doubtRead moreThe restrictions limit access for some irrigators and are intended to preserve water for critical human needs and the environment.It follows periods of low rainfall in the catchment throughout the past 12 months, with experts warning of a growing risk of summer fish kills unless flows down to the Menindee Lakes via the Darling-Baaka River improve.Menindee was the site ofcatastrophic fish killsin 2018, 2019 and 2023, which saw millions of dead fish wash up along stretches of the Darling-Baaka.“Government officials are predicting with a level of certainty that unless there’s more water flowing into the Baaka-Darling River that there will be fish kills at Menindee this summer,” said Prof Jamie Pittock of the Australian National University and the Wentworth Group of Concerned Scientists.“We need a major rainfall event to happen and for the state governments to prevent irrigators from pumping out the first flush of water.”Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletterGraeme McCrabb, who was one of the first Menindee residents to raise the alarm about the 2018-19 disasters, said the combined Menindee Lakes had reached “drought reserve volumes”.He said this effectively meant conservation of water “at all costs”. McCrabb said he was hopeful that recent rainfall in Queensland may result in some replenishment of the Menindee system.“There are some small inflows coming across the Queensland border now, which probably give us some hope for the summer. But we would need more on top of that,” he said.“If we don’t get inflows, the risk [of fish kills] would be very high in January or February.”He said a milder summer would also lower the risk.“I’m worried about fish kills to be honest,” McCrabb said.“It’s a tough time or sad time when the water starts to get that real green algal look.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith water levels low and long-range forecasts pointing to the prospect of a hot summer, the NSW water minister, Rose Jackson, said “no one is underestimating the challenge at Menindee this summer”.“Our focus is on doing everything we can to protect water quality and native fish through the months ahead,” she said.“Significant inflows would improve conditions but we aren’t sitting back and waiting for rain.”Jackson said in addition to temporary restrictions for some water users, the government had put in place a temporary fish passage to allow better movement of native fish and established a water quality working group.Days after winning the 2023 state election, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, and senior state ministersvisited Menindee and committed to an investigationof themass fish kills.An expert panel was established under thenorthern basin connectivity program, which recommended limiting upstream overextraction during dry periods to help maintain flows in tributaries into the Darling-Baaka River to the Menindee Lakes. This was to try to reduce the risk of catastrophes such as fish kills and large-scale drying.The panel delivered its final report two years ago butthe state governmentis yet to implement it.McCrabb said he was disappointed the government had not followed through on the recommendations of the connectivity panel.“Since the fish kills, government agencies have made no policy changes to improve water quality outcomes,” he said.Explore more on these topicsMurray-Darling BasinNew South Wales politicsWaterFishDroughtNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Worldwide legacy’: almost $20m raised to protect majestic tract of land in far north Queensland | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Bush Heritage hopes to buy Wooroora station, which links wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland and is home to 12 endangered species
Author: Joe Hinchliffe
Headline: Bush Heritage hopes to buy Wooroora station, which links wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland and is home to 12 endangered species
Content: Wooroora station in far north Queensland which could soon be bought by Bush Heritage.Photograph: SuppliedView image in fullscreenWooroora station in far north Queensland which could soon be bought by Bush Heritage.Photograph: SuppliedQueensland‘Worldwide legacy’: almost $20m raised to protect majestic tract of land in far north QueenslandBush Heritage hopes to buy Wooroora station, which links wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland and is home to 12 endangered speciesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJoe HinchliffeWed 28 Oct 2026 17.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA majestic tract of land in far northQueenslandthat links wet tropics and world heritage rainforest, and contains headwaters that flow to the Great Barrier Reef, could be bought and protected by Christmas, after a conservation group raised more than $19m in private donations to buy the cattle station.mapWooroora spans more than 20,000 hectares of largely intact wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland on the lands of the Jirrbal people about 100km south-west of Cairns – and borders Bush Heritage’s existing 43,575-hectare Yourka Reserve inone of the most biodiverse regions in Australia.Cassowary and tree-kangaroos are among at least 12 threatened species and more than 30 species of conservation significance that have already been recorded on Wooroora, which is also the northernmost refuge for koalas, and, according to the would-be owners, is almost certainly home to species yet unknown to science.View image in fullscreenWooroora station is the most northerly habitat for koalas.Photograph: John WybrowIn 2024 a plan toclear more than 500ha of Wooroora station for a 42-turbine windfarm was rejectedbecause of what the then environment minister, Tanya Plibersek, described as the unacceptable impact on the environment, including the spectacled flying-fox and the northern greater glider.The chief executive of Bush Heritage, Rachel Lowry, said Wooroora would be the organisation’s most ambitious single acquisition in its 35-year history to date.“This breaks the glass ceiling,” Lowry said. “And I don’t think it’s just for Bush Heritage, but for our sector more broadly.”Lowry said fundraising for the $24.7m to buy and manage the land for an initial five years has been going on for more than 18 months. She travelled to New York during the 2025 UN climate summit to make a presentation that helped result in a donation of almost $2.5m from the foundation associated with the US outdoor clothing company Patagonia.View image in fullscreen‘We’re leaving a legacy worldwide’ … Bush Heritage Australia’s chief executive, Rachel Lowry.Given the country is a global biodiversity hotspot, Lowry said the protection “forever” of Wooroora was “not just a gift for Australia”.“When we step in and we protect and manage country, like Wooroora, we’re leaving a legacy worldwide,” she said.An anonymous Australian philanthropist also donated $6m. Now Bush Heritage is appealing to the public to raise the final $5.3m it needs by the deadline of 24 December.Jirrbal senior elder Uncle Kurt Noble said the land purchase would allow traditional owners back on “proper Jirrbal land”.“There are a lot of stories within the family connected to this country,” he said. “Some of the Dreamtime stories, as well as a little bit of the history”.In a recorded interview from Wooroora provided by Bush Heritage, Noble said his great-grandmother was born on the station but that he had not previously had the opportunity to visit.View image in fullscreenA Lumholtz tree-kangaroo mother and baby at Wooroora station.Photograph: BG Thomson“Much of our land is under private ownership, you know, and to have access, to be able to come back and forward, has been very restricted over many years – over generations,” he said.Renewed access would not only enable care and restoration for the environment, he said, but also for “the cultural values of our land”. Noble said it would allow “our young people to grow up with a better understanding, not only of country, but of language, of song, of our cultural practices, of our different significant sites all over this country”.Traditional custodian and the Wabubadda Aboriginal Corporation chair, Liam Roberts, said in another recorded video that Jirrbal were hoping to jointly manage the reserve.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’ve got rangers. We’ve got work we’d like to do on country,” he said.Roberts said the station contained “sacred artefacts” along old Jirrbal trails and creeks.“It’s beautiful camping country, it’s beautiful fishing country, it’s beautiful ecology,” he said.“In the old days the pathways were very much running from the dry country to the wet country, seasonally, and this is a key part of country that we can’t find anywhere else.”Bush Heritage’s head of Queensland and the Northern Territory, Dr Jo Axford, said Wooroora includes one of the region’s largest unprotected stretches of wet sclerophyll forest – toweringeucalyptusgrandisthat forms a transition zone between ancient wet tropics rainforest and seasonally dry savannah woodlands.From its neighbouring reserve at Yourka, Bush Heritage had been actively seeking to acquire the station since 2010 because it provides the “missing piece” in a 429,000-hectare nature corridor that runs up to Cape York.View image in fullscreenUncle Kurt Noble, senior Jirrbal elder, said securing access to the land was vital for future generations.Photograph: Supplied“The amazing thing about Wooroora is that it’s this long, narrow property – if you look at a map, Wooroora itself is almost like a key,” Axford said.Wooroora rises to about 1,000m above sea level, but falls to 660m in 10km, which Axford said creates a diverse mosaic of habitat that will allow threatened species such as the critically endangered magnificent brood frog to find refuges and hopefully adapt to a changing climate.This “really unusual” topography makes Wooroora one of the only places on Earth home to both the rainforest dwelling southern cassowary and the plains roaming emu, where Lumholtz’s tree-kangaroo clamber through canopies near koalas, she said.But Axford said she is confident the station also harboured undescribed species.“Nobody’s looked at the invertebrates, nobody has gone into all those gullies and valleys, these huge rhyolite outcrops,” she said.“I’ve had the advantage of being able to fly over it in a chopper – and you just know there must be so many hidden secrets in there”.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandConservationEndangered speciesWildlifeAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program | Aukus | The Guardian
description: As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, retired admiral Peter Briggs says personnel is one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces
Author: Narelle Towie
Headline: As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, retired admiral Peter Briggs says personnel is one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces
Content: The USS Colorado Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarine at HMAS Stirling base in Perth.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPView image in fullscreenThe USS Colorado Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarine at HMAS Stirling base in Perth.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPAukus‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine programAs USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, retired admiral Peter Briggs says personnel is one of the ‘huge issues’ it facesFollow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastNarelle Towiein PerthWed 28 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels underthe controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned.As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program.We want you! ADF recruitment rates are growing, even as the odds of conflict rise. Why are people signing up?Read moreAs part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its six diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete.The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – more than double the number needed for the Collins class.The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.“Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said.“By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.”But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats.“We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said.View image in fullscreenCapt Justin Reeves talks to the media on the USS Colorado at HMAS Stirling in Perth.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP“You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.”About 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-Aukus submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK.“The personnel side is a huge issue but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said.Hegseth calls US-built nuclear submarines the ‘apex predator’ of the seas. But are they right for Australia?Read moreThe former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements.The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track.Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians.After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program, which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet.From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCrew members on the USS Colorado.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPPaul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated.Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment.The USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”.Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons.It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port.View image in fullscreenSleeping quarters on the USS Colorado.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPThe demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties.In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms.Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”.Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said.“Being nuclear-powered is a massive advantage.”Explore more on these topicsAukusAustralian militaryUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Death toll rises to 68 with dozens injured after high-speed train collision in Spain – as it happened | World news | The Guardian
description: Pedro Sánchez says the government will act with urgency to ‘clarify what has happened, why this tragedy occurred’
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Pedro Sánchez says the government will act with urgency to ‘clarify what has happened, why this tragedy occurred’
Content: 11.41 EDTWhat we know so far - summaryJakub KrupaAt least 68 people have been killed after two passenger trains collided in Toledro province in central Spain,and the death toll may rise further.A similar number of people remain hospitalised,including 15 in serious or critical state (15:44).The two trains with 544 people on board in total (10:46) were travelling in the same directionon the high-speed line from the Spanish capital, Madrid, to Seville in the south-west of the country.Video footage from the scene showed extensive damage to both trains (12:23,13:52).Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez said the country was “in mourning”as he insisted the government will get to the bottom of incident and address potential failures with “utmost firmness” (15:49).Transport minister Óscar Puente said initial review of the evidence pointed to an “inexplicable” decision to order trains to go aheadafter a signalling failure (15:01), implying a human error.The investigation islikely to focus on 17 minutes between the trains were halted and the crash.Spanish media reported that the controller responsible was questioned by investigators this afternoon (16:40).Today’s collision is the second high-profile train crash in Spain this year(11:00), and the third deadliest incident on its railway in the last 50 years (12:55).Spain is expected to declare three days of mourninglater today (15:54).Both main parties suspended their campaigning activities ahead of next month’s parliamentary election,but the far-right Vox party continued with its rallies (12:11).ShareUpdated at12.10 EDT

title: Putin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of Starlink | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Russia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack Ukraine
Content: Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk during a summit with African leaders in Moscow.Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/ReutersView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin praised Elon Musk during a summit with African leaders in Moscow.Photograph: Maxim Shipenkov/ReutersUkrainePutin hails Elon Musk’s ‘genius’ amid plans for Russian version of StarlinkRussia plans to build own version of US billionaire’s satellite communications to help attack UkraineDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 28 Oct 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine.The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’sSpaceXwith Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation.“Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Russian leader said, according to the Tass news agency. “How many of these [satellites] does he have in orbit? More than 5,000, and we’re only taking the first steps.”The true number of active SpaceX satellites is estimated at about 10,000, which provide the high-speed internet service that has been the subject of a diplomatic row between Musk, the US andUkraineearlier this month.A military version of Starlink, called Starshield, was suddenly restricted one night in the middle of October, preventing Ukraine from conducting medium drone attacks and hampering some of its anti-drone air defences.Initially, Musk, an ally of the US president, Donald Trump, denied that he had ordered a throttling of the internet connection, before saying at the end of last week that he had closed a loophole in which the civilian Starlink had been used by the military.Putin appeared to be trying to flatter Musk, whose control of the communications technology has raised questions about the US billionaire’s leverage over the White House and the impact he is able to have on Ukraine’s war effort.View image in fullscreenElon Musk is a controlling shareholder in Starlink and an ally of Donald Trump.Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and ​to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.Starlink does not work inRussiaand its use by Russia inside Ukraine was restricted earlier this year. Meanwhile, Moscow has begun to develop an alternative system, though, with an estimated 26 working satellites, its capacity is limited.Last week, after about 10 days of restriction, Ukraine’s president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, announced that “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored” and that the speeds were “now where they need to be”.Few believe the issue is permanently settled, with relations between Zelenskyy and Trump fraught in the run-up to the US midterm elections next Tuesday. Trump has also reached out to Putin, agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow early in October in an effort to reduce the oil price before Americans go to the polls.Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he hoped proposed trilateral peace talks, involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, would take place between 6 and 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE, shortly after the midterms.“We are waiting for the American side. I think that they’ll be ready with all the answers after the elections,” the Ukrainian leader said at a press conference in The Hague with the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier, Zelenskyy said he had spoken to Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, as it emerged that Britain would provide £10bn in extra financing for Ukraine over the next three years – and an immediate £500m for air defence systems.The additional aid was, Zelenskyy said, “a truly strong and very timely step” that came “as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone” as the war heads towards what is expected to be its most difficult winter yet.John Healey, the UK chancellor, announced the extra funding as part of the government’s annual budget. “The prime minister and I called President Zelenskyy to tell him about our commitments in the budget today. He told us: ‘You’ve made my day’.”The Dutch government also said it would provide €500m in military support for the winter, and a further €1.2bn in non-military aid, partly to help fund urgent repairs to Ukraine’s utilities and manufacturing.Kyiv has been relentlessly attacked by Moscow this autumn as Russian forces fail to make progress on the frontlines in the east of Ukraine.Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since the middle of October, Zelenskyy said overnight, hitting power plants and other key targets in an effort to cause a humanitarian crisis in the capital.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaElon MuskVladimir PutinSpaceXEuropeVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in Spain | Spain | The Guardian
description: Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives
Content: The small town of Urda, near where the crash occurred, was swiftly transformed into a frantic emergency response centre.Photograph: Andrea Comas/APView image in fullscreenThe small town of Urda, near where the crash occurred, was swiftly transformed into a frantic emergency response centre.Photograph: Andrea Comas/APSpain‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of deadly train crash in SpainPassengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 livesAt least 68 killed in Toledo train crash – full reportSam Jonesin UrdaWed 28 Oct 2026 14.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”View image in fullscreenJosimar Medina and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, from Peru and Brazil respectively, were thrown across their carriage of the fast train from Madrid to Seville after it collided with another train on the track.Photograph: Sam Jones/The GuardianThe Peruvian stood recounting the details ofWednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south ofSpain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.View image in fullscreenA member of the Spanish Red Cross embraces a woman as they wait for news of passengers on the two high-speed trains that collided near Urda.Photograph: Susana Vera/ReutersFredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.“One guy was shouting: ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”View image in fullscreenFrederich and Arabella Barilea, originally from the Philippines but currently living in Dubai, were passengers on the Iryo train that the fast train from Madrid hit from behind.Photograph: Sam JonesAround the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending. Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second major rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of theAdamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.View image in fullscreenMedical staff converted a nearby sports centres into a temporary medical facility.Photograph: Andrea Comas/APBut, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly collisions that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With asnap general electionjust a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly and thoroughly as possible.For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.“Mejor no verlo,”she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.Explore more on these topicsSpainTrain crashesRail travelRail transportEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network | Train crashes | The Guardian
description: Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%
Content: Rescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault.Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault.Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty ImagesTrain crashesAnalysisSecond fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail networkAshifa Kassamin MadridQuestions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTShareSpain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive inEuropeand the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety.Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesdaymorning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers.Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track.Soon after, the central command in Madrid instructed one of the trains involved in the crash to resume service at normal speeds, sending it colliding into a train that was still sitting stationary on the tracks, said Puente. “It was the control centre – via its operators – that made the decision to resume operations, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he added.State-owned rail operator Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”.The accident follows acrash in January that killed 46 peopleand left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.View image in fullscreenA Guardia Civil officer collects evidence at the site of January’s fatal rail crash near Adamuz in Andalucía.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APMedia on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network.The first crash sparked conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued.Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” theunion saidearlier this month.Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.”mapIt has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo.The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country wheretravel by trainaccounts for about 57% of all transport.While the causes of the January crash remain under investigation, a preliminary report suggested that it could have been the result of defects in the track or in a weld between two sections of track. The report noted, however, that several other possibilities were also being investigated.Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain.The governmentsays it has increasedspending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the 2013 crash near Santiago de Compostela that claimed 80 lives.Photograph: ReutersSpain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU.Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU.On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister said measures would be taken to rebuild trust in the country’s high-speed rail system. “Because it is simply unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have,” said Sánchez.The crash was Spain’s worst rail accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.Explore more on these topicsTrain crashesSpainEuropeRail transportanalysisShareReuse this content

title: New book makes fiery claims about Jared Kushner’s finances in Trump’s first term | Jared Kushner | The Guardian
description: Kushner threatens to sue, denying allegations that two slush funds were set up to influence his Middle East role
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: Kushner threatens to sue, denying allegations that two slush funds were set up to influence his Middle East role
Content: Jared Kushner speaks during a Board of Peace open session in New York on 23 September 2026.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJared Kushner speaks during a Board of Peace open session in New York on 23 September 2026.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesJared KushnerNew book makes fiery claims about Jared Kushner’s finances in Trump’s first termKushner threatens to sue, denying allegations that two slush funds were set up to influence his Middle East roleMartin PengellyWed 28 Oct 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new book containing incendiary claims aboutJared Kushner’s financial dealings duringDonald Trump’s first term has ignited a political and media firestorm.The book by author Matthew Cole is calledPrinces and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle Eastand was released in the US this week. Anexcerpt was published by Vanity Fairlast Thursday, and immediately drew a furious response from Kushner, who called its claims “completely insane”. The book contains numerous allegations about Kushner, whose father-in-law is Trump and who has served as one of his top diplomatic envoys in the Middle East – the most explosive of which are claims linking him to huge bank accounts allegedly funded by Gulf states.Kusher denounced the bookon his sitelast week, and writingon X: “We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” He has demanded that Vanity Fair retract the excerpt and has threatened legal action against the book’s publisher, Simon & Schuster.He added: “During the period in question, I was one of the most scrutinized people in the world, subjected to intense media coverage, multiple congressional investigations, and a special counsel investigation. I voluntarily cooperated with these investigations, providing over 30 hours of testimony. None of these allegations ever surfaced, because none of these events ever happened.”The Guardian contacted Kushner’s legal counsel from Clare Locke as well as Chad Mizelle for comment and received no response.Cole’s sources are predominantly anonymous and he does not print images of emails or other documentation to support his reporting. Extensive footnotes indicate sources of information, including confidential interviews.In the book, the top intelligence official in the United Arab Emirates, Ali Al Shamsi, is reported to have called Kushner “the most expensive employee we’ve ever had”. The book details alleged payments into two “slush fund” bank accounts allegedly set up for Kushner by Emirati prince Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Saudi Arabian prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) during Trump’s first term. The Guardian contacted the Saudi Arabian and Emirati embassies for comment and did not receive a response.In the book, Cole claims the accounts were partially managed by Kushner on an iPhone hacked by Russian and Dutch intelligence.But despite the Emirati spymaster’s opinion of Kushner, Cole alleges that the New Jersey real estate scion was not entirely trusted. Cole describes a dangerous world in which blackmail is as common a tool of statecraft as torture and murder, as in the cases of the Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, killed on theordersof MBS in Turkey in 2018, and the Emirati journalist and poetHabib Al Sayegh, whose killing by agents of MBZ in 2019 is described by Cole.Kushner continues to steer US foreign policy despite having no official role, with questions about his business interests accompanying him as he travels the world with New York real estate magnate Steve Witkoff, this weekseekingpeace in Ukraine, if on terms favorable to Russia.In response, an attorney “who has represented President Trump in multiple defamation lawsuits”, Alejandro Brito, told Cole that, “during his time working for President Trump, Kushner ‘always represented and sought the interests of the United States and the President of the United States and did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.’” He further said that “[a]ny allegation that Kushner knew of, had access to, had authorization for or engaged in or directed any conduct related to any government-funded or government-linked bank account is totally false and defamatory”.Brito told Cole that “‘there are no accounts and never were.’” Cole writes that the Dutch government refused to comment in response to his questions about the alleged hacking of Kushner’s phone.According to Cole, MBZ and MBS wanted Kushner to help achieve their “vision of a new Middle East, one in which Israel would become an integral part of the region, recognized diplomatically by Gulf Arabs today and eventually by the rest of the Arab world; the Palestinians would end their conflict with Israel and accept a peace built on prosperity; Islamic extremism would be defeated; and Iran’s expansionism and militancy would retreat, either by persuasion or force.”Nearly 10 years later, the US and Israel are planning new strikes in their eight-month war with Iran; Saudi Arabia is at war with Houthi rebels in Yemen, and Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.Kushner entered Trump’s first administration with his wife, Ivanka Trump, as close presidential advisers. MBZ and MBS, Cole claims, saw a chance to secure the best access money could buy. Cole alleges that in early 2017 the two princes “proposed to give Kushner a fund, a bank account, which the two leaders, working with Jared, would use to identify and pay for projects and foreign policy goals to advance for President Trump’s benefit”.According to Cole, an idea to fund Trump’s proposed wall on the US border with Mexico apparently did not work out but the author claims that “MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2bn into at least two banks for Kushner.” Classifying the accounts as “Alpha” and “Beta”, Cole claims the Alpha account was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in UAE, and contained “roughly $750m” to be “used as a foreign policy fund” overseen by Kushner and MBZ and meant to help end the Israel-Palestine conflict.Cole quotes a source who says he knew of the UAE’s alleged deal with Kushner as saying: “‘Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy.’” Cole writes: “This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. ‘Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off,’” the source alleged.The same source claimed that “a slush fund – a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives – was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption … ‘The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.’”Citing “a person briefed on the Beta account”, Cole claims it contained “roughly $1bn” and at the suggestion of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was moved by MBZ to the Israeli Central Bank via Azerbaijan, a favored conduit for laundering money.“It is … unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him,” Cole alleges, “but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit.”Kushner’s attorney, Brito, told Cole his client “had no financial relationships with any foreign countries or leaders”, adding that his “complete financial disclosures are publicly available in his OGE [office of government ethics] form 278e filings during this period.”Cole alleges that the “Alpha” account established for Kushner in Trump’s first term was drained by failed schemes and Kushner’s access was cut off. “It is unclear if the Israeli government allowed Kushner access to the Beta bank account” after the end of Trump’s first term, Cole writes.Cole also examines thewidely reported storyabout how Kushner ultimately secured Qatari investment in 666 Fifth Avenue, a marquee Manhattan property, thereby profiting from interests on both sides of a bitterly divided Middle East, given Saudi Arabia and UAE’s rivalry with Qatar. (Kushner has denied engaging in any conflicts of interest.)In Trump’s second term, Kushner’s diplomatic work has been dogged by questions about another massive financial asset: a$2bn investmentby the Saudi sovereign wealth fund in Kushner’s Affinity Partners private equity firm, made after Trump left power in 2021. Cole quotes an unnamed Arab official and Affinity investor who claimed: “We don’t pay Jared because he’s a savvy investor. We pay him to keep him happy. That keeps his father-in-law happy.”Cole writes: “Deep relationships with MBZ, MBS, Emir Al Thani [of Qatar], and Bibi Netanyahu were useful as [Kushner] shuttled between capitals, trying to find a way to end the daily slaughter in Gaza. But as it had been when he was a government employee, there was little record of what his investors were negotiating with him.”In his epilogue, Cole writes that Kushner “declined multiple requests for an on-the-record interview for the book”, adding that he “first contacted him with a list of questions in May 2026 and followed up via email twice more, asking additional questions.”Through his lawyers, Kushner denounced all of Cole’s reporting. Also on X, Chad Mizelle, a Trump administration lawyer who identified himself as “Jared’s attorney”,said: “The central allegation in this book is categorically false. These are not questions of interpretation or competing recollections: there are no bank accounts. They don’t exist. These are egregious and defamatory claims without a shred of evidence to substantiate them.”Explore more on these topicsJared KushnerTrump administrationUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricaUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Coalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majority | Israel | The Guardian
description: Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that drew highest turnout in decades
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that drew highest turnout in decades
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu claimed without evidence that Arab Israeli parties had ‘stolen the election’, while Gadi Eisenkot appeared to rule out a coalition with Palestinian parties.Composite: AFP and Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu claimed without evidence that Arab Israeli parties had ‘stolen the election’, while Gadi Eisenkot appeared to rule out a coalition with Palestinian parties.Composite: AFP and Getty ImagesIsraelCoalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majorityProjections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that drew highest turnout in decadesIsrael election: what we know so farAnalysis: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscapeJulian Borgerin JerusalemWed 28 Oct 2026 15.58 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 01.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s future hung in the balance on Wednesday as it became clear thatBenjamin Netanyahuhad lost his governing majority. His political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot’s bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister’s bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots – about 14% of the total electorate –yet to be fully counted.With the remaining 86% of the votes tallied,both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.On Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and the success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming they had “stolen the election”. He did not offer evidence, butsaid on Xthat his Likud party had sent “hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence” to the central elections committee and the Shin Bet internal security agency.Both those agencies have been politicised under Netanyahu’s government. The elections committee had sought to ban Arab Israeli parties before the poll, but the attempt to exclude them was overturned by the country’s supreme court.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu at an election night event for his Likud party in Jerusalem.Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesDonald Trump took credit for Netanyahu’s better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am (the United Arab List).“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid. And if we don’t put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan wrote on X.Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscapeRead more“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.Noa Landau, a commenterwriting in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can’t be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu’s government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot at an election night rally in Tel Aviv.Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to their rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other’s camps.Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.View image in fullscreenThe scene outside the Knesset in Jerusalem on Wednesday.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAThe Palestinian parties and Jewish centre-left have been urging the opposition to focus on finding common cause in the Knesset, replacing the speaker and pursuing legislation that the factions can agree on, such as ordering an independent review into the security failures that led to the 7 October attack by Hamas in 2023.On Wednesday, Herzog urged all parties to keep an “open mind” in trying to build a new government coalition.“We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said.The election happened in the midst of Israel’s war in Gaza – barely mentioned in the course of the campaign, despite the fact that Israel has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and Netanyahu is wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.View image in fullscreenProtesters take part in an anti-government demonstration calling for an end to the war in Gaza near Netnayahu’s residence in Jerusalem on Wednesday.Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty ImagesA UN commission of human rights expertsreported on Mondaythat Israel had continued to commit genocidal acts against Palestinian civilians in Gaza after a ceasefire was declared in October 2025. Since then 1,431 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military, including 300 children.The report, by the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said: “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Daniel Meron, rejected the report as an “attempt to destroy the Jewish state” and “to undermine Israel’s ​legitimacy and deny its fundamental right to exist and defend itself”.Eisenkot and much of his bloc support the war in Gaza, and sought to make the election a referendum on Netanyahu. The turnout was nearly 78%, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting.View image in fullscreenNetanyahu supporters celebrate in the early hours of Wednesday.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesPolitical deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, he and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war alongside the US against Iran.Explore more on these topicsIsraelBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition | Israel | The Guardian
description: Incumbent could turn defeat into another term in office as rival parties erect confected barrier to unseating him
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Incumbent could turn defeat into another term in office as rival parties erect confected barrier to unseating him
Content: A supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu shows his excitement on election night in Jerusalem.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu shows his excitement on election night in Jerusalem.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelAnalysisIsrael’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalitionEmma Graham-Harrisonin Tel AvivIncumbent could turn defeat into another term in office as rival parties erect confected barrier to unseating himFull report: Coalition talks loom in IsraelAnalysis: Rise of Palestinian parties will redraw political landscapeWed 28 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 20.21 EDTShareHours before the final results fromIsrael’s electionswere in, several things were clear.
