Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.But most ofIsrael’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.The self-imposed ban on abroader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaperIsraelHayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”View image in fullscreenMansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, holds his daughter as he casts his vote in Maghar, Israel.Photograph: Rami Shlush/ReutersOther Israelis were even more direct. “If you stop being racist two amazing things will happen to you,” musician Yali Sobol wrote in a Facebook post. “First, you will stop being racist. Second, you will discover you have won.”While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperinsaid.But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.Former generalGadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot waves to supporters at an election night rally.Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty ImagesPalestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List,said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”The Islamist Ra’am party put a Jewish former police chief in second position on their slate, in a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis.A precedent from three decades ago, whenYitzhak Rabinrelied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict, gets little mention in contemporary Israeli political debate.Netanyahu put racism at the heart of his campaign, in a strategy critics said was designed both to bolster voter support and complicate post-election coalition negotiations for the opposition.A slogan featured on many of his election posters, “The right or Palestine”, framed 20% of the population as an enemy within Israel’s borders.A bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives for now – and we are more divided than ever | Dahlia ScheindlinRead moreOn election night he shrugged off the loss of about 10 seats from the 64 seat-coalition he assembled in 2022 – a severe rebuke from voters by most counts – to claim that his vision for Israel had been vindicated in the poll.The Knesset overall has shifted further right, as have young Israelis, and after the results came in, he issued an open invitation to put their opposition to Palestinian parties ahead of their opposition to him.“The rightwing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public,” he said. “We must form a strong national-right government”.Many in Israel described this election as existential, as they struggled to halt the erosion of democracy inside Israel’s pre-1967 borders, and secure a State Commission of Inquiry into the 7 October attacks.For Palestinian citizens facing surging crime, discrimination and home demolitions inside Israel and watching family and friends endureethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bankand a war of annihilation in Gaza, that was viscerally true, and they came out in record numbers.Israel describes itself as a Jewish and democratic state. If the representatives of Palestinians are now effectively excluded from government because of their race, Netanyahu will have turned that promise into more of a choice – between a Jewish future or a democratic one.Explore more on these topicsIsraelBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence | Jafar Panahi | The Guardian
description: Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’
Content: The Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that authorities were cracking down on cultural figures.Photograph: Carlos Álvarez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that authorities were cracking down on cultural figures.Photograph: Carlos Álvarez/Getty ImagesJafar PanahiIranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentenceCharges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’Deepa ParentWed 28 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Iranian court has handed the award-winning film directorJafar Panahia new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.The 66-year-old, whowon the Palme d’Orat Cannes last year forIt Was Just an Accident, was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned toIranin March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said the sentencing, and the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, could violate Iran’s constitution, unless the authorities establish a clear legal basis linking the property to an alleged offence.Speaking to the Guardian while in the US earlier this year,Panahi warnedthat the current “cycle of violence” in Iran could continue.“What I have been depicting in this film is when the cycle of violence continues, then it becomes very difficult to stop it,” Panahi said. “Unfortunately, because of the savagery that is being carried out by the state, the fear is that this cycle of violence will continue.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I think of those I left behind in prison’: Iran’s Jafar Panahi on life as a banned film-makerRead moreThe latest sentence has raised concerns among fellow artists over the risks facing those who continue to work independently in Iran.The Iranian actor Setareh Maleki, who was forced into exile after starring in Mohammad Rasoulof’s Oscar-nominated filmThe Seed of the Sacred Fig, told the Guardian: “One of the greatest fears of a dictatorship is losing control over the stories people tell. When those stories cross borders and reach the world, they become impossible to silence. Jafar Panahi has told his stories too, and his sentence proves once again just how deeply the Islamic Republic fears even the act of storytelling.”Inside Iran, a film-maker currently shooting a film in secret expressed support for Panahi. “We all support him, who brings us great pride. He hasn’t remained silent and instead voices demands of the Iranian people,” said the film-maker, who did not want to give her name.She said she believed Panahi’s latest sentence was linked to his calls for unity during the January protests and his support for diverse voices inside Iran, including supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s former shah.The Iranian-British actor Nazanin Boniadi also condemned the ruling, saying: “Jafar Panahi has spent decades turning censorship into cinematic resistance, bearing witness to the suffering and resilience of the Iranian people. His latest draconian prison sentence is yet another attempt to silence a courageous artist whose work exposes the realities of repression in Iran.”In a recent report, the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that Iranian authorities are intensifying their crackdown on artists, writers, poets, musicians and other cultural figures, “pulling peaceful voices into the same coercive security and judicial apparatus used to suppress dissent across Iran”.Explore more on these topicsJafar PanahiIranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand tells trial it was wrong to use fame to ‘facilitate’ sex with women  | UK news | The Guardian
description: Former comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, says he misused position but ‘consent is more important than sex itself’
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Former comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, says he misused position but ‘consent is more important than sex itself’
Content: Russell Brand gave evidence at Southwark crown court for four hours on Wednesday.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRussell Brand gave evidence at Southwark crown court for four hours on Wednesday.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockUK newsRussell Brand tells trial it was wrong to use fame to ‘facilitate’ sex with womenFormer comedian, in court on rape and sexual assault charges, says he misused position but ‘consent is more important than sex itself’Emine SinmazWed 28 Oct 2026 17.28 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand has told a court that he was wrong to have used his fame and success to “facilitate” sexual activity with women.The 51-year-old comedian said he had “misused” his position “very selfishly” and dedicated his life to “reckless philandering and idiocy”.But he insisted that “consent is more important than sex itself” and that the criminal case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life.Brand is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Wearing a dark suit, white shirt and tie, he appeared in the witness box for four hours on Wednesday as he gave evidence at Southwark crown court.He said he had achieved “staggering fame” after marrying the US pop star Katy Perry in 2010 but that now nobody would “touch him with a bargepole”.View image in fullscreenRussell Brand denies all the charges. At the start of his evidence, he repeatedly said ‘no’ when the individual claims were put to him.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAHe blamed his downfall on “devastating” 2023 media reports about his alleged sexual misconduct, which he said had led to him being barred from visiting his baby son when he was having open heart surgery at Great Ormond Street hospital.He also said he had failed to persuade a single person with relevant information to give evidence on his behalf at his criminal trial. “Would they touch you with a bargepole?” his barrister, Ian Winter KC, asked. Brand replied: “No.”The TV personality gave confident answers in a booming voice to Winter, issuing a series of terse “no” replies when asked if he had raped women in a hotel room, at his home and in a bar toilet, and sexually assaulted radio and TV workers.He told the court he was “innocent” of all the charges and said: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself.”He later added: “Consent is an ongoing process and at any point anybody can withdraw their consent.”During the course of his evidence, Brand told the court he does not remember some of the incidents in the charges and remembers only consensual sexual encounters in others.He admitted saving the telephone number of a woman who accuses him of anal rape in 2009 with the letter “T” next to her name, meaning “tart”.The woman alleges Brand raped her at his north London townhouse, a few days after she had willingly engaged in a threesome with the star backstage at the Hammersmith Apollo venue in London.When Winter asked what he meant by the word “tart”, he replied: “That was what I used to denote casual hook-ups.”He also put two asterisks next to the woman’s name, which he told the jury meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.”Brand used colourful language to describe some of his accusers. He described a woman who alleges he raped her at the Labour party conference in 1999 as “vivacious and loquacious” and an MTV worker who accuses him of oral rape in 2004 as having “prominent eyes”. “She was lithe, elfin, pixieish, energetic,” he said.But there were tense moments during cross-examination in which Brand stared at the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, in silence for several seconds. Occasionally he could be seen moving his lips before speaking out loud.The prosecutor probed him about alleged inconsistencies in his previous statements and what he has told the jury with regards to the woman who accused him of anal rape. Brand said: “Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree. Since these events occurred there’s been escalating recollection.“It’s been a deeply traumatic episode of my life I’ve focused on at the expense of my marriage, my children and health. I ask your forgiveness, well, not your forgiveness.“I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that.”And when asked if the young fan was “just another sexual conquest” in his attempt to sleep with 5,000 women, Brand told the court: “I really don’t know the number, but it’s difficult to dispute that’s how I conducted myself in the pursuit of willing sexual partners.”As he came to the end of his cross-examination, Karmy-Jones challenged Brand on what he had done to upset the woman so much. “I think I was in a position of fame, a successful person who was admired and I misused that commodity very selfishly,” he said.“You were in a position of power in respect of each of these women,” the prosecutor continued, to which Brand replied: “As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong.”Karmy-Jones also confronted him with extracts from his 2007 book, My Booky Wook, in which Brand said he “would never have relented until I received my birthright orgasm”. Responding to one of the passages, Brand said: “I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.“With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I’ve been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy.”The prosecutor said that Brand’s book included a picture of himself as a seven-year-old with the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took fifteen years to produce results.”View image in fullscreenExtracts from Brand’s My Booky Wook were read to the court on Wednesday.Photograph: Metropolitan policeThe first alleged rape victim has told the court she believed Brand was gay when they first met at a Labour party conference fringe event, which led to her agreeing for him to come to her hotel room.The prosecutor asked Brand: “That’s something you would do, wasn’t it? That was something you would do to make girls trust you?”“No,” Brand replied.Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Mr Justice Bennathan told jurors they should find Brand not guilty of the indecent assault allegation after he concluded “there was insufficient evidence” to support the charge.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Budget 2026: Healey hikes taxes on banks and landlords to fund £100 handouts to 20m households | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Few surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisis
Content: Andy Burnham, the prime minister, hugs John Healey, the chancellor, after delivering his first annual budget.Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham, the prime minister, hugs John Healey, the chancellor, after delivering his first annual budget.Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesBudget 2026Budget 2026: Healey hikes taxes on banks and landlords to fund £100 handouts to 20m householdsFew surprises as chancellor uses low-key speech blaming ‘global economic storms’ for stoking energy prices and cost of living crisisBudget 2026: key points at a glanceBriefing: key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa CrerarEditorial: Budget’s bold ambitions and welcome first stepsHeather Stewart,Jessica ElgotandRichard PartingtonWed 28 Oct 2026 16.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund a £100 winter handout for 20 million families as official forecasts made clear there is no end in sight for the cost of living crisis.In his first budget, the chancellor blamed “global economic storms” for the grim outlook, as the war in Iran drives up oil and gas prices.But he also faced criticism for failing to squeeze more money from profitable banks, punishing savers and not giving enough help to the poorest.In a low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, Healey was at pains to stress he was sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, and there were few surprises in his hour-long address to MPs.Budget briefing: the key questions answered by Heather Stewart and Pippa CrerarRead moreBut with households facing soaring energy prices, and mortgage bills rising amid higher interest rates, Healey offered a £100 cost-of-living payout, which will be sent to all English households in council tax bands A-D..It formed the centrepiece of a cost of living package, which he said would “take the pressure off in the coldest months, and see people through to the spring”.The £2.6bn cost of the £100 giveaway includes funding for the Scottish and Welsh governments, which Healey said he hoped they would use to implement a similar scheme.“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said.But the government’s independent forecaster warned households face a “grim picture” on living standards, as it slashed the outlook for the economy in 2027 and said there was “virtually no growth” in disposable income for households.The Guardian view on Labour’s budget: bold ambitions and welcome first steps | EditorialRead moreHealey also came under fire for an unexpected 2p increase in tax rates for income earned on property or savings. As well as hitting savers and landlords, theOffice for Budget Responsibility(OBR) said it risks “leading to a steady rise in rents”, by deterring landlords from the market and cutting supply, as well as passing on costs to tenants.Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation thinktank, criticised the £100 handout, arguing it would have been better to give more generous support to the poorest consumers.“The chancellor has missed the mark with badly targeted support that has left families facing a tough winter as energy bills rise,” she said.As expected, the chancellor also cancelled fuel tax rises planned by Rachel Reeves, and extended the VAT cut on electricity prices previously announced to next summer.Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.The cost of the household support measures will be met by a doubling of the additional levy banks pay on their profits, to 6%; as well as the higher taxes on income from property and savings..The additional bank tax will only last for 15 months and marked a less significant rise than some in the industry had feared. Banks’ share prices were among the highest risers in the blue chip FTSE 100 index on Wednesday.Laura Suter, director of personal finance at AJ Bell, said: “Savers will be hit with another hefty tax rise on their savings interest, adding to the squeeze on their savings over the past few years.”She added that the higher tax on rental income “could be passed on to tenants, with rent hikes a potential lever for landlords to mitigate any increase in tax”.“Equally, we could see yet more landlords selling up, in favour of investing their money in other assets that have lower taxes and less government tinkering,” she said.The NewEconomicsFoundation thinktank accused Healey of failing to be bold enough. Hannah Peaker, its deputy chief executive, said: “As households prepare to be hit by a wave of price rises this winter, the chancellor has shown the right instincts but not yet the right scale.“The £100 support with energy bills will provide some welcome relief, but the chancellor could have been braver in the face of what we are up against.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEnergy provider EDF predicts that the Ofgem price cap – which determines consumer bills – is set togo up by £466 in January. And despite Healey’s promise of a “breathing space,” in the teeth of the crisis, official forecasts published by the OBR alongside the budget pointed to a challenging winter.Presenting the forecasts, the OBR’s David Miles highlighted a “pretty grim picture” for household finances, as inflation rises to almost 4%..Even by 2030-31, it only expects real disposable household incomes – its favoured measure of living standards – to be 2% higher than before the Covid pandemic. It now expects anaemic economic growth of 1% next year, about half a percentage point lower than expected in March.Healey said higher inflation and interest rates had hit the government’s finances too, ratcheting up the government’s interest bill by £14bn this year alone, but promised to stick to Labour’s fiscal rules.The OBR said Healey would meet the most important rule – to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – with a diminished headroom of £15bn by the target date of 2029-30, against the £24bn Rachel Reeves had built up in the spring.Borrowing is scheduled to be higher than expected in the short term, but the chancellor promised to rebuild the buffer against the rules to £22bn by the end of the five-year forecast period.“That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can,” he said. Bond markets appeared unruffled by the higher-than-expected borrowing.The deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, to argue Burnham was keeping his options open on an early general election.Burnham doubled down on his promise not to call one, however, telling reporters on Wednesday that he could rule one out for at least 12 months. “I’m not thinking about my own party and its prospects. I am thinking about people, and I’m thinking about what I can do to help them.”Badenoch said Britain had “overspent, overborrowed and overtaxed”, and criticised Healey for delayed decisions on defence spending and welfare cuts. Healey has said he will tackle welfare after reports from Alan Milburn on youth unemployment and Sir Stephen Timms on disability benefits, expected next month..Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that by sticking to the tight spending plans bequeathed by Reeves, Healey could be storing up trouble for the spending review due next year.“History warns us to be sceptical of tight spending plans in later years of the forecast. Next year’s spending review will be a crunch point, and looks very tough for many departments, whose budgets will be squeezed by higher inflation forecasts,” she said.“The plans for overall spending set out in the budget mean that spending choices at next year’s spending review will be much harder than those made so far this parliament.”Buried in the budget was a hint at an easing of some migration restrictions, including some industries that will be allowed to lower the salary thresholds for visas to allow companies across the country to hire international talent.Among the winners was London mayor LordSadiq Khan, who received new powers to extend the Bakerloo line in London and a pledge that cross-Channel trains will now also stop at Stratford International in east London. There was also cash to explore hosting the Olympics in “a northern city” – and former Greater Manchester mayor Burnham may have a candidate city in mind.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyBudgetUK cost of living crisisTaxTax and spendingFamily financesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Knifeman on LNER train ‘caused terror and fear on unimaginable scale’, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder passengers and staff on board a London-bound train last November
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder passengers and staff on board a London-bound train last November
Content: A photo of Anthony Williams, 33, on an LNER train  last year, which was shown to the jury at Cambridge crown court.Photograph: British Transport Police/PAView image in fullscreenA photo of Anthony Williams, 33, on an LNER train  last year, which was shown to the jury at Cambridge crown court.Photograph: British Transport Police/PAUK newsKnifeman on LNER train ‘caused terror and fear on unimaginable scale’, court hearsAnthony Williams is accused of attempting to murder passengers and staff on board a London-bound train last NovemberNeha Gohil and press agencyWed 28 Oct 2026 15.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA knifeman “caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale” to passengers when he stabbed 10 people on a London-bound train, a court has heard.Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on an LNER train on 1 November last year and stabbing four people in the 24 hours before.Christopher Paxton KC told jurors at Cambridge crown court on Wednesday: “The defendant, Mr Williams, armed with a knife, caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale, moving up and down a busy train from which there was no escape, stabbing several people as he did so.”During his opening statement, Paxton showed a CCTV clip of a passenger, Stephen Crean, attempting to wrestle a knife from Williams. He said Williams asked Crean: “Do you want to die?”“We say, clear evidence of the defendant’s intention to kill, as was the use of the knife to stab so many, and to stab and cut Mr Crean in his hand, head and lower back,” Paxton said.Paxton described the “terror” of the attack, which led some train passengers to run “for their lives” and hide away in toilets, store cabinets and under seats.The prosecutor also praised the “extraordinary bravery” of the passengers who tried to wrestle the knife off Williams.This included Scott Green, who was stabbed while he attempted to grab the knife from Williams. A member of the train crew, Samir Zitouni, was also stabbed multiple times as he tried to use a frying pan to stop Williams, jurors heard.“In the face of that threat and the defendant’s sheer brutality some stood tall to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage, defending themselves and putting themselves in harm’s way to protect strangers,” Paxton said.Paxton also praised the train driver for his decision to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon.Williams, of no fixed abode, previously admitted a series of offences, including the wounding of 12 people, but denies 14 counts of attempted murder.Paxton told the court Williams posed a “dangerous threat” to the people he encountered before the train attack on the evening of 1 November.Jurors heard Williams had approached a 17-year-old boy on the Docklands Light Railway in London in the early hours of 1 November and asked him if he was “beefing the devil” before he knifed him in the face and hand.Williams also attacked three people in Peterborough on the evening of 31 October, the court heard, including a 14-year-old boy.“Across the Halloween weekend last year, to the many people he encountered, the defendant, Anthony Williams, posed a dangerous threat, marauding through towns and cities, on streets and trains alike, armed with a knife,” he said.“He stabbed many, seeking to end their lives with deadly intention, striking out at them when they were defenceless and in fear.”The trial continues on Thursday.Explore more on these topicsUK newsCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage skips budget in Commons over seating ‘altercation’ concerns  | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Reform UK leader ‘shocked’ by £10bn pledged to Ukraine and doubles down on cutting tax for crypto investors
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Reform UK leader ‘shocked’ by £10bn pledged to Ukraine and doubles down on cutting tax for crypto investors
Content: Farage said at a press conference in Westminster that he had decided to give parliament a ‘wide berth’ on budget day.Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFarage said at a press conference in Westminster that he had decided to give parliament a ‘wide berth’ on budget day.Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockBudget 2026Nigel Farage skips budget in Commons over seating ‘altercation’ concernsReform UK leader ‘shocked’ by £10bn pledged to Ukraine and doubles down on cutting tax for crypto investorsBudget 2026: key points at a glanceRowena MasonWhitehall editorWed 28 Oct 2026 15.42 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage skippedthe chancellor’s first budgetbecause he was worried he would get in a “physical altercation” with another MP in a row over seating arrangements.The Reform UK leader was not present in theHouse of Commonsbut gave a press conference afterwards in which he said he was “shocked” by the £10bn going to support Ukraine and doubled down on his party’s policies on cutting tax for crypto investors.In a joint event with Robert Jenrick, his party’s Treasury spokesperson, Farage said he had decided to give parliament a “wide berth” as he was concerned he would get into a fight because another MP had removed a green paper slip saving him a seat. He said this situation had turned physical on a previous occasion.“At the state opening of parliament, I got involved in, I didn’t want to, but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber,” he said.“I didn’t make a fuss about it. I didn’t complain. But I could see, given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation, and just sometimes, it’s better to avoid conflict, is one reason. Second reason is, actually, I sat going through the budget with the economists in the office line by line.”It later emerged that the seat reservation was removed for not being properly stamped with the date.A House of Commons spokesperson said: “There are clear and long-established arrangements for members to reserve their own seats in the chamber using prayer cards displaying a valid date stamp. Today, a prayer card placed on a seat did not display a valid date stamp and was removed in line with the usual chamber protocol.”In his response to the budget, Farage said John Healey’s small giveaways suggested there would be a general election in May next year and added that Reform would be ready for one as early as December.Farage criticised the extra taxation announced on gambling shops through higher machine-games duty, saying it would be bad for the horse-racing industry and drive gambling offshore and through crypto.Asked whether Reform still had a policy of cutting capital gains tax on cryptocurrency, which could benefit its big donors, Farage said his plans still stood and would not benefit his backers overall.He said his policy was trying to “bring crypto in from the cold … A 10% tax rate on crypto gains is a way of incentivising people to come into the system, to go straight in a new regulated industry.”OnUkraine, Farage said he was “surprised by the amount” of promised economic and military aid but that he did not “mind the amount, provided I can be absolutely assured it’s not going to get swallowed up in corruption and making Ukrainian officials richer than they already are”.He claimed to be more worried about Vladimir Putin’s “rationality” than at any point before in the conflict, but said he was “shocked by the size of [the aid package]” and was “really concerned the money’s going to get used properly and spent well”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBudget winners and losers: pensioners and households gain as banks and betting shops hitRead moreFarage has previously expressed admiration for the Russian president and in 2024 suggested the west “provoked” Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, although he has supported the UK’s position in the war and declined to repeat Donald Trump’s harsher criticisms of Kyiv.Asked whether he preferred Healey’s budget or the disastrous one given under Liz Truss in 2022, which he previously praised but led to Truss’s demise as prime minister, Farage said he had liked the top lines of the Truss budget but “what I hadn’t understood was they didn’t cut spending”.He added: “That was their mistake … If they cut spending radically, they could have cut taxes, and that was the big lesson that came from it.”The Reform leader also gave his response to Tommy Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists, saying the far-right agitator’s behaviour had obviously been “very wrong”. But he repeated suggestions that his party’s members would not be penalised for admiring Robinson, saying just because they liked a social media message “doesn’t make them full-blown marchers in support of their cause”.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026Nigel FarageHouse of CommonsReform UKBudgetTax and spendingCryptocurrenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Budget 2026: £100 energy payment for millions and rise in bank tax as watchdog warns on stalling living standards – as it happened | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: OBR says that living standards are forecast to rise by just 1% over the whole post-Covid decade
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: OBR says that living standards are forecast to rise by just 1% over the whole post-Covid decade
Content: 11.18 EDTOBR: living standards forecast to rise by just 1% over whole post-Covid decadeTheOBRreportsays RHDI (real household disposable income – one measure of living standards) is rising at a record slow rate – less than 0.1% per decade. That means, by the end of the decade, it will be just 1% higher than its pre-Covid level, it says.double quotation markOur central forecast represents a continuation of the historically weak growth in RHDI per person since the global financial crisis. Chart 2.7 shows the rolling 10-year average annual growth in RHDI per person. This slowed significantly in the aftermath of the financial crisis, due to lower growth in productivity and real wages. Growth reached a historic low over the 10 years to 2025-26, averaging just ¼ per cent a year, and we expect it to fall further in the near term. By 2029-30, our central forecast sees growth over the prior 10 years averaging less than 0.1 per cent a year. As a result, 10 years on from the onset of the pandemic, RHDI per person would be just 1 per cent higher than its pre-pandemic level.Rolling average growth in RHDIPhotograph: OBRShare

title: Tributes pour in for labor leader Dolores Huerta: ‘Fought for farm workers to the very end’ | California | The Guardian
description: Lawmakers, activists and union leaders across the US remember the co-founder of United Farm Workers union
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: Lawmakers, activists and union leaders across the US remember the co-founder of United Farm Workers union
Content: People walk past a Dia de los Muertos display with a photo of Dolores Huerta at an eponymous elementary school in San Francisco.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a Dia de los Muertos display with a photo of Dolores Huerta at an eponymous elementary school in San Francisco.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APCaliforniaTributes pour in for labor leader Dolores Huerta: ‘Fought for farm workers to the very end’Lawmakers, activists and union leaders across the US remember the co-founder of United Farm Workers unionMaanvi SinghWed 28 Oct 2026 18.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFollowing the news that Dolores Huerta – the civil rights icon who popularized the rallying cry “Sí, se puede! – had died at the age of 96 on Wednesday, activists, lawmakers and civil rights leaders paid tribute to Hureta’s long and lasting legacy.In California – where Huerta helped found the United Farm Workers (UFW) union – her death was deeply felt. It was in California’s central valley that she laid the foundations for the United Farm Workers, and helped organize the1965 Delano grape strike– a national boycott of table grapes that resulted in better wages and working conditions for grape pickers. Several schools in California bear her name, and murals across the state depict her likeness. And in 2018, California declared 10 April – her birthday – Dolores Huerta Day.Dolores Huerta, California labor leader and civil rights champion, dies aged 96Read more“From the fields ofCaliforniato the halls of Congress and the White House, Dolores dedicated her life to ensuring that every voice – especially those too often silenced – was heard,” said Hector Sanchez Barba, the president of the voter mobilization organization Mi Familia Vota. “Her historic rallying cry, ‘Sí, se puede,’ is not just a slogan; it is a living call to action that continues to unite and inspire millions across the world.”“Our greatest monument to her memory is for the union she helped found to continue to grow. Dolores fought for farm workers to the very end of her life,” said UFW president Teresa Romero. “The greatest possible tribute to her life is for her work of organizing to continue.”Huerta’s legacy is national and international; her portrait hangs at some US embassies and schools in several US states are named after her. She helped negotiate national immigration policy, and remained, until her death, intimately involved in promoting civil and labor rights in Washington DC and across the US.Tributes also came from some of California’s biggest political names, including Nancy Pelosi, the former House speaker, Gavin Newsom, the governor, and former vice-presidentKamala Harris.“Dolores was a dear friend, and we all responded to her rallying cry, ‘Sí se puede,’ which inspired generations of Americans to believe in the power of collective action,” said Pelosi. “May it be a comfort to her family and loved ones that so many mourn their loss and are praying for them at this sad time.”“I was blessed to know Dolores for many years and proud to organize alongside my dear friend to champion working families and immigrant rights,” said Harris. “I will always be grateful for her support and friendship. We will honor her legacy by continuing the fight for the dignity of every person.”“Dolores Huerta represented the best of us,” said Newsom. “California – and the United States – would not be what we are today without her resolute spirit, her passion for justice and fairness, and her commitment to those overlooked and forgotten.”“The best tribute we can pay is to carry on the work, which means standing with workers, defending civil rights and organizing for a more just California,” echoed Alex Padilla, US senator representing California.“¡Adiós, Dolores! You were everywhere. You did everything,” said Xavier Becerra, the former California attorney general and former US health secretary who is running for governor. “If you want to know where a leader will take you, know where they come from. Dolores never let us forget where she came from. Si, se pudo [Yes, we did].”Dolores Huerta – a life in picturesRead moreLawmakers across the US, including Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, the New York congressperson, also hailed her trailblazing legacy. “For decades after the Delano Grape Strike, she continued to organize for the rights of working people, women and immigrants. She continued to fight for the idea that when ordinary people come together, they can change the course of history,” said Ocasio Cortez. “While we mourn her devastating loss, we will continue her fight to build a country where every worker, regardless of race, gender, or economic status, is treated with dignity.”Lawmakers thanked Huerta for her efforts to promote female candidates to public office.Eloise Gómez Reyes, the state senator who brought legislation in 2018 to mark 10 April as Dolores Huerta Day in California, said that she was mourning “the loss of someone who profoundly shaped my own life”.“Dolores Huerta taught generations of us that we did not have to accept the world as it was. That ordinary people, working together, could challenge powerful institutions, overcome injustice, and build something better. She didn’t simply open doors for women like me. She taught us that we had the power to open them for others,” Reyes said.Hilda Solis, a former Democratic congresswoman who became the first Latina to serve in a cabinet position as Barack Obama’s labor secretary, thanked Huerta for her mentorship. “Growing up in the San Gabriel Valley, I rarely saw Latinas in positions of leadership. Dolores was one of the few women who showed me what was possible,” she said. “From the state legislature to Congress and my time serving in President Barack Obama’s cabinet, Dolores remained a constant in my life. We joined demonstrations and rallies, stood with workers fighting for their rights and demanded action when people in power looked away … Dolores understood the importance of showing up, bearing witness and refusing to let the suffering of women go ignored.”Huerta for years was considered the second-in-command to UFW co-founder César Chávez – and spoke about how she had to fight the sexism within the movement, and was often forced to cede credit to Chávez. Earlier this year, in the aftermath of a New York Timesinvestigation uncovering Chávez’ pattern of sexual abuse of women and girls, Huerta revealed that Chávez had raped her, too.“I believed that exposing the truth would hurt the farmworker movement I have spent my entire life fighting for,”shesaid, explaining why she had stayed silent about her abuse for so long.But after sharing her story, she learned that her fear would not bear out. Across the US, officials looked to renaming streets that once bore Chávez’s name with Huerta’s. Murals centering Chávez were replacedwith Huerta’s image, or images depicting the larger farmworker movement.“Her guidance transcended generations, nationalities, and borders. She touched so many people as she fought for justice, peace and equality. She never backed down,” said actor Rosario Dawson, who portrayed Huerta in a 2014 biopic of César Chávez. Dawson, who cofounded the organization Voto Latino, had worked with Huerta to rally voter turnout, and at timeshad openly disagreedwith her politics, said that the civil rights leader had been a “mentor and a beacon of light”.“¡Sí, se puede, Dolores! May we carry your light and joy as we forge the path for new generations,” she added.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaUS unionsNancy PelosiGavin NewsomKamala HarrisWest CoastAlexandria Ocasio-CorteznewsShareReuse this content

title: Microsoft posts $92.3bn quarterly revenue after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees | Microsoft | The Guardian
description: Software giant reports $36.6bn in profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as Azure cloud computing division grows 48%
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Software giant reports $36.6bn in profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as Azure cloud computing division grows 48%
Content: The Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Microsoft campus in Redmond, Washington.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersMicrosoftMicrosoft posts $92.3bn quarterly revenue after offering buyouts to 60,000 employeesSoftware giant reports $36.6bn in profit, beating Wall Street expectations, as Azure cloud computing division grows 48%Agence France-PresseWed 28 Oct 2026 18.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMicrosoft gained billions of dollars in stock market value Wednesday afternoon after it reported better than expected revenue and profit, just days after it offered voluntary buyouts to some 60,000 employees.The office software giant’s growth was fueled by its Azure cloud computing division, which grew by 48% in the September quarter.Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cutsRead more“We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost-efficiency for customers across our entire stack,” Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said in a statement.The technology giant recorded $92.3bn in total revenue and more than $36.6bn in profit, the company said in a securities filing Wednesday. Analysts had expected around $90.6bn in revenue and $35.1bn in profit, according to FactSet.The quarterly earnings report comes two days after Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence investments.It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year, after giving seven percent of its US workforce the option to retire early in April.Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.Earlier this month, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips and will cost more than $2,500. Apple announced a similar touchscreen Macbook this week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud datacenters, where running AI is slower and more expensive.Explore more on these topicsMicrosoftComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms  | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%
Content: Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference in Washington DC on 29 July 2026.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh speaks during a news conference in Washington DC on 29 July 2026.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesFederal ReserveFed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midtermsFed chair Kevin Warsh said politics played no role in pause of interest rate hikes, despite inflation remaining above 3%Gaya GuptaWed 28 Oct 2026 15.26 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USFederal Reserveleft interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%.Inflationhas hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, thepause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, whosaidthat “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.Warsh declined to comment on a remark fromDonald Trumpthat, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists arepredictingone more rate hike before the end of the year.“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Wallersaidearlier this month.The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveUS politicsDonald TrumpUS economyInflationUS interest ratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Embattled CBS leader Bari Weiss downplays concerns about weak 60 Minutes ratings | CBS | The Guardian
description: CBS News editor-in-chief sidesteps viewership concerns and says flagship show doing ‘tremendously well’
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: CBS News editor-in-chief sidesteps viewership concerns and says flagship show doing ‘tremendously well’
Content: Bari Weiss at an event in New York City.Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty Images for the Free PressView image in fullscreenBari Weiss at an event in New York City.Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty Images for the Free PressCBSEmbattled CBS leader Bari Weiss downplays concerns about weak 60 Minutes ratingsCBS News editor-in-chief sidesteps viewership concerns and says flagship show doing ‘tremendously well’Jeremy Barrin WashingtonWed 28 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCBS News editor-in-chiefBari Weisshas spoken publicly for the first time about the ratings challenges the network has experienced under her year-long tenure, sidestepping concerns about diminished viewership at the Sunday show 60 Minutes by saying it was not her top priority.“I could never build anything if I were focused on the precise number of people that happen to tune in to the second feature on 60 Minutes on a given Sunday,”she said at an industry conferenceon Wednesday organized by the tech publication the Information. The news organization did not offer press credentials.Overall, Weiss said the show was doing “tremendously well”.Weiss completely overhauled 60 Minutes in late May, ousting the show’s executive producer and parting ways with three top correspondents, including Scott Pelley. But the show has struggled to even match last season’s viewership, which averaged 9.1 million viewers per episode.The show’s most recent episode drew just 5.64 million viewers, “one of the smallest audiences for the program in years”,Variety reported. The show was the lowest-rated sixth episode of the weekly show this century, a feat also achieved bythe fourth episode of the show.The show’s ratings are heavily dependent on whether it is preceded by a highly watched NFL football game. Ratings for the show have been low despite a strong run of guest bookings and news-making segments. Viewership hasn’t been all bad, either – the 4 October edition of the show drew an average of more than 10 million total viewers.Weiss was also asked about parent company Skydance’s recent merger with Warner Bros Discovery, the parent company of CNN. While Weiss was initially rumored to potentially lead the cable news network, chief executive David Ellison instead opted to keep CNN chief executive Mark Thompson in place – for the time being, at least.Asked whether she might be interested in running CNN, Weiss replied: “I want to focus on doingCBSNews, trust me. This is a big enough challenge.”Weiss said she is not focused on criticism of her tenure at CBS News, which has come from inside and outside the building. Her strategy has been to “put the blinders on, tune out the noise and focus”, adding: “I’m not doing anything I’m doing for popularity’s sake.”Explore more on these topicsCBSBari WeissUS television industryTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says government to ‘terminate’ Biden-era methane emissions rules | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Critics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billions
Author: Sara Sneath
Headline: Critics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billions
Content: Donald Trump at the rally in Lubbock on Tuesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at the rally in Lubbock on Tuesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump says government to ‘terminate’ Biden-era methane emissions rulesCritics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billionsSara SneathWed 28 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 21.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump said his administration was “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding oil and gas companies accountable for large leaks of planet-warming methane during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday evening.“Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators. The change would save consumers and energy producers $45bn and unlock 210m barrels of oil, he said, which is equivalent to about 10 days of US petroleum consumption.Ina press release, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, praised what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act. The proposal is expected to produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic ft of natural gas, according to the EPA.The EPA’s proposal violates the Clean Air Act’s duty to protect public health and welfare and would seriously harm communities near oil and gas development, as well as the wider public, said Darin Schroeder, the methane legal and regulatory director at Clean Air Task Force (CATF). “EPA’s crusade against limits for emissions scientifically proven to harm public health and the environment must stop, and the agency must rescind this unlawful proposal and implement the 2024 rule without delay.”Curbing pollution from the oil and gas industry is critical to protecting public health, said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. “This not only carries environmental consequences, but leaks can also release harmful pollutants like volatile organic compounds that worsen air quality and carcinogens like benzene and formaldehyde,” he said. “If finalized, this proposal would help polluting industries avoid cleanup and harm the communities who bear the brunt of dirtier air and a warming planet.”At a Trump rally in Corpus Christi earlier in the day, Trump shouted outHarold Hamm, saying the founder of Continental Resources was in the audience. In April, Continental Resourceswrote a letterto the EPA pushing back against measures in the methane rule that prohibit routine flaring of associated gas.Although some oil and gas executivesspoke publiclyin favor of the landmarkmethane rule, industry trade groups and corporations worked behind the scenes to gut the methane regulations, according to trade association materials and records obtained via the Freedom of Information Act byFieldnotes, an oil and gas watchdog organization.The 2024 methane rule required oil and gas operators to eliminate and minimize leaking, flaring and venting of methane and of volatile organic compounds, which are harmful to human health.It was thefirst timethe federal government had set nationwide requirements to limit methane emissions from existing oil and gas facilities. An earlier rule finalized under the Obama administration in 2016 applied to new and modified sources. Under the rule’ssuper emitter program, companies had to investigate major leaks near oil and gas facilities detected by third parties using EPA-approved remote sensing technology.In March 2025, EPA administratorLee Zeldin announcedthat the agency was reconsidering the Biden-Harris regulations “to ensure that they do not prevent America from unleashing energy dominance and continuing our trajectory as a leader in clean energy and emissions reductions”.Last year, theUS emitted more methanefrom its oil and gas sector than any other country in the world. Methane is responsible forat least a quarterof today’s warming.Julia Kane, a researcher for Fieldnotes, said the Trump Environmental Protection Agency was giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they want. “The oil and gas industry says it’s a ‘good-faith’ partner eager to help craft regulations, but time and time again it’s worked behind the scenes to delay and weaken them,” she said.Records obtained by Fieldnotes, including calendar events, presentation slides and meeting request forms, show that industry groups and companies met with the EPA to discuss methane regulations at least 38 times during the current administration’s first year.“I do think it’s just an extraordinary level of access,” Kane said, adding that industry groups themselves were pleasantly surprised by their access under Trump. For example, during a conference call with industry representatives last year, the Independent Petroleum Association of America executive Lee Fuller described a discussion with EPA staff, saying: “It was one of the more fascinating meetings that we’ve ever had, just because they were suddenly willing to talk to us. And they were also suddenly willing to talk about things that we’ve been trying to get them to do for years, and they’ve never even let it come on to the radar screen.”Since the EPA announced it would no longer enforce oil and gas regulations in March 2025, oil and gas operators have leaked, vented or flared$7bn worth of natural gas, according to calculations by the Environmental Defense Fund.Rosalie Winn, senior director and lead counsel at the Environmental Defense Fund, said theTrump administrationwas seeking to curtail the federal government’s ability to do anything to address climate pollution across all of the largest sectors responsible for emissions.“What this administration is doing is enabling the worst polluters in the industry to continue to make ever more money off the back of American consumers while they’re wasting energy,” she said.Robert Mackey contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationGreenhouse gas emissionsDonald TrumpOil and gas companiesUS Environmental Protection AgencyClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s inflation rate rises to 4.3%, fuelling fears of fifth interest rate hike this year | Inflation | The Guardian
description: CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisis
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisis
Content: Australia’s inflation rate has risen, fuelling fears the Reserve Bank will hike interests rates for the fifth time this year.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia’s inflation rate has risen, fuelling fears the Reserve Bank will hike interests rates for the fifth time this year.Photograph: James Gourley/Getty ImagesInflationAustralia’s inflation rate rises to 4.3%, fuelling fears of fifth interest rate hike this yearCPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisisFollow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettandPatrick ComminsTue 27 Oct 2026 22.17 EDTFirst published on Tue 27 Oct 2026 20.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, with a key gauge that strips out volatile prices also elevated, sharpening expectations of another interest rate rise next week.The Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred measure of consumer prices, called underlying inflation, came in at an annual 3.6% to September.RBA officials have strongly indicated the board may need to lift borrowing costs further to drag price growth back toward its 2.5% target, citing concerns of a“materially worse” inflation outlook.Odds of fifth interest rate hike this year shorten as RBA deputy warns inflation outlook ‘worsening’Read moreThe CPI release comes shortly ahead of the central bank’s next monetary policy decision on 3 November, when most economists are tipping another cash rate increase.The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, described the inflation numbers as “too high” at Senate estimates on Wednesday, shortly after the data was released.He said there was a “nightmare” risk that longer-term inflation expectations would pick up, making it harder to get inflation out of the system.“We don’t think it is necessarily crystallising yet, but it is a particular risk,” Hauser said.Chart of inflation, showing a gradual increase from June 2025 to 4.3% in September 2026The cash rate, which informs lending rates including mortgages,already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years, after four rate hikes in 2026.A fierce political debate has erupted in Australia over what is driving the cost-of-living squeeze, with critics pointing to a mix of high fuel prices caused by the Iran conflict, government spending and poor productivity.Inflation is ‘too high’, but RBA says Australia is not heading for recession – videoThe treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said on Wednesday that while “we accept our part in the fight against inflation”, high oil prices and a recovering private sector were the main causes of the rise.“The most important thing that can happen for Australians under pressure is to see an end to this war in the Middle East,” Chalmers said.“This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living and for inflation, right around the world.”Growing uneaseCPI figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday show that costs for everyday goods and services are rising at the same time asunemployment lifts, making life uncomfortable for households.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTransport costs have risen 8.7% over the past 12 months, due in large part to escalating fuel prices stemming from the US and Israel conflict with Iran.While higher fuel prices are trickling through the economy, there are price pressures everywhere.Food prices have also jumped another 3.2% in a year, and housing costs were up 5.2%.Stephen Smith, partner at Deloitte AccessEconomics, said the RBA had “little appetite to allow inflation expectations to drift higher after such a prolonged period above target”.“The difficulty is that the economy is already slowing. Household spending is subdued, the labour market has softened and the housing market has weakened,” Smith, who is expecting a rate rise next week, said.The escalating expenses have fed into the growing political unease in Australia and elsewhere, as voters express their discontent with cost-of-living pressures.Housing, which is the single biggest category in the CPI, was the largest contributor to annual inflation, according to the ABS, followed by transport costs.Builders have been passing on higher costs for materials and labour for new dwellings, while electricity prices are also elevated.Josh Gilbert, market analyst at eToro, said inflation was turning into a “higher-for-longer” story in Australia.“Anyone holding out for rate relief may need to pack plenty of patience, because another hike looks imminent after today,” Gilbert said.Explore more on these topicsInflationEconomicsInterest ratesAustralian economyCost-of-living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Plan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant a ‘terrible deal’ for UK taxpayers, MPs say | Sizewell C | The Guardian
description: The public accounts committee has said the risk to billpayers is ‘extraordinary’
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: The public accounts committee has said the risk to billpayers is ‘extraordinary’
Content: The government expects Sizewell C to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn and for construction to be completed by 2043.Photograph: Sizewell CView image in fullscreenThe government expects Sizewell C to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn and for construction to be completed by 2043.Photograph: Sizewell CSizewell CPlan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant a ‘terrible deal’ for UK taxpayers, MPs sayThe public accounts committee has said the risk to billpayers is ‘extraordinary’Jillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentTue 27 Oct 2026 20.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog.MPs on the public accounts committee (PAC) have warned the government that the cost of theSizewell Cnuclear reactor could spiral to almost £48bn, leaving bill payers on the hook to provide an extra £9.8bn to construct the plant before 2040 and a further £12bn over its 60-year operating life.Taxpayers and consumers face a “high level of risk”, according to PAC, after the government agreed to take a near-45% stake in the nuclear plant, which is considered a successor project tothe heavily delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear plantin Somerset.Spending watchdog warns £38bn cost of Sizewell C nuclear plant is ‘risky’Read moreUnder the terms ofthe multibillion-pound deal, which will be paid for through taxes and energy bills, the UK government holds a 44.9% stake while French state nuclear developer EDF has a 12.5% stake.The rest of the funding has come from private investors including the British Gas owner Centrica, which holds a 15% share, alongside the Canadian investment group La Caisse, which holds 20%, and the investment manager AmberInfrastructure, which has a 7.6% stake.The UK government was forced to take a larger than expected share of the project after buying out Chinese state nuclear developer CGN, which had been allowed to hold a 20% stake in Sizewell C before national security concerns emerged.The watchdog warned that while the British public could be called on to shoulder multibillion-pound cost overruns, the nuclear project’s private investors would only need to put in an extra £30m.Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the PAC chair, said: “The high level of risk borne by taxpayers and consumers for the construction of Sizewell C is extraordinary. Private investors look set for significant returns on their investments, while customers are likely to be saddled with higher energy bills.”He urged the government to “focus on the successful delivery of this project”, and in building confidence in the UK’s nuclear industry more broadly, so that taxpayers will “never be put in this position again”.A government spokesperson said the report “completely ignores that investors are incentivised to complete construction as cheaply and quickly as possible” through the terms of the deal.“Once operational, Sizewell C could save £2bn a year across the energy system, cutting costs for families up and down the country, and the project is already making good progress with over 2,000 workers on site,” the spokesperson added.Sizewell C is projected to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn, with construction completing between 2039 and 2043. The committee has called on the government to provide the scenario analysis it used to underpin its cost estimates for the project within the next three months. It also asked ministers to provide an update on the project’s development every six months to keep track of its progress.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCritics of the project, including Alison Downes of the Stop Sizewell C campaign group and Prof Steve Thomas of Greenwich Business School, who provided joint evidence to the committee, have suggested that the cost of abandoning the project today would be lower than the cost of paying inflated energy bills over 60 years “multiple times over”.They called on the government to rule out using this funding model for future nuclear projects. “All it offers is a free ride for investors and financial pain for households,” they said in a joint statement.Tom Greatrex, the chief executive of the Nuclear Industry Association, said Sizewell C would provide “clean, reliable and constantly available power” that could save households billions from paying the cost of balancing the grid or building extra network connections.“Currently, the consumer is footing a bill of £2.8bn so far this year to manage a dysfunctional grid, paying both for wind to stop generating at some times, and for gas-powered backup at others,” he said.This article was amended on 28 October 2026. Costs for Sizewell C are regulatory threshold projections, not a government estimate as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsSizewell CNuclear powerEnergyEconomicsInfrastructureGovernment borrowingEconomic policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Chiefs sign Justin Tucker in wake of sexual misconduct allegations as Butker struggles | Kansas City Chiefs | The Guardian
description: The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad
Content: Justin Tucker won a Super Bowl with the Ravens.Photograph: Tim Warner/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJustin Tucker won a Super Bowl with the Ravens.Photograph: Tim Warner/Getty ImagesKansas City ChiefsChiefs sign Justin Tucker in wake of sexual misconduct allegations as Butker strugglesTucker was banned under NFL’s conduct policyButker has missed five of 16 FG attempts this seasonGuardian sportWed 28 Oct 2026 15.59 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheKansas City Chiefshave signed the former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad after Harrison Butker’s poor start to the season.Tucker was widely considered one of the best kickers in NFL history until the Ravens released him in May 2025. The Ravens said his departure was a “football decision” after a slump in form, but the move came months after he wasaccused of inappropriate sexual behaviorby massage therapists. Tucker denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges but heserved a 10-game NFL banfor violating the league’s personal conduct policy.Don’t tell Harrison Butker working women helped him win three Super Bowls | Melissa JacobsRead moreMore than a dozen massage therapists from spas and wellness centers in the Baltimore areaaccused Tuckerof inappropriate sexual behavior. One therapist who spoke to the Baltimore Banner, which broke the story, described Tucker’s alleged behavior as “really degrading”. Another said: “I can’t watch sports anymore. I see his face everywhere.”The 37-year-old has not played in theNFLsince he was released by Baltimore. During his time with the Ravens, he made seven Pro Bowls and won the Super Bowl in his rookie season. His final season in Baltimore, in which he made just 73.3% of his field goals, was statistically the worst of his career. Tucker’s career average for field goals is 89.1%.On Wednesday, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid said he was not worried about Tucker joining the team.“He’s done his suspension, took care of that business there,” Reidsaidin response to a question about what message the move sent to the team’s female fans. “I’ll leave it at that.”When asked about Tucker’s past, Reid said: “We try to do our homework the best way we possibly can and talk to a lot of people, make sure things are OK.”Butker, who has won three Super Bowls with the Chiefs, has missed five of his 16 field goal attempts this season. The 31-year-old Butker has also been involved in off-field controversy.During a commencement addressat Benedictine College in 2024, he criticized Pride month, working women, Joe Biden’s leadership during the Covid-19 pandemic and abortion.“I think it is you, the women, who have had the most diabolic lies told to you,” Butker said during the speech. “Some of you may go on to lead successful careers in the world, but I would venture to guess that the majority of you are most excited about your marriage and the children you will bring into this world. I can tell you that my beautiful wife Isabelle would be the first to say her life truly started when she started living her vocation as a wife and as a mother.”Reid said Butker had not been “as consistent as he wants” this season.“We love Harrison,” Reid said. “He’s one of my favorite guys. Sometimes things don’t go quite the way you want them, and you work on that. He understands the business and how it works. He’s struggled a little bit. Butker will get most of the reps this week. We’ll just see where it goes. It’s fluid.”Explore more on these topicsKansas City ChiefsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ernie Johnson, beloved host of Inside the NBA, to step away from show at end of season | US sports media | The Guardian
description: Ernie Johnson, the widely loved host of Inside the NBA, has announced he will step away at the end of the current season after 37 years in the role
Author: Guardian sport
