Villa initially survived when Bizot superbly tipped on to the crossbar and behind to thwart the Cherries right-back Juanlu at the end of a marauding run.However, Cook took the resulting left-wing corner short and, after receiving the ball back from Gannon-Doak, caught out Bizet with a low in-swinging cross which crept in at the near post.Quick GuideCarabao Cup quarter-final drawShowFleetwood v Everton or NewcastleManchester City v Bradford CityCrystal Palace v SunderlandLiverpool v BournemouthTies will take place during the week commencing 14 DecemberWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Villa midfielder João Gomes saw an opportunity to halve the deficit saved by Di Gregorio, while the defender Harwood-Bellis went close with a header.Hopes of a comeback ended in the 69th minute when Rodríguez burst into the penalty box and lashed his second goal of the season into the bottom-right corner after Tyler Adams intercepted a loose pass.Garnacho was denied a consolation by Di Gregorio after racing clear before his fellow replacement Alysson headed a golden chance wide as Bournemouth’s defence held out to make it a hat-trick of 3-0 wins. They now travel to Liverpool in the quarter-finals.Sunderlandheld on to beatBrentford3-2, with Chemsdine Talbi, Timur Tutierov and Malick Fofana on target – and the winger Jocelin Ta Bi had a hand in all three goals for Régis Le Bris’s much-changed team.Callum Wilson pulled one back within three minutes, tapping in off the bar from four yards out, after Vitaly Janelt’s scuffed shot had fallen to him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIgor Thiago set up a thrilling finish when the goalkeeper Melker Ellborg failed to deal with his header in the fourth minute of five added on at the end of the contest. However, the Black Cats held on to book a place in the last eight of the competition for the first time in five years – when they were a League One team.View image in fullscreenMalick Fofana of Sunderland (right) celebrates with Dayann Methalie after scoring his team’s third goal.Photograph: Ian Horrocks/Sunderland AFC/Getty ImagesBrentford started strongly and after the visiting captain, Nathan Collins, directed a free header into the arms of Ellborg, Malick Diouf’s cross was turned into the side-netting by Thiago. Jannik Schuster’s header shortly after crashed against the bar before the rebound saw Michael Kayode direct an effort against the foot of the post.Ellborg also made a stunning flying save to turn Mamadou Sangaré’s volley over the bar, before Sunderland made them pay for those wasted chances.Although Thiago went close to levelling, Ta Bi brilliantly created the second at the other end by beating his man and putting a chance on a plate for Tutierov to convert.With six minutes remaining of the first half, the excellent Ta Bi crossed to the back post for Fofana to head into the roof of the net and make it 3-0.Brentford responded quickly. Three minutes before the break Wilson pulled a goal back and the striker went close to adding a second before the half-time whistle. After the restart, Janelt’s long-range effort brushed the side-netting and Dango Ouattara headed wide at the far post as Brentford looked to close the gap further.Although Thiago’s header from Mathias Jensen’s delivery eventually squirmed under Ellborg to give Sunderland a late scare, there was to be no equaliser, and the hosts next travel to Crystal Palace.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupBournemouthSunderlandAston VillaBrentfordnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This isn’t supposed to happen’: giant-slaying Fleetwood revels in fairytale Arsenal win | Fleetwood Town | The Guardian
description: Fishing town in disbelief the morning after its footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penalties
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Fishing town in disbelief the morning after its footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penalties
Content: Zsofia Wright, the retail manager at Fleetwood Town, said victory celebrations went on until about 1.30am.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenZsofia Wright, the retail manager at Fleetwood Town, said victory celebrations went on until about 1.30am.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianFleetwood Town‘This isn’t supposed to happen’: giant-slaying Fleetwood revels in fairytale Arsenal winFishing town in disbelief the morning after its footballing minnows beat mighty Arsenal on penaltiesHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a wet and windy night on the north-west coast of England, a League Two sidesensationally knockedthe Premier League champions out of the Carabao Cup. But this is not justa fairytale story of giant-slaying: Fleetwood Town and Arsenal have an unlikely history that stretches back long before Tuesday night’s game.Arsenal played at their iconic Highbury stadium until 2006, and Fleetwood’s ground has the same title, being named after Highbury Avenue, the adjoining street.Fleetwood also play in red shirts with white sleeves in the style of the classic Arsenal kit. Nobody is exactly sure why, but according to Ray Curtis, a barman in the town’s King’s Arms: “Fleetwood’s first ever kit, the home kit, was given to them by Arsenal.”And in the 2000s, not long after Patrick Vieira captained Arsenal, Fleetwood boasted a namesake star: a Brazilian striker called Magno Vieira.At the 5,300-capacity Highbury on Wednesday morning, the floodlights that Fleetwood had hired for the occasion were being packed away. “It’s back to reality, back to being a League Two team, that’s our normal,” said Zsofia Wright, the ticket office and retail manager.View image in fullscreenTelevision equipment is removed from the Highbury stadium on Wednesday after the match between teams 84 places apart in the football pyramid.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianOn Tuesday, the excitement and anticipation started early. “We started getting what team had turned up, who’d flown in, and the whispers started, and it’s like, ‘oh, they’ve gone quite strong’,” Wright said.“So we were all planning to just enjoy the occasion. And then obviously, we went 1-0 up and everyone was kind of looking at each other, like this isn’t supposed to be happening.”She said it was back to reality when Arsenal equalised except that “the clock kept on going and the score didn’t change”.View image in fullscreenChris Newman came to the club shop to pick up some souvenir programmes.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianWright said everyone was on the pitch after the dramatic penalty shootout that saw the Premier League champions and Champions League finalists ousted from the competition. The next stop for players, fans and management was the stadium bar.“Just incredible,” Wright said. “We were here till about half one last night. It was brilliant, amazing.”“The atmosphere was crazy,” said Chris Newman, 33, who was at the match with his son. He returned to the club shop on Wednesday to pick up two souvenir programmes. “Everything happened so quick,” he said. “I just didn’t expect it at all.”The shop has done a roaring trade over the past 36 hours, with half-and-half Fleetwood and Arsenal scarves proving especially popular. One buyer with a London accent said: “I’m a Spurs fan, it’s brilliant.”Wright said the town was abuzz the morning after: “Bars, pubs that are struggling, they were open till God knows what time yesterday. We just hope it can continue throughout the season, just hope that attendances start to pick up, and get consistency back again through the gates.”The club’s nicknames – the Cod Army, the Fishermen, the Cods and the Trawlermen – all derive from theLancashiretown’s fishing industry.Sharon Brooks, who was visiting a fishmonger by the harbour, said: “We thought it’d be three, four or five nil, but they did so well to get a draw and then win on penalties, and five brilliant penalties. It’s nice for a town like Fleetwood, and [against the] Premier League winners last season, they just surprised you didn’t they?”Her 12-year-old son, Ryan, who is an Arsenal fan, said: “Even though I wanted [Arsenal] to win it, I’m pleased for them.”View image in fullscreenSharon Brooks with her Arsenal-supporting son, Ryan, who said he was still pleased his local team won.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDonald Maclean in the King’s Arms in Fleetwood town centre. He said such a result ‘had never been heard of before’.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianIn the King’s Arms, everyone was eagerly awaiting Wednesday night’s draw, which will decide who Fleetwood plays next.Donald Maclean, who missed the game because he was on duty at a nursing home, said: “I saw the goals this morning and I was delighted, over the moon, imagine Fleetwood taking down the Gunners! Never been heard of before, so yes, we’re all delighted about it. Brilliant!”The Cod Army’s victory has delighted fans partly because it was so unexpected – Fleetwood sit 84 places below Arsenal in the football league pyramid.Michael Houton said he had thought the result impossible “because Arsenal shouldn’t have got beaten should they? Not against Fleetwood.”View image in fullscreenFleetwood Town’s club shop has been doing a roaring trade in half-and-half scarves.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianPaul Dagger was so pessimistic about his team’s chances that he had staked £200 at half-time on Arsenal to win at odds of 10/7. “Gyökeres [of Arsenal] scored within five minutes of the start,” he said. “I thought, oh here we go, money’s coming in now. You live and learn.”Fleetwood fans hope it will be the start of something bigger than just a victory for lovers of the game. “The town needs it,” Dagger said. “As you can see, it’s full of charity shops and vape shops.”View image in fullscreen‘I think it’s fantastic for the town,’ said Paul Dagger.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGarry Gill said other teams would now be ‘frightened’ of coming to play Fleetwood.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianGarry Gill, a retired crane operator, said: “I am a Fleetwood fan and I think it’s fantastic for the town. It’s going to bringcoin.“Ifthey play with the determination they did last night, any team that comes to play now is going to be frightened. And normally, that’s not the case, they think it’s an easy win.”Jim Buckley said: “It’s magic. We’re a Mickey Mouse town of 25,000 people, there’s no train station. I mean at the Emirates, they can fit three towns the size of this town in there.”He was not far out – Arsenal’s stadium can hold 60,000 fans.The drinkers in the King’s Arms said the travelling Arsenal fans had had a good day out despite the embarrasing defeat.Dagger said: “Two pound twenty a pint in here, two pound fifty a pint over the way. They couldn’t believe it, they were going, facking ‘ell, it’s eight quid where we are.”View image in fullscreenBethany Taylor, right, at the Shark Chippy near Fleetwood harbour. She said she was expecting defeat until she heard the roar of the crowd at the final whistle.Photograph: Colin McPherson/The GuardianBack near the harbour, at the Shark Chippy, there was a lunchtime rush. Dishing up cod and chips, Bethany Taylor said she lived near the ground and could tell the result from the roar of the crowd and the flares. “It was good, brilliant,” she added. “We weren’t expecting it.”“It’s an incredible result isn’t it?” said her colleague Louisa Smith.But do they think Fleetwood can lift the Carabao Cup? “It’d be a struggle, but hopefully they will,” Smith said. “We wish them luck.”Explore more on these topicsFleetwood TownNorth of EnglandLancashireArsenalEnglandCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnley turn to former CSKA Moscow manager Fabio Celestini as new head coach | Burnley | The Guardian
description: Swiss replaces sacked Nicky Hayen with the club languishing in 22nd in Championship.
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Swiss replaces sacked Nicky Hayen with the club languishing in 22nd in Championship.
Content: Fabio Celestini is unveiled as Burnley’s new head coach after Nicky Hayen’s sacking on Saturday.Photograph: Burnley FCView image in fullscreenFabio Celestini is unveiled as Burnley’s new head coach after Nicky Hayen’s sacking on Saturday.Photograph: Burnley FCBurnleyBurnley turn to former CSKA Moscow manager Fabio Celestini as new head coachSwiss, 50, also had successful spell at BaselHe replaces Nicky Hayen with club 22nd in ChampionshipPress AssociationWed 28 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBurnley have announced former Switzerland midfielder Fabio Celestini as their new head coach four daysafter sacking Nicky Hayen.Burnley, who have won only one of their 12 league games this season after relegation from the Premier League, have not disclosed the length of Celestini’s contract. They heralded his appointment by saying in a statement that the 50-year-old “arrives with a proven capacity to win and to adapt to different football environments”.‘This isn’t supposed to happen’: giant-slaying Fleetwood revels in fairytale Arsenal winRead moreThe club’s chief football officer, Diego López, himself a new name at the club this week, said: “Fabio brings the passion, experience and knowledge we were looking for. He showed extraordinary determination and conviction to come to Burnley. We want people who truly want to be here and help this club grow. Fabio is a clear example of that.”Celestini’s last managerial role was at CSKA Moscow, who he left in May this year, and he has also had spells at Swiss clubs Lugano, Luzern, Sion andBasel. He led the latter from bottom of the table to a league and cup double in the space of 18 months.The new head coach told Burnley’s website: “I look at Burnley and I see a club with big potential and players with real quality, who can help us achieve our supporters’ ambitions. I know the situation we are in, and I have lived it before. Our supporters deserve to see a team playing with belief from the first whistle.”The former midfielder, who spent 10 years as a player in France and Spain and won 35 caps for Switzerland, will take charge of his first match in Saturday’s home league game against Portsmouth.Explore more on these topicsBurnleyChampionshipBaselnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthony Edwards to undergo knee surgery as Timberwolves star faces up to two months out | Minnesota Timberwolves | The Guardian
description: Anthony Edwards will undergo arthroscopic surgery on his right knee after a blistering start to the NBA season, with his return timetable uncertain
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anthony Edwards will undergo arthroscopic surgery on his right knee after a blistering start to the NBA season, with his return timetable uncertain
Content: Timberwolves guard Anthony Edwards celebrates during a game against the Miami Heat on 21 October in Miami. Edwards is set to undergo arthroscopic surgery on his right knee and is expected to miss several weeks.Photograph: Issac Baldizon/NBAE/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTimberwolves guard Anthony Edwards celebrates during a game against the Miami Heat on 21 October in Miami. Edwards is set to undergo arthroscopic surgery on his right knee and is expected to miss several weeks.Photograph: Issac Baldizon/NBAE/Getty ImagesMinnesota TimberwolvesAnthony Edwards to undergo knee surgery as Timberwolves star faces up to two months outFour-time All-Star needs arthroscopic procedure on kneeEdwards averaging 33.3 points through first four gamesAbsence could rule Wolves star out of awards contentionAssociated PressTue 27 Oct 2026 22.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinnesota guard Anthony Edwards needs an arthroscopic procedure to alleviate issues with his right knee and will miss several weeks, a person with knowledge of the matter said Tuesday.The person spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because the Timberwolves had yet to make any public announcements of Edwards’ plan to have the operation. A more precise timetable for Edwards’ return will be known after surgery, the person said.‘We’re not doing great’: Gilgeous-Alexander in tears after Williams suffers gruesome leg injuryRead moreEdwards had been listed on recent injury reports with a right knee issue. Periodic knee pain has dogged him for some time, though the specifics of the current problem were not clear. The Timberwolves had listed him as questionable for their game against Golden State on Wednesday, before the decision was evidently made to go forward with the surgery.Edwards was off to a flying start this season, averaging 33.3 points and leading Minnesota to three wins in their first four games. He scored 45 points in the season-opening win at Miami, then had 47 points in a loss to Cleveland on Monday night. His 133 points through the first four games is a Timberwolves record, breaking the old mark of 120 – set by him two seasons ago.But there were some signs that all was not right. Edwards had a two-handed transition dunk late in the first half of Minnesota’s win over Toronto on Sunday, seemed to head down to the defensive end very gingerly after that play, then spent the next Timberwolves offensive possession standing in the right corner and squeezing his knee for a few seconds.If he is out for two months, that would mean he remains sidelined until around Christmas – when Minnesota play an Oklahoma City team that also have major injury concerns. The Thunder lost Jalen Williams (leg, ankle) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) earlier this week; both will have surgery that could be season-ending.A two-month absence would also sideline Edwards for around 25 games, meaning he would again fall short of the NBA’s 65-game threshold for end-of-season awards such as the All-NBA team and MVP.Edwards was limited to 61 games last season, mostly because of knee-related issues. It was the first season in which he missed any significant time; Edwards missed 19 out of a possible 400 games in his first five NBA seasons.The four-time All-Star, two-time All-NBA pick and member of the 2024 US Olympic team thatwon gold at the Paris Gameshas averaged 24.6 points in his career. Since Edwards entered the league, only the Los Angeles Lakers’ Luka Dončić, Denver’s Nikola Jokić, Oklahoma City’s Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Miami’s Giannis Antetokounmpo have scored more points than the No 1 overall pick in the 2020 draft.Explore more on these topicsMinnesota TimberwolvesNBABasketballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Elonville’: US residents say Musk’s xAI offered to buy homes if they don’t sue over datacenter noise | Mississippi | The Guardian
description: Several homes have been purchased near datacenters and one resident said realtor outlined target to buy more than 400
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Several homes have been purchased near datacenters and one resident said realtor outlined target to buy more than 400
Content: Jason Haley looks on near one of the xAI datacenters close to his home in Southaven, Mississippi, on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brandon Dill/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Haley looks on near one of the xAI datacenters close to his home in Southaven, Mississippi, on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brandon Dill/The GuardianMississippi‘Elonville’: US residents say Musk’s xAI offered to buy homes if they don’t sue over datacenter noiseSeveral Mississippi homes have been purchased near datacenters and one resident said realtor outlined target to buy more than 400Oliver Milmanwith data visuals byDaniel WolfeWed 28 Oct 2026 11.32 EDTFirst published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople in aMississippineighborhood, many of whom dislike a nearby power plant central toElon Musk’s artificial intelligence ambitions, have received a stark offer – to sell their houses to his company and make way.Real estate agents have been going door to door in Southaven,Mississippi, on behalf of xAI, touting a deal to purchase houses as long as the owners agree to not join a lawsuit against the company over the power plant’s noise. (Musk’s AI company officially became SpaceXAI in July and has lately been rebranded as SpaceXSI but to neighbors of the datacenter in Mississippi, it remains xAI.)This plan could potentially swallow up almost the entire neighborhood of Colonial Hills, on the western flank of Southaven. A realtor told one resident there is a target to purchase 418 homes, with 18 homeowners already agreeing to sell, according to a recording of a conversation heard by the Guardian. xAI did not respond to questions over these numbers and its plans for the neighborhood and has previously said it intends to be be a good neighbor; it denies all claims in the noise lawsuit.A satellite map of the development progress in the town of Southaven, Mississippi. It shows three datacenters along the Tennessee and Mississippi border. South of that there are gas turbines highlighted. To the right of the turbines is the neighborhood of Colonial Hills with the sold properties called out.The homes, the realtor and the local mayor say, will house xAI staff as the company continues its explosive expansion in the area, with three of its datacenters springing up in Southaven and adjoining Memphis, Tennessee, in just the past two years. This frantic pace, and the all-hours noise from gas turbinesinstalled without permits to power the datacenters, has dismayed some locals.“It sounds like an airplane engine but it’s continuous, it’s incredibly loud,” said Elizabeth Rose, a piano teacher, of the xAI site which sits about two miles from her home. “I’ve been woken up at 2am by it, I’ve been woken up at 3am by it. I sometimes have to just get away from it because it makes me so angry.”Rose said she was shocked when the power plant, a former Duke Energy site housing 69 temporary gas turbines to feed the new datacenters, began its low-level growl in August last year. “All of a sudden there was a plant there,” she said. “And now I get the feeling they are trying to expand the buyout to the entire neighborhood. It will become Elon Musk’s little playground, basically. Elonville.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth Rose at her home in Southaven, Mississippi, on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brandon Dill/The GuardianThe market value offers for these homes, in an area where the average house price isabout$180,000, is a comparatively small outlay in creating the world’s largest cluster of AI supercomputers as envisioned by Musk, a technologist who is the world’s richest person and a major Republican donor.Since July 2024, xAI has constructed three vast datacenters – called Colossus I, Colossus II and Macrohardrr – in the Memphis and Southaven conurbation, which sprawls across Tennessee’s border with Mississippi. Musk is currentlyspendingup to four nights a week in an Airstream trailer in the Memphis area as he personally oversees the build-out of the datacenters to further develop the Grok AI chatbot.“We’re seeing the fastest growth I’ve ever seen in my life for Grok bot,” Musk said during aSpaceXearnings call this month. “I’ve never seen anything grow this fast.”Muskhas spent about half a billion dollarshelping elect Republicans in the last two election cycles and his zeal for datacenters is shared by Donald Trump, who has said anyone who opposes such development will become “backwards and poor”.‘A different set of rules’: thermal drone footage shows Musk’s AI power plant flouting clean air regulationsRead moreAs is common in the broader grassrootsbacklash against datacenters, however, some residents in Southaven say they have been trampled upon in this gold rush. Three locals, anguished by the din of expansion, filed alawsuitin June complaining of “near-constant noise, vibrations and other nuisance-level harms” from the nearby xAI power plant.Jason Haley, one of the three plaintiffs, said he never considered himself an activist or political in any way but had been driven to distraction by the noise of the gas turbines that sit about half a mile from his home, which he has owned for the past 20 years.“There’s a high-pitched hum and then another sound like an airplane over your house,” he said. “It’s been so torturous I can’t sleep, I just leave the house or turn on some music until I fall asleep completely exhausted. It drives you insane. You also lose hope because you’re being ignored or dismissed. There’s no escape.”Exasperated by fruitless exchanges with Southaven’s mayor and enraged by Tate Reeves, the Republican, pro-AI Mississippi governor,claimingthat curbs on datacenters are “surrendering the future of technology to China”, Haley lodged the lawsuit and startedpostingvideoson social media of himself monitoring the rumbling noise levels.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators rally in opposition to a plan by xAI to use gas turbines for a new datacenter, in Memphis, Tennessee, on 25 April 2025.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images“I thought I’d make some noise of my own because of this bullshit,” said Haley. “I didn’t know anything about Elon, still don’t know the man. But our governor saying I don’t love America because I don’t like being tortured by noise? That is just asinine and ignorant. We’ve got to hold people accountable when they are harming other people, I don’t care who you voted for, who you pray for or who your favorite team is.”The allegations of heedless noise are denied by xAI, which has previously said that “we care deeply about being good neighbors” and has varied its power output and built sound-dampening walls. In a letter handed to nearby residents in Colonial Hills, MZX, the xAI subsidiary that operates the site, states that it “requires property for its business purposes” and is prepared to buy nearby houses with a contractual condition – that they do not join Haley’s class-action lawsuit.This offer is starting to see results. Since 9 October, five neighborhood homes have been bought by MZX, according to DeSoto county records. Gavin Foust, who lives near Haley and said his elderly neighbors have just agreed to sell, predicts more will follow.“They are ideal neighbors and planned to live their rest of their lives in that house but they want to get out of Dodge now because they don’t want to be bothered by these turbines,” said Foust, who added he won’t accept the offer himself due to its requirement not to sue.“My hearing was damaged when I was in the army but I can still hear this thing, it’s like a jet engine. Why would you put it in a city? Why push people out? It’s reckless and shameful.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFoust, a paramedic, grew up in the unassuming western reaches of Southaven, a district filled with affordable, 1960s homes and quiet, close-knit communities. This serenity has been upended by the noise from the xAI power plant, he said, as well as its air pollution.Dozens of temporary, truck-sized gas turbines have been running at the xAI premises without permits required by federal law,the US Environmental Protection Agency has determined. The EPA has also said the permit requirements are a matter for the state to enforce.View image in fullscreenGeese fly near one of the xAI datacenters in Southland, Mississippi, on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brandon Dill/The GuardianWhile no on-site air pollution monitoring has been done, the Southern Environmental Law Centerestimatedthe toxic emissions from these turbines, which aretypicallyhighly polluting, have caused $44m in annual health costs.In April, environmental groups and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP)suedin federal court to stop use of the turbines, only for the US Department of Justice tounsuccessfullytry to block the lawsuit by arguing xAI technology has been used to wage war on Iran and is therefore required for national security reasons.“It’s been pretty shady from the get-go,” said Foust. “A lot of people in this neighborhood suffer from conditions exacerbated by all the nitrogen oxide, formaldehyde and other garbage put out by these turbines. For kids with asthma or elderly people with COPD [chronic obstructive pulmonary disease] it’s a mess all round. It’s pretty frustrating.”In July, xAI agreed with state regulators to transform the power plant into a newer, permanent gas-fired facility by next summer, which should lessen the noise coming from the temporary turbines. Given the company’srepeated use of gas turbines without a federal permitand separate fines itmay facefor storm water violations, though, opponents remain wary.“I’ve had hopes all along that haven’t come through,” said Haley. “The same company said it wasn’t polluting the air. I’m still hopeful but I’m not confident.”The opposition to the datacenter influx hasn’t been universal, Haley acknowledged. Some locals aren’t too bothered by the noise while others actively champion the influx of cash into one of the poorest states in the union. Local businesses have experienced a surge in new activity, with the mayor hailing the datacenters for helping deliver new jobs and opportunity to the area.View image in fullscreenJason Haley stands beside a noise-monitoring device near one xAI’s datacenters in Southaven, Mississippi, on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brandon Dill/The Guardian“This development will produce unprecedented tax revenue for DeSoto county taxpayers that will enhance the quality of life for all,” said Darren Musselwhite, Southaven’smayor, who oversaw a land swap deal with xAI that resulted in a new police and firefighter training center for the city.“The buyout is not intended to be a company city at this point,” Musselwhite said of the property purchases. “This has never been mentioned to me. The buyout has multiple purposes which are to provide homes for some employees and a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for those who perceive the industrial development near them as a negative.”Musselwhite said dealing with the noise was a “top priority” for him but that city monitors had not detected a breach of a local noise ordinance limit of 70 decibels. Critics point toevidencethat lower levels of noise, of 50 decibels or more like that recorded near the power plant, may be linked to adverse health impacts if persistent.For those who can’t stand this noise, there is little to celebrate. Haley said the controversy had drawn the community together and made him question how AI is being “pushed down everyone’s throat”. He added: “Put it this way, I’m now registered to vote.” Rose, the piano teacher, said her roommate would accept three or four times the value of their home but she would still be opposed to such a sale.“I wouldn’t take the offer if it was up to me, just to make things difficult for Elon,” she said. “I hate AI, I never understood why it was invented. I refuse to use it because I know touching it will cause that plant to crank up.”Explore more on these topicsMississippiDatacenters – USElon MuskSpaceXAir pollutionAI (artificial intelligence)Law (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care laws | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Labor government under pressure to create social media watchdog as new online safety standards bill passes lower house
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Labor government under pressure to create social media watchdog as new online safety standards bill passes lower house
Content: Communications minister Anika Wells says content that promotes misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured under digital duty of care laws.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenCommunications minister Anika Wells says content that promotes misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured under digital duty of care laws.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPAustralian politics‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care lawsLabor government under pressure to create social media watchdog as new online safety standards bill passes lower houseFollow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerWed 28 Oct 2026 01.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 02.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe federal government wants to ban AI chatbots which seek to create “emotional intimacy” after prime ministerAnthony Albaneseraised the alarm in a heartfelt speech about children treating these agents as their “best friend”.But Labor is coming under increasing pressure to empower the telecommunications ombudsman to become a watchdog for social media and AI to give Australians an external complaints mechanism and allow the “naming and shaming” of big tech.The digital duty of care bill passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday and will be debated by the Senate in coming weeks. The government hopes to pass the bill by the end of 2026, but its pathway through the upper house remains unclear. The Greens support the bill, whilethe Coalition has said it will not vote for it, though Labor still appears keen to win the opposition’s support andremains open to amendments.The planned framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. Labor said it would place “an overarching obligation” on tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians” and replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content. It would also require social media platforms to offer an “opt-out” feature for its algorithm and suggested content.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe communications minister, Anika Wells, has suggested content that that promotes misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorderswould be captured by the laws. On Wednesday, the government accepted amendments from crossbencher Kate Chaney which would add certain AI chatbot activity to the list of harms, requiring platforms to ban “material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child’s dependence on it in place of human relationships”.In an emotional address on Tuesday night, where he again implored the Coalition to consider voting for the bill, Albanese said: “the stories we hear about people identifying a chatbot, a non-person as their best friend, should be a huge wake up call for every member of this parliament to be prepared to act.”View image in fullscreenPrime minister Anthony Albanese speaks during question time in the House of Representatives at parliament House in Canberra on 27 October.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPThe opposition voted against the bill in the House, alongside One Nation. Political opponents haveaccused Labor of an “Orwellian” system of “censorship”and of seeking to influence conversations online – claims Wells strongly denied.“If they really care, the test is simple here, they should bring an amendment, not a slogan to ‘kill the bill’,” Wells told ABC radio on Wednesday.Another Chaney amendment accepted by Labor would require the algorithm opt-out features to be “accessible, easy to use” and “prominently available” on platforms, amid concerns that social media firms may offer only small or hard-to-find features.The bill now moves to the Senate, where the Greens have set up an inquiry to probe the laws due to report back in late November. Senator Sarah Hanson-Young backed a digital duty of care, calling for the government’s legislation to be strengthened. The Greens want Australians to have the right to pursue private legal action against platforms and for penalties to be increased.1:18OpenAI admits misstep in handling AI agent interactions with Australian government sites – video“Australians also need an external complaints pathway, free from the profit-driven whims of big tech’s content moderation,” she said.Independent MP Sophie Scamps had proposed changes to the bill to expand the remit of the telecommunications industry ombudsman. She said such a watchdog – which does not currently exist for big tech – would allow ordinary social media users to seek remedies to their accounts being hacked or inaccessible, including compensation, and investigate broader issues to name and shame companies behaving badly.Labor did not accept this amendment in the lower house and Wells declined to voice support for such an idea, but the Greens will push for such a reform in their Senate negotiations.The telecommunications industry ombudsman, Cynthia Gebert, said her office would be well placed to carry out such a role for big tech. She said such roles were funded by the industries they regulate and that expanding its remit could be financed by big tech.“There are some real strengths in the DDOC [digital duty of care] because it’s putting the onus on platforms to make things safe … but I think the area that needs to be strengthened is giving people somewhere to go if they can’t get their complaints resolved with the platform,” Gebert said.“It risks leaving Australians in the safe place they are now, where they get automated responses or escalation procedures that don’t go anywhere.”Gebert said the government should make it mandatory for big tech to be part of an ombudsman scheme, saying it would “hold industry to account and drive system improvement”.“[The telecommunications industry ombudsman] can help with your Telstra account, but we can’t help with your Gmail account. Consumers come to us sometimes and ask, ‘why this, not that?’,” she said.“We want to help but don’t have the powers to do so now.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

After consulting dermatologists and putting them to the test, we have crowned a brand new number oneThe best anti-ageing creams, serums and treatmentsSarah MatthewsUpdatedWed 28 Oct 202611.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLED face masks are booming in popularity – despite being one of the most expensive at-home beauty products to hit the market. They claim to reduce the appearance of fine lines, stop spots and calm redness, with some even combining different types of light to enhance the benefits.However, it’s wise to be sceptical about new treatments that are costly and non-invasive, and to do your research before you buy. With this in mind, I interviewed doctors and dermatologists to find out whether these light therapy devices work.They’re not a miracle cure for deep-set wrinkles, but experts say the best light therapy masks can promote collagen production, improve elasticity and help smooth skin with sustained use. And while it may seem like a new technology,research from the 1990sshows the efficacy of light therapy in wound healing, acne treatment and skin rejuvenation.Red and infrared light are safe to use on all skin types, but be warned that blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones.I’ve tested some of the most popular devices on the market – including infrared masks – to narrow down my favourite LED face masks for treating a range of skin concerns.At a glanceBest LED mask overallCurrentBodySeries 3£499.99 at CurrentBodyBest budget LED face maskSilk’nLED face mask 100£99.99 at LookfantasticBest LED mask for full facial coverageTherabodyTheraFace mask Glo£299 at Space NKBest LED device for acne-prone skinLustreSolo£60 at LustreBest LED mask for quick treatmentsDr Dennis GrossSpectraLite FaceWare Pro£465 at Space NKBest LED mask for travelSilk’nLED face mask Pro£259 at LookfantasticWhy you should trust meI’ve been reviewing health and beauty tech for the past five years. During this time I’ve witnessed many beauty fads come and go. Naturally tight-fisted and a sceptic, I was initially struck by the cost of these masks. How on earth can an elaborate LED light strip set you back more than £300?But after testing multiple light therapy masks, I’ve come to understand the technology behind them – and, sadly, you won’t be able to engineer your own light therapy system with a costume mask and a set of LED string lights.I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles to test on, but I can comment on how blue-light treatment affects acne because I’ve suffered from it since I was a teenager – despite my mum’s assurances that it would clear up after puberty. The experts I spoke to agreed on the efficacy of red and infrared light for anti-ageing.Are LED face masks worth it?Light therapy masks are fantastic additions to a skincare routine, helping to smooth, firm and reduce blemishes. Since I started using one almost two years ago, my skin is calmer, less prone to redness, and has a more even tone.However, LED masks can be expensive, and if you’re not disciplined enough to use one regularly, you won’t see results. Before you splash up to £500, keep in mind that light therapy masks are most effective when paired with agood skincare routine. It’s crucial to make sure skin is properly cleansed before treatment and protected from sun damage afterwards.If you don’t already have askincareroutine nailed down, don’t buy a light therapy mask just yet. Consider starting out using a gentle cleanser and moisturiser, with anSPFfor daytime. You could also incorporate targeted skincare serums, such asretinolandvitamin C, to help firm and brighten the skin without the need for an expensive light therapy mask.How I testedView image in fullscreen‘I tested the fit, comfort levels and usability of 18 of the most popular light therapy masks.’Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianSince LED treatments take a while to show visible results, it’s difficult to test multiple light therapy masks at once (at least, without spending a few years testing them), so I enlisted the help of dermatologists who were familiar with light therapy treatments long before they were commercially available.I spoke to Dr Barbara Kubicka, an expert in aesthetic medicine; Dr Derrick Phillips, a consultant dermatologist and spokesperson for the British Skin Foundation; and aesthetic doctor Dr Priya Verma, an authority on the science of skin ageing.I asked these experts to identify which light therapy mask features – such as bulb quality and quantity, light wavelength and treatment time – matter the most, to inform my choices. They also outlined the suitability of light therapy for different skin types and its associated risks.Armed with their advice, I tested the fit, comfort levels and usability of 18 of the most popular light therapy masks and other targeted LED devices. Getting hands on with the masks allowed me to pinpoint any of the key features the experts recommended, as well as features I found helpful as a consumer.I’ve been using a light therapy mask regularly for almost two years, so I can identify a good mask from a bad one. My tests also included monitoring results after four nightly sessions, with the obvious caveat that only very minimal changes could be observed after such a short-term treatment. I then tested my favourite masks over several months, too, helping me to verify any unique treatment claims – as well as giving me plenty of opportunities to scare my boyfriend by sneaking up on him wearing each one.Only masks that use the brightest, flicker-free bulbs, fit comfortably and are easy to use made the final cut. After testing, I returned the masks sourced for this article to the manufacturers.
