You have to bite down on the mouthpiece to keep it in place, which is far less comfortable than just wearing a mask with a strap around your head.Number of LEDs:30;number of settings:two;treatment time:5mins;lightwavelengths:amber (605nm), red (633nm), dark red (660nm), near-infrared (830nm), deep near-infrared (1,072nm);timer countdown:noSilk’nLumiLips LED lip maskfrom£49£49 at Currys£63.20 at LookfantasticWhat we loveDeep near-infrared light and concentrated treatmentWhat we don’t loveLess comfortable to wear than a maskPeep Club heated eye wand LED+Peep ClubHeated eye wand LED+from£85£85 at Peep Club£85 at Victoria HealthWhat we loveDedicated, soothing treatment for eye areaWhat we don’t loveSmall LED light coverageView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£85 at Peep Club£85 at Victoria HealthBest for:reviving and soothing the undereyesLED face masks usually arrive with guards to protect your eyes from the light, which means they neglect to treat the delicate skin around the eyes – an area particularly prone to fine lines, wrinkles and discoloration.The Peep Club heated eye wand is a nifty little gadget that was designed in collaboration with optometrists, primarily as a hot compress to help with dry, tired eyes. The LED+ model includes a small LED light, which glows red to reduce fine lines and amber to decrease the visible blood vessels that cause dark circles. There’s also green light for soothing inflammation, although the evidence around green light is shaky.During testing, I found it soothed my irritated eyes after long days staring at a screen. The amber light setting seemed to reduce my dark circles, too, after a few weeks of consistent use. As recommended, I used it with thePeep Club coconut eye balmto give the wand a bit of slip, which avoided irritating the delicate skin under my eyes.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s not as convenient to use as a dedicated mask, since you have to glide it over the skin. Its LED light is small, so you need to dedicate a lot of time to treatment to get the best results. While I love using the coconut eye balm and a 40ml tub lasts a long time, it leaves an oily slip on the skin after treatment, and the need for this extra running cost may be off-putting.Number of LEDs:not listed;number of settings:five, three with LED;treatment time:5mins;lightwavelengths: amber (605nm), red (633nm), green (525nm);timer countdown:yesPeep ClubHeated eye wand LED+from£85£85 at Peep Club£85 at Victoria HealthWhat we loveDedicated, soothing treatment for eye areaWhat we don’t loveSmall LED light coverageThe rest of the testI’ve tested many more LED devices than can fit on this page, and while I don’t usually draw attention to bad products, I came across so many poorly designed models that I feel it necessary to shed light on the LED masks that overpromise and underdeliver.First, we have theRevolution Pro Miracle LED face mask, which costs just £59.99 at full price. Believe me, I wanted this mask to be a winner, but its solid plastic structure, with no eye shielding or padding, made it so wildly uncomfortable to wear that it was an almost instant write-off. The straps are another problem; they come together around the bottom part of your head, causing the mask to constantly fall. It also seems built for very small faces, so it constantly slipped down my face, pinching my nose and making it difficult to breathe properly – even if I used it without the straps and lay flat during treatment. Throw in fewer LED bulbs than average and dim lights, and this mask is impossible to recommend.A high price tag doesn’t guarantee how good the mask is either, as evidenced by theForeo FAQ 202 LED mask, £719 at full price. Its light weight and comfort level, along with an array of treatment options via its app-based controls, meant it impressed initially. However, its silicone design felt incredibly flimsy, and after a week of use, it had already started peeling away from the central battery pack.This might be forgivable if Foreo offered a full warranty and repair service. There’s atwo-year warrantycovering defects and faulty workmanship, but this does not cover “cosmetic deterioration caused by fair wear and tear, or damage caused by accident, misuse or neglect”. To access accidental damage coverage, you have to pay Foreo’s £9.99/month subscription. Even if you’re happy to risk it, at the time of testing in June 2026, you still had to shell out £4.99/month to access the mask’s full suite of preset treatments. Add to this the scale of advertising you’re bombarded with in the app – some of it unskippable. When you consider its price, this brazen money-grubbing leaves a very bad taste.Through testing this family of devices, I had also been hoping to find an undereye brightening LED patch to usurp the Peep Club wand, which requires constant movement across the eye area. I had hoped that theLustre GoGlowbrightening and de-puffing patches would fit the bill. They come in a handy headphone-like charging case and have a clever wireless design. However, when positioned under the eyes as advertised, the light was incredibly bright, which made it tricky to see. The sticky pads, although small, were uncomfortable to remove, and my skin was left feeling irritated for a day afterwards. The search for the perfect undereye LED patch continues …What you need to knowView image in fullscreenRed light is just one of several LED wavelengths used to target different skin concerns.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianWhat is LED therapy, and how does it work?“LED (light-emitting diode) therapy is a non-invasive treatment that uses specific wavelengths of light to stimulate various cellular processes in the skin,” says aesthetic medicine expert Kubicka. “Depending on the colour or wavelength, LED light can target inflammation, promote collagen production, accelerate healing and even kill bacteria.”Light therapy is a great addition to your skincare routine – for me, it’s helped reduce breakouts, improve healing and reduce the appearance of my acne scars. LED face masks are quick, gentle and non-invasive, and suitable for most skin types (although as mentioned above, blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones, according to the experts I spoke with). The masks are effective and foolproof to use, and the daily treatments also force you to take a little time for yourself – perfect for a morning pick-me-up or an evening wind-down.Does red light help with anti-ageing?“Red-light therapy can reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles through a process called photobiomodulation,” says consultant dermatologist Phillips. “It energises mitochondria, which are the batteries of the cells, powering the production of collagen and elastin by fibroblasts, the factories of the skin.”Elastin and collagen are “the building blocks of firm, youthful skin”, says Kubicka. Stimulating the production of these molecules can “improve skin density, elasticity and overall smoothness” as long as you complete treatments regularly.I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles, but I’m keen to avoid more by using red-light therapy for “preventive ageing”. However, “most of the clinical evidencefocuses on treating visible signs of ageing or repairing damaged skin, rather than long-term prevention in younger skin”, as aesthetic doctor Verma explains.Still, Verma reassured me my efforts wouldn’t be in vain. “Using LED light consistently and appropriately may help support overall skin health […] especially when combined with sun protection and a good skincare routine.”For more, readdo you really need an LED face mask?What different colours of light therapy are available?Several colours are available, with each wavelength said to target a different skin concern. These colours correlate to the visible light spectrum, and each can have a different effect on the skin.Red light has a wavelength of between 630 and 700nm and is the most widely known form of light therapy, loved for its non-invasive potential anti-ageing benefits. Near-infrared light above 700nm “penetrates the skin more deeply to support tissue repair and reduce inflammation”, according to Kubicka. Blue-light therapy (415nm), on the other hand, has been proven to target acne-causing bacteria, leading to a reduction in breakouts over time. Kubicka also says blue light can help regulate oil production – another common problem for those with acne.The effects of some types of light on the skin are better researched than others.Near-infrared,red lightandblue lightare backed by scientific studies that identify the biological processes that each type of light triggers in the body.Meanwhile, research into green and yellow light is more limited. One study questions theefficacy of yellow-lighttherapy and claims that a previous study may have been influenced by the placebo effect. Similarly, a study ongreen light therapysuggests that more research is needed to provide a solid recommendation for use as an anti-ageing treatment.How and when would you recommend using light therapy?The “how” is simple: always use light therapy masks on freshly washed, dry skin, before applying serums and creams. This will give the light the most direct access to the skin.Despite what some instruction manuals advise, don’t jump into daily treatments straight away – you may end up with slightly irritated skin. Start by introducing treatments two to three times a week, and monitoring the impact on your skin. If you don’t notice any sensitivity, you can incorporate more treatments, if permitted by the manufacturer’s guidelines.Once your skin is used to the treatment, “home devices should be used three to five times a week, for 10-20 minutes a session,” says Phillips. But treatment times vary between devices, so always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, and don’t expect instant results. If you’re hoping to reduce breakouts, you should “see a reduction in redness and the frequency of acne breakouts within two to four weeks”. Those using red light for anti-ageing benefits will need to wait a little longer: “It typically takes six to eight weeks to see visible changes.”Is light therapy safe for all skin tones?“LED light therapy is generally very safe when used correctly,” says Verma. This is because, unlike laser hair removal, it only uses low-level, non-thermal light. “The most common side effects are mild and temporary, such as slight redness, dryness or irritation.”“People with known photosensitive disorders or taking medications that make them more sensitive to light (eg certain antibiotics) should consult their doctor,” says Phillips. He also warns that those with darker skin tones should exercise caution when using blue light, since “some blue wavelengths have been associated with hyperpigmentation”. The Lustre Solo patches recommended above offer exclusively blue light, but the other masks in this roundup have blue-light-free settings if you do find that it causes sensitivity.How much should I spend on an LED therapy mask?There are hundreds of light therapy masks available at different prices, but the quality varies wildly. You may see results from a budget-friendly mask, such as theSilk’n LED face mask 100reviewed above, but spending more will generally get you a larger quantity of bulbs that offer a greater range of wavelengths. You’re also more likely to get a mask with a better fit and coverage.The best mask for you will depend on your skin concerns and budget. Those hoping to invest in a mask with anti-acne properties will be able to spend less, since blue light is more widely available, but if you’re looking for the best anti-ageing deep near-infrared light therapy, you will need to part with more cash.High-end red-light therapy masks can cost upwards of £500; if you spend that much, just make sure you use it regularly, or you won’t see results.How to clean an LED face maskCleaning instructions for LED masks will differ slightly from brand to brand, based on the different materials used. As a general rule, you want to steer clear of using chemical or alcohol-based cleansers since these can damage a mask’s delicate silicone and padded components. Always check the instructions for your specific mask before jumping into cleaning.The usual best practice is to use a non-abrasive cloth, such asmicrofibre, dampened with water to wipe down your mask after every use. Try not to use too much water and never submerge the mask, as doing so will damage the electrical components. Always make sure your mask is unplugged and switched off before cleaning, and wait for the mask to dry completely before storing, charging or switching it on.For more:The best concealers for camouflaging blemishesThe best retinol and retinal serums for smoother, firmer skinThe best eye creams for banishing bags, puffiness and fine linesShark FacialPro Glow + DePuffi reviewSarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, andcan sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’sdisciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)This article was originally published on 19 September 2025. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. This article was amended on 27 October 2026; the CurrentBody Series 3 and Therabody TheraFace Mask Glo masks were added after testing, two masks were removed, and prices were updated throughout.Explore more on these topicsSkincareThe FilterBeautyGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from? | Games | The Guardian
description: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry
Content: Oddly compelling or just slop? Minecraft and Fornite mashup.Photograph: @moreshiina/YouTubeView image in fullscreenOddly compelling or just slop? Minecraft and Fornite mashup.Photograph: @moreshiina/YouTubePushing Buttons newsletterGamesSocial media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industryDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 28 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarremashups of popular video games. Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from.Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube forthis informative video, which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more.Claude is now able to spit out a game’s source code from its compiled version overnight. Tell it to combine two games and it will help with that, too. There is not zero human involvement: from what I understand, the best of these mashups have needed significant human tweaking. But this has completely transformed video game modding because you now need drastically less time and computing knowledge to be able to pull off massive projects. It now takes an evening rather than months of work.View image in fullscreenSkateboards and swords … World of Warcraft and Skate 3 mashup.Photograph: @kimmo3223/YouTubeAs a person with zero coding knowledge, I was curious about how easy this was to do. I asked Claude how I’d go about making my own mashup, I picked one relatively obscure game and one extremely popular one, just to be annoying. Claude gave me comprehensive instructions and background on some modding and emulation tools, which was super interesting but ultimately of no use to me, because I had no idea what I was doing. So I just asked it if it could build me this in a browser.Four minutes later, it spat out a rubbish but playable game, with further instructions on how I could get the visual assets from the source games so that Claude could incorporate them for me and host it as a local file to avoid copyright issues. In half an hour, I had made something that’s still rubbish, but good enough for a 15-second TikTok. Except I haven’t made anything at all – the machine has done it for me. Istillhave no idea what I’m doing.This probably doesn’t seem that different from people using AI to create fake images of Jesus shaking hands with Trump to post on Facebook – and it isn’t, really. But people who DO know what they’re doing have gone much further with this AI-assisted source-code bonanza. I have seen relatively recent games such as Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom running in web browsers. Github is full of open-source code for Steam-like game launchers that draw from all the emulated codebases available, essentially giving you a vast library of retro games for free. Most consequentially, PlayStation 5 emulation has made an enormous jump: you can now run almost any PS5 game on a PC. For free.Much of this is obviously extremely illegal. Regarding the PlayStation 5 situation, I have seen a lot of angry videos describing this as a justified response to Sony’s abandonment of physical games: if you can’t buy a game anyway, how can you steal it? Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 emulation has also become astonishingly easy, thanks to AI-assisted launchers and mod hubs with beautifully clean interfaces. Speaking as a former prodigious teenage pirate (I wasn’t always so technically illiterate), you used to have to accumulate some secret knowledge to avail yourself of this stuff. That is no longer the case.There are enormous consequences here for any video game publisher that would rather nothave all of their game’s code freely available online for people to do what they want with. And that, presumably, is all video game publishers. AI is a technology built on the theft of creative work, as all writers and artists know – but up until now, it has not affected corporations to the same extent. Now that it does, will AI companies finally be forced to pump the brakes?What to playView image in fullscreenAll-consuming … Nintendo Switch Sports ResortPhotograph: NintendoMy house has been completely overtaken byNintendo Switch Sports Resort, which brings motion-controlled sports from skateboarding to thumb-wrestling to your living room, alongside more normal options such as tennis, golf and bowling. This is obviously a game in the Wii Sports lineage, and it fully embraces that landmark game’s accessible, fun-first philosophy, while also building on it to keep your interest going, from competitive leagues and online play to peaceful plane and jetski tours around the titular resort. My kids are obsessed with it. And because they’re up and moving, I felt perfectly fine about letting them play it for four straight hours while we were trapped in the house by Storm Boelo over the weekend.Available on:Nintendo SwitchEstimated playtime:anywhere from 20 minutes to 20 yearsWhat to readView image in fullscreenNight moves … Keith Stuart has investigated the best new horror games, such as The Killing Stone.Photograph: QuestionIf you’re looking forsomething to playfor a cosy Halloween night in, Keith Stuart has investigated the best newindie horror gamesfor spooky season.Microsofthas just offered voluntary redundancy to 60,000 people, including many working at Xbox game studios. AsVGC points out, that is a quarter of its entire staff. (The 1984-esque wording stood out to me – MS is calling this a “voluntary exit offer”.)The storied developer behind Mass Effect, Dragon Age and Knights of the Old Republic,BioWare, has been shuttered by EA. I could have written thousands of words on this – these were some of the defining games of the 00s and early 2010s, a hugely significant gaming period, and BioWare’s more recent history absolutely stinks of mismanagement – but I’ll leave it at this:it’s devastating.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickLara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blundersEA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereftCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 – a thrilling airport novel of a game | ★★★★☆Nintendo Switch Sports Resort – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games | ★★★★☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenGeographically accurate … Microsoft Flight Simulator.Photograph: gamespressReaderChrisasks:“I’m currently on a Field Trip in Iceland guiding a group of school students. It made me think whilelooking at the stunning volcanic scenery: what games are the most geographically accurate?”The boring answer to this is, of course,Microsoft Flight Simulator, which is 100% geographically accurate because it draws on satellite images of the entire Earth. I also played a strange experimental game last year calledPrologue: Go Wayback!, which a team in Amsterdam made – it procedurally generates accurate northern European wilderness for you to survive in, based on an impressively complex algorithm.Plenty of games have created architecturally accurate cities – all of the Assassin’s Creeds, Tom Clancy’s The Division, Yakuza/Like a Dragon and of course Grand Theft Auto – but fewer have made geographically accurate places that don’t have a volcanic lava-land in troublingly close proximity to a jungle. Forza Horizon’s versions of Mexico, Japan and the UK feelaccurate, but aren’t. ApparentlyKingdom Come: Deliveranceis based on a geographically accurate recreation of 15th-century Bohemia, which doesn’t surprise me at all given that game’s devotion to historical believability.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterAI (artificial intelligence)PiracyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity | Jeanette Winterson | The Guardian
description: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed
Author: Aida Edemariam
Headline: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed
Content: ‘What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted’ … Jeanette Winterson at home in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted’ … Jeanette Winterson at home in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe ideas interviewJeanette WintersonInterview‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanityAida EdemariamThe author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceedWed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Iam a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.”She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded byFrankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.When we meet, Winterson is just back from China, where, she tells me, her first novel, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit, a fictionalised account of her childhood, has sold more than a million copies in the past six years; more than 200,000 mostly young women tried to come to see her speak. She thinks this is because, in a world of long work hours and looming AI-engendered precarity, this fictionalised account of her own escape from an entrapped childhood gives readers permission to imagine a different future for themselves. She has since written 13 novels for adults, as well as nonfiction, short stories, children’s books and screenplays. Now she wants to persuade the production company Goalhanger to give her a podcast. “I want to do one called The Rest is Human,” she says, sitting at a bare wooden table inher home, a Georgian set of rooms above a shop – which she also owns – in Spitalfields, east London. “To see what we retain for ourselves in this absolute scramble to outsource everything we thought we were.”View image in fullscreenWinterson: ‘We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for.’Photograph: Posed by models; SDI Productions/Getty ImagesBecause we are, she argues, at a turning point in our story as a species. Until the Industrial Revolution, change was all about “Mother Nature and the slow process of becoming”, but then we “massively intervened. And that’s a decisive moment.”Computing, 70 years ago, was another step. Artificial intelligence – which she would prefer to call alternative intelligence – is next, and “an evolutionary leap. That’s what this is. AI is much more than a tool.” Given this, a certain understanding of the irreducibly human – our feelings, our imaginations, our centuries of study of who we are and what we have done – must be central to how well or badly things might go.She’s often strikingly optimistic about it. She imagines a relationship with AI, for instance, where you can “have a chat to your system. It’s going to look at everything. It’s going to go at such speed. It’s going to look at transport. It’s going to look at utilities. It’s going to look at employment, going to look at job hours, going to say, ‘What do these weird things called humans thrive on? What do they like? And have they always liked it?’ We could do this in a genuinely utopian way and say, ‘Right, we’re going to make it better.’” We are at a deeply significant moment of choice, she believes, that mirrors the choice we had in the Industrial Revolution – namely, “What future shall we build?”But in failing to distribute its gains fairly, the Industrial Revolution ushered in an era of unprecedented wealth for the few and unprecedented levels of misery for the many – a state of affairs many predict is not only already echoed but will be dwarfed by the fallout from AI:a permanent underclass, entire continents left behind and starved of current sources of income. Not to mention the environmental impact of datacentres at a time when the world can least afford it.The problem is not AI, she insists, but us. “There is no inevitable dystopia.” If things go wrong, it will be because of “old-fashioned thinking laid over this brand-new reality”. Specifically, “the idea of meaningless endless work being good for the soul is a 19th-century madness designed to keep people in their place. Most of what we fear about AI and jobs comes down to the political and economic choices our masters will make, just as they did in the Industrial Revolution.” She isn’t blindly optimistic. She does know that, “Yes, we are on track to mess up this chance to fundamentally change our relationship to the world of work” – but that’s because “our masters are using out-of-date, not-fit-for-purpose economic models”.View image in fullscreen‘What we know about humans is they love monopolies.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianBut it isn’t only the old winner-takes-all, “rational” ends-justify-the-means economic models that are the problem. Our flawed assumptions, and our prejudices, being the material on which large language models (LLMs) are trained, are built into the very fabric of AI. Not to mention the characters and the moral imaginations of those developing it. When we meet, Winterson is reading Jill Lepore’sThe Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and reiterates Lepore’s argument that we are now living “the sci-fi books that these [men who are] ruling the world read when they were 13. And she said, ‘We are now all under the covers with these boys and their flashlights. And the thing is, they didn’t read them as warnings about how to preserve what’s good in us. They read them as instruction manuals.’ It’s absolutely terrifying.”One big thing they seem to havetaken from these books, and Winterson cannot help but be fascinated by, is “the ultimate goal of Silicon Valley … to get out of the body and off the planet” – not least because she is so aware that humanism, in which everything is brought back to ourselves, our perceptions and our bodies, is historically so recent. People say, “These are machines, you can’t have relationships with them,” she says. “I look at them and say, ‘billions of people on this Earth right now are having their most profound relationship with a non-biological entity they call their sky god.’ Right? It’s always been so! We are absolutely primed not to worry about biology being everything about us. That’s why religion was invented – it is the world’s first disruptive startup. It’s there to say, this is not it. This is not the end, this doesn’t matter, this is a transition.”View image in fullscreenAn illustration of a mill in Leeds, during the second Industrial Revolution.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSo we’re literally making our own gods? “Totally! What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted,” which is, at its most basic level, a solution to the problem of death. “I mean, has there ever been a time where religion and science are asking the same question, since the Enlightenment? They’re both saying, ‘Is consciousness obliged to materiality?’ And religion has always said no. And science has always said yes. And now science is saying, ‘Um, noooo.”’ You know, to me, where I come from” – a childhood of fundamentalist Christianity in 1960s Accrington, and training as a preacher – “this iscompletelyfascinating.” Later, on email, she adds, “I love my body, but I would be happy to shape shift. Happy to slip out of it into pure consciousness one day and of course people say there is no consciousness without a body, and that was the scientific belief. But now? Haha.”I would, I have to say, argue the opposite, that advances in neuroscience, immunology and psychotherapy mean it ismore the scientificbelief than ever. Not to mention the fact that AI is also entirely dependent on a physical system, otherwise known as datacentres. Although, as she points out it’s important to remember that “the machines don’t have a limbic system. They’re only neural networks. But we’ve got two systems – we’re like a hybrid car with two powertrains, so we’ve got the neural network, our rational processing self, and we’ve got the limbic system, which is much older and that’s the fight-flight-freeze, and where all our feelings come from.” Perhaps detaching from the limbic is the next stage, she says, and it definitely isn’t all good. “Maybe we’ll decide that we don’t need this feeling machine … that is where the tech bros are heading. I don’t know if you’ve ever sat in a room with some of these bigger guys, because it’sveryinteresting. They are not connected to their feelings. They find them kind of bothersome.”This tech-enabled possibility of a kind of transcendence seems to have arrived alongside a requirement for faith – in the technology, in the future it is making, in the people building that future, in its predictions both of utopian heaven and various shades of hell, all by high priests who jealously guard access to what’s actually going on. “What we know about humans is they love monopolies,” says Winterson, “because it’s a concentration of power. Of course it can be corporatised, monopolised to such a degree that it becomes the worst prison imaginable,” as told in Joanna Kavenna’s brilliant 2019 dystopian novelZed. “That is a real possibility,” she says. “And that’s why we need people who are sort of free-range humans, who canthink.”View image in fullscreenWinterson … ‘Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story.’Photograph: Posed by models; MoMo Productions/Getty ImagesThe problem then is how we support – or develop – such humans. “There are basically two ways to know you have a future,”claimedAlex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, recently. “One, you have some vocational training. Or two, you’re neurodivergent.” Daniela Amodei, the president of Anthropic and herself a literature graduate, when asked more or less the same thing, had a different take. “I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” she said, because “the things that make us human will become much more important instead of much less important.” Which makes the bonfire of the humanities in the UK somewhat concerning: in the year to December 2024, 4,000 jobs in the social sciences, humanities and artswere lost. Exeter University recently announced it would be cutting 150 roles, affecting eight in 10 academics in the faculty of humanities, arts and social sciences, while last month Nottingham said it would be ending its modern languages and its music degrees. At some universities the humanities, according to areportin this paper, risk being “extinguished” altogether.Why save the humanities? One answer might be that they teach a sense of where we come from and who we are, which also feels threatened. “Massive numbers of students are going to emerge from university with degrees, and into the workforce, who are essentially illiterate,” one professortoldNew York magazine, responding to the first tranche of AI natives arriving in higher education. “Both in the literal sense and in the sense of being historically illiterate and having no knowledge of their own culture, much less anyone else’s.” It risked, areportfrom MIT claimed, being a kind of generational “cognitive surrender”.Another is the processes by which people should be taught – reading, and being critical of what is read, and then having to write cogent defences of those critiques. Having to tussle your intuitions into an essay helps you to discover what – and how – you think, and how the ideas of others work. Winterson, who studied English at Oxford, and has been professor of new writing at the University of Manchester for 14 years, as well as teaching “a free-thinking class about creativity”, agrees. But she is dismissive of much of the current system. “Maybe I’m controversial here but I do think higher education needs a top-down restructure. I don’t think it’s viable and I don’t think it’s delivering in its present form.” The thing is, “We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for. Is it for jobs? Is it for personal growth? There are a lot of worthless higher education courses which are not helping, either. I think it’s always better, being a practical northern girl, to face the facts to start with.”View image in fullscreenIn her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, Winterson imagined a world populated by robots and people who never age.Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty ImagesWe need to think, she says, about “what’s reserved to us that isn’t going to be done bigger, better, faster, stronger by the machines. And that’s where higher education really comes in. The question that’s sitting on top of all these things about, ‘Why are these jobs going?’, ‘What’s happening in these courses that aren’t getting any applicants any more?’, is ‘What sort of humans will we need in the world to come? What are humansfor? What are we going to do withus?’”. And that “takes us back to the idea of, well, OK, how do you develop a mind? How do youprotecta mind? Because the mind is this massive, monstrous place where anything can happen.”And for this, “a humanist education is essential. We have to centre the human here. By changing how we educate our kids from the start we can foreground creativity, play, problem-solving, thinking, because it’s fun to think, the arts because humans are naturally creative. Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story or do a dance or paint a picture or have an imaginary friend. This isn’t imposed and it isn’t elitism. It’sus.”Even an hour a week, she thinks, would make a difference. “Let’s ask what you think about the world. ‘Why do you think that?’ It’s not costly. It’s actually about will.” Teach maths and arts and science, she suggests, at least to A-level, even if they aren’t examined. “Of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people. Everything is interesting! Humans are born with a big brain. Mostly we don’t use it.”View image in fullscreen‘Artists make something out of nothing every day.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianOnce past formal education, she would embed artists and public intellectuals at every level. “The arts aren’t a leisure industry,” as she puts it in 12 Bytes. “The arts have always been an imaginative and emotional wrestle with reality – a series of inventions and creations. A capacity to think differently, a willingness to change our understanding of ourselves. To help us to be wiser, more reflective, less frightened people. Artists make something out of nothing every day.”We meet before Jacob Coxonquithis job at Anthropic to warn of a 10% chance AI might erase humanity, sending a wave of panic across the world. Afterwards, I check in about how positive Winterson is feeling now. The worst “could happen”, she repeats. But “the immensity of the good outcome is just as real as the totality of our failure to get this right”. Above all, “this is a human decision and a human predicament. This is our big chance. Maybe our last chance, just like Turing’s colleague Jack Good said when he called AI our last invention. It’s all to play for.”We can only hope it’s not too late.Jeanette Winterson’s most recent book is One Aladdin, Two Lamps. She also writes atjeanettewinterson.substack.comOne Aladdin Two Lamps by Jeanette Winterson (Vintage Publishing, £12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy for £10.39 atguardianbookshop.com. title: Castle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared mess | Television | The Guardian
description: Billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’
Content: ‘Another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces’ … Castle Walls is the first fully AI-generated series to premiere on a major streaming platform.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video / YouTubeView image in fullscreen‘Another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces’ … Castle Walls is the first fully AI-generated series to premiere on a major streaming platform.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video / YouTubeTelevisionReviewCastle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared messBilled as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’Luke BuckmasterWed 28 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust as the world reels from Elon Musk’s AI-poweredThe Odyssey remake– though “remake” feels rather generous for a seven-minute splat of synthetic sludge – another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces. For Prime Video’s AI-generated TV series Castle Walls, produced by Turkish production studio Ay Yapım using a melange of generative video tools, has arrived, billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series to premiere on a major streaming platform.‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey filmRead moreIt’s certainly more epic than Musk’s production, consisting of two 17-minute episodes. Set in the 11th century, the show revolves around the historic Alamut Castle, although it’s entirely absent of any real sense of time or place. I was briefly intrigued by the opening images, with their bold palette of blues and mustard browns and yellows – but as soon as the “people” appeared, looking like Vaseline-smeared Madame Tussauds creations slowly melting in the sun, everything came crashing down.View image in fullscreen‘Like Vaseline-smeared Madame Tussauds creations slowly melting in the sun’: Castle Walls.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeThere are lots of heady moments across the first two episodes of this oddly paced show, with cranky-looking men aplenty and over-milked visual metaphors involving the likes of snakes, blood and fire. Everything looks like it was cooked up with the prompt: “Give me eye-watering visuals.” The opening shot depicts an eagle being transported across a desert in a cage (“make it look cinematic”), followed by a longshot of the castle (“make it more cinematic”), then an aerial shot of men arriving on horseback (“make it MORE MORE MORE cinematic”).View image in fullscreen‘Overloaded with grand and imposing imagery’: Castle Walls.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeWe learn of the arrival in Alamut of a “freak” who “doesn’t eat or drink” and is intent on claiming these sweet digs for himself. This is Hasan Sabbah, who is supposed to be charismatic but looks plasticky and spectral, with a complexion like wet glue. He has somehow inspired an army of followers and ventures into the castle’s dungeons to recruit one more: the notorious warrior Azazil.The frame is overloaded with grand and imposing imagery: when Azazil says goodbye to loved ones, of course the scene takes place in front of a milky sunset. When he fangs it across the desert on a horse at night, of course there’s a white full moon glowing resplendently above. When the doors of the mighty castle creak open, in the lead-up to a big moment in episode two, of course incandescent orange sunlight streams through the widening gap.View image in fullscreen‘Viewers understandably seem less interested in what the technology promises than in what it threatens to take away: art imbued with humanity.’Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeMake no mistake: the technology powering this is amazing and will profoundly alter the state of motion pictures. Productions such as Castle Walls are among the first out of the gates, and therefore prone to snarky commentary. Perhaps these early AI-generated workswill end up being broadly comparable to early silent films: revolutionary at the time, but quickly eclipsed by more sophisticated applications of the technology. But whereas the earliest motion pictures, famously dubbed the “cinema of attractions” by the historian Tom Gunning, provided some carnival-like wonder, these AI works tend to evoke a more cynical response from the general public. Viewers understandably seem less interested in what the technology promises than in what it threatens to take away: art imbued with humanity.The sensible path forward is surely for human and machine to enter into a reciprocal and carefully collaborative process, where artists only use algorithms and prompts to enhance, rather than replace, human creativity. On that front, Castle Walls did use human voice actors and was reportedly written by actual human screenwriters: Kerem Deren and Çisil Hazal Tenim. “This is not a production that bypassed human skill; it is one that used AI to amplify it,”Ay Yapım has said.But that’s hardly something to crow about, given how banal and chuckleheaded the writing is, puffed-up with lines like “I’ve stopped being a decent man” and “If I am the sheaf, you are the sword”. Were they really trying to make good art? Maybe that’s a question for ChatGPT.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTurkeyDramaAI (artificial intelligence)Amazon Prime VideoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Carney is celebrated abroad – while he guts hard-won protections at home | Shiri Pasternak | The Guardian
description: The Canadian prime minister’s reckoning with Trumpism in Davos clashes with his attacks on environmental, Indigenous and labour rights
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Canadian prime minister’s reckoning with Trumpism in Davos clashes with his attacks on environmental, Indigenous and labour rights
Content: ‘To what image of nationalism is Carney hewing?’Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreen‘To what image of nationalism is Carney hewing?’Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APOpinionCanadaMark Carney is celebrated abroad – while he guts hard-won protections at homeShiri PasternakThe Canadian prime minister’s reckoning with Trumpism in Davos clashes with his attacks on environmental, Indigenous and labour rightsWed 28 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTShareThe Canadian prime minister is a hero around the worldfor his Davos speechthat reckoned with a reconfiguration of power in the shadow of Donald Trump.But at home, Mark Carney is mirroring the US president by radically centralizing power within his office and cabinet and taking a hatchet to dozens of laws protectingenvironmental,Indigenousandlabour rights, all in order to enact his economic agenda.His globalsale of Canadian land and resources comes just weeks after another major Canadian export –wildfire smoke– decimated First Nations communities in northern Ontario, leading to mass evacuations and warning the world of the impact of a fossil fuel economy.The BuildingCanadaStrong Act, Bill C-39, is a 250-page piece of omnibus legislation introduced on 21 September by the transport minister and House leader, Steven MacKinnon.The new bill expands his previous legislation that created an expansive fast-tracking designation for “projects of national interest” to “regions of national interest”, which could exempt vast areas of Canada from labour and Indigenous rights, and environmental protections.Geographic regions can be given this sweeping new designation by federal ministers, diminishing the sovereignty of parliament and bypassing local elected officials and affected citizens in these special economic zones.Arms-length environmental review boards are also being done away with. Decision-making for new pipelines, nuclear facilities, highways and other major infrastructure has been shifted to the very bodies charged with promoting these sectors. The Canada Energy Regulator now directly assesses energy projects, while the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission directly approves nuclear/uranium projects.Cabinet approval has also been removed entirely for most pipelines under the amended framework, now strictly reserved for pipeline projects requiring more than 300km ofnewright of way. Even if a significant pipeline is proposed, if it hews close to existing corridors, it is now exempt from federal cabinet oversight.This is what Carney believes it takes to make good on his oft-repeatedpromisethat Canada “has what the world wants”.As Narwhal magazinereported, these changes follow lobbying by the oil and gas industry in the form of a literal wishlist of demands to speed up project reviews for fossil fuel projects. A public pressure campaign by the CEOs or executive chairs of 14 companies wasreleasedlast March, calling on the prime minister to undo the former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s modest climate policies.It is not only environmental protections that are impeding the economy Carney hopes will stabilize Canada’s GDP. The new bill also explicitly adds the power toend a legal strikein the Canada Labour Code.ForIndigenous peoples, the rollback is just as massive. They have fought for decades to constitutionally enshrine their rights to consultation on development affecting their lands.But with fast-tracked projects and a new guarantee to industry of a one-year timeline for decisions, communities must determine all cumulative impacts in the early stages of assessment, virtually wiping out their opportunity to influence the project direction, given the time-consuming nature and costly nature of impact assessment.What is the former central banker’s vision for Canada? To what image of nationalism is Carney hewing?Carney’s approach has been called a “carve-out” system of legal exceptionalism. These aren’t the sensational executive orders of Trump’s bombastic political style, but more sophisticated and sly swipes at our existing framework of law.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is no coincidence that this omnibus legislation came down following the major Canada Investment Summit that Carney held in Toronto in September. It replaced what many feared was the worst rollback in rights Canadians had ever seen –Bill C-5- with something even worse.The leakedpitch bookfor the Investment Summit showed 167 projects being sold to the highest bidder among the 200+ private equity and sovereign wealth funds reps who attended. The projects include AI datacentres, publicly owned airports, defence manufacturing, and dozens of energy and mining projects.Carney hasclaimedthe summit raised over $500bn in new foreign investment commitments to Canada. But how will he accommodate the needs of capital to make these projects viable? The Building Canada Strong Act is the most crucial way, through regulatory concessions. But it’s part of a buffet of public wealth on the table.Only one day after the summit, Carney introduced the Productivity Mega Deduction, allowing businesses to deduct the cost of a much broader range of assets right away, including pipelines, mining property, aircrafts and bridges. The effective tax rate went from 13% to 6.4% – the lowest of any major economy, including the US.Carney also promised to distribute C$280bn in federal subsidies to industry by way of tax write-offs and shifting risk from capital to taxpayers via cheap credit and loans from the Canada Growth Fund, the Canada Infrastructure Bank, and Export Development Canada.To survive Trump’s trade war, the doors of Canada have been flung open to a giant sale of resources to industrial projects that would not be viable without the public backstop of financing and corporate license to plunder.Though Carney is popular, Canadians arewaking upto this elitist agenda. Rather than rescuing Canada, it is endangering the survival of our country and people.Shiri Pasternak is an associate professor in criminology at Toronto Metropolitan University and a member of the Infrastructure Beyond Extractivism research team, a collaboration between critical scholars and Indigenous land defenders across North AmericaExplore more on these topicsCanadaOpinionAmericasMark CarneyIndigenous peoplescommentShareReuse this content

title: Will it be AI or the climate crisis that ends humanity? We can make it neither | Adam McKay and Philip Eubanks | The Guardian
description: Both of these threats have the same roots: private entities seeking to cash in. We have the power to stand against them
Author: Adam McKay
Headline: Both of these threats have the same roots: private entities seeking to cash in. We have the power to stand against them
Content: ‘At the heart of this sits the same fundamental question: who decides our future?’Photograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreen‘At the heart of this sits the same fundamental question: who decides our future?’Photograph: Paul Sancya/APOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Will it be AI or the climate crisis that ends humanity? We can make it neitherAdam McKayand Philip EubanksBoth of these threats have the same roots: private entities seeking to cash in. We have the power to stand against themWed 28 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTShareA summer of extreme heat, entire villages obliterated in Nepal, a superEl Niñobreaking records, Exxonpublicly sayingwe may reach 3C by 2050 – could it possibly be any worse?How about throwingAIextinction in the mix?As climate activists and funders, we’ve spent years warning about a self-evident, imminent, avoidable climate calamity. Whether by making award-winning films (Don’t Look Up and Just Look Up) to warn the public, or by funding protest groups across the planet that bravely stand up for a livable future, we’ve been sounding the alarm to wake the public up.Lately, as climate disasters and AI expansion wreak havoc on communities globally, warnings are arriving from everywhere all at once.Daniel Kokotajlo, a former AI forecaster for OpenAI,recently testifiedbefore the Senate that today’s AI models are now trained to pursue goals no human gave them, and then they hide the fact that they’ve done it. Kokotajlo put the odds of AI companies automating their own work by the end of 2028 at about 50%, and, if that happens, the AI safety community warns the technology could improve faster than humans can monitor it, and eventually become too difficult to shut down.I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis | AnonymousRead moreThese speculative warnings have earned alarm from mainstream media, politicians and civil society alike. Some critics suggest the warnings are marketing ploys by the AI industry to set up an arms race, using the false specter of AI apocalypse to capture government funding. Others think it might be an attempt to avoid accountability: by treating the machines as gods, we might conveniently forget their maker.Either way, the debate keeps missing the damage AI is doing right now, polluting communities around the world, or the damage of new AI partnerships with the oil and gas industry. And we don’t just mean emissions from datacenter infrastructure alone. The harms run much deeper.Arecent study in a Natureportfolio journal revealed an alliance between oil majors and the tech industry to use AI for new exploration and extraction – in effect adding up to 1.8 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide (the equivalent of Russia’s annual emissions) to the atmosphere annually.double quotation markIt feels as if we’re in a race over which apocalyptic ending comes first. How about none of them?Meanwhile, AI is flooding our information ecosystems with disinformation that erodes public trust, or it “hallucinates” nuclear threats,almost sparking war between the US and China.It feels as if we’re in a race over which apocalyptic ending comes first. How about none of them?At the heart of this sits the same fundamental question: who decides our future? Right now, whether the threat is AI or climate, or a mix of both, the answer is the same: a handful of private corporations, billionaires and their political enablers, making choices that will enrich them but devastate billions of people.A datacenter that drains water from a drought-stricken town, burns gas for power, and runs AI that helps oil companies find more oil isboth a climate fight and an AI fight.Communities are resisting, and winning.Data Center Watchcounted at least 120 US datacenter projects worth nearly $200bn blocked or delayed in the first half of 2026, with opposition in 49 states.Heatmap Newsfound at least 20 canceled outright in the first three months of the year alone, a record.AI and the climate crisis pose existential risks. The law offers a way to reduce them | Robert ReichRead moreThese are the early stages of what we believe is poised to become a global movement against corporate and billionaire capture of our water, the land that grows our food, and the air we breathe.At Climate Emergency Fund, we’ve put half our funding toward grassroots groups at the forefront of this fight, and we hope to scale that up before the year is out. We’re asking other funders to join us in this work, which at its core is meant to build thriving communities, not AI datacenters.This fight can continue to grow into a cohesive, sustained, strategic movement. It is one of our last best chances to tackle not only climate change, but also a corporate billionaire class that has decided it has the right to control and steal the future for the rest of us.The goal is a future in which the possibility of the end of the world no longer needs a daily check-in. Our existential threats are the result of human activity – systems built by people, on purpose, for money. Things built that way can be unbuilt, and we can choose to build another, better, world.“Solving” these crises doesn’t require settling whether the machines or the seas get us first. It only requires deciding we don’t want to learn the answer. We have everything we need, except time.But with the time we have, we can take drastic action now. And instead of pouring billions into datacenters and tech IPOs, we must fund those fighting for a thriving future.Adam McKay is the Academy Award-winning director of The Big Short, Vice and Don’t Look Up; the founder of Yellow Dot Studios; and a board director for Climate Emergency FundPhilip Eubanks is the executive director of Climate Emergency FundExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionClimate crisisDatacentresDon't Look UpcommentShareReuse this content

title: We are seeing the rise of psychopatriarchy everywhere | V (formerly Eve Ensler) | The Guardian
description: Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalism
Author: V (formerly Eve Ensler)
Headline: Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalism
Content: ‘It is propelled by its own mad trajectory.’Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘It is propelled by its own mad trajectory.’Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersOpinionUS newsWe are seeing the rise of psychopatriarchy everywhereV (formerly Eve Ensler)Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to racism, colonialism, imperialism and capitalismWed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 16.25 EDTShareFor those of us who have spent our lives trying to dismantle this endlessly destructive paradigm of patriarchy, it has become increasingly clear in recent months that something more terrifying is afoot.The wheels are off the cart. We are in the midst of a chaotic, demented acceleration of the most violent and cruel aspects of this system which has evolved into what I am calling Psychopatriarchy.Psychopatriarchy is a reaction, a backlash against the progress we have made on all fronts: women’s rights, civil rights, immigrant rights, workers rights, trans rights etc.It has birthed an authoritarian fascist reality, poisoning our social and psychological environment with terrorizing violence, cruelty and precarity. It has consolidated the billionaire class who are driven by the mindset summed up in the slogan “move fast and break things.” Or, one might say, grab things, rape things.Psychopatriarchy is found in the 120 people who own more money than half the population on Earth, in the systems of oppression, surveillance and violence which become more and more sophisticated and widespread, in the few mainly white men with extreme wealth and power who are now merged with the government and own the systems of communication, AI, police or state militias like ICE.America must reverse Trump’s moral squalor | Robert ReichRead morePsychopatriarchy is a sanctioning of extreme hatred and violence against women from the top, many of whom are rapists, batterers, pedophiles and abusers or men who openly support them.The president of the US is a civilly adjudicated sex abuser and has not only flippantlydismissed allegationsof sexual violencemade against othersin his orbit, but made it fashionable and popular attitude for the men in his delusional cult.He has created a suffocating atmosphere of misogyny and predation. We only have to look to the manosphere, or the rape academies online where millions of men exchange best practices for drugging and raping their wives, girlfriends, sisters or deepfake pornography which is destroying thousands of women’s lives or sex robots.Orrape islandswhere some of the most powerful men in the world are alleged to have raped underage girls and not one has been prosecuted. Or universities where young men allegedly gang-rape an incapacitated woman or where young women can’t put down a drink at a party without fear of being drugged, where they are blamed for being assaulted.Psychopatriarchy is women dying preventable deaths because abortion care is denied or delayed or the introduction of extreme constitutional amendments such asNorth Carolina House Bill 1232, where menmight belegally allowed to kill women who have abortions. This bill will hopefully not pass, but the fact that it is even being considered is an example of how deeply far we have fallen.Psychopatriachy is the open and unapologetic death of compassion; asElon Musk said: “Empathy is the fundamental weakness of western civilization.” This means a kind of contempt for anything that appears to be emotional, alive, feminine, caring.Strength in the form of dissociation is revered. When you feel nothing, no guilt, no shame, no horror at your actions, you can better serve your goals and the state. When you are ruled by your blind devotion to the president, the boss, the father, you become capable of doing anything in his name.Psychopatriachy is renaming the Department of Defense the “Department of War”, well, the “High-T Department of War”,as Hegseth calls it, wanting all military personnel aged 30 and over to “have the right testosterone levels” to operate at their “absolute best” and to optimize “natural capabilities”, “longevity”, and “readiness”. Preparing a psycho army driven by chemicals beyond their control.Psychopatriarchy iswanting to livestreama firing squad. It’s the endless genocide in Gaza, the outright murdering of babies, toddlers, mothers, fathers, journalists, doctors. It’s the US bombing a girls school in Iran and murdering 120 girl children and 26 teachers, and no one ever taking responsibility for one of the worst war crimes since Vietnam.It’s illegally kidnapping presidents and randomly murdering people by bombing them in boats in the middle of the sea. It’s masked men dragging away wailing children from their parents.It’s killing activists in the streets: Renee Good and Alex Pretti. It’s intimidating and threatening deportation to those who disagree with you: Ilhan Omar. It’s creating the conditions for the lynching of Black people across the United States.It’s tearing down ancient grandmother trees to build walls to keep suffering people out or to landscape a golf course. It’s the coldhearted, discompassionate billionaire class taking everything, erasing everyone.Psychopatriarchy is the decimation of all forms of accountability. Infinite impunity. No supreme court, no Department of Justice, no leaders, no Congress. Withdrawing or refusing to be part of any international courts or abiding by international law. When there is no accountability, when there is no place to turn for justice, a society loses its moral footing and begins to fall.Psychopatriachy is not just a political notion. It’s a state of existence, a blight on the condition of humanity locking us into daily terror, cruelty, depression, malaise, a manufactured sense of powerlessness, alienation and a desire to disappear.It is a kind of low-level anxiety, an ongoing foreshadowing or feeling of imminent destruction coming from multiple directions at once, and rather than reducing these threats (AI, nuclear weapons, climate catastrophes, pandemics), the psychopatriarchs are accelerating all these things. AI is charging forward with no regulation, escalating the nuclear arms race, increasing drilling of oil at breakneck speed.Psychopatriarchy is jet fuel to all the other -isms: racism, colonialism, imperialism, capitalism.It is propelled by its own mad trajectory. We can try to block it (courts); we can starve it (strikes); we can remove it (vote and get them out office). We can name and shame it (speaking out, marches and rallies), refuse to normalize it (write about it, make art about it); we can prosecute it.We can create a parallel world that is so inviting, generous and caring that even those who are still struggling to break out of the cult will eventually be emboldened.But what we cannot do is go to sleep, become small and still, with the childlike fantasy that they will not find us. What we cannot do is succumb to it or become them – numb, selfish, hollow and cruel.Our feelings, our pain, our empathy, our rage, our love, our refusal to turn away will be our salvation. Psychosis is the inability to tell what is real from unreal. Our work is to say what we see and trust what we know, to keep speaking truth to power and go to any lengths to stay connected to reality and each other.V (formerly Eve Ensler) is a playwright and activist and the founder of V-Day, a global movement to end violence against women and girlsExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Donald TrumpUS politicsAbortionReproductive rightsRape and sexual assaultcommentShareReuse this content

title: Jay-Z is the perfect Super Bowl shill for a league of billionaires | NFL | The Guardian
description: The rapper lends the NFL a veneer of credibility but is unlikely to push back on the establishment figures who run the league
Author: Lee Escobedo
Headline: The rapper lends the NFL a veneer of credibility but is unlikely to push back on the establishment figures who run the league
Content: NFL commissioner Roger Goodell and Jay-Z greet each other at the announcement of NFL and Roc Nation’s agreement in 2019.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Roc NationView image in fullscreenNFL commissioner Roger Goodell and Jay-Z greet each other at the announcement of NFL and Roc Nation’s agreement in 2019.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Roc NationNFLJay-Z is the perfect Super Bowl shill for a league of billionairesLee EscobedoThe rapper lends the NFL a veneer of credibility but is unlikely to push back on the establishment figures who run the leagueWed 28 Oct 2026 05.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 06.51 EDTShareOn Monday the NFLnamed Jay-Zas the headliner for this season’s Super Bowl half-time show. His company, Roc Nation, produces the show under a 2019 dealreportedlyworth $5m a year, and the agreement was extended for another five years in 2024. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said his one request when the partnership began was that Jay-Z “take the stage himself one day“.Goodell’s wish makes total sense:Jay-Zis the perfect choice for the half-time show, and that’s not a compliment. The NFL wants a shill who can still pass for a rebel, and nobody in American music plays that part better than Jay-Z.Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people | Howard BryantRead moreJay-Z’s origin story has become an American legend. Years before he sold records, Shawn Carter grew up in Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses andsold crackas a teenager. When labels passed on him, he hawked CDs from the trunk of his car on college campuses. Then he put out Reasonable Doubt in 1996 on his own label, Roc-A-Fella. “Nobody would sign me,” he said later. The money followed. In 2013, he performed Picasso Baby, a track about the paintings he wanted to own, for six hours straight at aChelsea gallery, and Marina Abramović joined him. By the time of The Story of OJ in 2017, he washanding out financial advice. Forbes puts his fortune at about$2.8bn. He raps for the rich now, a Black oligarch who seems about as cut off from the rest of the country as the rest of the billionaire class.His bootstraps story mirrors the platitudes Americans have been told for decades – work hard and you’ll get what you deserve. On paper, he’s the perfect avatar for America’s polluted ideas of capitalism. But the country Jay-Z is rapping to is in terrible shape. How many of us can relate to his lyrics in 2026? Gas and grocery prices have rocketed. SNAP enrollmentfell more than 13%in a year as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act tightened the rules. Only 63% of adults say they couldcover a surprise $400 expense.You can see why the NFL would use Jay-Z as someone who can give the appearance that the league, with its huge conservative fanbase, is actually progressive. Hewore Colin Kaepernick’s jerseyon Saturday Night Live in 2017 after the quarterback had sparked a protest movement against police brutality by kneeling for the national anthem. Jay-Z then dedicated The Story of OJ to Kaepernick onstage. A year later, on Apeshit, he bragged about turning down the Super Bowl and told the NFL it needed him more than he needed it.Things would soon change.In June 2019, Forbes named himhip-hop’s first billionaire. A few months later, Roc Nation signed its deal with the NFL. But at the news conference announcing his NFL partnership, Jay-Z no longer appeared as receptive to Kaepernick’s approach to protest. “We’vemoved past kneeling,” he said. That same year, Kaepernicksettled his collusion grievanceagainst the league after he said his protests had effectively ended his playing career.The 2019 deal also put Roc Nation to work onInspire Change, the league’s social justice initiative. It’s safe to say that Kaepernick was unimpressed. “I just want you to know, one, you’re serving the culture up to a bunch of racists and, two, they don’t care about you,” Kaepernicklater recalled saying to Jay-Z. “You’re the music guy to them. They quite literally need a Black face – and have said as much.”Seven years later, Jay-Z is still battling Kaepernick, the man who says he was blackballed by the NFL. This summer, Jay-Z linked up with Target, whichhad been boycottedby many Black customers after it rolled back its diversity and inclusion policies. Kaepernick, on the other hand, said he would not allow his memoir to be sold at any of the chain’s stores. At a concert in July, Jay-Z rapped that Kaepernick had allowed himself to be silenced by signing his grievance with the NFL (sources close to Kaepernickhave denied this). “Buddy took a check, I ain’t even mad at him, but along with that check you have to sign a non-disparagement. I’m the one [the NFL] can’t control,” Jay-Z rapped to the crowd at Yankee Stadium.Maybe that’s true, but it doesn’t appear that Jay-Z is doing much to control – or change – the league either. In 2021,USA Today’s Mike Freeman wrote: “There isn’t a single, tangible thing you can point to that shows Jay-Z helping with the league’s social justice efforts.” That’s a little unfair; through Inspire Changethe NFL has funnelled millionsinto charities across America. At the same time, the NFL is mostly run by the same old, rich conservatives it always has been. There is still no Black majority owner of a team, and Forbes now puts the combined value of theleague’s 32 teamsat more than $300bn. In 2025, Donald Trump, who once called NFL players who protested during the national anthem“sons of bitches”, becamethe first sitting president to attend a Super Bowl, and that same week the leaguepulled “End Racism”from the endzones in New Orleans. That slogan had been on NFL fields since 2020 as part of Inspire Change.Conservatives have noticed. Acolumnpublished onSport & Statehailed Jay-Z as a “legend” and told readers there likely wouldn’t be any anti-ICE activists onstage at this season’s halftime show, adding that “after last year’s Bad Bunny debacle, Jay-Z offers a compromise.”That’s about right. Jay-Z won’t have anybody to push against at theSuper Bowl. The NFL is Roc Nation’s client, and the team owners are its partners. As we saw with the Target debacle, whatever Jay-Z says up there, he’s unlikely to go against the people who pay him.Explore more on these topicsNFLSuper BowlJay-ZUS sportsColin KaepernickcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disaster | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: Once the midterms are over, Trump will be free to pursue vendetta politics. But with will and diplomacy, he can be reined in, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: Once the midterms are over, Trump will be free to pursue vendetta politics. But with will and diplomacy, he can be reined in, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: Donald Trump at a campaign rally in Crossroads Arena, Corinth, Mississippi, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a campaign rally in Crossroads Arena, Corinth, Mississippi, 26 October 2026.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpTrump is in a corner and likely to lash out at Iran again. Here’s how to avert that disasterSimon TisdallOnce the midterms are over, Trump will be free to pursue vendetta politics. But with will and diplomacy, he can be reined inWed 28 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.40 EDTShareAs another Iran catastrophe looms, one question matters more than any other: how to stop it before it’s too late? Whatever the eventual outcome of Israel’s election and next week’s US midterm polls, Donald Trump, playing the Lone Ranger, and Benjamin Netanyahu, his badass Tonto, appear hell-bent on resuming theillegal war of choicethey began in June last year and expanded in February. Like a Shakespearean tragedy moving inexorably to a bloody denouement, the worst is yet to come. And yet three things seem certain: the US and Israel will again fail to totally destroy Iran’s largely hypothetical nuclear capabilities; its regime will survive; and millions of ordinary people, there and around the world, will pay the price for this unjustified, reckless aggression.Ducking and weaving, Trump is desperate to dodge the blame for the Republicans’ anticipated midterm meltdown, largely triggered by war-related fuel and consumer price inflation. He claimedUkraine’s attacks on Russian refinerieswere responsible, but that didn’t wash. He cut atreacherous diesel deal with Vladimir Putinbut, as usual, Russia’s smirking mafioso conned him. He urged US allies to tap their strategic reserves but, unsurprisingly, vilified and sidelined European leaders, who view his war as an unmitigated disaster and declined to bail him out. Trump alsoreportedly rebuffedlast-gasp, electorally driven pressure from Netanyahu to hit Iran this month, fearful it would unleash a Democratic tsunami.Yet once the midterm polls close, and whatever the results, all these considerations fall away. What voters think will no longer matter to Trump. At that point, he can do more or less what he wants, in foreign and defence policy, for his final two years. And what he wants has little to do with imaginary Iranian nukes, a democratic uprising in Tehran, or any of his other bogus justifications for waging war. Trump will be free to do what he does best: vendetta politics. Iran’s greatest sin is to have defied the imperial will. He wanted aneasy Venezuela-style, regime-altering victory (and sweetheart oil deals). What he got was a middle digit, burnt fingers and a forever war. Just as he vengefully pursues opponents at home, so he now victimises Iranians. It’s not rational or ideological. Like everything with Trump, ultimately it’s personal.Netanyahu’s reasons for wanting another bash are thoroughly dishonourable too, but in a different way. Given his myriad, chronic failures before and after the 2023 Hamas massacres, his trashing of Israel’s international reputation by his criminal actions in Gaza and Lebanon, and his Trump-ish slide into bigoted, ultra-nationalist authoritarianism, Netanyahu is fighting for his job and, potentially, his freedom. He insists, despite his record, that only he can ensure Israel’s security. He suggests, outrageously, thatopposition victory could pave the wayfor Israel’s destruction in a second, nuclear Holocaust. Israel’s military chiefs suspect he may restart the Iran war in order to dominate and manipulate the inevitable post-election coalition talks – hoping to stay in power and out of jail.The likely, mortifying consequences of a renewed US-Israel onslaught after 3 November should be fully understood. For starters, the price of oil will spike again, perhaps to unprecedented levels, negatively affecting people all around the world. Pentagon officials, possibly peddling disinformation,suggest Iran is preparing to retaliatewith missile and drone attacks against Saudi and other Gulf oil refineries, infrastructure and underwater internet cables, while reinforcing blockades of the strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab strait. The impact on international energy supplies, transportation and international trade generally could be far worse than last spring.Trumpreportedly plansa shock-and-awe, time-limited assault – primarily on the mountain complex where Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium is supposedly stored, plus its missile bases and energy grid. If this sounds familiar, it is. Trump’s chief gunslinger, Pete Hegseth, and his air-force cowboys claim to have destroyed many of these targets already, some more than once. Total success will probably elude them again. What’s more likely is that the war’s duration will lengthen, and more Iranian civilians will suffer the fate ofover 100 schoolgirls killedin a Tomahawk missile strike in Minab in February.
