For that atrocity and others, Trump and Hegseth have never admitted responsibility.Other foreseeable consequences include: the spread of related conflicts, involving Iranian allies and proxy militias, to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Lebanon; attacks on US embassies and personnel from Jordan to Kuwait; intensified, opportunistic settler violence and land grabs in the West Bank; stepped-up Iranian freelance assassination and sabotageoperations in Europe; further undermining of US and Israeli democracy from deliberate obstruction of war-zone accountability, official cover-ups and blatant lying, and restrictions on independent media reporting; another hugely damaging split between Washington and its reluctant European allies; and another geopolitical free lunch for the west’s anti-democratic challengers, Russia and China.Here are two more questions. By what right does the US, in particular, presume to behave in this way? Forget, if you can, Trump and Netanyahu. What does the American public (or at least, those who vote Republican) say? Have they not learned by now, after so many disastrous interventions that the world does not want, and does not need, to be saved by the US? In the age of Maga, this vulgar exceptionalism has surely had its day. Second, reformulated question: how may this looming catastrophe be prevented? Resumed warfare, leading to a wider, globally destabilising conflagration, is not inevitable. But urgent action is necessary now.A talks process, mediated by Qatar, though neglected and boycotted by the White House, has not completely collapsed. Negotiations could yet produce viable outcomes if given a chance, Badr Albusaidi, Oman’s foreign minister,told the Guardianthis week. A longer-term solution, he suggested, could be a non-aggression pact involving all six Gulf states, plus Iran and Iraq, acting on the premise that they, not the US, would be the primary, joint providers of future regional security. As Albusaidi spoke, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on a last-ditch mission to pre-empt resumed hostilities. All power to them. At least they’re trying.It would be reassuring to think Trump and Netanyahu are listening. But the bottom line is that, for their different reasons, both men probably want this war. A firm, united course of rapid, preventive action is required to head them off. Britain, its European allies and like-minded governments took a tentative,defiant step in Istanbullast weekend, urging diplomacy over violence. Now they and all the world’s democracies must stand as one and, in a formal demarche, tell the US and Israel they risk a permanent rupture with immediate and long-term negative economic, diplomatic, commercial, military and security consequences if they ignore global opinion and go to war again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump is not king of the world. And Netanyahu cannot do as he likes with impunity. It’s high time they were told.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS-Israel war on IranIran nuclear programmeIranBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: I’ve mailed off my vote in the US midterms. It will be a nail-biting watch, but easier from outside Trump’s America | Eleanor Limprecht | The Guardian
description: I’m hopeful these elections will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris
Author: Eleanor Limprecht
Headline: I’m hopeful these elections will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris
Content: Virginians cast their ballots during early midterm voting in Alexandria on 27 October. The 2026 US midterm elections are on 3 November.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenVirginians cast their ballots during early midterm voting in Alexandria on 27 October. The 2026 US midterm elections are on 3 November.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAOpinionUS midterm elections 2026I’ve mailed off my vote in the US midterms. It will be a nail-biting watch, but easier from outside Trump’s AmericaEleanor LimprechtI’m hopeful these elections will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubrisWed 28 Oct 2026 18.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTShareRecently I made my own envelope out of a sheet of paper and sticky tape, signed it and affixed a sticker. Then I took it to my nearest Australia Post shop in Sydney and mailed it.In other words, I voted from abroad in the US midterm elections. Because my last place of residence in the US was the state of Virginia, I can register to vote and request a ballot online, but the ballot still needs to be printed, signed, sealed in an envelope made of folded paper, signed again, placed inside another (store-bought) envelope and mailed in. There was nosausage sizzleor cake stall to reward me for my civic duty, and no spectre of a fine if I didn’t complete it.I give a wide berth to anything resembling a craft project (haunted by the ghosts of Easter hat parades past) but I would cross-stitch a ballot if it lessened the power that President Trump wields over my country of birth. Hell, I would papier-mache an airplane and decoupage a pilot’s licence to deliver my vote in person.What are the races to watch in the US midterm elections and why do they matter?Read moreUnfortunately, not everyone is as fervent: voter turnout in the midterm elections in the US is typically less than half the eligible voting population. The midterms are viewed as less important; in-person voting is arduous and inconvenient (with long queues, on a weekday rather than a Saturday) and some voters view state-based elections as secondary to the presidential election.3:38US midterms: what are they and why do presidents dread them? – explainerThe current administration is trying to reduce voter turnout even more because things are not looking good for Republican candidates. They have gerrymandered, sued the state of California for refusing to disenfranchise 20,000 voters, tried to restrict mail-in voting (this wasblocked by the supreme court)and alreadymade a challengeto Alaska’s Senate election results if the incumbent Republican senator Dan Sullivan does not win.Can you smell it from here? That’s not raw sewage overflow from the recent heavy rains, that’s Trump’s fear.Democrats only need three seats to gain majority in the House of Representatives and four to gain majority in the Senate. If theDemocratscontrol Congress it will be far more difficult for Trump to get his laws through. They could create committees to investigate the president and even begin an impeachment trial.Trump’s egregiously named Operation Epic Fury has caused the price of fuel to skyrocket and most Americans (two-thirds) now view the ongoing war against Iran as a mistake. As the price of fuel goes up, Trump’s approval rating sinks. (His dismantling of democracy and campaign of disinformation didn’t seem to disturb voters in the same way that this hit to the hip pocket does.)I am cautiously hopeful. I’ve spent the past two years wishing I was Canadian and rushing to turn off the radio or television at the sound of Trump’s hyperbole. Perfecting my simultaneous sigh and shrug when people hear my accent and ask me to explainhowandwhythe bully-in-chief was re-elected.Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must change | Kathryn SikkinkRead moreBut I keep recalling the awful events of 6 January 2021, when in the wake of a Trump rally, an angry rightwing mob attacked the US Capitol building after his defeat in the 2020 elections. Five people died and 174 police officers were injured while the rest of the world watched in horror. As a child in Arlington, Virginia, I visited those rotundas and chambers on field trips. As an adult here in Australia, I worried over friends and family who live and work in Washington DC. If the Republican candidates are defeated in these elections, will the administration accept the results?4:10The key Capitol attack footage shown on day two of Trump’s impeachment trial – videoThere are three million Americans who live abroad and more than 110,000 here in Australia (around 60% of us have Australian citizenship). It will be nail-biting to watch the 3 November midterm elections, but easier from afar than from within Trump’s America: a country where immigrants are endangered, abortion rights have been eroded, artificial intelligence has grown without regulation and foreign aid, environmental protections and domestic social services have been gutted. Even Trump’s tariffs are backfiring for the United States, uniting the countries they are aimed against, such as Canada. Elbows up!These midterms, I am hopeful it will be a win for democracy rather than dictatorship, for peace rather than war, and humanity rather than hubris.Just please, whatever happens, don’t ask me to explain theelectoral collegecome 2028.Eleanor Limprecht is the author ofCul de Sac,What Was Left,Long Bay,The PassengersandThe CoastExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsTrump administrationRepublicansDemocratscommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget | Aditya Chakrabortty | The Guardian
description: The financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent moment, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Author: Aditya Chakrabortty
Headline: The financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent moment, says Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionBudget 2026Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budgetAditya ChakraborttyThe financial guru’s fingerprints are all over John Healey’s red book – but Lewis is not a politician. His everyday fixes can’t meet this turbulent momentWed 28 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 14.50 EDTShareWas this Andy Burnham’s budget – the bold vision of a new prime minister who burns with a passion to topple “40 years of neoliberalism”? Fat chance. Was it John Healey’s budget – the repair job of a cautious chancellor fretting about record-high taxes, £3tn of public debt and an economy stuck in first gear? Little sign of that.This budget was cast in the image of a man who isn’t in Burnham’s government or even a Labour politician – but who appears almost every day on TV, on podcasts and is probably better known than 649 of the MPs at Westminster. Today’s budget was theMartin Lewisbudget.Lewis is theMoneySavingExpert, whose weekly Money Tipsemail advises 10 million British subscribers on cheap mortgages, Black Friday deals and how to score two pizzas for £10. Tips and tricks to stave off rising prices and make the most of the money you have. Given that the Bayeux tapestry is French, and the Koh-i-noor is Indian, Lewis may be the closest thing Britain has to a genuine national treasure.Over the past four years, since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine and sent energy prices soaring, Lewis has become more political and wielded greater influence in Westminster. His fingerprints were all over this “red book”. This morning, before the cabinet had even had its traditional pre-budget pep talk, Lewis had gone to Downing Street for a personal briefing from the chancellor on its key measures. On Radio 4’s Today programme, he was the big budget interview, rather than any politician or BBC editor.No wonder, because the most eye-catching of thebudget’s measureshad been written by the money saving expert. Scrapping standing charges on gas bills, shielding more pensioners from income tax and fixing energy bill credit against council tax bands – all of these came from Lewis’s wishlist. Beyond policies, he has also informed Burnham’s politics. At last year’s Labour conference, Lewisadvised any new prime ministerto “pick a hundred things that piss people off and fix them at one a day for the first hundred days”.Et voilà! The King of the North has vowed to end loudcasting on public transport, crack down on unfair parking fines and introducemore drop boxesfor the post … and more and more.ForLabourministers, government by MoneySavingExpert may seem a no-brainer. After a wretched couple of years under Keir Starmer, they can pose as the people’s champion, for ever on your side. Best of all, all these micro-policies cost micro-money. Today’s budget had 98 measures – more than any I can remember in decades of covering fiscal events, yet they all cost trifling sums.Which brings us to the killer problem: Lewis is one of the most trusted people in Britain. But he’s not a politician. He’s never claimed to be. He speaks the language of terms and conditions, not financialisation – and he knows his limits. To quote aNew Statesman essaylast week on the new MoneySavingPolitics: “As governments have embraced retail policies and suggestion-box-style politics in his image, Lewis has been raising the alarm that there are too many people who can no longer help themselves and it is time for structural change.”The difference was clear today. In her first budget, Rachel Reeves announcedextra spendingworth £74bn by the end of the period. By comparison, Healey announced agrand totalof £380m. For all Burnham’s grand ambition and soaring rhetoric, his first budget was only 0.5% of Starmer’s first budget.This is obviously not how the King of the North wants you to see him. Listen to Burnham speak, and you hear a changemaker, an ideas man, a leader with a 10-year plan. But does he put his money where his mouth is? Does he heck. The anxiety I have heard for months from so many of his advisers and MPs was borne out in this budget: he’s big talk and small stick.The best line of the day came from Kemi Badenoch. “The prime minister came to power promising to end 40 years of neoliberalism, and instead we got 4p off gherkins,”the Tory leader said, while Burnham and Healey frowned like men caught bang to rights. What’s the point of cut-price marmalade when a few months ago you promised to nationalise Thames Water?Why, for that matter, chuck out the old boss when the new one is less ambitious? Whacking banks with a tax in order to cut energy costs is good politics, but this new government should have been much more ambitious. A hundred pounds is a token saving when the typical household’s fuel bill is about to top £2,000. Given how harsh thisEl Niño winteris likely to be, I imagine the government will have to cobble together another intervention before the new year.Ministers are now caught in a pincer movement between Badenoch to their right, who can argue they aren’t tackling the really big problems and, to their left, the Greens and Plaid, as well as the Scottish nationalists, who will keep on saying they aren’t doing enough for their own voters. In a day of grim economic forecasts, perhaps the worst was from the Office for Budget Responsibility,which said thatin the face of high inflation, earnings willnot rise at all next year– while 2030 would see households with take-home pay just 2% above where it was before Covid struck in 2020. Put those two figures together and – despite all the Westminster chat – you can forget about a snap election that delivers Labour a new majority.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf ministers can’t offer any protection against an economic outlook that bleak, they will face an angry and mutinous public. If the Labour party wants to be re-elected, it needs to give people a reason to go out and vote for it. Pointing to bond markets isn’t a defence, because markets aren’t in open rebellion. Yes, government borrowing is a lot more expensive than it was in the post-crash years of cheap money and the interest bill on the nation’s debt is high. But no one thinks Britain is France. Gilt traders today looked at a government running down its financial buffer and were completely unruffled. Had Healey borrowed much more to invest in social and cheap housing, he could have argued that such spending would soon enough bring down benefit bills – and markets would have believed him.I write this as someone who wants Burnham to do well – and certainly to do better than today’s tiny raft of tweaks. Unlike many Labour politicians, he can talk sincerely about where disastrous rightwing politics have led this country. When he promises a new economic and political model, I – and many others – am up for it. In contrast to Starmer he doesn’t act as if he hates 80% of his own party members. Unlike Starmer’s advisers, his team doesn’t subsist on a diet of received wisdom and petty vindictiveness. But at some point, the grand rhetoric and the romantic notions need to cash out into a programme of change. Otherwise, voters will draw the conclusion that this summer’s coup against a recently elected prime minister had no grand motivation apart from saving the skins of Labour MPs and fanning a few egos.A Martin Lewis budget is fine, but Labour chose Andy Burnham as its leader and the public were promised a Burnham budget. They’re still waiting.Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist and the Guardian’s senior economics commentatorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026OpinionBudgetTax and spendingOffice for Budget ResponsibilityJohn HealeyAndy BurnhamMartin LewiscommentShareReuse this content

title: Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel responds | Polly Toynbee, Hettie O'Brien, Rohan Sathyamoorthy, Kevin Cashman, Nik and John McDonnell | The Guardian
description: Amid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Amid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AFP/REX/ShutterstockThe panelBudget 2026Will John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ budget deliver what Britain needs? Our panel respondsPolly Toynbee,Hettie O'Brien,Rohan Sathyamoorthy,Kevin Cashman,NikandJohn McDonnellAmid global economic storms, the new chancellor has promised to steer the course – with promises of more help to come. Will it be enough?Wed 28 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShare‘Growth in every postcode’? Not yet, but hope at lastPolly ToynbeeGuardian columnistFirst, he did no harm. Then he scattered sprinkles of feel-goods. He told the truth about the state we’re in, deep in anextra £14bn of expensive debt, and, though he put it politely, at the mercy of the monster in the White House’s whims on Iran and tariffs.The losers were popular targets: the banks and gambling companies. But plainly bank threats to decamp partly paid off. Their shares leapt up on the news that their surcharge would rise to only 6%, not its original 8% before Tory reductions. They expected to pay more, and indeed they should. Gambling company shares jumped up too, with Rank up more than 10% on the day when the companies were only hit with five percentage points more tax on high-stakes machines, a missed chance, but better than nothing. The Treasury makes£4bn from gambling. Time to ban their advertising next.The chancellor gave a gracious nod to his predecessor. He should be grateful, as she took the pain and he takes the gain for her £66.6bn in tax rises, in NI for employers andfrozen income tax thresholdsthat slide by unseen, but yield mightily until 2031.The publicexpected more personal taxes, according to Ipsos. It didn’t happen. Labour can take comfort that they think the Conservatives and Reform would both raise tax and cut public services.Instead, help comes for their energy costs, one of the greatest causes of household debt, with bills set to rise brutally in January. Homes in council tax bands A-D get £100 and the VAT reduction has been extended until July, while abolished standing charges leave 60% of homes better off. But the rumbling discontent that has upended our politics since Brexit is easily explained by the unprecedented long fall inmedian household income, only in the last year rising back to levels six years ago.Yet people’s priorities remain perverse: immigration stays top of their concerns, above inflation and the economy. Spending more on tougher border controls is second only to the NHS as the most popular expenditure. What do you do? Give in and let Shabana Mahmood be her harshest – or start telling people about the trade-off? Visas for work for another 200,000 migrantswould bring the Treasury £18bn, says the Office for Budget Responsibility. Think what people could have for that.Is this the “growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” Andy Burnham promises? No, not yet, not yet … Wait for his 10-year plan, spending review and an election with a new manifesto. And hope.Voters might have been hoping for something bolder than thisHettie O'BrienWriter on the Guardian’s morning newsletter First Edition, the Guardian Long Read, and the author ofThe Asset ClassWhile Keir Starmer promised to tread more “lightly” on voters’ lives, interpreting political disaffection as a sign that people wanted to hear less from their politicians, Andy Burnham has interpreted this loss of faith as a demand for more political action. But there was always a risk that without a theory of power, his premiership would come to resemble the Downing Street equivalent of the TV show Rip-Off Britain, giving voters “everyday fixes”, starter ISAs and cheaper gherkins while failing to change the economy or society as a whole.The charitable reading of John Healey’s budget is that it was better than it could have been (and better than the Treasury, which briefed this as a “low-key” event, wanted us to expect). His energy package, including a £100 cut to bills for houses in council tax brackets A-D, will help ease the cost of living and should lower inflation. He also proposed a series of changes that should help to bring down energy bills in future. But there was no help for low-income renters, nor any plans for funding public services that are facingreal-terms cuts. Bankers, meanwhile, will be breathing a sigh of relief after Healey imposed a temporary 6% tax on bank profits, below the pre-crisis level of 8%.For a government that has promised to turn back 40 years of neoliberalism, you might have been hoping for something much more radical than this. Small, short-term fixes and making it easier to cancel your Netflix subscription don’t equate to a political philosophy, let alone a programme capable of convincing voters that difficult trade-offs – whether on defence spending or the costs of an ageing society – will be worth it. Governing, as Mark McVitiewrote recently, requires political imagination and a sense of where you want to end up. Let’s hope that Andy Burnham has more to offer than this.Budget cuts to fund military spending will lead to job losses and lower growthKevin CashmanResearcher at Transition Security Project, a centre founded by Common Wealth and Climate and Community InstituteJust last month, the prime minister made the significant promise to “break with the direction of the past 40 years” and “build a new economy and a new politics”. John Healey’s budget, unfortunately, doesn’t do enough of either.Department budgets were alreadyslashed this summerto help finance the Ministry of Defence’s demand for an extra £15bn. Now, this budget adds £3bn more in cuts.In July,Transition Security Projectestimated that the defence investment plan, funded partly through £6.8bn in cuts, would result in more than 10,000 net job losses. With a further £3bn in cuts, those losses are now likely to exceed 15,000.The reason is simply that military spending is a weaker driver of growth than the investment being sacrificed to fund it. Too much of the money leaves the country – flowing, especially, to the United States.These cuts also undermine programmes that would help bring down the cost of living. The budget confirms a £1bn cut to Warm Homes, which supports heat pump grants. The additional help with household energy bills is welcome. But directing up to £5bn from the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank towards defence reinforces the same misplaced priorities when these resources could have been invested in areas that help with living standards.Burnham does not have to accept these constraints. Healey has left the detailed funding route to the Nato spending targets until next year’s spending review. These targets – pushed by the US – imply a colossal transfer of wealth from the public to the military sector. Burnham should abandon these targets he inherited, which will steal more investment from every other department.Healey was right that wars are driving up our energy bills and making Britain less safe. But let’s be honest about the role the government is playing. The US used British bases in its unprovoked attack on Iran, and our government is now backing Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen. Diplomacy and de-escalation are part of a serious cost of living strategy – not bombing.Welcome news on apprenticeships, but otherwise little cheer for young peopleRohan SathyamoorthyWriter from south-west LondonLook hard enough at this budget, and there are some signs that the chancellor is serious about bridging the age divide: an increase in tax for Britain’s banks, increased investment in apprenticeships and a new scheme for first-time buyers will be a welcome relief for many young and working people who are tired of bearing a disproportionate share of Britain’s economic burden. However, the limitations of even these mild reforms are already apparent:bank stocks roseconspicuously this morning on news that the rise would be temporary and only a mere three percentage points. And although the first-time buyer ISA will help young savers in the immediate term, in the long run it is only continuing to subsidise the housing crisis at the expense of the taxpayer, rather than intervening directly in the market to bring prices back down to an affordable level.Furthermore, while pensioners, businesses, workers, women, carers, families and even nightclubs all received explicit support from Healey, outrageously absent was any real help for young people, nor any mention of the student loan crisis. The only mention of young people not in employment, education or training was made in the context of reforming welfare. Instead of addressing the problems facing young people and making clear that he would tackle intergenerational fairness, Healey made his priority clear, with “the biggest increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war”.Ultimately, it will be impossible to fully judge this budget until we see the one that succeeds it. This “breathing space” budget will be beneficial only if it really is just that – buying time for the government to solve the painful, unignorable issues still crippling Britain’s young people: jobs, student loans, soaring rents. If the mixed rhetoric today is anything to go by, I won’t be holding my breath.I wish more had been done to help us pay our rent and fill our fridgesNikParticipant in theChanging RealitiesprojectThe chancellor said “hope starts with a home”, but for me, it’s the cost of my home that keeps me in poverty. I work multiple jobs just to pay my rent, and nothing in today’s budget will make that situation better. Where is the “breathing space” for families like mine, or hope for the future?Families struggling through the storms of living on a low income deserve more than modest, micro-policies and everyday fixes to protect them from the incessant headwinds.Extending the removal of VAT from electricity bills to next summer is being presented as help for households, but for rural families like mine, it offers little (or no) meaningful relief. I have no access to mains gas and can’t afford heating oil, so I depend on electricity to heat my home. Yet this measure does nothing to address the reality of living rurally without affordable alternatives. A record number of people now live in very deep poverty, with incomes that don’t cover the basics of food, housing or energy. We need meaningful, targeted support, not policies that offer some households a small saving while leaving others struggling to keep warm. In Cornwall, many homes rely on heating oil, and removing the kerosene tariff may help, but any savings depend on supplies holding up and suppliers passing them on.The chancellor promised a distinctly Labour approach to welfare but I know many will feel incredibly fearful about the white papers to come later this year, afterAlan MilburnandStephen Timmsdeliver their reports on youth unemployment and disability benefits.What we know from this budget is that families will be able to save about 40p on the weekly shop, assuming toffees and caramels are a part of your weekly essentials. Food poverty directly impacts health, productivity and social inclusion. I wish more had been done to help fill our fridges.This budget buys time to go bigger and bolder in next year’s spending reviewJohn McDonnellLabour MP for Hayes and Harlington. He was shadow chancellor for Labour from 2015 to 2020The chancellor has called his budget a “breathing space” budget and that’s exactly what it is. It’s less a break with Keir Starmer, but hopefully the start of a step away.The range of small-scale cost of living assistance offered on energy and food costs are all welcome elements of relief, but the harsh reality is that they provide an extremely limited breathing space.The government has to be extremely careful that the goodwill that Andy Burnham’s arrival has generated does not degenerate into disappointment and disillusionment. Reform UK may have dipped in the polls but the rise of the far right in Germany, France and Italy demonstrates all too clearly where that disappointment can lead to.This budget indicates to people that the government appreciates their concerns and is on their side, but it is absolutely critical that the time this budget may buy is used to demonstrate that it also has the plan needed to tackle the financial pressures people are under.Next year’s spending review provides that opportunity.The government has committed to the large-scale capital investment programme in council housing, home insulation and alternative energy that can stimulate the growth promised in every postcode.But there has to be demand in the economy too. That means putting money to spend in people’s pockets by modernising our taxation system to redistribute wealth and tackle the underinvestment in our public services, low pay and poverty that have held our economy back.Nobody doubts the pressure John Healey has been under as a result of the crass geopolitical nightmares caused by Donald Trump’s attacks on Iran. Both Benjamin Netanyahu and Vladimir Putin have played Trump like a fiddle to their own advantage, and we are all now paying the economic price. With the potential change in the midterms, perhaps it’s also time for leaders to start talking less about defence spending and more about peace making.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026The panelTax and spendingJohn HealeyHousingMilitarycommentShareReuse this content

title: The RBA has primed the market for an interest rate rise. But what will it mean for unemployment?  | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: Central bank forecast that unemployment might have to move even higher makes it clear how much more the RBA cares about inflation than full employment
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: Central bank forecast that unemployment might have to move even higher makes it clear how much more the RBA cares about inflation than full employment
Content: Australian unemployment rose from 4.1% in January to 4.7% in September.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenAustralian unemployment rose from 4.1% in January to 4.7% in September.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPGrogonomicsInterest ratesThe RBA has primed the market for an interest rate rise. But what will it mean for unemployment?Greg JerichoCentral bank forecast that unemployment might have to move even higher makes it clear how much more the RBA cares about inflation than full employmentFollow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastWed 28 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.21 EDTShareBack in July, the June inflation figures killed off chances of a rate rise; yesterday, however, theSeptember inflation figuresall but guarantee a rate rise next week.The September figures are a bit quirky because the Bureau of Statistics published both the monthly and old quarterly ones.The monthly measure had annual inflation jumping up from 4.0% to 4.3%; while the quarterly measure – which the RBA has in the past said was more important – remained steady at 3.9% (and if anything fell very slightly):Click here if this graph does not displayBut that did not matter: all focus was on the 4.3% number, even though monthly figures are much more erratic and subject to jumps and falls in certain prices.Cost-of-living crisis? You wouldn’t know it by looking at these companies’ profits | Greg JerichoRead moreIn September, as was the case in July and August, petrol prices were the big driver. Automotive fuel rose 9.4% in the month. They also look set to rise another 7% when the October figures come out next month:Click here if this graph does not displayIt means that around half of the increase in inflation in September came from fuel prices. This was followed by holiday costs, which always go up at the start of spring:Click here if this graph does not displayThe impact of petrol prices over the past three months is, of course, all driven by oil prices oddly refusing to react to either the RBA raising rates or Donald Trump declaring mission accomplished in Iran:Click here if this graph does not displayThe impact of petrol prices since June on overall inflation is obvious when you look at inflation with and without those prices. Without petrol prices, inflation would be at 3.6% – well below the 4.3% official rate:Click here if this graph does not displayAnd yes, 3.6% is higher than the Reserve Bank would like, but it does perhaps give an indicator of what we are dealing with here.Inflation isn’t galloping ahead due to domestic pressures; rather, it is remaining higher than the RBA’s target due to the flow through of oil prices into costs (including holidays) and directly in fuel prices.We are also seeing the impact of AI datacentres on inflation.As with last month, once again the price of games increased. That’s because we are not talking about board games, but those which require computer chips –the same type that are in such high demand for datacentres.The ABS noted that the 15.5% price rise for games, toys and hobbies in the past year was “driven by price increases in memory and storage components being passed on to consumers”.So that’s nice:enjoy paying more for Grand Theft Auto VI.But look, anything I tell you here isn’t going to make a lick of difference. The RBA is going to raise rates next week.Before the CPI release, the odds were about 61%. Afterwards they rose to 87% and a rise to 4.85% is fully priced in to happen in December:skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClick here if this graph does not displayWhat is interesting, though, is it makes it clear just how much more the RBA cares about inflation than its other mandate of full employment.When the September unemployment figures of 4.7% were released, the market quite rightly dropped the likelihood of a rate rise to a less than one in five chance. But the RBA was clearly not happy with that.Last week, the deputy governor of the RBA, Andrew Hauser, participated in afireside chatto Citigroup investors. He made it clear the RBA was not happy with things, saying “the inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in the August report”.He further said that there is “an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that maybe 3% to 3.5% is the new normal … that is the central banker’s nightmare”.And boom, the odds of a rate rise increased from 22% to 51%, and they kept going up.Click here if this graph does not displayThat means the RBA can now easily justify raising the rate next week – after all, they primed the market to do so.Hauser yesterday walked back his comments somewhat when the RBA appeared before the Senate estimates committee. He said that it was surprising “how well anchored inflation expectations remain”.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereAnd as for the increases in unemployment? That is rather less of a concern for the RBA.Greens senator Nick McKim asked Michele Bullock whether she was “worried … about the pace of the increase in unemployment, specifically what rise in unemployment would give the RBA cause for a reasonable concern that we would head into recession?”.He asked this due to unemployment rising from 4.1% in January to 4.7% in September. Claudia Sahm, a US economist, argues a 0.5% rise in the three-month average of unemployment over a year is the point at which an economy enters recession conditions.Right now, Australia’s three-month average unemployment rate has risen 0.45% in the past year, and if the October rate remains at 4.7%, it will break through the 0.5% mark:Click here if this graph does not displayBullock replied: “We’re not worried about the pace of increase in the unemployment rate at this stage. We do forecast that it has to gradually move up … I can’t be specific about what that number is. What I can say is we think that it’s probably above where the unemployment rate is at the moment.”So that’s nice. Sleep well knowing that Australia’s unemployment rate is rising but the central bank will increase rates again, knowing it might send it up even higher.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsInterest ratesGrogonomicsInflationReserve Bank of AustraliacommentShareReuse this content

title: A bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives for now – and we are more divided than ever | Dahlia Scheindlin | The Guardian
description: Exit polls gave the opposition hope, but then reality dawned. With most votes going to rightwing parties, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleak, says Tel Aviv-based political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin
Author: Dahlia Scheindlin
Headline: Exit polls gave the opposition hope, but then reality dawned. With most votes going to rightwing parties, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleak, says Tel Aviv-based political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin
Content: A supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu reacts to the first exit polls at a Likud party election event in Jerusalem, Israel, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAView image in fullscreenA supporter of Benjamin Netanyahu reacts to the first exit polls at a Likud party election event in Jerusalem, Israel, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAOpinionIsraelA bitter night in Israel for all who craved a fresh start. Netanyahu survives for now – and we are more divided than everDahlia ScheindlinExit polls gave the opposition hope, but then reality dawned. With most votes going to rightwing parties, the prospects for the left and centre now look bleakWed 28 Oct 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTShareFollowing Israel’snail-biting election, nearly every political community in the country experienced triumph and despair. The initial results swung wildly from the first exit polls to the slow real-vote count; the bloc of parties loyal to the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, might yet win, and each side feels that its fate hangs in the balance.So far, only one certainty remains: Israel’s bitter divisions are deeper than ever.At 10pm Jerusalem time, three television stations published their exit polls by veteran pollsters showing a stinging loss for Netanyahu’s current government. In all three, his current coalition won just 50 out of 120 parliamentary seats, with 70 for the opposition. It was small consolation for Netanyahu that his Likud party held a slight lead over the main challenger, the Yashar party led by former IDF chief of staffGadi Eisenkot.Millions of Israelis who voted for opposition parties felt exhilarated. Together, four Zionist lists within the opposition ran a two- or three-seat lead over Netanyahu’s bloc, though neither of those groupings was close to a 61-seat majority. Eisenkot gave a passionate speech about the defeat of the “coalition of failure”, by a “larger and stronger Zionist majority”. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, another leading opposition figure, declared that the “alliance of those who served” had won – referencing Israelis who have served in the military, while Netanyahu’s government had shielded Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jews from service during Israel’s longest and bloodiest war.Those first polls also showed an unprecedented gain for parties representing Arab-Palestinian citizens of Israel, with 17 or 18 seats out of 120. That community, about one-fifth of the population, had a powerful turnout ofmore than 75%. In earlier years, their turnout rates had lagged behind those of Jewish voters. Many Arab citizens preferred to avoid legitimising elections in a country that has discriminated against them since its founding, alongside ongoing occupation and now full-blown war against Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.But the community was seized by the urgency of ousting ultra-nationalist, anti-Arab extremists in the current government. Calls to boycott elections nearly vanished, and the first results made Arab parties look like kingmakers for coalition bargaining.Netanyahu’s camp would have been dejected at first. To be sure, two additional exit polls showed more flattering results for his bloc, but these were commissioned by right-leaning channels that many viewed as biased. Throughout the campaign, their poll findings had been outliers.View image in fullscreenOpposition leader Gadi Eisenkot celebrates the release of the exit polls at the Yashar party’s campaign headquarters in Tel Aviv, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Paulina Patimer/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThen the counting began. Within hours, Netanyahu’s bloc staged a reversal, pulling significantly ahead of the four opposition Zionist parties many hoped would replace him. The Arab parties retained a strong showing but lower than the original heady projections. But three of the four Zionist parties preferred to exclude them for coalition-building purposes. As a result, even if the total opposition vote outweighs support for the outgoing government, Netanyahu might have done it again.It is not yet clear if any one group of parties can reach a 61-seat majority. Negotiations to form a coalition will take dizzying twists in the coming weeks; maybe a minority government or a stalemate will be the unsatisfying result. But one thing is certain. Israel’s divisions have never been more profound. Blocs, camps and tribes have never been more irreconcilable.The majority of Israelis who voted for any opposition party cannot fathom how they will survive under another extremist, anti-democratic, pro-war coalition led by Netanyahu and his theocratic allies.Yet the clear majority of the voters supported ideologically rightwing parties, who hold perhaps 74 seats at present, including Netanyahu’s bloc and at least two clearly rightwing opposition parties led by Avigdor Lieberman and Bennett. The centre and left wing in Israel cannot fathom how they will survive under these nationalist, militarist, illiberal lawmakers with a firm majority in Knesset, regardless of the government.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArab citizens could suffer the most severe disappointment. In return for their greatest-ever political participation, with the singular aim of ousting a government that loathes them, their efforts may have gone for nought.Israel’s moderately leftwing Democrats party appears on course to reach around nine seats, more than twice the parliamentary strength of an equivalent party in the last Knesset. But for roughly 20% of all Israelis who call themselves leftwing, who dream of a country that no longer lords it over Palestinians and still dares to hope one day for peace, there is little horizon for hope.Israel has always been famously divided, yet managed somehow to hold together. Now, the lively disagreements of the past have given way to fundamental, even existential questions about whether the people of Israel have anything in common with each other; and whether some will simply give up and go.Dahlia Scheindlin is a political analyst in Tel AvivExplore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahucommentShareReuse this content

title: The climate crisis will destroy our economies – we learned this 20 years ago. When will we act?  | Fiona Harvey | The Guardian
description: The radical Stern report showed that a low-carbon future is also good economics. But it seems that capitalism needs a reminder, says Fiona Harvey, an environment editor at the Guardian
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: The radical Stern report showed that a low-carbon future is also good economics. But it seems that capitalism needs a reminder, says Fiona Harvey, an environment editor at the Guardian
Content: Flood water at Fishlake, in Doncaster, South Yorkshire, November 2019.Photograph: Richard McCarthy/PAView image in fullscreenFlood water at Fishlake, in Doncaster, South Yorkshire, November 2019.Photograph: Richard McCarthy/PAOpinionClimate crisisThe climate crisis will destroy our economies – we learned this 20 years ago. When will we act?Fiona HarveyThe radical Stern report showed that a low-carbon future is also good economics. But it seems that capitalism needs a reminderWed 28 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTShareSaving the only planet we have makes good economic sense. There is, after all, no money to be made on a dead Earth. There may be costs involved now, but they are worth paying to protect our children from certain destruction.These propositions seem self-evident now. But two decades ago, mainstream economists had very different ideas. They had proved that the climate crisis would be a mere economic blip, easily absorbed by growing economies and therefore not worth spending money on. In their accounting, they considered ice caps and glaciers functionally worthless, that trees only add to GDP when they are cut down, and that a livable climate shouldn’t even merit a line on a spreadsheet.What changed? Twenty years ago this week an earth-shaking report was published by Nicholas Stern, a former World Bank chief economist turned adviser to Gordon Brown. His review, The Economics of Climate Change,upended conventional wisdomamong economists and dragged them into a new century. It set out, for the first time, in clear and bold terms, why investing in a low-carbon futuremakes economic sense.TheStern review, in 700 dense pages full of graphs and data, is a model of transformative thinking. Using standard economic tools and methods, and in ways that other mainstream economists could understand, Stern made three key, and at the time radical, conclusions: that the costs of inaction on the climate were greater than the costs of action; that the climate crisis was a market failure; and that economic growth was compatible with cutting greenhouse gas emissions.Stern’s crucial insight, the revolutionary idea on which his whole thesis turned, was that future generations have as much right to be born as we did. Traditional economicsmistrusts anything that could happen in the future, applying a “discount rate” to it. Likely future profits are reckoned as lower in value than those of the present, as are likely future losses.View image in fullscreenEconomist Nicholas Stern at COP26 in Glasgow, November 2021.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersThat might make sense when compiling companies’ accounts, as it prevents them over-selling themselves on optimistic assumptions. But applying a discount rate where the climate is concerned is a gross distortion – effectively, it means future lives are assigned less value, and so taking actions now that protect children when they grow up are made to appear uneconomic.To gauge how startling this proposal was at the time, consider William Nordhaus, former professor of economics at Yale, whose work was the previous standard for climate economics. He confidently asserted in the early 1990s thatcountries should budget for “moderate” global heating, of about 3C to 4C above preindustrial levels, because below that the cost of cutting greenhouse gas emissions would outweigh the damage of climate change. In order to reach these conclusions, Nordhaus’s work relied on the same “discounting” assigned to future damage and future lives that Stern set out to challenge.The vitriol poured on Stern by fellow economists –including Nordhaus– was intense.I covered it at the time for the Financial Times, and I remember the spluttering outrage of traditional economists, fuming that the discount rate – a central tenet of Treasury forecasting around the world – could be meddled with. The ethical point appeared to elude them. Ethics have little place in GDP.But Stern stuck to his analysis, and in the 20 years since it has been found sound – if anything, he underestimated both the rapidity of heating and economic consequences, and overestimated the cost of renewable energy. Stern’s work liberated many governments: they could now justify bold climate strategies to investors, aid donors and the ever-present bond markets. Conversely, laggard administrations could be challenged at the ballot box and, increasingly,in court.Today, Stern says, if he were re-doing the review, he would place more emphasis on the role of nature, as the collapse of biodiversity around the world is a key economic andnational security threat that has been grossly underestimated, and neglected as a result.It might seem, in 2026, as if Stern has won the argument. But traditional economic approaches to the climaterefuse to go away. In 2018, even after a deluge of science showing that3C heating would leave coastal cities under waterand swathes of agricultural land as desert, Nordhaus published apaper claiming that 3C would reduce global GDP by just 2.1%, and even a 6C increase would incur just 8.5% GDP loss. However, other climate scientists have indicated that at 6Cwidespread faminecould leave billions of people, in economic terms, suboptimally productive. Or, as the rest of us might say, dead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2018, Nordhaus was awarded the Nobel prize. His work on the climate wasprominent in the citationand his prize lecture. In hundreds of universities around the world, economists arestill being trained todayin those same traditional growth models he used. And sunny predictions that the climate crisis could shave just a few per cent off GDP arestill in use, shockingly, among governments, businesses and international institutions, even as temperatures shatter records and thesupercharged El Niñothreatens trillions of dollars in damages.The results are plain to see: governments refusing to act, markets over-valuingfossil fuel companies, investorspunishing businessesthat dare to prepare for a low-carbon world. Many insurance companies, supposedly the enforcers of probity in capital markets, are alleged to knowingly be fudging their figures to massage climate risk away, as the Guardianrevealed this month.If we are to have a thriving future economy, as well as a living planet and robust human societies, we need a new system of economics thatvalues these things. Stern showed the way. Twenty years later, the rest of the world must catch up.Fiona Harvey is an environment editor at the GuardianExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionNicholas SternEconomic policyGreen economyFossil fuelscommentShareReuse this content

title: I couldn’t afford food on jobseeker after bills and rent. Is this really what ‘no one left behind’ looks like?  | Travis Gilbert | The Guardian
description: Trying to make ends meet on around $58 a day is a cruel joke bestowed upon those who find themselves unemployed in the ‘lucky country’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trying to make ends meet on around $58 a day is a cruel joke bestowed upon those who find themselves unemployed in the ‘lucky country’
Content: ‘Right now, the jobseeker payment is too low to enable people to participate in the things that can help them move from “welfare to work”.’Photograph: Stefan Postles/AAPView image in fullscreen‘Right now, the jobseeker payment is too low to enable people to participate in the things that can help them move from “welfare to work”.’Photograph: Stefan Postles/AAPOpinionWelfareI couldn’t afford food on jobseeker after bills and rent. Is this really what ‘no one left behind’ looks like?Travis GilbertTrying to make ends meet on around $58 a day is a cruel joke bestowed upon those who find themselves unemployed in the ‘lucky country’Tue 27 Oct 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 02.33 EDTShareIn 2022, when Anthony Albanese was making his pitch to voters to change the country by changing the government, I was briefly encouraged by one aspect of Labor’s platform.Albanese pledged a new social contract for Australia, with “no one held back and no one left behind”.Three years later, as I found myself receiving jobseeker for the first time in two decades and with just $45.95 a week left after paying my landlord, I suddenly realised I was feeling both held back, and a long way behind my employed peers.I am not alone.Foodbank’s report on food insecurityreleased on Monday has again brought the lived experience of poverty back into the spotlight.Welfare in Australia is a cruel shambles. How about we actually try to help people not squish them | First Dog on the MoonRead moreThere are up to 900,000 people in Australia asked to make ends meet on around $58 a day. That is a tough enough ask for those in social housing; in the private rental market, it is a cruel joke bestowed upon people who find themselves unemployed in the “lucky country”.In the age of “conditional welfare” we are asked to attend fortnightly compliance appointments with publicly funded, privately owned job agencies, maintain an internet and phone connection to upload proof of compliance with their “approved activities” and get frequent texts about the consequences of not meeting their monthly “points target”.With my $46 a week, I prioritised internet ($17.50), mobile phone ($5) and paying my electricity in advance ($24).While grateful to live in a country with a “safety net”, it only covered these four expenses.There was no money for contents insurance, food, GP visits, medication or public transport to and from the fortnightly appointments with my compliance officer (“employment consultant”). The payment would not even stretch to cover a bus fare – a problem in the age of conditional social security.One of the compulsory activities I must attend or else earn demerit points (like a recalcitrant driver) and go from the “green zone” to the red zone (“wilful non-compliance” and $0), is a fortnightly face-to-face appointment 8km from my flat.I walk a lot, but a 16km round trip to confirm I am no better off than I was a fortnight ago is beyond my level of fitness.I was fortunate enough to gain temporary employment on a project which gave me a few thousand dollars to draw down on to buy food, pay to see a doctor, buy medication, and insure the contents of my flat. Others on jobseeker are not so lucky, and the lie that it is a temporary payment is borne out in the department’s own stats, that show half the people rely on it for more than two years.For me, living in suburban Canberra, the jobseeker payment is about $120 a week below where it needs to be in order to afford food and things like medical appointments, medication and insurance.Food pantries and charities become essential for those on jobseeker, especially if you want to avoid predatory lenders.My defiant (though not optimistic) hope is this government, or the one that replaces it, finally accepts the enormous weight of evidence from welfare rights advocates, business groups, community legal centres, the OECD and parliament’s own economic advisory body.That evidence says unequivocally that a substantial and permanent increase to the jobseeker payment is long overdue, and is needed to ensure it is fit for purpose as a safety net that supports people who can, to re-enter the workforce.Right now, the payment is too low to enable people to participate in the things that can help them move from “welfare to work”.Raise the rate for good. Help restore dignity and transform lives.Travis Gilbert lives in CanberraExplore more on these topicsWelfareOpinionCentrelinkAustralian economyInequalitycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Israel’s elections: Netanyahu lost his mandate. If opponents unite, he’ll lose power too | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: His chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work withPalestinian Israeli parties
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: His chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work withPalestinian Israeli parties
Content: ‘Mr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine”.’Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Mr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine”.’Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/GettyOpinionBenjamin NetanyahuThe Guardian view on Israel’s elections: Netanyahu lost his mandate. If opponents unite, he’ll lose power tooEditorialHis chief rival should reject the prime minister’s anti-democratic vision and work with Palestinian Israeli partiesWed 28 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.55 EDTShareBenjamin Netanyahu haslost his mandatebut not, so far, power. While final votes are still being tallied, most voters picked his opponents on Tuesday. His bloc’s share of seats remains the largest, but appears to have slumped by around 10, leaving it below the 61 needed for a majority in the Knesset. Palestinian Israeli parties surged, and are projected to almost double the 10 seats they held. The result is that Mr Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the military, now faces a choice: fall into line with Mr Netanyahu’s racist fearmongering or work with Arab-led parties.The prime minister who oversaw shocking security failures ahead of the Hamas atrocities of 7 October 2023 still pitches himself as “Mr Security”.On trial for corruption, he has persistently attacked democratic institutions, especially the judiciary. He embraced and then indulged the ultra-right as they cheered onbrutal settler violencein the occupied West Bank. (Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich lost ground in these polls, but perhaps due to their vision’s permeation of mainstream politics more than a revolt against it.) Mr Netanyahu’s war on Iran has destabilised the region. The tens of thousands of Palestinians killed by his government’s genocidal war on Gaza have barely featured in the election campaign, butits cost for Israeli hostagesand international support for Israel have been noted by voters.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot.Photograph: JNA/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockMr Netanyahu relied on fear, campaigning with the slogan “the right or Palestine” andaccusingPalestinian citizens of Israel, around a fifth of its population, of trying to “steal the election”. They haveoften boycotted their democratic right, in a system stacked against them, with politics moving rightwards. Mr Eisenkot’s bloc gives themlittle reason for optimism; Tuesday’s turnout testifies totheir desperation to see an endto the most extreme government in Israel’s history. Millions of Palestinians living under illegal Israeli occupation got no vote at all.Mr Netanyahu, the consummate survivor, maypin his hopes on another election. For now, as incumbent, he holds extra cards. The greatest danger is that he pushes Donald Trump into a renewed offensive on Iran after the midterms, seeing perma-war as political salvation.Mr Eisenkot, one of many burned by their dealings with the prime minister, is unlikely to risk a “unity government”. His bloc could remove Mr Netanyahu “if it is brave enough”,observed Ahmad Tibiof the Joint List ticket of Palestinian parties. In campaigning, most opposition Israeli politicians ruled out a coalition with the Joint List or Ra’am (the United Arab List) – except on termsthat they will not accept. But the Palestinian parties have made clear that they are open to cooperation and there is precedent. Mr Netanyahu himself reportedlymade overturesto Ra’am in 2021; instead it joined the coalition that unseated him.“We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,”wrote Yair Golan, head of the centre-left Democrats – noting that Mr Netanyahu talks of a Zionist majority but relies on the support of non-Zionist Harediparties. Mr Eisenkot may fear that supporters will not tolerate a deal but they will not thank him for failing to boot out Mr Netanyahu when given the chance. That would also allow the prime minister to turn this result into an ideological victory. Israel defines itself as Jewish and democratic. Mr Eisenkot and his partners should accept every vote and citizen as equal.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
