title: The bare-handed beekeeper who looks like something out of The Odyssey: Holly Lynton’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. “Should I put them on my face?” he said. “Sure!” I replied’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. “Should I put them on my face?” he said. “Sure!” I replied’
Content: ‘I got a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up’ … US photographer Holly Lynton’s Bare Handed Les, Honeybees.Photograph: Holly LyntonView image in fullscreen‘I got a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up’ … US photographer Holly Lynton’s Bare Handed Les, Honeybees.Photograph: Holly LyntonMy best shotPhotographyThe bare-handed beekeeper who looks like something out of The Odyssey: Holly Lynton’s best photograph‘Les didn’t wear gloves as he needed to be able to feel the bees so he didn’t crush them. “Should I put them on my face?” he said. “Sure!” I replied’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 28 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe jumping-off point for myBare Handed serieswas a bird becoming trapped in the netting around the raspberry bushes in my backyard. It made me think of the problem humans have interacting with the natural world. How do we navigate obtaining food and the other things we need while still being good stewards of the land? I’d seen work by photographers demonstrating how Big Agriculture was destroying the environment. I wanted to find people who took a respectful approach, tried to work in tandem with it, but who might be in a fearful or dangerous situation.I approached Les, the man in this picture, after speaking to the director of an exhibition space in Albuquerque, New Mexico, who had hired him to remove a feral beehive from his tree. I’d already tried to photograph another beekeeper who wore a full protective suit, but he might as well have been an astronaut. With Les, I was able to stay nearby and work with him over three days. The first couple involved straightforward documentary pictures of him tending his hives. Then, on the third day, his apprentice Amber showed up to help.Les had the queen bee in a cage in his shirt pocket and asked Amber to take it out. Wherever the queen is, the rest of the colony will swarm. There’s a picture I made whereLes and Amber are joined together by bees, and that was my “ah ha!” moment. Amber took out the queen and placed her in Les’s hand, which is where the bees went next. He looked at me with his hands full of bees and said: “Should I put them on my face?” I said: “Sure!”Les slowly moved his hands up to his face.Beesdon’t like hair, which is why they’re not in his beard or the top of his head. He closed his eyes for a few minutes, and I photographed. Afterwards, he said: “You know, I couldn’t hear anything but the buzzing.” I don’t think he’d ever done that before. People sometimes have their own ideas, which I just go with. One of the reasons I like spending some time with them is that when they’re engaged in work, it’s almost like watching a dance and waiting for the right gesture.double quotation markThe bees were landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see themLes didn’t wear gloves when handling the bees. He said he needed to be able to feel them so he didn’t crush them, and that it was too hot to wear a suit. I wore a shirt that buttoned up tight at the wrists and tried wearing a beekeeper’s veil, too, but I abandoned that after finding it hard to focus through the mesh. I did get a bee buzzing in my ear and had to walk away until she let up.I was using a medium-format analogue camera, and the bees were also landing on my hands while I was looking through the lens. I could feel them but not see them. That was disconcerting, but Les advised me just to move slowly, as he did. That worked: I didn’t get stung.A grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photographRead moreFor a while, the photograph of Amber and Les joined together by bees was the one I preferred. I was worried people would find the bees on his face over the top. The themes of the project were quickly reinforced when I photographed wolves in a sanctuary with their trainers, and then went out with a family of catfish noodlers in rural Oklahoma. “Noodling” involved them catching these fish with their bare hands – even though they can weigh 45kg and really fight back. I realised none of these people had any fear. They were all experts at whatever it was they were doing, and for them this was a spiritual, meditative practice. That became the focus for the series.Before I started taking photography classes, I planned to be a psychologist and a writer. But what I love about photography is that you can create ambiguous narratives, a multilayered story in a single frame. A lot of my work references cultural memory. Rather than straight documentary, I’m aiming for something more mythic, and gestures that happen spontaneously can sometimes seem to reference a certain myth or biblical allusion. This photograph leans more towards Greek mythology, even if it doesn’t directly reference an exact story. Les isn’t Odysseus but, like him, he elects to hear rather than protect himself, which makes him feel like he’s a part of The Odyssey, somehow.View image in fullscreenHolly Lynton.Photograph: Holly LyntonHolly Lynton’s CVBorn:Boulder, Colorado, 1972High point:High points occur when my photographs are both made and shown. When photographing, a high point is when everything aligns – the light, content, composition – and I create an unanticipated image that transcends the moment. One that elicits allusion, mystery and wonder. In terms of exhibitions or publications, it’s often what is recent. In the past few years, institutions as varied as the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City and Bristol Cathedral in England have exhibited my work. I’m thankful that institutions have enabled people from many different backgrounds and perspectives to see my photographs. Talking with viewers and hearing their reactions has been a real gift. My book Bare Handed, published by L’Artiere, was another high point.Top tip:Right now, the quest for authenticity instead of artifice feels crucial, and what I’d urge photographers to undertake. I’d also say there is no such thing as too much curiosity (even though some people might make you think so). Don’t be afraid to change your mind about what you are working on, the meaning behind it or how to go about it. Reframing is what I like to call it. Follow your intuition. And find the joy in the practice of making work and being creative. Difficult moments will occur, and ones that feel like failures, but it’s the journey, not the end goal.Holly Lynton’s exhibition,Beyond the Bounds, is at Bristol Cathedraluntil 15 November, part ofBristol photo festivalExplore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotBeesInsectsAnimalsFarmingArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars glory | Movies | The Guardian
description: Oozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it up
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: Oozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it up
Content: Spanish civil war meets Grindr … singer Guitarricadelafuente makes his acting debut in La Bola Negra.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyView image in fullscreenSpanish civil war meets Grindr … singer Guitarricadelafuente makes his acting debut in La Bola Negra.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyMoviesInterview‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars gloryRyan GilbeyOozing panache and bagging awards already, La Bola Negra is an eye-popping war and prejudice epic starring Penélope Cruz in a blond wig and Glenn Close speaking Spanish. We meet the ex-lovers who dreamed it upWed 28 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – the directing duo known in their nativeSpainas “Los Javis” – began writing their queer epic La Bola Negra, they weren’t thinking about whether it would be stylish (which it is) or win numerous awards (which it has) or capture what they refer to as “the anti-fascist zeitgeist” (which it does). Instead, they thought only of scale. “I’m done with LGBTQ+ movies being niche,” says Ambrossi. “I was like, ‘Let’s make the biggest, gayest war movieever.’” Job done.At Cannes this year, the best director prize was awarded jointly to them and to Paweł Pawlikowski, who made the Thomas Mann road trip filmFatherland. La Bola Negra is now an Oscars frontrunner, with best picture and best director nominations all but guaranteed. Brimming with panache, the movie darts back and forth between three stories set in Spain: in 1932, a young man applying for membership of an exclusive casino is rejected on the grounds of his suspected homosexuality; in 1937, a callow nationalist soldier develops tender feelings for the injured republican prisoner under his watch; and in 2017, a queer historian inherits an unfinished story by Federico García Lorca. That story lends the movie its title and provides the thread that sews its strands together.double quotation markPeople are videoing themselves before watching it – then afterwards when they’re crying and huggingThrow in spectacular set pieces, Ken Russell-style visual flair, cameos from a blond-wiggedPenélope Cruzand a Spanish-speaking Glenn Close, and the result is a maximalist collage where the Spanish civil war sits side-by-side with Grindr hook-ups. “We loved imagining scenes that you don’t usually have in queer movies,” says Ambrossi, citing the spectacular opening sequence in which a Spanish village is bombed by Italian fascists. “A lot of people have said they’ve been missing something like this. They want to buy popcorn and be given a big movie like Titanic.” His eyes widen. “This is the gay Titanic!”View image in fullscreenBeating Scorsese … Penélope Cruz entertains the troops in the film.Photograph: Carla Oset/Netflix/AltitudeRelaxing at a corner table in the restaurant of a London hotel, Los Javis represent a study in contrasts. Ambrossi is 42, dinky and loquacious, his impish face crowned with a laurel of curls. He leans forward as he talks, arms folded on the white tablecloth. The taller, taciturn Calvo, 35, is gravely handsome. Battling jet lag, he repeatedly stretches his limbs like a cat, sneaking a glance at himself in the mirror next to the table as he does so. Both men have black caterpillar eyebrows, as well as cheekbones that could double as clothing rails.On this chilly autumn morning, Los Javis could do with some extra layers. They rub their bare arms furiously until an assistant arrives bearing hoodies. Then again, maybe the three of us have goosebumps not from the cold but from discussing their film. Ambrossi approves of this theory: “There’s a trend on TikTok where people video themselves – ‘This is usbeforewatching La Bola Negra’ – and then it cuts to afterwards when they’re crying and hugging. All this togetherness from the cinematic experience is beautiful.” No wonder Los Javis insisted on an extended theatrical window for their film before selling the US rights to Netflix. La Bola Negra will remain in US cinemas for 47 days, a record for the streaming platform. Even Scorsese didn’t get that.The movie also marks a personal breakthrough for the pair, who first met when they were actors. “Friends who read the script said to us, ‘Oh, you’re goingthere?’” recalls Ambrossi. “We’ve been writing together for 13 years about LGBTQ+ characters but it has always been, like, lesbians, trans women …” Previous collaborations include their 2017 debut film, Holy Camp!, which they adapted from La Llamada, their stage musical about a summer camp staffed by nuns. In one scene, God materialises to sing I Will Always Love You. Their 2023 series La Mesías (nowstreaming on Mubi) is a hypnotically bizarre tale of Christian pop stars, extraterrestrials and bad parenting. But no gay men.View image in fullscreen‘I was told to cut my hair, not paint my nails’ … Javier Ambrossi, Guitarricadelafuente and Javier Calvo on set.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWhat took them so long? “Sometimes you don’t want to talk about yourself,” offers Calvo, speaking up at last. “Many queer creators have projected themselves into other characters. Pedro Almodóvar, Lorca with The House of Bernarda Alba, Michael Patrick King with Sex and the City.” He flashes a rare smile. “Good show.”Ambrossi identifies a psychological dimension to the delay: “It’s true you don’t want to be too on-the-nose. But you start wondering if there is also another reason.” In the 1932 strand of the film, the elite casino members use a system of black and white balls to vote on admitting newcomers. The black ball for no–la bola negra– becomes a symbol of queer generational shame and rejection that must be wrestled with. Is it shame, then, that kept Ambrossi from addressing his own sexuality in his work? “In my case, yes. I wasn’t ready to talk about desire or sex because I felt ashamed in some way.”He and Calvo were already friends with their compatriot and hero Almodóvar, whose company El Deseo, meaning Desire, co-produced La Bola Negra. “I told Pedro, ‘I don’t deal well with desire.’ He looked at me and said, ‘You need to start.’ That’s when it clicked: if you don’t deal explicitly with desire, you are missing life.”View image in fullscreenLorca scholar … Glenn Close and Carlos González discuss the great Spanish writer.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyPerhaps that is why the word “explicit” crops up several times in Ambrossi’s conversation today: having been out as a gay man but under the radar in his work, he is eager now to emphasise the ways in which La Bola Negra is defiant or unequivocal. One aspect is the casting of gay actors in gay roles, most notably the Bambi-eyed singer Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his screen debut as the lovestruck soldier.“It’s not that straight actors can’t play gay,” says Calvo. “There are no rules in art. But …” Ambrossi jumps in: “We like to do it this way. When I was 10, I watched Rupert Everett in My Best Friend’s Wedding. I wasn’t sure I was gay, but I knew he was like me. There was a truth in his eyes that I want to get in my movies.” He sighs. “Rupert Everett was so brave. He should have been James Bond.”La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people’s choice awardRead moreCalvo had an unhappy experience as a young gay actor. “I was a teenager playing a gay role on TV,” he says. “When it finished, I didn’t get many auditions. I was advised to cut my hair, not paint my nails.” A short back and sides didn’t help, though. “I guess people could still tell. So I decided to write roles for actors who don’t have space in the industry.”Once the pair began dating as well as working together, the two-headed queer celebrity phenomenon of Los Javis was born. They were playwrights, film-makers, actors and reality TV participants, including regular judges on the Spanish version of Ru Paul’s Drag Race. Being an indispensable part of Spanish cultural life came at a price. Calvo points to this now as one of the reasons he and Ambrossi separated during the making of La Bola Negra. “People would talk to me in the plural all the time, ‘It was nice to meet you guys.’ I’d be like, ‘Huh? I’m standing alone here.’ I felt I’d lost my individuality.”View image in fullscreenMeet the judges … Ambrossi and Calvo (far right) in Drag Race España All Stars, 2024.Photograph: AtresplayerSpain didn’t cope well with the breakup. “It was a big deal,” Calvo admits. “There were cameras outside my door for a month.” Keen to move on, Ambrossi displays a flicker of irritation: “I think we’ve passed through this conversation. Imagine everyone talking about your ex forever! We love to write and direct together and we’re going to keep doing that.” The matter is closed.After all the diversifying and cross-platforming, Los Javis have reached their Pokémon-style final evolution. “From now on, we want to focus on movies,” says Calvo. No regrets, though. “The other things were important in making a statement,” Ambrossi points out. “I grew up thinking directors should be serious and monolithic. We represented a new way.” Calvo lifts a finger: “A non-binary way,” he says. “We don’t see life as stiff. We mix genres. A more flexible time is coming. Take the work seriously but not yourself.”La Bola Negra review – the complicated secrets of gay sexuality in Spain are brilliantly toldRead moreBefore they go, there is a line in La Bola Negra that I ask them to unpack. When the modern-day researcher Alberto asks the Lorca scholar played byGlenn Closefor advice on what he should do with the pages of that incomplete story, she tells him: “You’ve inherited something and you don’t know what to do with it. You are truly a Spaniard.”Calvo is happy to help. “In Spain, we always have to be reminded by foreigners that we have a rich, interesting culture and history,” he says. Ambrossi elaborates: “It is as if pride is shameful. When someone is doing well and winning awards all over Spain, people are like, ‘Hmm. That’s not very Spanish.’ Unless it’s football.” Where does that attitude come from? “Maybe religion,” muses Calvo. “Maybe dictatorship.”Does it apply to them? Are they destined to underplay their triumphs for ever? They offer their best you’ve-got-to-be-kidding looks, then answer in unison: “Not us.”La Bola Negra is in UK cinemas from 6 November.Explore more on these topicsFilmPeriod and historical filmsPenélope CruzGlenn CloseFederico García LorcaSexualityLGBTQ+ rightsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I knead the audience, like a baker!’ House music legend Peven Everett on life after cancer and vanquishing the ‘Disco Sucks’ movement | Music | The Guardian
description: The prolific house and soul musician is the subject of a new documentary which follows him from child trumpet prodigy to becoming ‘everyone’s favourite artist, you just don’t know it yet’
Author: Kate Hutchinson
Headline: The prolific house and soul musician is the subject of a new documentary which follows him from child trumpet prodigy to becoming ‘everyone’s favourite artist, you just don’t know it yet’
Content: ‘Everyone’s favourite artist – you just don’t know it yet’ … Peven Everett.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘Everyone’s favourite artist – you just don’t know it yet’ … Peven Everett.Photograph: PRHouse musicMusicInterview‘I knead the audience, like a baker!’ House music legend Peven Everett on life after cancer and vanquishing the ‘Disco Sucks’ movementKate HutchinsonA new documentary follows the Chicagoan from child trumpet prodigy to Gabriel-singing icon and DIY maverick. ‘Not everybody wants to see musical genius’, he saysWed 28 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt We Out Here festival in Dorset in August, thousands of people could be heard singing a trumpet melody as if it was a giant brass-band karaoke session. On stage was Peven Everett, performing a rendition ofGabriel, one of the most celebrated anthems in dance-music history. Co-created with producer Roy Davis Jr, the best-known version, which blew up in UK clubs in the mid-90s, is a spiritual garage-house track about the “archangel of love” that can bring both punters and DJs to tears.But Everett is much more than one song. Damon Albarn ofGorillaztells me that “Peven has a once-in-a-generation voice … he’s a great inspiration to us all.” We Out Here founder, Gilles Peterson says that the Chicagoan is, alongside Detroit’s Moodymann and Amp Fiddler, “the closest thing dance music has to a Prince-type figure”. A prolific multi-instrumentalist and one-man cottage industry, Everett’s catalogue spans more than 500 tracks, across house, neo-soul, hip-hop, samba and more.As with Prince, Everett’s audience can expect something different with each performance; they’re often improvised and don’t have strict setlists. “I’m kneading the audience into position, like a baker,” says the 51-year-old. He claims the Prince-fluence goes both ways after the latter attended one of his shows in the mid-to-late 2000s. “He started going more into dance music at that exact time,” says Everett. “He knew what I was doing: he’d seen it for himself.”View image in fullscreenA still from Peven Everett: Voice of a Generation.Photograph: PRWhen we speak, Everett is preparing to join Gorillaz for the Chicago stop of their world tour. It’ll be the first time he’s been on stage with them since 2022, having contributed to their 2017 album Humanz. “It’s going to be one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to do,” he says. “I used to have some control over how much I gave emotionally, but tomorrow, I don’t think I’ll have that.” Two years ago, Everett was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer, just as his career was gathering pace. “A part of me feels like I let the people down by getting sick,” he says. “I missed a step.”He’s now completed treatment and his life and artistry is the subject of a new documentary by Denholm Hewlett (son of Jamie, the visual artist behind Gorillaz). “People always refer to him as a house music artist,” says Hewlett. “But he was a trumpet prodigy by the age of 12 and was raised by jazz royalty.” Before dance music, Everett gave up a scholarship at Boston’s Berklee College of Music to go on the road with his mentor, Betty Carter, and the Marsalis brothers, Wynton and Branford. When he was 21,a 1995 New York Times articleasked whether Everett was the next Miles Davis.But Everett returned to Chicago to look after his ailing mother, where he teamed up with the producer Roy Davis Jr. Out of those mid-90s sessions came 1999 deep house staple Watch Them Come, as well as Gabriel. The original version of Gabriel has more of a typical four-to-the-floor beat but it was its Live Garage Mix that resonated in the UK as DJs found that its swung drums matched the pace of the nascent UK garage scene.Roy Davis Jr: Gabriel ft Peven Everett – videoIt was rereleased in 1997, reaching No 22 in the charts. At the time, US dance music was often associated with a big “diva” vocal; in the documentary, producer Marc Cary claims that Everett “brought a richness to house music” that previously didn’t exist.Peterson says the song has become a dance-music standard, while Everett recalls dancing at Chicago’s Red Dog club in the early 2000s, when he claims that Thomas Bangalter of Daft Punk and vocalist Benjamin Diamond approached him. Two years earlier, they had a huge hit with Music Sounds Better With You under the name Stardust. “That was funny. They were like, ‘Yo,we made Stardustbecause of Gabriel, we used that as a template.’ I guess it’s kind of a compliment. At least they had the grace to tell me.”Though some early Gabriel promos did not mention his name, and some have knownthe song as a Roy Davis Jr track, Everett says he was not simply a hired hand (he also played that unmistakable trumpet part). “When I go into any studio,” says Everett, “I make the vocals: I arrange them, I sing them. I make the horn and keyboard parts: I arrange them, I play them.” In the past, Everett has raised the subject of his contributions to the track on social media; today he can only say “the situation itself is still pending”.Despite releasing other contemporary house classics such as 2007’s Stuck – and soundtracking theHermès catwalkat Paris fashion week last January – Everett is far from a household name. In an interview in the documentary, Moodymann says Everett is “everyone’s favourite artist, you just don’t know it yet”; elsewhere in the film, he is compared to Stevie Wonder and James Brown.View image in fullscreen‘Peven has a once-in-a-generation voice’.Photograph: Frazer Harrison/Getty Images for CoachellaYet Everett runs a DIY enterprise, and has self-released more than 50 albums on his Studio Confession Entertainment label. “He’d make an album in one week and then burn it on to CDs and sell them at record stores in Chicago,” says Hewlett. “People haven’t been able to keep up.”“For the majority of my career, I’ve been blacklisted,” Everett claims obliquely, citing his home town music industry in particular. Why? “For being a musical genius,” he replies. “Not everybody wants to see that.”‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating strokeRead moreEverett sees himself as following on from where musical greats such as Marvin Gaye and Barry White left off in the late 1970s, as disco’s name was being sullied by the racist, homophobic “Disco Sucks” movement. “That didn’t sit right with me, it was hateful,” Everett says. “It tarnished great music. So I said, guess what? I’m gonna make the records that I know should have happened right after.”The day after our interview,a videocirculates of Everett and Albarn at Gorillaz’s Chicago show, as an emotional Everett prepares to sing the late Bobby Womack’s part on the Gorillaz tune Stylo. Artists as varied as Shirley Manson of Garbage, Kelela and Honey Dijon commented on the video with words of support. Everett says that his time was always supposed to be now. “I’m glad that I did it this way,” he says. “I maintain control of my catalogue, I still have the enjoyment of making music, and I got through a huge disease. I feel blessed.”“He’s going to have his moment,” adds Hewlett. “It feels like he’s just getting started.”Peven Everett: Voice of a Generationpremieres on 30 October at the Barbican, London, as part of the2026 Doc’n Roll film festivalExplore more on these topicsMusicHouse musicBarbicanGorillazDance musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Their orchestra is not a sacred object but a tool for struggle – Paris’s musicians join the frontline  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: L’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s young musicians went viral for their defiant performances during the last week’s protests in France. They belong to a fine tradition of radical orchestras. Also, today, what music should soundtrack the Traitors?
Author: Tom Service
Headline: L’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s young musicians went viral for their defiant performances during the last week’s protests in France. They belong to a fine tradition of radical orchestras. Also, today, what music should soundtrack the Traitors?
Content: Conductor Etienne Jarrier (centre) and the ONM perform during protests over the rising cost of living in Paris, France on 17 October 2026Photograph: Sipa US/AlamyView image in fullscreenConductor Etienne Jarrier (centre) and the ONM perform during protests over the rising cost of living in Paris, France on 17 October 2026Photograph: Sipa US/AlamyTom Service on musicClassical musicTheir orchestra is not a sacred object but a tool for struggle – Paris’s musicians join the frontlineTom ServiceL’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s young musicians went viral for their defiant performances during the last week’s protests in France. They belong to a fine tradition of radical orchestras. Also, today, what music should soundtrack the Traitors?Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTShareThey were the last people standing – or rather playing – during last week’s student protests in France, as gas canisters landed in double-bass cases. L’Orchestre du Nouveau Monde, co-founded by young conductor Étienne Jarrier and his friends when they were still teenagers, aren’t a typical orchestra. With theirmanifesto of activism and social justice, the orchestra is not “a sacred object of beauty, but a tool for struggle”, through civil disobedience, outreach in schools, demonstrations and concerts, all to “present a different kind of classical music – one reconnected to reality”.The new world Jarrier and his group dream of is “anti-racist, anti-capitalist, feminist, environmentalist and committed to de-growth”, and their way of working is deliberately provocative, not only to so many of the dominant directions of travel in the political world, but also to the institutions of classical music. They play scrappily passionate performances of La Marseillaise, of music from The Avengers, of Dvořák’s New World Symphony and protest songs but the ONM judge the quality of their performances not by playing the right notes in the right order, but by their consciousness-raising impact, whether they’re staging performances at Place de la République inParisor at the foot of a glacier.double quotation markThey don’t want their audiences to listen in silence but to sing with them, move with them and shout with them.This is not an orchestra trying to find hermetically sealed concert halls to perform in perfect acoustics. It’s a group that wants to be out on the streets, outside television studios and the headquarters of corporations, institutions or industries they choose to protest against. They don’t want their audiences to listen in silence but to sing with them, move with them, shout with them.All of this seems like a radical overturning of the way that orchestras usually function – and the ONM is arguably the most self-consciously radical orchestral assembly right now in how it fuses its political purpose to its musical ideals.But it’s not the first. In its political idealism and aesthetic radicalism, the ONM is a contemporary cousin of two British orchestras founded in 1969 and 1970: the Scratch Orchestra and the Portsmouth Sinfonia. Composers Cornelius Cardew, Howard Skempton and Michael Parsons founded theScratch Orchestra in 1969. Cardew’sThe Great Learning, based on texts by Confucius, is the Scratch Orchestra’s magnum opus, its notation and performance realised the Scratch Orchestra’s goals: to make music as open as possible to participants of all abilities and backgrounds. Instead of classical music’s polished perfection, the Scratch Orchestra’s experimentalism was an aesthetic of radical inclusion – socially, musically and aesthetically. The Great Learning’s greatest learning of all was that music of this ambition and scale belongs to anyone who wants to play it. The Scratchers went on to be welcome by the very institutions they critiqued,playing the Proms in 1972; but Cardew’s increasingly devoted leftwing activism took his music down a different course and the orchestra disbanded in 1974.View image in fullscreenBreaking convention … the Scratch Orchestra’s Cornelius Cardew listening to a man operating a jackhammer in 1969.Photograph: Tony Barette/Daily Mail/RexFor the Portsmouth Sinfonia, the self-styled “world’s worst orchestra”, the point was to try to play the classics – piano concertos, symphonies, orchestral hits – on instruments that the musicians, which included Gavin Bryars, Brian Eno and Michael Nyman, didn’t actually know how to play. The delirious, joyous and utterly deliberate cacophony that resulted remade everything from Beethoven’s symphonies toHandeland Hooked on Classics. (The Portsmouth Sinfonia’s attempt to disco-ify the classical repertoire parodied the Royal Philharmonic’s chart-topping kitschorama, and reached no 38 in the charts in 1981: Classical Muddly.Listen to it here, and enjoy.And even if the anarchy of the Portsmouth Sinfonia is no more, plenty of UK groups today are leading even more serious missions to reorient the priorities of orchestras towards social and political engagement. Here’s just a few: theMulti-Story Orchestra in Peckham, which amplifies the voices of the pupils and students it works with in south London as performers, composers and administrators; inclusive ensembles led by disabled musicians such as theNational Open Youth Orchestra,RNS Movesand theParaorchestraare all examples where social activism meets orchestral possibility, making the sounds of social change; whileContemporary Music for All (CoMA)continues a message of radical inclusion for new music, creating a repertoire of hundreds of pieces for non-professionals to play.View image in fullscreenThe Orchestre du Nouveau Monde’s concert in Place de la Republique on 17 October was disrupted when police used tear gas as broader demonstrations over living costs, education and public services drew large crowds.Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Even so, the ONM’s commitment to direct political action makes them stand out in today’s musical world – but their manifesto has a clue to an even deeper history: they want classical music to be “reconnected to reality”. That’s the point: classical music only exists across the world today because of its often-problematic connections to conceptions of nationhood and political orthodoxy, from the courts of Vienna in Beethoven’s time to the concert halls of Shostakovich’s era in Soviet Russia. You can’t have the power of all that music without the complicated and compromised politics that produced it. The attempt to pretend that these connections don’t exist in the later decades of the 20th century and beyond is part of the problem with classical music’s often self-inflicted irrelevance, as if the art form were untethered to the world around it, existing only in glitzy concert halls and glossy programmes. The ONM’s performances and protests, and the police’s reaction to them, is a wake-up call to remind classical music where it comes from – and yes, to reconnect it to today’s realities.With Celebrity Traitors– the latest series ofthe most successful TV franchiseon the planet – drawing to a close this week, here’sthe BBC’s Mark Savage analysinghow the deliberate duplicities and misdirections of the show’s music are made, not leastthe “Braaams”of the composer Sam Watts’s opening titles. But is it just me or is there less of the Lacrimosa from Mozart’s Requiem, and less classical as a whole, in the soundtrack for the death marches and backstabbing this time round? I have a challenge to the music supervisors: next series, why not use only classical to soundtrack it all? There’s vast reserves of dark and doomy tunes and arias of treachery and treason to choose from after all –the Traitors Promthe summer before last was a mere drop in the ocean of classical melodramas. My choice for the opening titles? The opening ofWagner’s Walküre, which has enough storm, threat and malice in its opening minutes to dramatise any celebrity face-off. What would you suggest?View image in fullscreenHow to soundtrack the treachery? Maya Jama, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Professor Hannah Fry, on the current season of Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PAThis week Tom has been listening to:I can’t get past The Portsmouth Sinfonia’s Classical Muddly, because who doesn’t need more joy and chaos in their lives? Also it’s not on the streamers, which only adds to the joy. If ever there was music made that the algorithms can’t touch, it’s this.See also:Tom Service on Stephen KovacevichExplore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicParisProtestFranceExperimental musiccommentShareReuse this content

title: Castle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared mess | Television | The Guardian
description: Billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’
Content: ‘Another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces’ … Castle Walls is the first fully AI-generated series to premiere on a major streaming platform.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video / YouTubeView image in fullscreen‘Another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces’ … Castle Walls is the first fully AI-generated series to premiere on a major streaming platform.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video / YouTubeTelevisionReviewCastle Walls review – Prime’s first fully AI-generated show is here, and it’s a Vaseline-smeared messBilled as the first end-to-end AI-created series on a major streaming service, this Turkish show looks like the result of the prompt ‘make it cinematic’Luke BuckmasterWed 28 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 21.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust as the world reels from Elon Musk’s AI-poweredThe Odyssey remake– though “remake” feels rather generous for a seven-minute splat of synthetic sludge – another bucket of AI gunk is dropped on to our faces. For Prime Video’s AI-generated TV series Castle Walls, produced by Turkish production studio Ay Yapım using a melange of generative video tools, has arrived, billed as the first end-to-end AI-created series to premiere on a major streaming platform.‘Meaningless as a laptop screensaver’: reviewers slate Musk’s AI-made Odyssey filmRead moreIt’s certainly more epic than Musk’s production, consisting of two 17-minute episodes. Set in the 11th century, the show revolves around the historic Alamut Castle, although it’s entirely absent of any real sense of time or place. I was briefly intrigued by the opening images, with their bold palette of blues and mustard browns and yellows – but as soon as the “people” appeared, looking like Vaseline-smeared Madame Tussauds creations slowly melting in the sun, everything came crashing down.View image in fullscreen‘Like Vaseline-smeared Madame Tussauds creations slowly melting in the sun’: Castle Walls.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeThere are lots of heady moments across the first two episodes of this oddly paced show, with cranky-looking men aplenty and over-milked visual metaphors involving the likes of snakes, blood and fire. Everything looks like it was cooked up with the prompt: “Give me eye-watering visuals.” The opening shot depicts an eagle being transported across a desert in a cage (“make it look cinematic”), followed by a longshot of the castle (“make it more cinematic”), then an aerial shot of men arriving on horseback (“make it MORE MORE MORE cinematic”).View image in fullscreen‘Overloaded with grand and imposing imagery’: Castle Walls.Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeWe learn of the arrival in Alamut of a “freak” who “doesn’t eat or drink” and is intent on claiming these sweet digs for himself. This is Hasan Sabbah, who is supposed to be charismatic but looks plasticky and spectral, with a complexion like wet glue. He has somehow inspired an army of followers and ventures into the castle’s dungeons to recruit one more: the notorious warrior Azazil.The frame is overloaded with grand and imposing imagery: when Azazil says goodbye to loved ones, of course the scene takes place in front of a milky sunset. When he fangs it across the desert on a horse at night, of course there’s a white full moon glowing resplendently above. When the doors of the mighty castle creak open, in the lead-up to a big moment in episode two, of course incandescent orange sunlight streams through the widening gap.View image in fullscreen‘Viewers understandably seem less interested in what the technology promises than in what it threatens to take away: art imbued with humanity.’Computer-generated: Amazon Prime Video/YouTubeMake no mistake: the technology powering this is amazing and will profoundly alter the state of motion pictures. Productions such as Castle Walls are among the first out of the gates, and therefore prone to snarky commentary. Perhaps these early AI-generated workswill end up being broadly comparable to early silent films: revolutionary at the time, but quickly eclipsed by more sophisticated applications of the technology. But whereas the earliest motion pictures, famously dubbed the “cinema of attractions” by the historian Tom Gunning, provided some carnival-like wonder, these AI works tend to evoke a more cynical response from the general public. Viewers understandably seem less interested in what the technology promises than in what it threatens to take away: art imbued with humanity.The sensible path forward is surely for human and machine to enter into a reciprocal and carefully collaborative process, where artists only use algorithms and prompts to enhance, rather than replace, human creativity. On that front, Castle Walls did use human voice actors and was reportedly written by actual human screenwriters: Kerem Deren and Çisil Hazal Tenim. “This is not a production that bypassed human skill; it is one that used AI to amplify it,”Ay Yapım has said.But that’s hardly something to crow about, given how banal and chuckleheaded the writing is, puffed-up with lines like “I’ve stopped being a decent man” and “If I am the sheaf, you are the sword”. Were they really trying to make good art? Maybe that’s a question for ChatGPT.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTurkeyDramaAI (artificial intelligence)Amazon Prime VideoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Kovacevich - a pianist who risked oblivion to know what it’s like out on the edge | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The death of Stephen Kovacevich, aged 86, was announced yesterday. Tom Service pays tribute to a pianist whose performances were full of beauty, clarity – and danger
Author: Tom Service
Headline: The death of Stephen Kovacevich, aged 86, was announced yesterday. Tom Service pays tribute to a pianist whose performances were full of beauty, clarity – and danger
Content: Intimacy and intensity: pianist Stephen Kovacevich rehearsing at London’s Queen Elizabeth Hall in March 2013.Photograph: Amy T Zielinski/Redferns/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIntimacy and intensity: pianist Stephen Kovacevich rehearsing at London’s Queen Elizabeth Hall in March 2013.Photograph: Amy T Zielinski/Redferns/Getty ImagesClassical musicStephen Kovacevich - a pianist who risked oblivion to know what it’s like out on the edgeThe death of Stephen Kovacevich, aged 86, was announced yesterday. Tom Service pays tribute to a pianist whose performances were full of beauty, clarity – and dangerAnd, here,in a piece published on Kovacevich’s 75th birthday, Andrew Clements picks his favourite recordings.Tom ServiceWed 28 Oct 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was just a couple of weeks ago that Stephen Kovacevich and I were last in contact. He was in hospital, recovering from a hip operation, and we were talking aboutHiromi, and where the latest generation of pianists were coming from. The players who had the brilliance, fire and commitment to the moment that his favourite players had: Vladimir Horowitz, Sergei Rachmaninov – his greatest of the greats – and his friend and occasional mentee, Yuja Wang.Among other things, he told me about a Charles Munch performance of Berlioz’sSymphonie Fantastique he had discovered on YouTubethat made him exclaim: “How the hell did he get an orchestra to play like that?” Conversation with Stephen was always like that: utterly intense, totally opinionated, with the feeling that the spirits he was talking about, whether performers or composers from Chopin to Beethoven to Brahms to Mozart to Bach, were in the room with you, conjured into being as real, passionate people and presences.Which was, of course, what you felt and heard in his playing. His long career devolved into name changes (Bishop, Bishop-Kovacevich, then Kovacevich) and relationship changes, as partnerships with conductors he loved to work with were intensely productive and then suddenly disappeared. Listen to any of the concerto recordings with Colin Davis to hear the adventure of what they made together, from Bartók to Mozart.View image in fullscreenStephen Kovacevich with cellist Jacqueline du Pré in London in 1964. The two made an acclaimed recording ofBeethoven’s Cello sonatas.Photograph: Erich Auerbach/Getty ImagesWhat was constant was a spirit of going to the edge of a performance to find the place where the music is most powerful and most vulnerable; risking oblivion to know what it’s like there, out on the edge. Stephen talked openly about how often his performances failed him, but he rejoiced in his successes, particularly the technical ones of the last decade or so of his life, whenhe recovered from a severe strokein his late 60s, and combatted nerves, to play Schubert and Rachmaninov with an intimacy and intensity that was breathtaking.He was driven by capturing the sensual spirit at the core of all the music he loved to play. This was a dangerous occupation, as it should be. Getting that close to the white-heat of Beethoven’s sonatas or Brahms’s concertos is all about being burnt and scarred, and plunging back in again to those cauldrons of extremity, the psychic and emotional places where music like that is made, and where performances like Stephen’s are born.One of his complaints about classical music right now was that performers often don’t take enough risks, that their music-making isn’t dangerous enough. I agree with him. His own playing was the perfectly imperfect response: that’s why his Beethoven sonatas are my favourite on record, because you’re with him in the moment of the attempt to reach the mountaintop, with everything on the line, throwing it all at the impossibility of the moment. In that struggle and that realisation, there’s more truth and more transcendence than most pianists will find in a lifetime. I’m going to miss him.More on Stephen Kovacevich“I don’t live in a subversive way. But I certainly believe in it” –a 2001 interviewTo celebrateKovacevich’s 75th birthday, Andrew Clements picked his favourite of his recordings.Wereview his 70th birthday concertat the Wigmore Hall, London, anda 2015 concertof music for two pianos with Martha Argerich.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? by Judi Dench review – whatever you do, don’t call her a ‘national treasure’ | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos and why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relic
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos and why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relic
Content: Judi Dench.Photograph: Paul StuartView image in fullscreenJudi Dench.Photograph: Paul StuartAutobiography and memoirReviewIs It Too Late to Make a Run for It? by Judi Dench review – whatever you do, don’t call her a ‘national treasure’The actor waxes lyrical on directors, dildos and why she hates being referred to as though she’s a dusty old relicFiona SturgesWed 28 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the late 1950s,Judi Denchwas invited to meet a major Hollywood producer about a possible career in the film business. The producer looked at her for a long time and said: “Very nice to meet you but you’ll never make a movie because you have every single thing wrong with your face.” As she left his office, Dench – who was 23 and about to make her professional debut as Ophelia in Hamlet at the Old Vic – breathed a sigh of relief and resolved to concentrate on theatre. Though she dabbled in film and TV, it wasn’t until the 1990s that she became a bona fide movie star, playing M in the Bond films and winning an Oscar for her portrayal of Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love. Yet, she notes: “Being onstage is where I feel safest. Yes, I’ve appeared in films, but I’d never consider myself a film actor.”Dench’s reflections on her working life form the backbone of Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, a memoir built around her conversations with the actor and theatre director Brendan O’Hea, Dench’s friend with whom she also collaborated on 2023’s Shakespeare: The Man Who Pays the Rent. This book confirms much of what is already known about Dench: that she is impishly funny, swears like a sailor, and that, despite that film producer’s unkind comments, she has “no hang-ups about what I look like on camera … Acting for me is not about looking glamorous. It’s whatever’s needed for the story.” We also learn that Dench, who is 91, can’t resist a prank: while playing Brecht’s Mother Courage at the Barbican in London, she replaced the drinks her character serves to two soldiers with cider vinegar – “It was a joy watching them knock it back, made even more glorious by the fact they had to ask for a top-up.”In keeping with her previous book, this one is delivered in a question-and‑answer format. The chapters are thematic and cover faith, animals, directors and directing, comedy, choosing a part, which means the chronology is all over the place. While the book starts quite reasonably with Dench’s early life in York as the daughter of a GP, it ends, oddly, with a chapter called Starting Out, in which we learn what she did after her A-levels. And while she has an easy chemistry with O’Hea, there are times when his line of questioning gets tediously granular, as in: “What’s your favourite dressing room?” Such are the perils of having an actor interview an actor.But despite the shoptalk and the haphazard structure, there are enough witty anecdotes and oddball facts to keep it clipping along. We learn that Dench has a waste-collection truck named after her: “Dame Foodie Dench”; that she had a cat called Bernard the Duck Fucker (though O’Hea neglects to ask how he earned his name); and that, on the opening night of Madame de Sade, Dench’s co-star Frances Barber gave her a double-ended, bendy dildo which she wore as a scarf when the company gathered for director’s notes. Elsewhere, Dench pays touching tribute to departed friends including the late Maggie Smith, whom she says was “a very complex person – intensely private, and I suspect quite lonely at times; she’d occasionally erect an electric fence around herself”.The whole project is kept afloat by Dench’s rare humour and warmth which long ago elevated her to national treasure status (an appellation she loathes as it makes her sound “like a dusty old relic”). Her eyesight is now poor, but her memories are pin-sharp, relayed through a prism of amused self-deprecation and passion for her job. The book’s title references Dench’s professional nerves, which lead her to keep her bag by the rehearsal room door in case she is compelled to do a runner. Learning lines may have become more difficult, but she has no intention of stopping work. “Take the keys out of the ignition and the car will conk out,” she cautions. “Don’t retire, do not go gentle, and don’t even think about going quietly.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
