title: Film buffs love it. Trump and Tom Hanks hosted it. Can TCM survive a Hollywood mega-merger? | Movies | The Guardian
description: Since 1994, Turner Classic Movies has been a haven for old film lovers. Now with Skydance’s David Ellison calling the shots, fans are panicking over its unclear future
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: Since 1994, Turner Classic Movies has been a haven for old film lovers. Now with Skydance’s David Ellison calling the shots, fans are panicking over its unclear future
Content: ‘TCM has been like a close, comforting friend during some very dark hours of my life,’ said Karie Bible.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘TCM has been like a close, comforting friend during some very dark hours of my life,’ said Karie Bible.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesMoviesFilm buffs love it. Trump and Tom Hanks hosted it. Can TCM survive a Hollywood mega-merger?Since 1994, Turner Classic Movies has been a haven for old film lovers. Now with Skydance’s David Ellison calling the shots, fans are panicking over its unclear futureAlaina DemopoulosWed 28 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTShareI have made many attempts to lessen the existential disaster we call Tuesday – tacos, trivia – but lately only one thing works. Every night just before 8pm, I hide my phone under a pillow in the next room, plate up a carb-heavy dinner, and turn on Turner Classic Movies (TCM) for Sweater Weather, a series of films dedicated to the transitional season.Every Tuesday in October, Alicia Malone, an affable Australian film historian wearing business casual and a flippy bob, introduces a double feature. These are often midcentury melodramas featuring striking leads, serpentine plots, and the burnt hues of fall rendered in indulgent Technicolor. Like All That Heaven Allows (1955), about a widow who finds herself crushed under the weight of 1950s suburban conformity – and the teeny waistline of her swing skirts – while nursing a crush on her much-younger gardener. Or Leave Her to Heaven (1945), about a beautiful socialite so obsessed with her hapless husband that she will kill anyone who threatens their bond.In these films, everyone has theiroriginal teethand no onetakes Ozempic. It’s my weekly break from doomscrolling, from whatever-maxxing, from the maddening norm of vertical content. I want to live in the world of Sweater Weather cinema all year long.View image in fullscreenTed Turner lights a cigar in his office at CNN, in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1989.Photograph: Robin Rayne/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockTCM has aired old movies since 1994, when the cable channel was launched by CNN’s founder, Ted Turner. The businessman was obsessed with movies – his favorite, Gone with the Wind, christened the network’s first broadcast – and had acquired MGM studio’s big film catalog from which to pull titles. At the time, deeper-cut movies rarely played on major networks, and real buffs had to trawl library archives to find what they were looking for.From the start, TCM projected a reverence for the medium, airing uncut films in a wide range of genres – a 1930s screwball comedy in one slot, an 80s slasher flick in the next. Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy are never interrupted by commercials for car insurance or pharmaceuticals. The network’s present-day hosts – led by Ben Mankiewicz, grandson of Citizen Kane scribe Herman J Mankiewicz – and guest stars serve up insider stories as they present each film. Tom Hanks oncespokeon TCM of having to tell Bette Davis, then an intimidating grande dame of the screen, that she had stolen his wife’s seat at an Academy Awards afterparty. When Amy Madigan won an Oscar earlier this year for best supporting actress in Weapons, TCM brought her on totalkabout past roles, including one alongside the lateGene Hackman.Even Donald Trumpappearedon TCM, in 2007, where in typical fashion he compared himself to Charles Foster Kane, the wealthy yet pitiable tycoon from Mankiewicz and Orson Welles’s masterpiece, Citizen Kane.Letterboxd’s most eager reviewers are changing cinema etiquette: ‘I was excited to pull out my phone’Read moreI am not someone who feels sentimental about brands or companies. I like to think I’m smart enough to know they will never love me back. But TCM is different. Karie Bible, an author and tour guide at Hollywood Forever Cemetery, interment site of many icons, feels the same way.Bible started watching the channel as a college student in the 90s. “It’s kind of emotional to explain, but TCM has been like a close, comforting friend during some very dark hours of my life,” she said. “When I was in the hospital about to have a kidney operation I was watching it.”Bible remembers lying on a gurney after surgery, watching Alfred Hitchcock’s Rear Window and then the 1960s horror flick What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? “When they came to wheel me out, I told them I wasn’t going until Baby Jane was over,” Bible said. “My dad had to take away the remote so they could take me off the table.”TCM does not share ratings, but in 2020,68.2m homeshad access to it: retirees, small-town kids and director Martin Scorsese, who reportedly keeps TCM on in his editing suite. I would not say I am dating my boyfriend solely for his TCM subscription, but when he dropped that he had one during our first date, I decided there would be a second. It signals something charmingly analog, an instinct to choose careful curation over autopopulating recommendations on streamers such as Netflix, Amazon Prime and HBO.Can a network like TCM, which is programmed by people who clearly think a lot about what to put on air, survive in this media ecosystem?View image in fullscreenThe Skydance logo is displayed at the New York Stock Exchange in New York City,  on 8 October 2026.Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersIn early October, when Paramount Skydanceannounced its acquisitionof Warner Bros Discovery – and therefore a collection of cable channels including CNN, MTV and TCM – fans panicked. A flowchart allegedlyproduced by the new mega-media company Skydance listing its new properties made theroundson a Reddit forum for TCM viewers; TCM’s logo was notably absent. “This is very ominous,” one user wrote. “Doomed,” wrote another. (The image is of unknown origin; Skydance’s websiteincludesTCM on a list of brands.)It felt like deja vu. In 2023, after the $43bn merger of Warner Bros and Discovery, executives laid off several TCM executives,includingits longtimehead of programming, Charles Tabesh, an enthusiastic champion of both obscure and well-known movies. The move disturbed film buffs, who saw it as a death knell for the network. Heavyweight TCM fans including Scorsese and fellow directors Paul Thomas Anderson and Steven Spielbergcalled Warner Bros Discovery’s head, David Zaslav, who acquiesced by bringing Tabesh back (though not the 70 TCM staffers also cut). There was a sigh of relief among certain circles: art had prevailed.double quotation markJust the fear of something going away makes you want to watch it even morePeter SarafNow comes Skydance. Staff are reportedlybracing for layoffsacross the company, which carries$80bn in debt due to the merger.“One of the easiest ways to remedy some of that debt is to sell some of the linear TV assets,” said Gabriel Miller, co-founder ofthe Industry, a newsletter about film production. “Obvously [Skydance CEO] David Ellison isn’t going to sell CNN, but something like Comedy Central or BET might be something that potentially ends up getting sold.”TCM, too? The officiallineis that the network is staying put for now, IndieWire reported. A representative for TCM declined to comment on the record to the Guardian. A representative for Skydance did not comment on the company’s intentions for TCM.TCM has spent decades cultivating its fanbase.Because the network does not air commercials, it cannot make money off of ads. It instead relies on carriage and streaming fees (there is an app available for people who already have a TV subscription through traditional cable or a live TV streaming service).It also hosts live events, including a Los Angeles film festival and “classic film cruise” that set sail earlier this month.Marsha Gordon is a history professor who penned abiographyof Ursula Parrott, the 1920s novelist who is credited for inventing the word “ex-wife”. Gordon spoke at a recent TCM festival, introducing a 35mm print of The Divorcee, an adaptation of Parrott’s work that is older than the Empire State Building. The screening took place at 10am on a Friday morning; Gordon expected maybe 30 people in the audience. Nearly 500 people showed up. “They were reacting exactly as you would imagine people would have reacted in 1930: laughing and holding their breath and booing at the right places,” she said.View image in fullscreenThe Dorothy dress worn by Judy Garland in The Wizard of Oz at a media preview of Bonhams and Turner Classic Movies Treasures from the Dream Factory at Bonhams in New York, on 19 November 2015.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersProgrammers for the festival and the daily TV schedule have a “sense of play”, Gordon said. They want viewers to have a good time. See: Creepy Cinema, an annual celebration of campy Halloween co-hosted by the Sex and the City actor Mario Cantone, who often uses his airtime to give impressions of stars such as Joan Crawford or Bette Davis.In February, social media users (gleefully) accused TCM ofsending a messagewith its decision to air Gaslight before Trump’s State of the Union. The 1944 film, about a husband who slowly convinces his wife that she has gone insane, spawned the eponymous term relating to the type of psychological manipulation Trump and other men have been accused of. “The counter programming at @tcm remains unmatched,” comedian Patton Oswaltpostedon Threads. The timing could have been coincidental: that night, TCM scheduled a series of remakes that had been nominated for Academy Awards, a category that Gaslight falls into. (A representative for TCM declined to comment on the theory at the time.)Coincidences like this might not go over well with David Ellison, son of Larry, the eighth-richest man in the worldand a Trump ally whodonated $45mto a Pac supporting his candidacy in 2024. The younger Ellison hasdownplayedhis own connection to the Trump administration, saying he doesn’t “want to politicize” Skydance and highlighting its “good relationship[s]” with the Biden administration and the Democratic California governor, Gavin Newsom.Then again, Ellison has one thing in common with me: he claims to love film. The industry scion originally founded Skydance to produce his passion projects. “I think he’s someone who actually cares about cinema and is going to try to make [TCM] work,” said Miller of the Industry newsletter.Goodbye Warner, hello Skydance: how will the major merger really impact Hollywood?Read moreChris Yogerst, an author and media historian who wrote abookon the original Warner brothers, is similarly optimistic. He could see a near future where TCM pivots to streaming-only – like the highbrow Criterion Collection, which is celebrated for its library but lacks the friendly host set-up of TCM. “They could make a hub [on HBO Max] or an app where the brand still serves the same format, but it’s just adapting to the digital era a little bit more effectively,” Yogerst said.Reports of TCM’s death may be exaggerated – and are also great PR, said Peter Saraf, chair of New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts. “When Zaslav tried to shut down TCM, he actually did it such an amazing promotional favor,” Saraf said. “So many people came out and said, you cannot do this. Just the fear of something going away makes you want to watch it even more. I think it would be very foolish of Ellison to even consider touching it.”So Sweater Weather cinema continues, at least for the rest of fall. And as always, I will be there. This week, a friend suggested making plans for Tuesday night. I countered with happy hour, explaining my prior commitment. She said that’s fine, and that we should meet up close to my apartment – she would like to come over after and watch TCM, too.Explore more on these topicsFilmParamount PicturesWarner BrosShare

title: Peter Medak, veteran director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88 | Movies | The Guardian
description: The film-maker enjoyed a long and varied film and TV career, from horror movies and true-crime thrillers to Cannibal and Breaking Bad
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The film-maker enjoyed a long and varied film and TV career, from horror movies and true-crime thrillers to Cannibal and Breaking Bad
Content: Peter Medak directing A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972).Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyView image in fullscreenPeter Medak directing A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972).Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyMoviesPeter Medak, veteran director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88The film-maker enjoyed a long and varied film and TV career, from horror movies and true-crime thrillers to Cannibal and Breaking BadAndrew PulverWed 28 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 15.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Medak, the British-Hungarian director of The Changeling, The Krays and Let Him Have It, has died aged 88. Medak’s family announced he died peacefully in Los Angeles on Tuesday.Medak enjoyed a long and varied career across film and TV, which included spirit-of-the-times classics A Day in the Death of Joe Egg and The Ruling Class (both from 1972), cult horror The Changeling with George C Scott, and The Krays and Let Him Have It, period true crime films made in the early 1990s. He also directed numerous episodes of high-profile TV drama, including the 80s revival of The Twilight Zone, Homicide: Life on the Street, and Hannibal.View image in fullscreenGary Kemp, left with Martin Kemp, right, and Billie Whitelaw in Medak’s biopic of the Kray twinsPhotograph: Warner Bros./Sportsphoto/AllstarBorn in Hungary in 1937, Medak was forced into hiding along with his Jewish family during the second world war, and then escaped the country during the Hungarian uprising. He came to London, where his aunt Lotte Medák was an internationally renowned opera singer and through her contacts Medak wastaken on as a traineeat newsreel producers Associated British-Pathé, working his way up through the studio departments, including a spell working in the editing room with future Chariots of Fire director Hugh Hudson. Medak then worked as assistant director to Joan Littlewood on Sparrows Can’t Sing and Guy Hamilton on Funeral in Berlin before making his own feature directing debut in 1968 with erotic thriller Negatives, starring Peter McEnery and Glenda Jackson.Medak then followed this up with two adaptations of celebrated plays: Peter Nichols’ A Day in the Death of Joe Egg, with Alan Bates, and Peter Barnes’ The Ruling Class, starring Peter O’Toole. Both were well received on their release in 1972, with O’Toole nominated for the best actor Oscar, but Medak would swiftly hit trouble two years later with Ghost in the Noonday Sun,a still-notorious Peter Sellers vehiclethat went vastly over budget, partly due to Sellers’ erratic behaviour, and which was only released on home video more than a decade later. (Calling it the “biggest disaster of my life”, Medak would later make a documentary about the experience, which screened at the Venice film festival in 2018.)Following the Graham Chapman comedy The Odd Job, Medak re-established his credibility with The Changeling, the creepy 1980 George C Scott horror about a composer who rents a haunted house. Calling it “filled with sadness and dread”, it was named by Martin Scorsese asone of his favourite horror movies. After spells on Shelley Duvall’s anthology series Faerie Tale Theatre and The Twilight Zone, Medak returned to features with two high-profile British crime thrillers. The Krays, released in 1990, cast Spandau Ballet’s Gary and Martin Kemp as the twin-brother gangsters, followed by Let Him Have It, about a controversial case which saw 19-year-old Derek Bentley hanged in 1953 for the murder of a policeman despite not pulling the trigger. Medak then returned to Hollywood with the Gary Oldman thriller Romeo Is Bleeding in 1993.View image in fullscreenPeter O’Toole in The Ruling ClassPhotograph: RONALD GRANTMedak pivoted back to TV and, starting in 1994, directed six episodes of acclaimed cop series Homicide: Life on the Street, and followed it up by directing an episode of The Wire in 2002. Later TV work included episodes of high-profile shows such as House,Breaking Badand Cannibal.Skyfall and No Time to Die writers Neal Purvis and Robert Wade, who worked with Medak on their first produced script Let Him Have It, told the Guardian: “Peter directed our first film and we couldn’t have hoped for a kinder, more respectful collaborator. It was wonderful to be treated as equals by this very experienced film-maker, who was enjoying a resurgence in his film career after the exciting and surprising The Krays. He was a good friend and we will miss the lunches and the talk of all the future projects he still burned to make.”Medak was married three times, to Katherine La Kermance between 1963 and 1972, Carolyn Seymour between 1973 and 1984, and Julia Migenes between 1988 and 2003.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsCrime filmsDrama filmsPeter BarnesPeter NicholsPeter SellersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bafta trustees may have broken charity law by accepting free guest tickets | Awards and prizes | The Guardian
description: Chair of membership council says legal advice obtained at own expense suggests offences could have been committed
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Chair of membership council says legal advice obtained at own expense suggests offences could have been committed
Content: Bafta is an independent arts charity famous for its annual film, television and games awards.Photograph: London Entertainment/AlamyView image in fullscreenBafta is an independent arts charity famous for its annual film, television and games awards.Photograph: London Entertainment/AlamyAwards and prizesBafta trustees may have broken charity law by accepting free guest ticketsChair of membership council says legal advice obtained at own expense suggests offences could have been committedNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 07.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBafta trustees may have breached charity and company law by accepting free tickets for guests at the organisation’s awards ceremonies, the chair of its membership council has claimed.Michael Pritchett told members at Bafta’s annual general meeting that legal advice obtained at his own expense suggested offences could have been committed by trustees who approved the charity’s accounts, which stated that no trustees had received remuneration or benefits.“I did not go looking for what I found,” Pritchett said. “I found it doing the job that you gave me.”He claimed trustees had received complimentary tickets for themselves and a guest at the film, television and games awards, potentially for as long as 20 years. The guest tickets were top-table seats, he said, with a second ticket at the film awards selling for £2,000.Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson to watch Bafta Scotland awards in separate ‘relaxed’ spaceRead moreBafta’s governing document states that trustees may not receive remuneration or other benefits from the academy. Pritchett said the charity’s 2024 and 2025 accounts stated that no trustees had received remuneration for their services, while its public register said trustees received no remuneration, payments or benefits.“Counsel advises that offences under theCharitiesAct and Companies Act are likely to have been committed by the trustees who approved those accounts,” he said. “I really wish I didn’t have to tell you this.”Pritchett, who is also a member of Bafta’s governance and appointments committee, also raised questions about possible tax liabilities, saying benefits of this kind were likely to have been taxable since 2016, with national insurance potentially payable by Bafta. He said he could not establish whether the arrangements had been reported to the relevant authorities.Bafta’s outgoing chair, Sara Putt, said the board had decided to end the practice of giving trustees a guest ticket to awards ceremonies in 2025, after a recommendation from its governance committee.“The separate guest ticket and accounting matters are being examined by an independent review group,” Putt said, adding that the board would update members in due course.Bafta trustees are volunteers, and it is understood they are invited to awards ceremonies in a working capacity, hosting tables and acting as ambassadors for the academy. It is also understood that guest tickets were a longstanding custom dating back to a time when demand for awards tickets was lower.Pritchett also criticised the refusal of a senior Bafta executive to provide records of who had received complimentary tickets, despite the committee’s terms of reference stating it could seek any information required from academy employees.“The records belong to the charity that you subscribe to,” he told members, noting that they had paid £4.7m in membership fees the previous year.Twelve-year-old wins Australian slam competition prize with poem about ChatGPT: ‘It’s totally unnecessary’Read morePritchett called on trustees to pay any taxes found to be due, repay any money owed and correct the accounts. Putt responded: “If we were told we had to pay those taxes, we would absolutely pay those taxes.”Putt said the legal advice obtained by Pritchett and fellow committee member Sara Curran was based on the information available to them, while Bafta’s own legal counsel had access to a fuller picture of the charity’s circumstances.A Bafta spokesperson said: “Trustees of Bafta are invited to attend events in a working capacity, representing the academy in an ambassadorial role, and prior to 2025 they could also bring a ‘plus one’ guest to accompany them.“In 2025 Bafta decided to review its guest tickets arrangements and discontinued the longstanding custom and practice of trustees inviting a plus one. The board has since established an independent review group to consider the historic guest ticket arrangement – the review is under way.”Explore more on these topicsAwards and prizesBaftasCharitiesVoluntary sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dear Charlie’: letter revealing move to snare future Rolling Stones drummer up for auction | The Rolling Stones | The Guardian
description: Brian Jones wrote to Charlie Watts in 1962 asking him to leave his R&B group and join his ‘far better’ band instead
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Brian Jones wrote to Charlie Watts in 1962 asking him to leave his R&B group and join his ‘far better’ band instead
Content: From centre clockwise: Brian Jones, Charlies Watts, Keith Richards, Mick Jagger and Bill Wyman.Photograph: Camerique/AlamyView image in fullscreenFrom centre clockwise: Brian Jones, Charlies Watts, Keith Richards, Mick Jagger and Bill Wyman.Photograph: Camerique/AlamyThe Rolling Stones‘Dear Charlie’: letter revealing move to snare future Rolling Stones drummer up for auctionBrian Jones wrote to Charlie Watts in 1962 asking him to leave his R&B group and join his ‘far better’ band insteadNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 06.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA handwritten letter from Brian Jones toCharlie Wattsin which he attempts to recruit the drummer to join the band that would soon become the Rolling Stones is being auctioned later this year.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Brian JonesThe 1962 letter, which comes directly from Watts’s sister and has remained in the family for more than six decades, will be revealed to the public for the first time.Watts was still working in advertising at the time while playing with Alexis Korner’s Blues Incorporated, one of the leading groups in London’s burgeoning rhythm and blues scene. He was initially reluctant to commit to Jones’s fledgling band, which had yet to be named.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Brian JonesThe letter comes with its original envelope and is addressed to “Mr. C. Watts” at his childhood home in Wembley. Jones begins: “Dear Charlie, if you consider this letter rather impertinent, please excuse me.”He goes on to enquire about Watts’s involvement with Blues Incorporated, before making his case for Watts to join his own band.“We are looking for a good drummer. Already we consider our band far better than Alex’s – we are getting a very tightly-knit sound.”In a particularly memorable postscript, Jones outlines the band’s existing lineup of two guitars, harmonica, piano and drums, noting their intention to eventually introduce a bass guitar, before offering a rather frank assessment of their current drummer: “Our present drummer is atrocious!”Despite Jones’s early overtures, it would take another seven months before Watts officially joined the Rolling Stones, in January 1963. By then, bassist Bill Wyman had also joined, completing the rhythm section that would become central to the band’s distinctive sound.On 2 February 1963, the Rolling Stones performed with their early six-member lineup of Watts, Wyman, Jones, Keith Richards, Mick Jagger and pianist Ian Stewart.The band’s desire to recruit Watts was later recalled by Richards in his autobiography Life, in which he described the lengths to which the musicians were prepared to go to bring him into the fold.Richards remembered that they had even cut back on food to afford the drummer, declaring: “We starved ourselves to pay for him!”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Brian JonesSotheby’s said the letter offered “a remarkable first-hand glimpse” into the band’s formative months and its determination to recruit Watts, who would become an integral part of their sound for nearly six decades.“Few documents bring us as close to the formation of a legendary band as this letter,” said Craig Inciardi, Sotheby’s music and pop culture specialist.“Written just weeks before the Rolling Stones’ first performance and months before Charlie Watts officially joined the group, it captures the excitement and ambition of a band on the cusp of history.“Having remained in the Watts family for more than six decades, it stands as an extraordinary first-hand record of the momentBrian Jonesset out to recruit the drummer whose distinctive sound would help shape one of the most influential bands in rock history.”The letter will be on public view at Sotheby’s New York from 2 December to 8 December, with online bidding open from 2 December until the Rock & Pop sale on 15 December. It is estimated to fetch between $70,000 and $80,000 (£52,000-£60,000).Watts would go on to remain the Rolling Stones’ drummer for nearly six decades, performing and recording with the band until his death in August 2021.Explore more on these topicsThe Rolling StonesCharlie WattsBrian JonesPop and rockShareReuse this content

title: Gulliver fans celebrate three centuries of Jonathan Swift’s classic satire | Jonathan Swift | The Guardian
description: Events in Ireland explore origins of Gulliver’s Travels, the Dublin clergyman’s book that became an instant hit in 1726
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Events in Ireland explore origins of Gulliver’s Travels, the Dublin clergyman’s book that became an instant hit in 1726
Content: A 1727 French engraving depicts Gulliver bound and surrounded by Lilliputians. Skewering human vanity and scientific arrogance, the book was an instant hit.Illustration: Digital Collections Department/Trinity College DublinView image in fullscreenA 1727 French engraving depicts Gulliver bound and surrounded by Lilliputians. Skewering human vanity and scientific arrogance, the book was an instant hit.Illustration: Digital Collections Department/Trinity College DublinJonathan SwiftGulliver fans celebrate three centuries of Jonathan Swift’s classic satireEvents in Ireland explore origins of Gulliver’s Travels, the Dublin clergyman’s book that became an instant hit in 1726Rory CarrollIreland correspondentWed 28 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn March 1726, an Irish clergyman visited London and arranged for a courier to deliver a manuscript to a publisher under cover of night. The dean of St Patrick’s Cathedral in Dublin knew his novel would cause trouble and wanted to publish it anonymously.His name wasJonathan Swiftand the story was called Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World. The satirical work was published that October and is better known 300 years on as Gulliver’s Travels.An immediate sensation, it skewered Georgian pretensions and entered popular culture through translations, children’s versions, comics and films. The anniversary is now being celebrated at Swift’s alma mater, Trinity College Dublin, and at events aroundIreland.View image in fullscreenThe Lilliputian army marches beneath Gulliver in Florence Dugdale’s Gulliver’s Travels Told in Simple Language (1912).Illustration: Digital Collections Department/Trinity College DublinExhibitions,festivals, seminars, art competitions and workshops are exploring the origins of Swift’s masterpiece, its retelling through a feminist lens, and its prophetic depiction of a society in thrall to a form of artificial intelligence.“Lemuel Gulliver’s first voyage to the land of Lilliput is the one most familiar to audiences today,” said Stephanie Breen, an assistant librarian and co-curator of the exhibition at Trinity. “This exhibition, however, brings viewers on a journey to all of the lands Gulliver encountered – Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa and beyond and the country of Houyhnhnms.”View image in fullscreenA 1726 edition of Jonathan Swift’s novel, initially known as Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World.Photograph: Digital Collections Department/Trinity College DublinThe exhibition, which runs until December and isavailable online, draws on the university’s collection of hundreds of editions and popularisations of Gulliver’s Travels, including engraved illustrations, pop-up versions, a 1976 Marvel comic and the only known surviving copy of an abridgement printed in 1761.The voice of Gulliver’s wife, Mary, who is neglected and left at home “big with child” until his eventual, grumpy return, was imagined through contemporary works such as Alison Fell’s The Mistress of Lilliput and Lauren Chater’s Gulliver’s Wife, said Aileen Douglas, a professor of English and exhibition co-curator.Gulliver’s experiences in Laputa, a floating island dedicated to arts and science, resonated with our era’s anxieties about technology, said Douglas. Its inhabitants seek to extract sunbeams from cucumbers and obtain knowledge via an “engine” of wires, handles and paper that can produce tracts on philosophy, poetry and mathematics “without the least assistance from genius or study”.In the kingdom of Luggnagg, Gulliver is at first enchanted and then horrified by the Struldbruggs, a race that is immortal but continues eternally to age and sicken.A panel discussion about the role of art in challenging power, and Gulliver’s attacks on human vanity and scientific arrogance, is to be held at Trinity on Wednesday. At the cathedral, a children’s choir willperform the premiereof a work by the composer Seán Doherty, along with organ recitals and extracts of Gulliver’s Travels read by the Swift scholar Brendan Twomey. An exhibition and lecture series at the Robinson library in County Armagh runs until December.Born in 1667, Swift combined posts in the Church ofIrelandwith pamphlets and essays that pioneered deadpan, savage satire, including A Modest Proposal, which suggested alleviating the plight of the Irish poor by selling their children as food to the wealthy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe wrote Gulliver’s Travels in Dublin and at an estate in County Meath, where it is said that some very tall and very small farm workers inspired the storytelling.When shipwrecked on Lilliput, Gulliver discovers diminutive inhabitants who are waging war against a rival kingdom in a dispute over which end of a boiled egg should be cracked – a satire on Europe’s sectarian conflicts. Gulliver captures the Blefuscudian fleet and douses a fire at a Lilliputian palace by urinating on it.View image in fullscreenGulliver puts out a palace fire in Lilliput by urinating on it in Gulliver, a retelling by Mary Webb, illustrated by Lauren O’Neill.Photograph: The O’Brien PressMarooned among giants in Brobdingnag, Gulliver’s stories about his “own dear native country” inadvertently reveal its corruption and cruelty, prompting the Brobdingnagian ruler to pillory humanity as “the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth”.Swift’s publisher, Benjamin Motte, did not know his author’s identity but the book’s success, and Swift’s literary record, enabled many to guess, said Douglas. “People sort of knew it was him.”Explore more on these topicsJonathan SwiftIrelandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mushroom Murders: Melanie Lynskey to star as Erin Patterson in new limited series | Television | The Guardian
description: Emmy-nominated actor is also executive producer of the Paramount+ series, which will dramatise the Australian true crime case
Author: Steph Harmon
Headline: Emmy-nominated actor is also executive producer of the Paramount+ series, which will dramatise the Australian true crime case
Content: Melanie Lynskey, who will be playing Erin Patterson, is best known for her roles in Two and a Half Men, The Last of Us, Yellowjackets and But I’m a Cheerleader.Photograph: Michael Tullberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMelanie Lynskey, who will be playing Erin Patterson, is best known for her roles in Two and a Half Men, The Last of Us, Yellowjackets and But I’m a Cheerleader.Photograph: Michael Tullberg/Getty ImagesTelevisionMushroom Murders: Melanie Lynskey to star as Erin Patterson in new limited seriesEmmy-nominated actor is also executive producer of the Paramount+ series, which will dramatise the Australian true crime caseSteph HarmonandSian CainTue 27 Oct 2026 21.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 22.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Emmy-nominated New Zealand actor Melanie Lynskey has been cast as triple murderer Erin Patterson in a new limited series titled Mushroom Murders: There’s More to Unearth, which will premiere on Paramount+ in 2027.The series follows the 97 days between the notorious 2023 lunch – at which Patterson allegedly served toxic death cap mushrooms to her estranged in-laws, hidden in individual serves of beef wellington – and her arrest.Served at her home in Leongatha, Victoria, the meal killed her husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, leading to Patterson’s eventual conviction.The case dominated headlines around the world, spawning podcasts, books and TV series, and becoming an obsession of true crime fanatics. In September 2025,Patterson was sentenced to life imprisonmentfor the murders, and for the attempted murder of Heather Wilkinson’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who spent weeks in hospital but ultimately survived.Patterson, 51, is appealing against the convictions, with her lawyers decrying what they called a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.Neighbours is being recut into a microdrama focused on Margot Robbie – and her co-stars aren’t happyRead moreLynskey, who will be playing Patterson, is best known for her roles in Two and a Half Men, The Last of Us, Yellowjackets and But I’m a Cheerleader. She announced the show at the Paramount+ and Ten upfronts, hosted at the MasterChef Kitchen in the Royal Melbourne Showgrounds – whereMegan, Duchess of Sussex, will be co-hosting Junior MasterChef Australia in 2027.From the stage, Lynskey said she was “very excited” to be playing Patterson in Mushroom Murders – an announcement greeted with gasps among the attending media and stakeholders.The show was written by Anya Beyersdorf, with all six episodes directed by Daina Reid for Soapbox Pictures. Beyersdorf, Reid, Lynskey and Deb Balderstone are listed as executive producers, with Lynskey saying the show “offers a compelling and unique perspective on the events that made headlines around the world. It’s really good. Because behind all those headlines there is still so much to unearth.”In a statement, Beverley McGarvey, the Network 10 president and head of streaming at Paramount+ Australia, said the series would bring “a gripping real-life story, that captivated Australia and the world to the screen with the scale, quality and creative vision audiences expect” from the streamer.It’s the second dramatisation of the true crime case, following a 2025 ABC announcement of Toxic, created by Elise McCredieand Tony Ayres. A release date for Toxic is yet to be confirmed.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionErin Patterson mushroom trialParamount+Australian televisionShareReuse this content

title: Danny Masterson loses appeal against rape conviction after arguing judge was biased against Scientology | US television | The Guardian
description: That ’70s Show actor was sentenced to 30 years in prison for two counts of rape against two women, who were also Scientologists
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: That ’70s Show actor was sentenced to 30 years in prison for two counts of rape against two women, who were also Scientologists
Content: Actor Danny Masterson, who is serving a 30-year sentence after being convicted of raping two women. His appeal against his conviction was denied on Tuesday.Photograph: Anna Webber/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenActor Danny Masterson, who is serving a 30-year sentence after being convicted of raping two women. His appeal against his conviction was denied on Tuesday.Photograph: Anna Webber/Getty ImagesUS televisionDanny Masterson loses appeal against rape conviction after arguing judge was biased against ScientologyThat ’70s Show actor was sentenced to 30 years in prison for two counts of rape against two women, who were also ScientologistsSian CainTue 27 Oct 2026 20.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 20.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDanny Masterson has lost the appeal of his rape conviction, meaning his 30-year prison sentence has been upheld.The actor, best known for his role on That ’70s Show, wasconvicted in 2023 of two counts of rapeagainst two women in 2003, while a third charge relating to a third plaintiff, who alleged she was raped by Masterson in 2001, was quashed.Masterson has insisted that sex with all three plaintiffs was consensual. In December he filed an appeal, questioning the plaintiffs’ credibility and claiming he didn’t receive a fair trial as the judge, Los Angeles superior court judge Charlaine F Olmedo, was biased againstScientology.In an89-page rulingfiled in the California court of appeal on Tuesday, a three-judge panel rejected Masterson’s arguments, finding that Olmedo’s statements during the trial showed “no animus or departure from neutrality regarding Scientology”.During the trial, prosecutors argued that Masterson, a prominent Scientologist, had used his role in the church – of which all three plaintiffs were also members at the time – to avoid accountability for the assaults. Prosecutors also argued the plaintiffs had delayed reporting the incidents due to their fear they would violate a Scientology rule against going to the police and be retaliated against.Two of his accusers testified that when they reported Masterson to Scientology officials, they were told they were not raped, were put through “ethics programs” which they likened to repeated interrogations, and were warned against going to police. One of the women said she was shunned and ostracised for doing so.Olmedo allowed a former Scientologist, Claire Headley, to testify as an expert about the church’s beliefs and practices. Headley told the court that Scientology regards going to law enforcement as a “suppressive act” that was sanctionable by excommunication.In his appeal, Masterson’s lawyers argued the court had improperly intruded into interpretation of church doctrine.“The jury in this case was not asked to determine the truth or falsity of Scientology doctrine or beliefs,” the appeals court panel wrote. “Admission of Scientology evidence for those purposes did not contravene the First Amendment.”The panel also rejected separate arguments about the statute of limitations and evidentiary rulings, and denied that he did not get an adequate defense.Masterson’s lawyers, Cliff Gardner and Eric Multhaup, called it an “unfortunate decision”, tellingVarietythey would appeal to the California supreme court.After Masterson was found guilty in 2023, the church of Scientology issued a statement to say the “testimony and descriptions of Scientology beliefs” during the trial were “uniformly false”.“The church has no policy prohibiting or discouraging members from reporting criminal conduct of anyone – Scientologists or not – to law enforcement,” the statement said.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUS televisionTelevisionRape and sexual assaultScientologyCalifornianewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: five sisters fight for justice after a shocking murder in Belfast | Television | The Guardian
description: A family continues its search for answers following a devastating killing. Plus: Hannah Fry investigates the future of superintelligence. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: A family continues its search for answers following a devastating killing. Plus: Hannah Fry investigates the future of superintelligence. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Paula, one of Robert McCartney’s sisters, who sought the truth after he was stabbed to death and no witnesses came forward.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenPaula, one of Robert McCartney’s sisters, who sought the truth after he was stabbed to death and no witnesses came forward.Photograph: BBCTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: five sisters fight for justice after a shocking murder in BelfastA family continues its search for answers following a devastating killing. Plus: Hannah Fry investigates the future of superintelligence. Here’s what to watch this eveningPriya Elan,Phil Harrison,Ellen E Jones,Hollie RichardsonandHannah VerdierWed 28 Oct 2026 02.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMurder in Belfast: Sisters Seeking Justice9pm, BBC TwoIn 2005, Robert McCartney was beaten up and stabbed to death in a gang attack outside a Belfast city pub. After that, witnesses (there were about 70) remained silent and evidence was destroyed. But Robert’s five sisters and fiancee continued their fight for answers – including finding out what happened to a survivor of the attack. This documentary follows their journey.Hollie RichardsonThe Future With Hannah Fry7.30pm, BBC TwoShe was a rubbish celebrity traitor, but Prof Hannah Fry is back doing what she does best: digging into the big facts, this time about the future of superintelligence. Could AI pose an existential crisis to humankind? It’s a mammoth topic and Fry is the right person to investigate.HRCelebrity Race Across the World8pm, BBC OneTo Borneo, where four celebrity pairings will be waving unwieldy maps at bewildered locals as they head in the general direction of Australia. It’s as gently likable as ever: Jeff Stelling and son Matt, Ella Eyre and bestie Nana, Princess Andre and brother Junior, and Sam Ryder and manager Kaz are our coconut-picking, taxi-haggling contenders.Phil HarrisonHow the Romans Conquered the Alps8pm, BBC FourConquering the Alps is no mean feat, but in 15BC Emperor Augustus drove a direct route through them. Little was known about the campaign, which happened over a single summer, but now archaeologists and ballistic experts piece together the weapons used and a team of volunteers reconstruct the Romans’ march.Hannah VerdierEllie & Natasia10pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenCracking … Ellie White (left) and Natasia Demetriou in Ellie & Natasia.Photograph: BBC/CPL ProductionsThe brilliant Asim Chaudhry is this week’s guest star in the second season of Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou’s cracking sketch series. There’s bizarre fun with a driving lesson, a gameshow called Find the Snakes and a bunch of battling politicians.HRFirst Dates10pm, Channel 4“I’m like Mother Teresa. With fake tits!” Daniella, the Essex firecracker, tells Fred. A new series begins with the 23-year-old TikTok relationship influencer meeting her potential match in Joey (also from Essex). Meanwhile, Meryl (from the first season of The Traitors) is searching for a partner as she hits the big 3-0.Priya ElanFilm choiceThe Monkey (Osgood Perkins, 2025), 10.40pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenScary movie … Theo James in The Monkey.Photograph: APOsgood Perkins made 2024’s scariest movie inLonglegs, but his follow-up, based on a Stephen King short story, is a raucous comedy-horror with more laughs and more life wisdom. title: ‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanity | Jeanette Winterson | The Guardian
description: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed
Author: Aida Edemariam
Headline: The author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceed
Content: ‘What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted’ … Jeanette Winterson at home in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted’ … Jeanette Winterson at home in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe ideas interviewJeanette WintersonInterview‘There is no inevitable dystopia’: Jeanette Winterson on AI and the future of humanityAida EdemariamThe author believes we are at a turning point as a species – and even in the shadow of big tech it’s up to us how we want to proceedWed 28 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Iam a storyteller by trade,” writes Jeanette Winterson on the first page of her 2021 book12 Bytes, an idiosyncratic and thought-provoking series of essays in which she considered just how artificial intelligence might change everything about our lives. “And I know everything we do is a fiction until it’s a fact: the dream of flying, the dream of space travel, the dream of speaking to someone instantly, across time and space, the dream of not dying – or of returning.”She had already been thinking about our possible futures for at least 15 years – her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, for instance, imagined a post-climate catastrophe world populated by robots and humans who never age, while 12 Bytes was preceded byFrankisstein: A Love Story, which alternates a recreation of the summer Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein with a trans doctor’s travels among present-day cryogenecists and AI-enabled robots.When we meet, Winterson is just back from China, where, she tells me, her first novel, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit, a fictionalised account of her childhood, has sold more than a million copies in the past six years; more than 200,000 mostly young women tried to come to see her speak. She thinks this is because, in a world of long work hours and looming AI-engendered precarity, this fictionalised account of her own escape from an entrapped childhood gives readers permission to imagine a different future for themselves. She has since written 13 novels for adults, as well as nonfiction, short stories, children’s books and screenplays. Now she wants to persuade the production company Goalhanger to give her a podcast. “I want to do one called The Rest is Human,” she says, sitting at a bare wooden table inher home, a Georgian set of rooms above a shop – which she also owns – in Spitalfields, east London. “To see what we retain for ourselves in this absolute scramble to outsource everything we thought we were.”View image in fullscreenWinterson: ‘We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for.’Photograph: Posed by models; SDI Productions/Getty ImagesBecause we are, she argues, at a turning point in our story as a species. Until the Industrial Revolution, change was all about “Mother Nature and the slow process of becoming”, but then we “massively intervened. And that’s a decisive moment.”Computing, 70 years ago, was another step. Artificial intelligence – which she would prefer to call alternative intelligence – is next, and “an evolutionary leap. That’s what this is. AI is much more than a tool.” Given this, a certain understanding of the irreducibly human – our feelings, our imaginations, our centuries of study of who we are and what we have done – must be central to how well or badly things might go.She’s often strikingly optimistic about it. She imagines a relationship with AI, for instance, where you can “have a chat to your system. It’s going to look at everything. It’s going to go at such speed. It’s going to look at transport. It’s going to look at utilities. It’s going to look at employment, going to look at job hours, going to say, ‘What do these weird things called humans thrive on? What do they like? And have they always liked it?’ We could do this in a genuinely utopian way and say, ‘Right, we’re going to make it better.’” We are at a deeply significant moment of choice, she believes, that mirrors the choice we had in the Industrial Revolution – namely, “What future shall we build?”But in failing to distribute its gains fairly, the Industrial Revolution ushered in an era of unprecedented wealth for the few and unprecedented levels of misery for the many – a state of affairs many predict is not only already echoed but will be dwarfed by the fallout from AI:a permanent underclass, entire continents left behind and starved of current sources of income. Not to mention the environmental impact of datacentres at a time when the world can least afford it.The problem is not AI, she insists, but us. “There is no inevitable dystopia.” If things go wrong, it will be because of “old-fashioned thinking laid over this brand-new reality”. Specifically, “the idea of meaningless endless work being good for the soul is a 19th-century madness designed to keep people in their place. Most of what we fear about AI and jobs comes down to the political and economic choices our masters will make, just as they did in the Industrial Revolution.” She isn’t blindly optimistic. She does know that, “Yes, we are on track to mess up this chance to fundamentally change our relationship to the world of work” – but that’s because “our masters are using out-of-date, not-fit-for-purpose economic models”.View image in fullscreen‘What we know about humans is they love monopolies.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianBut it isn’t only the old winner-takes-all, “rational” ends-justify-the-means economic models that are the problem. Our flawed assumptions, and our prejudices, being the material on which large language models (LLMs) are trained, are built into the very fabric of AI. Not to mention the characters and the moral imaginations of those developing it. When we meet, Winterson is reading Jill Lepore’sThe Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and reiterates Lepore’s argument that we are now living “the sci-fi books that these [men who are] ruling the world read when they were 13. And she said, ‘We are now all under the covers with these boys and their flashlights. And the thing is, they didn’t read them as warnings about how to preserve what’s good in us. They read them as instruction manuals.’ It’s absolutely terrifying.”One big thing they seem to havetaken from these books, and Winterson cannot help but be fascinated by, is “the ultimate goal of Silicon Valley … to get out of the body and off the planet” – not least because she is so aware that humanism, in which everything is brought back to ourselves, our perceptions and our bodies, is historically so recent. People say, “These are machines, you can’t have relationships with them,” she says. “I look at them and say, ‘billions of people on this Earth right now are having their most profound relationship with a non-biological entity they call their sky god.’ Right? It’s always been so! We are absolutely primed not to worry about biology being everything about us. That’s why religion was invented – it is the world’s first disruptive startup. It’s there to say, this is not it. This is not the end, this doesn’t matter, this is a transition.”View image in fullscreenAn illustration of a mill in Leeds, during the second Industrial Revolution.Photograph: Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesSo we’re literally making our own gods? “Totally! What tech is doing now is what religion has always wanted,” which is, at its most basic level, a solution to the problem of death. “I mean, has there ever been a time where religion and science are asking the same question, since the Enlightenment? They’re both saying, ‘Is consciousness obliged to materiality?’ And religion has always said no. And science has always said yes. And now science is saying, ‘Um, noooo.”’ You know, to me, where I come from” – a childhood of fundamentalist Christianity in 1960s Accrington, and training as a preacher – “this iscompletelyfascinating.” Later, on email, she adds, “I love my body, but I would be happy to shape shift. Happy to slip out of it into pure consciousness one day and of course people say there is no consciousness without a body, and that was the scientific belief. But now? Haha.”I would, I have to say, argue the opposite, that advances in neuroscience, immunology and psychotherapy mean it ismore the scientificbelief than ever. Not to mention the fact that AI is also entirely dependent on a physical system, otherwise known as datacentres. Although, as she points out it’s important to remember that “the machines don’t have a limbic system. They’re only neural networks. But we’ve got two systems – we’re like a hybrid car with two powertrains, so we’ve got the neural network, our rational processing self, and we’ve got the limbic system, which is much older and that’s the fight-flight-freeze, and where all our feelings come from.” Perhaps detaching from the limbic is the next stage, she says, and it definitely isn’t all good. “Maybe we’ll decide that we don’t need this feeling machine … that is where the tech bros are heading. I don’t know if you’ve ever sat in a room with some of these bigger guys, because it’sveryinteresting. They are not connected to their feelings. They find them kind of bothersome.”This tech-enabled possibility of a kind of transcendence seems to have arrived alongside a requirement for faith – in the technology, in the future it is making, in the people building that future, in its predictions both of utopian heaven and various shades of hell, all by high priests who jealously guard access to what’s actually going on. “What we know about humans is they love monopolies,” says Winterson, “because it’s a concentration of power. Of course it can be corporatised, monopolised to such a degree that it becomes the worst prison imaginable,” as told in Joanna Kavenna’s brilliant 2019 dystopian novelZed. “That is a real possibility,” she says. “And that’s why we need people who are sort of free-range humans, who canthink.”View image in fullscreenWinterson … ‘Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story.’Photograph: Posed by models; MoMo Productions/Getty ImagesThe problem then is how we support – or develop – such humans. “There are basically two ways to know you have a future,”claimedAlex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, recently. “One, you have some vocational training. Or two, you’re neurodivergent.” Daniela Amodei, the president of Anthropic and herself a literature graduate, when asked more or less the same thing, had a different take. “I actually think studying the humanities is going to be more important than ever,” she said, because “the things that make us human will become much more important instead of much less important.” Which makes the bonfire of the humanities in the UK somewhat concerning: in the year to December 2024, 4,000 jobs in the social sciences, humanities and artswere lost. Exeter University recently announced it would be cutting 150 roles, affecting eight in 10 academics in the faculty of humanities, arts and social sciences, while last month Nottingham said it would be ending its modern languages and its music degrees. At some universities the humanities, according to areportin this paper, risk being “extinguished” altogether.Why save the humanities? One answer might be that they teach a sense of where we come from and who we are, which also feels threatened. “Massive numbers of students are going to emerge from university with degrees, and into the workforce, who are essentially illiterate,” one professortoldNew York magazine, responding to the first tranche of AI natives arriving in higher education. “Both in the literal sense and in the sense of being historically illiterate and having no knowledge of their own culture, much less anyone else’s.” It risked, areportfrom MIT claimed, being a kind of generational “cognitive surrender”.Another is the processes by which people should be taught – reading, and being critical of what is read, and then having to write cogent defences of those critiques. Having to tussle your intuitions into an essay helps you to discover what – and how – you think, and how the ideas of others work. Winterson, who studied English at Oxford, and has been professor of new writing at the University of Manchester for 14 years, as well as teaching “a free-thinking class about creativity”, agrees. But she is dismissive of much of the current system. “Maybe I’m controversial here but I do think higher education needs a top-down restructure. I don’t think it’s viable and I don’t think it’s delivering in its present form.” The thing is, “We’ve got a market that doesn’t really know what education is for. Is it for jobs? Is it for personal growth? There are a lot of worthless higher education courses which are not helping, either. I think it’s always better, being a practical northern girl, to face the facts to start with.”View image in fullscreenIn her 2007 novel, The Stone Gods, Winterson imagined a world populated by robots and people who never age.Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty ImagesWe need to think, she says, about “what’s reserved to us that isn’t going to be done bigger, better, faster, stronger by the machines. And that’s where higher education really comes in. The question that’s sitting on top of all these things about, ‘Why are these jobs going?’, ‘What’s happening in these courses that aren’t getting any applicants any more?’, is ‘What sort of humans will we need in the world to come? What are humansfor? What are we going to do withus?’”. And that “takes us back to the idea of, well, OK, how do you develop a mind? How do youprotecta mind? Because the mind is this massive, monstrous place where anything can happen.”And for this, “a humanist education is essential. We have to centre the human here. By changing how we educate our kids from the start we can foreground creativity, play, problem-solving, thinking, because it’s fun to think, the arts because humans are naturally creative. Show me a child that doesn’t want to hear a story or do a dance or paint a picture or have an imaginary friend. This isn’t imposed and it isn’t elitism. It’sus.”Even an hour a week, she thinks, would make a difference. “Let’s ask what you think about the world. ‘Why do you think that?’ It’s not costly. It’s actually about will.” Teach maths and arts and science, she suggests, at least to A-level, even if they aren’t examined. “Of course we will specialise. We need doctors and chemists but we also need what used to be called well-rounded people. Everything is interesting! Humans are born with a big brain. Mostly we don’t use it.”View image in fullscreen‘Artists make something out of nothing every day.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianOnce past formal education, she would embed artists and public intellectuals at every level. “The arts aren’t a leisure industry,” as she puts it in 12 Bytes. “The arts have always been an imaginative and emotional wrestle with reality – a series of inventions and creations. A capacity to think differently, a willingness to change our understanding of ourselves. To help us to be wiser, more reflective, less frightened people. Artists make something out of nothing every day.”We meet before Jacob Coxonquithis job at Anthropic to warn of a 10% chance AI might erase humanity, sending a wave of panic across the world. Afterwards, I check in about how positive Winterson is feeling now. The worst “could happen”, she repeats. But “the immensity of the good outcome is just as real as the totality of our failure to get this right”. Above all, “this is a human decision and a human predicament. This is our big chance. Maybe our last chance, just like Turing’s colleague Jack Good said when he called AI our last invention. It’s all to play for.”We can only hope it’s not too late.Jeanette Winterson’s most recent book is One Aladdin, Two Lamps. She also writes atjeanettewinterson.substack.comOne Aladdin Two Lamps by Jeanette Winterson (Vintage Publishing, £12.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy for £10.39 atguardianbookshop.com. title: In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak review – what Madame Bovary thought of Flaubert | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark times
Author: Lara Feigel
Headline: This audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark times
Content: Mia Wasikowska and Henry Lloyd-Hughes in the 2015 film of Madame Bovary.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyView image in fullscreenMia Wasikowska and Henry Lloyd-Hughes in the 2015 film of Madame Bovary.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyBook of the dayFictionReviewIn One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak review – what Madame Bovary thought of FlaubertThis audacious portrait of the French author through the eyes of his women is Shafak’s love letter to literature in dark timesLara FeigelWed 28 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInFrantumaglia, her collection of essays on writing and reading, Elena Ferrante writes that she has sometimes dismissedGustave Flaubertas a “misogynist”, angered by his invention of as callous a mother as Emma Bovary. In other moods, however, she has wondered whether Flaubert allows his female characters to say what “women truly think and say and live but do not dare write”.Ferrante’s ambivalence is, I think, the most fitting feminist response to Flaubert’s novel. It’s tempting to castigate him as a male writer who kills his female character because he can’t imagine any other end for a transgressive woman; to reproach him for not giving Emma Bovary the profundity of emotion with which Tolstoy imbues Anna Karenina. But this isn’t the whole story, because Flaubert was so complex a figure: restlessly self-doubting even as he more than held his own in an age of cocksure egos; ecstatically happy in his solitary states of aesthetic creation precisely because they could throw him outwards into other people’s stories and minds.Elif Shafak’s audacious new novel is written out of this ambivalence. An opening chapter shows a devastated Flaubert killing what the narrator styles as “the only woman he has ever loved with heart, mind and soul”, by writing the end of Madame Bovary. The book then shifts briskly to Emma’s own voice, angry with her creator for denying her the freedom to learn from her mistakes (“Could it be because I am a woman?”). These two visions of Flaubert, teeming with creative passion for his own protagonist on the one hand and an exasperating misogynist on the other, become the twin poles of a vast 600-page novel exploring his life from every possible perspective. Thankfully, Shafak doesn’t attempt to ventriloquise Flaubert himself, master of themot juste. Instead, she has Emma summon the voices of 30 feminine figures, human or otherwise, encountered by Flaubert between birth and death, and alternates their accounts with that of the third-person narrator.This is the ideal vehicle for Shafak, who delights and often excels in giving voice to anyone and everyone, including, memorably, the tree protagonist inThe Island of Missing Trees. I have always admired Shafak’s storytelling verve while not quite falling for her whimsicality, and I balked slightly at the fancifulness of the chapters voiced by Opium (“Let me lighten up your load, ease the burden. I shall cradle you in my warm embrace”) and Syphilis (“I will damage your cells, burrow into your brain, penetrate your dreams”).double quotation markThis is the ideal vehicle for Shafak, who delights and often excels in giving voice to anyone and everyoneBut Flaubert himself might have been drawn to these extremes of literary inhabitation, which are a sort of extreme realisation of his own famous statement to Louise Colet: “It is a delicious thing to write. Today, for instance, as man and woman, both lover and mistress, I rode in a forest on an autumn afternoon under the yellow leaves, and I was also the horses, the leaves, the wind.” Certainly, I fell for Jamilah the camel (“I smile all the time. I cannot help it”), who comes at a point when the reader has either thrown the book aside in exasperation or been carried away by its abundance. “I saw those knives – and I smiled”: Shafak imbues Jamilah’s death with genuine tragedy, at a time when the inhabitants of defeated Paris are murdering zoo animals for restaurants to serve up as gourmet dishes.Throughout, Shafak powerfully evokes the minute-by-minute sensory experience of a sensitive child, and then of the adult still tragically caught up in his childhood world. She is astute and often moving on the main players in Flaubert’s life: the eventually overbearing mother who she suggests couldn’t quite bring herself to love him as an infant after losing several children before him; the sister whose death he never recovered from; the adored niece he allowed to be pushed into an unhappy marriage, despite understanding more profoundly than anyone in his century quite how unhappy such marriages could be; the lover who “thought I could help him, gently peeling off his loneliness like wallpaper lifted from a tired wall”.It’s with the invented minor characters that Shafak’s gift for storytelling finds its fullest expression. It’s as though she has tunnelled through Flaubert’s refined stylisation back into 19th-century chaos and exuberance, giving us a female murderer whose sister, passing as male, turns up to tutor the unteachable young Gustave; and the wife of the prosecutor who brought Madame Bovary to trial, laughing here at her husband’s secret hobby of writing pornographic poems. . By the end, Shafak’s powers of narrative invention become a kind of bravura performance, as unexpected, splendidly unlikely connections emerge between minor characters and disparate scenes.In an author’s note Shafak describes the novel as her “love letter to literature”. Certainly she shares Flaubert’s often idealistic sense that literature can help us even when everything else in our lives and world becomes bleak. “Without stories, without art, our descent into savagery would be even swifter,” she has Flaubert just about convincingly muse. Occasionally, I yearned for more of Flaubert’s cold analysis and sheer vitriol alongside the idealism. But this is unashamedly Shafak’s Flaubert, and I am glad of her faith in storytelling as a shaky light guiding us in dark times, even if I can’t always confidently share it.Lara Feigel is the author of Custody: The Secret History of Mothers (William Collins). In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak is published by Viking (£20). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Post your questions for Alex Cox | Movies | The Guardian
description: As the cult director of Repo Man and Sid and Nancy prepares to release his final film, Dead Souls, he takes your questions
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: As the cult director of Repo Man and Sid and Nancy prepares to release his final film, Dead Souls, he takes your questions
Content: Alex Cox.Photograph: Pool CATARINA/VANDEVILLE/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlex Cox.Photograph: Pool CATARINA/VANDEVILLE/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Alex CoxAs the cult director of Repo Man and Sid and Nancy prepares to release his final film, Dead Souls, he takes your questionsRich PelleyWed 28 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEverybody has their swansong, whether they know it or not. But for Alex Cox, his latest film Dead Souls – a darkly comic western loosely based on Nikolai Gogol’s 1842 novel – is billed as his final film.If it really is his last film, the fiercely independent British film-maker can look back on a helluva run. He broke through with 1984 punk classic Repo Man, then went on to direct Gary Oldman as Sid Vicious in Sid and Nancy. He made the political “western” Walker in 1987, starring Ed Harris – then from 1988 to 1994 introduced viewers to cult and overlooked films as the original presenter of BBC Two’s Moviedrome, essentially doing film nerd YouTube decades before YouTube existed.He ended up making films in Mexico in the 1990s, including the brilliant Highway Patrolman, then returned to his home town of Liverpool for Three Businessmen and The Revengers Tragedy. Back in the US Cox made Searchers 2.0 (an update of the classic western), Repo Chick (a sequel) and sci-fi comedy Bill the Galactic Hero.In Dead Souls, Cox also stars as Strindler – or is it Swindler? – a mysterious drifter roaming the American west offering to buy the names of dead Mexican labourers, before becoming tangled up with outlaws, crooked officials and his own increasingly tall tales. The cast also includes Edward Tudor-Pole – punk frontman, actor and former Crystal Maze host – so at least there’ll be someone around to tell Cox when his time is running out.So is Cox about to do a Tarantino? Post your questions below by midday on Wednesday 4 November, and we’ll print his best answers as part of our Readers’ Interview series.Dead Souls is on a Q&A tour from 4 November, in Bristol, Birmingham, Manchester, Liverpool, London and Oxford.
