title: Everest: The Other Side review – couple’s climb on the mountain’s toughest face comes with tricky moral questions | Movies | The Guardian
description: Immersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest’s north face
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Immersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest’s north face
Content: Anxiety-inducing … Jim Morrison in Everest: The Other Side.Photograph: Jimmy Chin Productions/PAView image in fullscreenAnxiety-inducing … Jim Morrison in Everest: The Other Side.Photograph: Jimmy Chin Productions/PAMoviesReviewEverest: The Other Side review – couple’s climb on the mountain’s toughest face comes with tricky moral questionsImmersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest’s north faceLeslie FelperinWed 28 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith some of its showings in the huge Imax format, this National Geographic-backed documentary feels like a callback to the early, glory days of large-format cinema when it was all about spectacle and scale, turning footage of natural-world wonders into an immersive experience. Those with a fear of heights or prone to vertigo may find this all a bit too immersive, in fact. That’s even more the case considering the point of the movie appears to be to provoke anxiety in the viewer for nearly the entire running time as we watch the subjects scale the steeper, far less travelled north face ofMount Everestand then, for reasons never quite adequately explained, ski back down it again.Such was the mission ofexperienced mountaineer Jim Morrison, an amiable-seeming fellow who, like all of those who pursue extreme sports, seems to feel a compulsion to put himself in the kind of grave danger that, should things go wrong, would put other people in danger rescuing him. His partner Hilaree Nelson shares his passion, and the two of them set off to be the first people to ski down Everest’s north face, and the first third of the film tracks them as they plan and eventually do practice runs to achieve this goal. Neither seems able to adequately explain why they’ve chosen to take such a risk, although Nelson tries a bit to articulate her mountaineering life almost as if it’s a career choice that her two teenage sons should simply accept as her choice to make, and maybe even thank her for – even if that means that should she be injured or lost they and Morrison (who is not the boys’ biological father) would also have to deal with the aftermath.We don’t want to give away what happens, but these moral questions hang over this film in a much more obvious way than they do in most other mountain-climbing films. (Interestingly, this is also a work co-directed by another couple, Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, who appear on screen to thrash out their own feelings on risk and reward.) Meanwhile, there’s some thoughtful footage of the various Nepalese guides who assist in Jim and Hilaree’s adventures, local men who have been climbing these mountains all their lives because they have far fewer career choices than the western tourists who come through town with camera crews, swathed in brightly coloured, prominently logo-bearing sports equipment.The lurid palette of this kit does in fact become a bit distracting when we get back to the mountain climbing stuff, and if you want to just relax and look at the stunning landscape you need to train your eyes to ignore the fluorescent jackets obstructing the view. That’s not criticising the cinematography itself; it is pin-sharp thanks to the most advanced kinds of lens and drone technology. But it’s safe to say the ethics aired here are a far murkier affair.Everest: The Other Side is out on 29 October in Australia, and 30 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMount EverestExtreme sportsMountaineeringSkiingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Asher: Everywhere Man review – music-biz face from Beatles-buddy pop act to superstar producer  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Backstory of modest industry veteran who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Backstory of modest industry veteran who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt
Content: Peter Asher, right, with Gordon Waller on Ready Steady Go in 1966Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenPeter Asher, right, with Gordon Waller on Ready Steady Go in 1966Photograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewPeter Asher: Everywhere Man review – music-biz face from Beatles-buddy pop act to superstar producerBackstory of modest industry veteran who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda RonstadtAndrew PulverWed 28 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRock’n’roll is notorious for its tales of bad behaviour: throwing TVs out of the window, mountains of cocaine, parades of groupies … but you won’t find any of that here. Peter Asher, brother of Jane, one half of Peter and Gordon, and super-successful producer of acts such asJames Taylorand Linda Ronstadt, appears to be about as nerdish and clean-living as a 60s/70s music industry veteran could be. Although that might just be what he wants us to think; what are the chances Asher is a complete reprobate away from the camera, and is just brilliant at hiding it? That glasses and ruffled shirt front combo definitely reminds you of someone a tad more sleazy, even before Asher himself reminds you about it in the final credits.Peter Asher on being music’s incredible ‘Everywhere Man’: ‘The secret is simple’Read moreWhatever the truth, Asher by any standards carved an amazing path, making the absolute most of being in the right place at the right time. Smartly structured around Asher’s anecdotes-and-music live show, the film stitches together a collection of clips, audio and musical performances that gallops through his personal backstory. His luckiest break, of course, was that his early partnership with schoolfriend Gordon Waller (modelled, it turned out, on the Everly Brothers) benefited from cast-off songs handed over by his sister’s boyfriend, one Paul McCartney; there’s an amusing moment where we hear John Lennon’s sneer at the lyric of what would become Peter and Gordon’s first and biggest hit, A World Without Love: “Please lock me away …” “Yes”. While the film clearly acknowledges the debt to McCartney’s songwriting (which presumably Lennon vetoed for the Beatles), it’s perhaps not quite ready to admit that without this connection, none of what followed would have happened at all.At one point Asher says he wasn’t much of a pop star, and subsequent events suggest he was probably right. He appears to have been more comfortable away from the spotlight, thereby allowing him to become a ubiquitous figure in the Beatles’ orbit in swinging 60s London to which the title alludes. He was a co-owner of supercool art gallery Indica (where Lennon first met Yoko Ono), though given it only lasted two years, possibly he wasn’t all that great at that, either. It was the Beatles’ connection, though, that allowed him to really come into his own, when he was appointed head of A&R at the newly formed Apple Records, with his own top floor office in the Savile Row building.Asher’s big discovery was Taylor, who had relocated to London after failing to get anywhere at home in the US; after producing Taylor’s debut album (which with characteristic modesty he says he messed up with Beatles-style orchestration), Asher followed Taylor to Los Angeles and settled into a quietly impressive second act as a producer and manager. After producing Taylor’s breakthrough second album, Sweet Baby James, Asher became a key figure in 1970s Californian soft rock, overseeing acts including Andrew Gold, Kate Taylor, JD Souther and – most successful of all – Ronstadt. Admittedly, this now looks a tad middle of the road, a musical era since vanquished by punk and new wave, but Asher later got on board with credibility-stoking artists such as Cher, Diana Ross and 10,000 Maniacs, and even produced albums by Boyzone and Morrissey.Throughout this parade of achievement, Asher cuts an impressively self-possessed figure, unassuming in many ways but also not hiding his light under a bushel. The appreciation he gets from his big-name collaborators is clear enough, but he also gives houseroom to somewhat more tangential figures, with Carole King in particular coming across strongly. But it’s the interactions with late former partner Waller that are probably the most resonant, with the virtual duet Asher sets up being especially moving.Peter Asher: Everywhere Man is in UK cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMusic documentaryPop and rockJames TaylorPaul McCartneyJane AsherreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Girls review – a story of friendship amidst extreme misogynist violence  | Stage | The Guardian
description:
Young Vic, London
Recalling Boko Haram’s abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok in 2014, Theresa Ikoko’s fierce and tender play reveals how three teenagers find hope and laughter under the most horrific circumstances
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Young Vic, LondonRecalling Boko Haram’s abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok in 2014, Theresa Ikoko’s fierce and tender play reveals how three teenagers find hope and laughter under the most horrific circumstances
Content: ‘Escape in fantasy’ … from left, Tara Tijani, Hannah Akhalu and Sewa Zamba in Girls.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreen‘Escape in fantasy’ … from left, Tara Tijani, Hannah Akhalu and Sewa Zamba in Girls.Photograph: Helen MurrayStageReviewGirls review – a story of friendship amidst extreme misogynist violenceYoung Vic, LondonRecalling Boko Haram’s abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok in 2014, Theresa Ikoko’s fierce and tender play reveals how three teenagers find hope and laughter under the most horrific circumstancesArifa AkbarWed 28 Oct 2026 09.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree girls huddle together, playing childish games to allay their fears from whatever terror stalks them. There are flashes of light and sounds, followed by sudden blackouts. At first, Theresa Ikoko’s play appears post-apocalyptic. Television screens line the back wall with radio frequencies tuning in and out. A strange structure looms overhead. Information about who they are, where they are hiding, who from, is parcelled out gradually.You learn that they are three Nigerian friends and schoolgirls living in a forest in 2015. Their captors are never named but you can infer they are part of theinsurgent Islamist group, Boko Haram, from the breadcrumbs of backstory. Director Ewa Dina makes this explicit in her programme note when she refers to the Chibok Girls, involving Boko Haram’s mass abduction of schoolgirls in Chibok, Borno State, in 2014.View image in fullscreenA new realiy … Girls.Photograph: Helen MurrayThese three girls, we realise, are being held hostage in a camp, forced to convert to Islam with rumours that they might be sent out as suicide bombers or fighters. They speak of not feeling like children any more, of seeing their homes destroyed, watching a woman being trampled to death, the smell of burning human flesh, and of the corpses lying in the well nearby. They tell each other childhood stories of a mythic forest god, yet feel the absence of such a deity in their damned corner of the forest. But they also laugh, play childish games of make-believe, talk about sex and fight, like any group of female friends.Each character is individuated and responds differently to the terror of the camp: Haleema (Tara Tijani) is belligerent and plans escape, Ruhab (Sewa Zamba) submits to this new reality and finds a version of love among her captors, and Tisana (Hannah Akhalu), flogged daily for refusing to attend Islamic prayers, finds escape in fantasy.This is certainly a play that reminds us of the fate of the Chibok girls, and violence against women at its most extreme, but it is also a story about female friendship, sometimes tender, other times mean and spiky, rather likeAva Pickett’s trio of friends in her Tudor-era drama, 1536. But it is also fierce and loyal to the last.There are a few too many breakouts with claps of stagecraft thunder and lighting, and some short scene changes that bring confusion. The final use of screens showing faces (presumably of real-life missing girls) is abrupt and unexplained. But those reservations aside, this play, a winner of the Alfred Fagon award in 2015 and joint winner of the George Devine award in 2016, is without doubt a gut-punch: imaginative, tender, shocking. Thataround 90 of the Chibok Girls are still believed to be missingmakes it all the more haunting, and infuriating.At Young Vic, London until 21 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreNigeriaBoko HaramYoung VicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How rebuilding old mosques is bringing Sikhs, Hindus and Muslims together in Punjab | Global development | The Guardian
description: Many Muslims saw their places of worship destroyed or abandoned during the sectarian violence of India’s partition in 1947. Now villagers of many faiths are coming together to revive them
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Many Muslims saw their places of worship destroyed or abandoned during the sectarian violence of India’s partition in 1947. Now villagers of many faiths are coming together to revive them
Content: Jaspal Sharma, left, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated a piece of his land for a mosque to be built in his village. All photographs by Cheena KapoorMany Muslims saw their places of worship destroyed or abandoned during the sectarian violence of India’s partition in 1947. Now villagers of many faiths are coming together to revive themByCheena KapoorSupported byAbout this contentWed 28 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear theazaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutalsectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”View image in fullscreenBibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh, donated family land to build a mosque in her village. ‘There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,’ she saysView image in fullscreenGajju Khan, who hopes to live long enough to see the mosque in his village completedDuring thepartition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.About 50 miles from Jakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.View image in fullscreenJaspal Sharma says donating some of his land to build a mosque was a neighbourly dutyView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe new mosque in Malerkotla, Punjab, welcomes worshippers for evening prayers“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of teawith his Muslim neighbourson the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.View image in fullscreenSadna Qasai, one of the many mosques in Punjab that fell into ruin after partition“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saintHazrat Mian Mirwas invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, theHarmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.Inspired by the formershahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed tomore than 165 such mosquesin the past nine years.View image in fullscreenSikh men in Punjab’s villages have been coming together to fund and help build or revive old mosques“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is aninquilab[revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayPeace and reconciliationIslamReligionSikhismIndiaSouth and central AsiaShareReuse this content

title: Cycling in the wild heart of the Netherlands: an autumnal break in the Veluwe | Netherlands holidays | The Guardian
description: The untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bike
Author: Suzanne Bearne
Headline: The untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bike
Content: A red deer in the Hoge Veluwe national park.Photograph: Laurens Verhoeven/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA red deer in the Hoge Veluwe national park.Photograph: Laurens Verhoeven/Getty ImagesNetherlands holidaysCycling in the wild heart of the Netherlands: an autumnal break in the VeluweThe untamed, magical landscape takes in a vast national park, palatial houses and a sculpture garden and museum stuffed with Van Goghs – all easily accessible by bikeSuzanne BearneWed 28 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 03.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne minute I’m cycling through an expansive dusty pink stretch of heathland with sloping sand dunes in the distant horizon, the next I’m winding through a fragrant Scots pine forest as sunlight filters through the branches of red-barked trees to make a kaleidoscope of white shapes on the trail floor ahead.I’m in Hoge Veluwe National Park, a 5,400 hectare (13,000 acre) nature reserve in Gelderland, about an hour and a half from Amsterdam. It’s crisscrossed by 25 miles (40km) of cycling paths, and around 2,000 free-to-use white bikes are available for visitors to explore the ever-changing scenery.I’ve been flitting back and forth to the Netherlands for years and have lost count of the times friends there have raved about the park and the wider Veluwe region, a forest-rich ridge of hills and diverse landscapes, stretching 37 miles, north to south. Finally I’ve come to see for myself and explore on foot and on two wheels over a few days – adding in a dash of culture at some of its historic towns and museums too.My trip starts atNatuurcentrum De Ginkel, a charming nature and visitor centre near Ede outside Arnhem. Here I meet nature guide Hanna Pol who takes me into the forest. “Veluwe is very biodiverse,” says Pol quietly as we walk past verdant oak, pine and birch. Trees with autumnal tawny-coloured leaves line one side of the path and wildflowers, with pops of bright yellow sunflowers and vivid red poppies, the other. Pol reels off some of the wildlife here: roe deer, five types of woodpecker, beavers, wild boar and wolves. As we crunch through a carpet of fallen leaves, we spy a small brown frog on a log, a woodpecker dancing around a tree, and the outline of two rust-red deers in the distance.View image in fullscreenDeelense Veld flessen in Hoge Veluwe.Photograph: Henk RuselerWe make our way to the wildlife observation area, an enclosed building with curved windows and a theatre-style set of wooden chairs. “The deer pass this way every night to eat,” says Pol. “Once we saw a really big fight break out.” She’s seen wolves too – they returned to the country in 2015 after about 150 years and it’s a controversial topic, with farmers worried about their livestock. We don’t see the elusive creatures, just a solitary bright white buzzard perching on a tree. On the shelves behind us, an assortment of skeletal remains includes antlers, skulls, the teeth of a wild boar and the foot of a deer.That night I stay in a stylish and sleek cabin with floor-to-ceiling views of the forest atBuitenplaats Petersburgon the edge of the park. It’s a peaceful haven of lodges with fairy lights strung around the woods and an enchanting Italian restaurant, Il Lupo, with an outdoor terrace.Besides its unspoilt natural wonders, Veluwe has plenty of other attractions. I visitPaleis Het Loo, a 17th-century royal palace in Apeldoorn, once the summer residence and hunting lodge of William of Orange III and his wife Princess Mary II Stuart. It’s an impressive building with ornate rooms, a staircase with the second biggest mural in the Netherlands, formal symmetrical gardens and an underground museum which tells the story of the Dutch royal family.Hotel de Echoput, a family-run modern hotel nearby, surrounded by the forest, is my home for the night. Its Grand Bistro Echo is a treat, with a menu that focuses on local ingredients – I enjoy fried mushrooms with a creamy Dordogne sauce and a vegan cheesecake with basil and white chocolate.View image in fullscreenCyclists at Otterlo.The next morning, after a brisk walk in the woods with barely a soul around, I visit the historic Hanseactic city of Harderwijk, on the shores of Wolderwijd lake. I wander the narrow cobblestone streets, medieval city walls and Old Town Hall with guide Marianne van Limbeek. “Harderwijk means hiding place for shepherds,” she tells me. We bump into Hendrik Kaper, a local street organist wearing a flat cap who treats us to a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody on his portable wooden organ.But it’s in Hoge Veluwe national park that I find the greatest sense of serenity – though one day a small adder with a dark zigzag stripe stops me in my tracks. Come outside peak times, as I have, and you might have some of the trails to yourself.View image in fullscreenPaleis Het Loo, near Apeldoorn.Within the park liesKröller-Müller Museum, a revered national art museum and sculpture garden founded by art collector Helene Kröller-Müller, who along with her husband, shipping magnate Anton Kröller, bought vast amounts of land in Veluwe (their private estate was later donated to the state). My timing is great as all 88 of its Vincent van Gogh paintings are on show together for the first time since 1984 (until 3 January).The sculpture park is one of the largest in Europe, and I stroll around the surrounding open grass and into the forest and stumble across various artworks (there are about 200 pieces dotted around). A short cycle away isJachthuis Sint Hubertus, the former country residence of the Kröller-Müller family with a watchtower more than 30m tall (apparently Helene loved afternoon tea at such lofty heights) surrounded by a lake with a very athletic bunch of jumping carp.I stop at Restaurant De Hoge Veluwe at Park Paviljoen for an early pasta dinner on the terrace before the sky turns a moody grey and rain looks imminent. Fortunately it’s only a 15-minute cycle to Otterlo, a pretty village with clusters of fairy lights and bunting decorating red brick houses andVakantieoord Het Lorkenbos, a charming holiday park surrounded by trees. My bungalow is cute and, feeling as if I’m in a twinkling winter wonderland, I light a candle and look up the Dutch word for cosy. It’sgezellig– a perfect description of how I feel after my nourishing break in this wild and restorative part of the Netherlands.The trip was arranged byVisit Veluwe. Entrance toHoge Veluwe national park€13.85per adult. Cabins atBuitenplaats Petersburgfrom€110. Camping atHet Lorkenbosfrom€23 a night, bungalows from €320 for two nights. Double rooms atDe Echoputfrom€169.Omioprovided train travel:Eurostar runs from London to AmsterdamExplore more on these topicsNetherlands holidaysCycling holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn excess custard into a fruity treat – recipe | Dessert | The Guardian
description: A fool is absurdly simple – just fruit stirred through custard or yoghurt with. maybe a bit of cream – and you can then add whatever bits and bobs you fancy from the fridge
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A fool is absurdly simple – just fruit stirred through custard or yoghurt with. maybe a bit of cream – and you can then add whatever bits and bobs you fancy from the fridge
Content: Tom Hunt’s blackberry, apple and custard fool.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s blackberry, apple and custard fool.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notDessertHow to turn excess custard into a fruity treat – recipeA fool is absurdly simple – just fruit stirred through custard or yoghurt with. maybe a bit of cream – and you can then add whatever bits and bobs you fancy from the fridgeTom HuntWed 28 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFool is one of my go-to desserts for two reasons: first, its pure simplicity – it’s little more than custard or yoghurt mixed with whipped cream and pureed fruit – and, second, its adaptability to the seasons. Gooseberry, rhubarb and strawberry are traditionally the most foolish fruits, but just about any fruit goes. British blackberries are still available and apples are in their prime right now, so I’ve gone for those, but use whatever you’ve got in store.I usually make fool with yoghurt, not least because it’s much less work than making custard from scratch, but I’ve got lots of leftover custard fromthis week’s Food Filter taste test, so I’m going for a custard base here. I’m always looking for ways to use up small amounts of bits and pieces in the fridge, such as the end of a pot of custard or yoghurt, then add a few other ingredients to elevate remnants into regalia.Blackberry, apple and custard foolA seasonal fool is a firm British favourite, so I’m rather surprised not to have covered it here before. As I come up to my 10th year of writing this column, I feel it’s time to revisit the classics, frombanana bread last weekto fool today, but with a zero-waste twist. For this recipe, finely dice the apple, so you can leave the skin on, to save on waste and to add fibre and texture.Serves2-4100g blackberries, plus extra to garnish1 apple, finely diced¼ tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ginger(ground or freshly grated)Sea salt3 tbsp honey100ml double cream, chilled150ml custardor yoghurt, or a mix of bothPut the blackberries, apple, cinnamon, ginger and a pinch of sea salt in a small saucepan, then add a splash of water. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for about 10 minutes, until the fruit is soft enough to mash with a fork. Mash everything together, leave to cool, then stir in three tablespoons of honey and refrigerate.When the puree is cold, whip the cold cream to soft peaks. With a metal spoon, gently fold in the custard, then fold in two-thirds of the fruit puree, or just enough so it ripples through the custard and cream base. Spoon the mix into two to four glasses, and top each with a spoonful of the remaining puree and a blackberry or two to garnish. Enjoy immediately or chill for a firmer set.Explore more on these topicsDessertWaste notFoodAutumn food and drinkFood wasteFruitBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vegetarian coconut curry recipes: Maunika Gowardhan’s spicy aubergine baingan and spiced vegetable stew  | Vegetarian food and drink | The Guardian
description: Coconut flavours the base of both these hearty curries – one with aubergines, one with gingery vegetables
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Coconut flavours the base of both these hearty curries – one with aubergines, one with gingery vegetables
Content: Maunika Gowardhan’sbhagare baingan, or aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenMaunika Gowardhan’sbhagare baingan, or aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.Vegetarian food and drinkVegetarian coconut curry recipes: Maunika Gowardhan’s spicy aubergine baingan and spiced vegetable stewAubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves, and a gingery vegetable stew with coconut and green chilliesMaunika GowardhanWed 28 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBoth these hearty curries use coconut as part of their base gravy. The region of Kutch in Gujarat is brimming with vegetable curries, and thebhagare bainganfeatures many classic Kutchi ingredients; it has several similarities to the Hyderabadi version, too. I’ve used baby aubergines, but if need be you can use regular diced aubergines instead.Avial, meanwhile, is often served at celebrations in south India, and this version is a Keralan recipe made with a flavourful coconut paste.Bhagare baingan, or aubergines cooked with coconut, chilli, tamarind and curry leaves (pictured top)Prep15 minCook1 hr 30 minServes4For the paste1 tbsp poppy seeds2 tbsp vegetable oil90gfinely chopped white onion1 tbsp sesame seeds1 tbsp grated fresh coconutFor the gravy160g fresh tomatoes4 tbsp vegetable oil150g thinly sliced white onions5 garlic cloves, peeled and ground to a paste¼ tsp turmeric powder1 tsp kashmiri chilli powder2 tsp ground cuminSalt, to taste8-10 baby aubergines, slit open lengthways1½ tsp tamarind paste½ tsp coarsely ground black pepper2 mild dried red chillies12 fresh curry leavesCoriander, to garnishRice or roti, to serveFor the paste, soak the poppy seeds in 70ml warm water 20 minutes. Meanwhile, put the oil in a small frying pan on a medium heat, then fry the onions for eight or nine minutes, just until they start to change colour. Add the sesame seeds and grated fresh coconut, and fry, stirring, for two minutes. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature. Once cooled, stir in the poppy seeds and their soaking liquid, then blitz the lot to a smooth paste.Meanwhile, put the tomatoes in a blender and blitz to a smooth puree. In a large, heavy-based frying pan for which you have a lid, heat the oil over a medium heat, then add the onions and fry, stirring regularly, for 17-18 minutes, until softened and lightly browned. Add the garlic paste, fry for 20 seconds, then stir in the turmeric, chilli powder and cumin, and fry, stirring for a few seconds, until fragrant.Add the pureed tomatoes and fry, stirring, for five minutes, until the mix splits and the oil leaves the side of the pan. Add the ground poppy seed and onion paste and fry, stirring continuously, for four minutes. Pour in 350ml warm water, season with salt to taste, then stir in the aubergines, cover and simmer on a low heat for about 15 minutes, stirring once halfway through. Add the tamarind paste and simmer for a further five minutes.Take off the heat and stir in the black pepper, whole dried red chilliesand curry leaves. Garnish with coriander and serve warm with roti or rice.Avial, or vegetable stew with coconut, ginger, curry leaves and green chilliesView image in fullscreenMaunika Gowardhan’savial, or vegetable stew with coconut ginger curry leaves and green chillies.Prep20 minCook40 minServes4For the paste200ggrated fresh coconut2½cm x 2½cmpiece ginger, peeled and roughly chopped½ tsp cumin seeds1 green bird’s eye chilliFor the curry3 tbsp vegetable oil1 tsp black mustard seeds1 dried mild chilli, roughly broken into pieces7-8 fresh curry leaves70g finely chopped white onion1 tsp turmeric powder200g medium carrots, peeled and cut into 1cm dice150g potato(use a good all-rounder such as red rooster), peeled and cut into 1cm dice200gfrench beans, all topped and cut into three roughly equal pieces½ tsp coarsely ground black pepperSalt, to taste3 tbsp greek yoghurtCoriander, to garnishRice or paratha, to serveFor the paste, put the fresh coconut, ginger, cumin seeds and chilli in a blender, add 200ml water and blitz to a smooth paste.Put the oil in a heavy-based saucepan on a medium heat. Add the mustard seeds, dried chilli and curry leaves. After 15 or so seconds, when they start to splutter and pop, add the chopped onions and fry, stirring, for seven or eight minutes, until they start to soften. Add the turmeric and the chopped carrots and potatoes, fry, stirring, for just a few seconds, then pour in 200ml water, cover and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook gently for 10 minutes, then add the chopped green beans and cook for another eight minutes, until all the vegetables are tender.Add the coconut paste and the ground black pepper, season with salt to taste, then stir and simmer for another two minutes. Whisk the yoghurt, then stir it into the pan and simmer for a minute more. Garnish with coriander and serve at once with rice or paratha.Maunika Gowardhan’s most recent book, Curry: Recipes from Indian Home Kitchens, is published by Quadrille at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsVegetarian food and drinkCurryFoodVegetablesHerbs and spicesIndian food and drinkTomatoesrecipesShareReuse this content
